n: AA Badenhorst CWG Akkerbos Grenache Blanc
d: Comparatively youthful 11-year-old vines on granite soils supply the raw material for this very exciting, foudre-aged Grenache Blanc. Pithy, tangy and mouth-wateringly fresh, it has aniseed and wet stone aromas, lovely minerality and flavours of citrus, cardamom and umami. The perfect grape in a warming world.

Seven different vineyards – four on Kalmoesfontein and three on Jakkalsfontein – contribute to this world-class Chenin Blanc from Adi Badenhorst. Offering a medley of citrus, greengage and yellow apple fruit, it has wonderful energy and zip, classic granite-derived minerality, lovely, waxy texture and definition and a saline finish.

Adi Badenhorst uses grapes from 94 different Swartland parcels to make this savoury, complex co-fermentation of Syrah with a supporting cast of 49% Tinta Barocca, Grenache Noir, Cinsault, Touriga Nacional, Cabernet Sauvignon and Souzão. More than the sum of its parts, it’s modern, concentrated and very lightly wooded with layers of fig, blackberry and liquorice and a fynbos top note.

Produced with a mind-boggling line-up of grapes, this Swartland blend is based on Chenin Blanc with the remaining 49% made up of Grenache Blanc, Verdelho, Clairette, Palomino, Muscat de Frontignan, Viognier, Sauvignon Blanc, Colombard and Chardonnay from 18 different parcels. Chamomile, orange peel and white flower aromas segue into a palate of pear, quince and tangerine and an appealing bitter twist.

The sort of thing you’d enjoy drinking at one of Adi Badenhorst’s epic pizza nights, this is an unfiltered, low-intervention blend of 17 different varieties, roughly half of which are white. Juicy, floral and easy-going, it has appealing rooibos tea and summer pudding flavours and a supple, palate-caressing finish.

Based on Chenin Blanc and Grenache Blanc, two of the pillars of the Swartland, this also contains some Roussanne and Verdelho. Wildflower, wet stone and gin botanical aromas lead you into a savoury, well-defined palate of citrus and cardamom with a hint of stone fruit.

A sublime bottling of Ramnasgras, this makes the most of this 1.4-hectare parcel of Cinsault, planted in 1963. Showing the concentration of its low yields, it has some clove and tobacco leaf notes from 30% whole bunches, granitic intensity, flavours of rosehip, redcurrant and Turkish Delight and shimmering tannins.

Ringmuur is a tiny parcel of just 0.18 of a hectare, planted on decomposed granite soils in 1964 on Kalmoesfontein. Fermented with 100% whole bunches before ageing in concrete, it has some subtle stony reduction, a waft of rose petal, succulent goji berry and wild strawberry flavours, filigree tannins and a racy, medium-bodied finish. Shows the quality of the vintage.

Entirely fermented and aged in concrete, this is a perfect introduction to the joys of the Swartland, combining Chenin Blanc, 21% Grenache Blanc, 16% Roussanne and 6% Viognier. Made without added sulphites, it’s a “natural wine you can drink”, according to Adi Badenhorst, with well-handled skin contact, flavours of quince and lemon zest and a sappy, refreshing finish.

One of South Africa’s most successful brands, the Secateurs Chenin Blanc now runs to a production of 500,000 bottles. Showing some subtle struck match reduction, it has layers of yellow apple, pear and passion fruit, a textured mid palate and supporting acidity. Just a great drink.

The Secateurs Red Blend is not as well-known as the Chenin Blanc, but it’s every bit as good. Syrah based with 11% Cabernet Sauvignon and 8% Cinsault, it has sage, tapenade and blackberry fruit flavours, smooth tannins and impressive palate weight.

n: AA Badenhorst Sout van die Aarde Palomino
d: Sourced from the same site as Eben Sadie’s Skerpioen – which adds Chenin Blanc to the blend – this is a varietal Palomino that is the “salt of the earth”, as the label would have it. Aged in foudres, it’s a coastal, Atlantic-influenced style with a briny top note, layers of almond, lime and citrus peel and some texture from foudre ageing.

This is the second release under the Turksvy label, sourced from a granite-rich vineyard that also supplies Duncan Savage, Jean Smit and the Mullineux. The firmest of the quartet, this has considerable grip, depth and intensity, understated oak, flavours of blackberry, tapenade and steak tartare and an undertow of tannin.

Praisy Dlamini has created one of the most dynamic and successful black-owned brands in the Cape. This is a crowd-pleasing cuvée of Chenin Blanc and 15% Muscat d’Alexandrie from Paarl, with an appealing medley of passion fruit, citrus and tangerine and 4.8 grams of sugar to fill out the mid palate.

Adara buy this Cabernet Sauvignon as a finished wine from Neil Ellis, who sources the grapes from the Bottelary Hills and the Jonkershoek Valley. Aromas of earth, toast and dried mint segue into a palate of bramble and blackcurrant leaf and a nuanced, well-balanced finish.

Made by Neil Bester from vines in the grounds of a luxury hotel and resort, this is one of two currently available releases of Chenin Blanc. Entirely unwooded, it’s tasty at the price with lime and pear fruit, some old-vine concentration and a textured, unfiltered finish.

A little fresher and lower in alcohol than the 2024 bottling, this is a crisper, more focused style of Chenin Blanc from Paarl that offers excellent value for money, with racy flavours of pear, peach and green apple and a hint of stony reduction.

Among the best-ever Cartology releases, this is a transparent expression of what Chris Alheit calls the “racy, pure” 2025 vintage. Using grapes from ten parcels across the Cape, it’s a typically harmonious cuvée of Chenin Blanc and 7% Semillon, using wild yeast fermentation in concrete eggs, foudres and old barrels. Savoury, leesy and wonderfully textured, it’s an unhurried wine with time on its side, all white flowers, gin botanicals and beeswax and a core of aniseed, almond, pear and lemon zest.

Fire by Night comes from the celebrated 22-hectare Nuwedam property that Chris Alheit purchased from Christa von La Chevallerie. Using two different sub-parcels – Ridge and Uitsig – it has the classic granite-derived intensity and energy of the Paardeberg, with chiselled, scalpel-like acidity, a salty undertone, layers of lime, green apple and chamomile and a mouth-watering finish.

I always enjoy a bottle of Hemelrand Vine Garden, as it reminds me of tasting at Chris Alheit’s cellar on the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge next door. Made with an intriguing medley of Roussanne, 27% Chardonnay, 23% Chenin Blanc, 11% Verdelho and 3% Muscat, it’s tangy, perfumed, finely judged white blend with layers of ginger spice, apricot, grapefruit and lemon zest and a focused, refreshing finish.

Hereafter Here is a young-vine Chenin Blanc from Bottelary, Malmesbury, Piekenierskloof and the Polkadraai Hills, partnered with some older material from the Paardeberg and Tyburgh. Your chance to acquire some Alheit magic at a very approachable price, it’s a sappy, racy, tangy white with aniseed and thatch aromas and an energetic palate of citrus peel and bay leaf.

It’s invidious to have to choose between Chris Alheit’s top Chenin Blancs in any given vintage, but choose we must. And in 2025, Huilkrans is primus inter pares, or first among equals, expressing the purity and focus of Jozua Visser’s Oudam farm at its best. Showing the effortless concentration of low-yielding vines planted between 1974 and 1989 at 450 metres, it has amazing depth and extract, blossom and jasmine aromas, savoury intensity and flavours of juniper, lemongrass and wet stones. Truly symphonic, this is a stunning white from a winemaker at the peak of his considerable powers.

Could the 2025 vintage of Magnetic North live up to the quality of the 100-point 2024 release? It’s very close. Made with low-yielding bush vines on red sand and clay soils at 520 metres, it’s another stunning release from one of the best Chenin Blanc sites in the world. Regal and patrician, it flirts with austerity, with chiselled, cut-glass minerality and transparency, top notes of kelp and oyster shell, a touch of umami and brooding complexity. One to tuck away.

How old is La Colline, the vineyard that supplies the grapes for this monumental Semillon? The records say 1936, but Chris Alheit thinks it could date back to the late 19th century. Sourced from the top part of the site at 330 metres, this has lots of energy and zip, layers of creamy lees, fennel and fynbos and a pithy, acid-driven finish. Still in its infancy, this will blossom in bottle.

First made in 2017, Nautical Dawn showcases what Chris Alheit calls the “raw talent” of the Rustenhof farm, overlooking False Bay, which has to be regarded as a Grand Cru site for Chenin Blanc. A little more exotic than the 2024 release, it has flavours of peach, pear and apricot tethered by Atlantic Ocean acidity, with a subtle lift of volatility and a granite-fresh finish.

Natasha Jacka is an exciting new name to keep an eye on, making wines of impressive purity and balance. This is a proudly 60% whole bunch fermented Grenache from Citrusdal Mountain with cumin, rose petal and white pepper top notes and a palate of cranberry, pomegranate and wild strawberry framed by fine-boned tannins.

Something to put a smile on the face of any Spanish wine lover, this is a rare example of a varietal Viura in the Cape. Made by exciting young winemaker Natasha Jacka, it’s a subtly oaked white with appealing zip and energy, flavours of celery, pear and lemon zest and a waft of white pepper.

Allesverloren makes other styles of wine too, but is best known for the quality of its Cape Vintage releases. Using six different Portuguese grapes, this is a fortified wine with time on its side, with good structure and intensity, fig, mulberry and liquorice flavours, wellintegrated spirit, 92 grams of residual sugar and a spine of tannin.

Allée Bleue is based in Franschhoek, but sources this amphora-fermented Semillon from what Edo Heyns calls a “very coastal” vineyard in Darling. Bay leaf, white pepper and rock pool aromas guide you into a palate of lime, wet stone and tarragon, complemented by a subtle earthy undertow.

n: Allée Bleue Blanc de Blancs CC
d: Using Chardonnay from Franschhoek, this is a finely judged Blanc de Blancs from Van Zyl du Toit. The base wine was barrel fermented with full malolactic, adding texture and interest to a palate of citrus, cardamom and brown toast complemented by creamy bubbles.

Isabeau is the top Chardonnay from Allée Bleue, sourced from a couple of older parcels on the farm. Made with a 60/40 combination of partially new wood and an amphora, it’s rich, dense and well made, with pear and lemon flavours and a hint of pineapple sweetness and a dab of cream from 30% malolactic.

n: Allée Bleue Old Vine OVP Cinsault

d: Building on the promise of the 2023 vintage under a new winemaking team, this is a refined, acid-driven Elgin Chardonnay that speaks of its cool climate. Deftly fermented in 42% new French oak, it’s tangy, bright and full of energy with aromas of chamomile and cinnamon and a palate of fresh lemons, crème fraîche and west stones.

Impressive stuff from Cameron Corney, this is a pithy, chiselled, cool climate Sauvignon Blanc that sits at the greener end of the variety’s stylistic spectrum. Nettley and herbal, it’s a little like an English Bacchus, with layers of elderflower, parsley and green asparagus and a crunchy, acid-driven finish.

An intriguing addition to the Alto range, this is a fortified Cape Vintage style made from Syrah, as opposed to the more common Portuguese varieties. Youthful, intense and concentrated, this has appealing fig, dark chocolate and blackberry jam flavours, understated oak and 101 grams of residual sugar.

Bertho van de Westhuizen makes this Stellenbosch cuvée with an unusual combination of Cabernet Sauvignon, 30% Syrah and 10% Cabernet Franc. Subtly wooded in 70% new oak, it’s a reassuringly traditional style that reflects the lighter vintage, with top notes of tomato leaf and aromatic spices and a palate of truffle, earth, dried herbs and sweet red berry fruit.

Made for the second vintage in a row – the release before that was the 2018 – this is a tribute to the male winemakers who have worked there over the years. Leafy, forward and appealingly balsamic, it’s an equal blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc, with mint, tobacco leaf and forest floor aromas and a palate of cassis and dried herbs framed by 100% new oak.

New to the Ampersand range, this Albariño hails from the Wolwedans farm in the Polkadraai Hills. Naturally fermented in plastic eggs and stainless steel, it’s a sappy, refreshing style of with chiselled, Riesling-like acidity, lime and passion fruit flavours and a lightly savoury finish.

Ampersand is the personal project of Gabriëlskloof’s viticulturist, Dean Leppan. Made with grapes from Stellenzicht’s young, virus-free plantings in Stellenbosch, this is a Cinsault for Pinot Noir lovers, with flavours of raspberry and Negroni spices, 40% whole clusters and a subtle bitter twist.

Definitely among the more elegant reds from Wellington, this is a well-judged Syrah from Shaun Meyeridricks that has nicely handled 50% whole bunches, sappy plum and black cherry fruit, subtle top notes of clove, pepper and Turkish bazaar spices and some stony reduction on the finish. Impressive at the price.

n: Angus Paul Wines Barbary Fictions Chenin Blanc
d: One of a quartet of impressive Chenin Blancs for Angus Paul, Barbary Fictions uses grapes from a 1972 block on the Mooiplaas farm in the Bottelary Hills. Showing some subtle struck match reduction, it’s a slow rumble of a wine that grows on you in the glass, with citrus, yellow apple and oatmeal flavours and a touch of stone fruit on the finish. The finish is classically granitic.

Angus Paul’s description of this Firgrove Cinsault is spot on: “weightless intensity”. Reflecting the proximity of False Bay, it’s all about purity and transparency, marrying aromas of tealeaf and rosewater with a palate of cucumber, red cherry and wild strawberry, savoury tannins and some clove spice from 100% whole bunches.

n: Angus Paul Wines Fantamtango Chenin Blanc
d: Fantamtango comes from a 1980 block on the Blaauwklippen Road t the eastern end of the Helderberg. Bottled a little later than usual because it was so “taut”, according to Angus Paul, despite full malolactic, it has some subtle skin phenolics, layers of citrus, cardamom and petrichor and a pithy finish. Entirely fermented and aged in concrete eggs.

n: Angus Paul Wines On a Flight of Furious Fancies Chenin Blanc
d: Angus Paul makes his wines in the Karibib estate, so he doesn’t have far to go to harvest this Chenin Blanc from a 1982 block on the property. Made in a low-intervention style, with minimal sulphites and full malolactic, it has a briny, sea breeze top note, layers of oatmeal, citrus and sourdough bread and a tangy, granitic finish.

n: Angus Paul Wines Transient Lands Chenin Blanc
d: Transient Lands combines raw material from Bottelary, the Helderberg and the Polkadraai Hills. Floral and enticing, it partners aromas of thatch, aniseed and juniper with a palate of yellow apple, pear and wet stones, some texture from full malolactic and a chiselled, tapering finish.

n: Angus Paul Wines Transient Lands Pinotage
d: The Transient Lands Pinotage is a 60/40 blend of grapes from the Polkadraai Hills and Bottelary. Fermented with 50% whole clusters, it’s another harmonious, deliberately understated wine from Angus Paul, who has got the best out of what he calls a “challenging grape”. Bramble and red berry flavours are complemented by subtle oak, savoury tannins and a touch of forest floor.

n: Anura Vineyards Chenin Blanc OVP Reserve
d: Stander Maas sources this Chenin Blanc from two parcels, planted in 1985 and 1990. Partial wild fermentation adds a savoury undertone here, contributing complexity to the old-vine fruit. Racy and well balanced, it has appealing pear, citrus and nectarine fruit, subtle wood and a tangy, palate-cleansing finish.

“We took a gamble and withstood the rains” is Matt Day’s honest commentary on the 2023 vintage at Anwilka. Combining Cabernet Sauvignon and 43% Syrah, it’s a wine that benefits from the input of Bordeaux consultant Hubert de BoŸard, who will know all about wetter growing seasons. Cut grass, rose petal and tarragon aromas segue into a palate of coffee bean, bramble and blackcurrant leaf framed by toasty oak.

Made for Johan Heyns by the brilliant Marelise Niemann, this is a separately fermented white blend of mostly Chenin Blanc supported by 17% Marsanne, 15% Grenache Blanc and 14% Roussanne. Bolder than the 2024 release, it has honeysuckle and aromatic spice top notes and a palate of subtle skin-tannin bitterness, quince and yellow apple and a tangy, acid-driven finish.

Tesame is a Rhône stye Cape red for people who appreciate the art of blending, as practised by Marelise Niemann. Partnering Grenache, 38% Syrah and 9% Cinsault, it’s a sappy, refreshing, medium-bodied style with some Negroni spices from 30% whole clusters, layers of redcurrant, goji berry and rooibos tea and a rose petal top note.

Using grapes from an old-vine parcel planted in 1962, this comes from the cooler climate of Piekenierskloof. Aged in a mixture of French and American oak – part of the house style at Arbeidsgenot – this is a tangy, racy style of Chenin Blanc, with yellow apple and pink grapefruit flavours and a subtly salty undertone.

Is Grenache Blanc part of the future in South Africa, a variety that does well in a warming world? I reckon so on the evidence of this and other wines. This is pithy, focused and acid driven with waxed lemon and green apple fruit, lots of stony intensity, a touch of oak sweetness and a mineral-rich core.

Why should Piekenierskloof have everything its own way when it comes to Cape Grenache? This is juicy, sappy and well-priced, with understated French and American oak, some subtle, stony reduction, flavours of goji berry and pomegranate and a nip of savoury tannins.

A producer to watch in the Swartland, this is a perfumed, well-judged Shiraz that carries its 50% new French and American oak lightly. Aromas of coconut and Asian spices segue into a palate of fig and blackberry complemented by fine, textured tannins.

Tannie Esther is a straw wine made from Muscat d’Alexandrie, dried on mats for two weeks to concentrate its sugar, extract and acidity. Aged for six months in 300-litre French and American oak, it’s intense yet refreshing, with orange peel, citrus and honey flavours, some patisserie spices and a refreshing, acid-driven finish.

Verdelho is a variety that ought to be more widely planted in the warmer parts of the Cape. This one from Jaco Brand was fermented and aged in fourth-use French and American oak and has plenty of zip and tension for a wine that underwent full malolactic. Stony, tangy and intense, it has lemongrass and green fig flavours and a patina of wood spices.

An impressive follow up the 2022 release, Michiel du Toit’s Chardonnay has a lot of flavour and texture for a medium-bodied style. Aromas of popcorn and brioche segue into a palate of citrus, pear and vanilla spice supported by granite-derived freshness.

n: Asara Wine Estate Owner's Selection Chardonnay
d: The soils are mixed on this single block in Stellenbosch, combining clay-rich granite and sandy loam. Fermented and aged in equal parts amphora and older French oak, it has aromas of hay and rice pudding, a waft of petrichor and pear and citrus fruit.

Anthony Hamilton Russell is determined to elevate Pinotage to the ranks of the world’s best varieties and he’s certainly doing his bit to put it there. Treated like a fine Pinot Noir, this is a medley of clones 6, 45 and 48 from a single one-hectare block on clay soils. Aromatic, detailed and refined, it has lots of mineral zip, sculpted, fine-grained tannins and flavours of plum, redcurrant and wild strawberry. The 30% new oak is right on point.

Now released within a year of the vintage, rather than kept back to develop in bottle, Sandstone is an unusual three-way blend of Sauvignon Blanc, 20% Chardonnay and 17% Semillon, benefiting from oak, concrete, amphora and ceramic egg ageing. Petrichor, saffron and wet stone aromas lead you into a palate of elderflower, beeswax and citrus zest and a lingering finish.

Aslina’s Western Cape Chardonnay is an 85/15 blend from the Simonsberg and Elgin. Very lightly wooded in older barrels and stainless steel, it has some mid-palate texture from ten months on lees, a palate of lemon butter, vanilla and pear and plenty of underlying zip and energy.

Delheim’s farm on the Simonsberg supplies the raw material for this consumer-friendly orange wine, made with Chenin Blanc that spent seven days on skins. Jasmine and subtle tangerine aromas segue into a palate of dried honey, aromatic spices and quince. Deliciously drinkable.

Umsasane is Ntsiki Biyela’s top red, made with grapes from Delheim on the Simonsberg. Combining Cabernet Sauvignon and 15% each of Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot, it has a scented frame of 15% new oak, top notes of mint and dark chocolate, impressive structure and depth and layers of blueberry and black cherry fruit.

Two blocks on the flank of the Kasteelberg supply the grapes for this very lightly wooded, foudre-aged Chenin Blanc from Albert Burger and Alan Cooke. Made in a low-intervention style, it has layers of greengage, Granny Smith apple and aniseed, sappy, palate-cleansing acidity and a waft of aromatic spices.

As well as being Donovan Rall’s home base, the Yellowwood Winery in the Swartland makes very good wines under its own Aspoestertjie brand. Fermented and lees-aged in third-fill barrels, this has the chiselled acidity that’s typical of Colombard, with the concentration of its 41-year-old vines and lime, citrus and grapefruit flavours.

The kind of thing the Swartland ought to make more of, this is a Chenin Blanc-dominated white blend that also includes 14% Viognier, and 2% each of Grenache Blanc and Roussanne. Lightly wooded, like all the Aspoestertjie wines, this is more than the sum of its parts, with ginger and saffron aromas, citrus, pear and juniper flavours and a savoury, slightly umamilike finish.

Anima’s Chenin Blanc includes a 20% amphora and qvevri component, adding an appealingly earthy undertone to the blend. Fresh, layered and well balanced, it has a nice medley of orange peel and waxed lemon flavours, some underlying tannic grip and a leesy finish. Something a little different from Corne Marais.

Cyclus is a stylish, seamlessly blended cuvée of Roussanne, 25% Chenin Blanc, 15% each of Semillon and Viognier and 10% Chardonnay. Including 25% that was aged in amphoras and qvevris, it has alluring saffron and jasmine aromas, flavours of quince, citrus peel and black tea and a nip of tannin on the finish.

Drawing on his experience in Georgia, Corne Marais fermented and aged this blend of Grenache and 30% each of Mourvèdre and Syrah in clay qvevris, including 12% whole clusters. The result is a firm, slightly earthy red with notes of blackberry and red cherry and an earthy, beetroot-like undertone.

A Helderberg estate to keep an eye on under new winemaker Dominique Modena, this is at the fresher end of the Chardonnay spectrum, exhibiting appealing purity and focus. The 39% new oak is well handled, adding some polish and perfume to a palate of lemongrass, fennel and lemon butter.

A series of cooler parcels on the Helderberg supply the raw material for this youthful, welljudged Syrah. Very lightly wooded in foudres and older oak, it has fynbos and white pepper aromas, lots of colour, layers of plum and black cherry and firm underlying tannins.

n: Avontuur The West Peak Cabernet Sauvignon
d: The West Peak comes from vines at the western end of the Helderberg close to Taaibosch and shows the ocean-kissed freshness of the site. Made with the 46 Cabernet Sauvignon clone, it has refined, mocha-scented 33% new oak, cassis and fresh herb flavours and some underlying tannic grip.

Reviewed a couple of years ago, but retasted as a more mature wine, this is a comparatively rich, yet well-balanced Chardonnay from Simonsberg-Paarl, with nutmeg and vanilla spice notes from 30% new oak, flavours of citrus, peach and macadamia nut, racy acidity and an appealingly toasty finish. The price is on the ambitious side, perhaps.

n: Babylonstoren In Die Wolke Pinot Noir
d: Pinot Noir is a rare find in Simonsberg-Paarl, but this one comes from a vineyard at 600 metres and has the benefit of a cooler site. Fermented with 20% whole bunches, it has impressive structure and backbone, a grippy, slightly ferrous undertone, a touch of wood spices and juicy plum and wild strawberry fruit.

Less oaky than it used to be – 80% new barrels instead of 100% – Nebukadnesar is a nicely crafted blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, 25% Merlot and 15% Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Petit Verdot. Ripe and approachable, it has gingerbread and cinnamon aromas, fig and blackcurrant pastille flavours and supple tannins.

This is the first vintage of a varietal Semillon from Babylonstoren – it used to go into a white blend – sourced from a block that was planted in 2008. Fermented and aged in 10% new wood, it has some subtle reduction, impressive focus and texture, layers of citrus and lanolin, subtle oak spices and a herbal undertone.

Shiraz is something of a signature variety at Babylonstoren. Serious, textured and well structured, this has appealing 30% new oak, layers of blackberry, fig and liquorice, sinewy, age-worthy tannins and the underlying concentration to develop further in bottle.

Sprankel is an ambitious bubbly from this showcase Simonsberg-Paarl property, made with a cuvée of Chardonnay and 10% Pinot Noir. Matured for 54 months on lees, with 10% of the base wine fermented in wood, it’s toasty, focused and appealing, with small bubbles, hints of hazelnut and citrus and 6.5 grams of dosage.

"There’s some chew on the wine," says Julia Blaine of this structured, age-worthy blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and 12% Malbec. Matured in 88% new French oak, it has appealing freshness from earlier picking in a warm vintage, flavours of mint and cassis, textured tannins and well-integrated wood spices.

A comparative rarity in the Cape, this is a delightful stand-alone Vermentino from Julia Blaine. Picked twice for added layers, it has appealing yellow apple, sake and clementine flavours, a touch of white pepper and a bitter quinine-twist that’s very Italian in style.

Il Principe – the prince in Italian – is a Tuscany-meets-Bordeaux blend of Sangiovese, 14% Malbec and 11% each of Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. A wine that lives up to its stylish label, it has assertive 42% new wood, savoury, tobacco leaf tannins, strawberry and redcurrant fruit and impressive underlying structure.

Il Sovrano – the sovereign in Italian – is a toasty, full-throttle cuvée of Cabernet Sauvignon, 29% Merlot, 20% Cabernet Franc, 9% Malbec and 3% Sangiovese. Matured in bold 92% new oak, it has layers of blackcurrant and damson, structured tannins and supporting acidity. The wood needs more time to integrate.

Full marks to Bacco Estate for making an ambitious rosé, made from an unusual combination of Malbec, 19% Syrah, 18% Sangiovese and 15% Vermentino. Fermented in older oak, it has appealing colour and texture, some underlying grip and tannic structure and flavours of tangerine, wild strawberry and gin botanicals.

Proof that Paarl is capable of making good Syrah, this is a savoury, lightly peppery red with top notes of incense and subtle vanilla spice, toasty 20% new oak and a core of blackberry and red berry fruit complemented by a waft of Mediterranean herbs.

The pick of the current Backsberg range, this hails from a pair of parcels in the Bottelary Hills. Curated in 12% new oak, it has aromas of mint, tarragon and cut grass, sinewy tannins and layers of plum, paprika and red berries. The finish is fresh and well balanced.

Droom – dream in English – is a wine that Bartho Eksteen has always wanted to make, sourced from an old-vine Semillon block in Franschhoek that was planted in 1905. Fermented in lightly toasted new oak, it carries its wood lightly, revealing layers of lanolin, cream and vanilla spice and a core of pear, tangerine and fresh green herbs. Not made in 2026, but let’s hope it will be back in 2027.

Fluister uses raw material from a 0.25-hectare, high-density block planted with the 115 and 777 clones. Fifteen per cent whole bunches add a layer of complexity to a savoury, wellstructured palate of mint, sage, red cherry and tomato leaf framed by one-third new oak.

Houtskool is a typically off-the-wall blend of Sauvignon Blanc from Cape Agulhas with 6% Semillon from Elgin. Very much an ocean-influenced style, it’s all about fruit rather than oak, pairing aromas of sea salt, nettle and sourdough bread with a palate of citrus, greengage and elderflower and a savoury, umami-rich finish.

Meester is the cheapest of Bartho Eksteen’s whites and serves as a good introduction to his winemaking style. Pairing Sauvignon Blanc and 6% Semillon from the Upper Hemelen-Aarde Valley, Cape Agulhas and Elgin, it’s a zesty, unoaked cuvée with rocket and blackcurrant leaf aromas, a palate of kiwi fruit and gooseberry and a herbal finish.

Aidan comes from the higher part of the Constantia Neck and is a blend of Merlot, 25% Syrah, 14% Petit Verdot and 7% Cabernet Sauvignon. Fresh in a wetter vintage, this has enough weight and concentration to carry its 69% new wood, with bramble, parsley and blackcurrant leaf flavours and a spine of fine-grained tannins.

Made in a low-intervention style – “we oxidise the shit out of it,” says Megan van der Merwe – this is a Viognier with lots of texture and layers, using different fermentation and ageing vessels, lots of lees work, flavours of quince, smoked lemon and pear and a hint of the creaminess that’s part of the variety’s DNA.

2023 was a vintage when you needed to spend a lot of time in the vineyard and that work has paid off at Beau Constantia. This is a blend of Cabernet Franc and 23% Merlot that’s certainly on the green and herbal side but has some tannic structure, plum and red pepper flavours, tangy acidity and stylish 60% new oak.

"Stupidly good," is Megan van der Merwe’s typically pithy description of the 2025 vintage. This superb assemblage of Sauvignon Blanc and 13% Semillon, sourced from vines at 360 metres, illustrates her point. Combining new and seasoned French and Austrian barrels and some ceramic clayvers, this has gunflint reduction, flavours of nettle, elderflower and pink grapefruit and some added structure from partial fermentation on skins.

A little on the funky side perhaps, but there’s no denying that this Constantia Syrah has lots of personality. Iodine, sage and subtle farmyard aromas segue into a palate of liquorice, blackberry and redcurrant, framed by 29% new wood, a touch of raw meat and a focused, granite-driven finish.

n: Beaumont Goutte d'Or Noble Late Harvest Chenin Blanc
d: Last made in 2021, Goutte d’Or is back with interest in the landmark 2025 vintage. Made with vine-dried and botrytis-affected Chenin Blanc bunches, it’s a subtly wooded delight, with 146 grams of residual sugar, peach, nectarine and patisserie flavours, low volatility and a core of racy, beautifully integrated acidity.

n: Beaumont Hope Marguerite OVP Chenin Blanc
d: A wine that I like to buy for my own cellar, given how seamlessly it ages, Hope Marguerite uses grapes from two blocks on the farm in Bot River, planted in 1974 and 1978. Expressing what Sebastian Beaumont calls a “great vintage”, it has wonderful focus and self-confidence, with scented 25% new oak, pear, wet stone and citrus zest flavours and a whisper of stone fruit sweetness.

Couched in a more modern style, this is dominated by grapes from younger vines at Beaumont, with 20% from older parcels. Deftly wooded in 30% new barrels, it’s a floral, tangy style with bramble and summer berry fruit, some clove spice from 15% whole bunches and a juicy, palate-caressing finish. Great by-the-glass stuff.

Among the best vintages of New Baby since the maiden 2015 release, this is seamless blend from what Sebastian Beaumont calls a “dream harvest”. Partnering Chenin Blanc, 25% Sauvignon Blanc and 12% Colombard from vineyards planted between 1974 and 1988, it has a sheen of subtle, vanilla-scented 25% new oak, flavours of pear, lemongrass and pink grapefruit and a stony, tapering finish.

Vitruvian is the red equivalent of the New Baby white in a sense, blending Mourvèdre, 21% each of Syrah and Pinotage and a further 10% each of Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot. Curated in 25% new oak, it has aromas of liquorice, barbecued meat and wild herbs and a palate of damson, blackberry and forest floor.

Making the most of “stuff that people can’t sell”, Abrie Beeslaar puts together this wine by blending purchased components with 20% of his own stuff. A pan-Stellenbosch cuvée from Banghoek and the Simonsberg, it’s a floral, youthful medley of Cabernet Sauvignon, 18% Pinotage, 17% Merlot and 14% Petit Verdot. Elegant, racy and fruit forward, with subtle 10% new oak and bramble and summer berry flavours.

Something of a movable feast, as the components change from vintage to vintage, this subtle Chardonnay comes from one vineyard in Barriedale and two in Stellenbosch. Barrel fermented without malolactic in 15% new wood, it has a macedoine of citrus, peach and green olive, a waft of cinnamon spice and a racy finish.

Very few people understand Pinotage as well as Abrie Beeslaar, who has been making worldclass examples of the variety for decades. This one hails from a 26-year-old bush vine block on shale soils and sits in the middle of the variety’s stylistic spectrum, with deftly handled 50% new wood, flavours of ginger, plum, liquorice and wild strawberry and judicious, palatecaressing tannins.

“The better vineyards perform well in shitty vintages,” says Abrie Beeslaar and here is the proof. Right up there with the best 2023 Stellenbosch reds, this is a profound, beautifully crafted assemblage of Cabernet Sauvignon and 40% Cabernet Franc from two sites on the Helderberg and in Banghoek. Even better than the maiden 2022 release, it has alluring espresso coffee and lead pencil aromas, sculpted tannins, subtle oak spices and layers of cassis, basil and red cherry.

n: Belle Rebelle A Bird In Hand Semillon

d: Chenin Blanc is the most planted white in the Breedekloof Valley, making consistently good wines. This one hails from a single parcel at 214 metres and is fresh, layered, medium-bodied style with a waft of vanilla spice, a hint of tannin from 5% skin contact and a core of saffron, citrus and Conference pear.

Mariëtte Stofberg is rightly proud of her bubblies, which are some of the best in the Breedekloof Valley. This all-Chardonnay Blanc de Blancs spent 78 months on lees and is a tangy, savoury, just off-dry style with fine bubbles, notes of croissant, wet stones and citrus and a tapering, well-balanced finish.

Using raw material from the granite soils of the Swartland as opposed to Belle Rebelle’s home base in the Breedekloof Valley, this is a stonier, more mineral-etched style of Chenin Blanc from Mariëtte Stofberg, with dryland intensity, good underlying grip and citrus and cardamom flavours.

Entirely sourced from vineyards that are over 35 years’ old, this stylish blend of Chenin Blanc, 30% Semillon and 10% Grenache Blanc is back after a break in 2024. Combining fruit from four regions – Cape Town, Franschhoek, Stellenbosch and the Voor Paardeberg – it’s a seamless Cape cuvée with lots of stony zip and intensity, scented 25% new oak and flavours of greengage, citrus and aromatic baking spices.

Pod is a comparatively unusual pairing of Pinotage and 45% Syrah from Stellenbosch and Darling, respectively. Matured in 40% new French oak, it has plenty of grip, concentration and tannin, blackberry, bramble and cinnamon spice flavours and the structure and intensity to develop further in bottle.

n: Bellingham The Bernard Series Basket Press Syrah
d: Combining fruit from the Polkadraai Hills and (for the first time) a 10% Swartland portion, this is the latest in a run of very good Syrahs from Richard Duckitt. Using 40% whole clusters and 25% new oak to good effect, it’s an intense, youthful, deeply coloured wine with damson, blackberry and liquorice flavours, grippy tannins and deftly integrated 25% new oak.

n: Bellingham The Bernard Series Bush Vine Pinotage
d: Three different Stellenbosch vineyards, predominantly located on granite-dominated soils are the source of this impressive Pinotage from Richard Duckitt. Concrete fermented before ageing in 40% new oak, it has ample colour and intensity, perfumed 40% new wood and sappy blackberry and bramble fruit.

n: Bellingham The Bernard Series Old Vine OVP Chenin Blanc
d: One of a pair of OVP Chenin Blancs from Ricardo Cloete, this is a blend of grapes from mostly Cape Town (aka Durbanville), with lesser components from Stellenbosch, Darling and Franschhoek. Matured in 30% new oak, it over-delivers at the price, showing stony intensity, aromas of hay and aromatic spices and a palate of wax, citrus and yellow apple and a granitic finish.

n: Bellingham The Bernard Series Old Vine OVP Chenin Blanc
d: An old-vine parcel planted in 1983 is the source of this excellent Chenin Blanc from young winemaker Ricardo Cloete. Fermented in 30% new barrels, it has the freshness of its cooler climate source in Durbanville, flavours of greengage, citrus peel and vanilla spice and a racy, well-balanced finish.

n: Benguela Cove Argonaut Blanc de Blancs CC
d: New to the range at this increasingly impressive property in Walker Bay, this is still youthful for a 2017 release. Made entirely from Chardonnay, it’s a pithy, racy, chiselled Cap Classique with brioche and waxed lemon flavours, deftly integrated 4.8 grams of dosage, a hint of aniseed and a refreshing, acid-driven finish.

Catalina is something of a counter-intuitive white, as it tastes good out of the traps but ages extremely well too. Fermented a little cooler in 2024 for more freshness, it has attractive 25% new wood, some subtle gunflint reduction, layers of padrón peppers, green herbs and citrus and a savoury, acid-driven finish.

Picked early for freshness, this is an appealing, mid-priced Chardonnay from Johann Fourie that has 30% new wood and ten months ageing on lees. Fermented with 20% malolactic to reduce the acidity a little, it has appealing pear, citrus and boiled sweets flavours, a note of lemon butter and a lightly toasty finish.

Collage is a cool-climate assemblage of the five red Bordeaux varieties, combining Cabernet Sauvignon, 20% Merlot, 19% Malbec, 15% Petit Verdot and 4% Cabernet Franc. The new oak component has come down to 40%, giving the site more room to express itself. Mint, dill and violet aromas are complemented by cassis, red cherry and subtle coffee bean flavours.

Johann Fourie sources this Sauvignon Blanc from cooler, southern slopes on shale soils close to the lagoon. Wild yeast fermented in 15% new wood and 10% ceramic eggs, it’s a textured, layered, complex wine with cool climate acidity, flavours of kiwi fruit and gooseberry and a racy, herbal finish.

Deliberately made with a little struck match reduction – Johann Fourie says it’s all about “nutrient deficiency” – this a nuanced, well-judged Chardonnay that reflects its cool Walker Bay climate. Finely wooded in 30% new oak, it has layers of citrus, Digestive biscuit and cinnamon spice, lively acidity and a flinty finish.

Petit Verdot might not be the first variety you’d choose to plant in one of the cooler parts of Walker Bay, but this example reflects good work in the vineyard and winery. Deeply coloured and intense, it has ample tannic backbone, damson and blueberry fruit, a waft of cedarwood and well-integrated 40% new French oak.

Vinography comes from a 1.5-hectare site with pronounced ocean influence – you can almost smell the proximity of the waves in the wine – making the most of the stellar 2025 vintage. Barrel fermented in 50% new barrels, with a ceramic egg component for added complexity, it has layers of citrus, lime and rock salt and a sheen of subtle baking spice sweetness.

Tres, or TR3S, is part of a museum-release range from Benguela Cove, produced as a threevintage blend from 2023, 2024 and 2025. More worked than the estate’s regular Chardonnay releases, it has toasty 30% new wood, flavour of butterscotch and popcorn and a steely, mouth-watering finish. A wine of two halves.

Diesel is the top-of-the-range Pinotage from Anri Truter, with ageing in 100% new oak to prove it. The price is on the ambitious side, but there’s no denying the quality of the wine. Soft, supple and intense, it’s a gratifyingly modern iteration of the variety, with layers of plum, wild strawberry and Asian spices, textured tannins and enough acidity to drive and freshen the finish.

Faith is what is known locally as a Cape red blend, made from equal parts Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinotage. The 100% new oak is a little too evident, but this is a wine that has the structure to evolve further in bottle, with decent underlying grip, flavours of coffee bean, cassis, plum and black cherry and supporting acidity.

The fact that Pinotage is an early ripening variety came in handy in the rain-affected 2023 vintage in Stellenbosch. Enticingly fragrant and intense, this is comparatively forward in style, with rose petal and baking spice aromas, subtle 30% new oak, raspberry, goji berry and forest floor flavours and a volatile lift.

One of a quartet of Pinotages from the Truter family, who have done as much as anyone to popularise the grape in South Africa and overseas, this Reserve bottling is way less oaky than it used to be, with layers of banana, summer berries and sweet patisserie oak, fine-grained tannins and wafts of saffron and rose petal.

Anri Truter is bringing a new focus and sensibility to his family’s winery, typified by this co-fermentation of Pinotage and 33% Chenin Blanc. Almost a rosé, it’s juicy, sappy and well balanced, with understated older oak, layers of rose petal, pear and rooibos tea and a refreshing, energetic finish.

Rebellion is a textbook introduction to the pleasures of Pinotage, priced at a level that lots of people will be able to afford. Scented supple and smooth, it has Pinot Noir-like flavours of raspberry and pomegranate, hints of candy floss and vanilla spice and layered, palatecaressing tannins.

Semillon and Franschhoek seem to go together like Laurel and Hardy. Proving that it doesn’t have to be oaked to be good, providing the grapes are wonderful, this is a scented, stainless steel-fermented style with layers of toast, lime and lanolin, a hint of cream soda and a tangy, low-alcohol finish.

n: Black Elephant Vintners Free Bird Bush Vines
d: Jacques Wentzel’s stylish Swartland red is a cuvée of Syrah, 8% Cinsault and 6% Grenache that’s deliberately made in a fresher, medium-bodied style. Enticing aromas of sage, thyme and fynbos lead you into a palate of blackberry, clove and red cherry, with sinewy tannins and a cola top note.

n: Black Elephant Vintners Free Bird OVP Chenin Blanc
Black Elephant Vintners Pinot Noir Brut Rosé CC
Black Elephant Vintners Three Men in a Tub with a Rubberduck
Black Elephant Vintners Two Dogs, A Peacock and A Horse

d: But Why? is a pure Cabernet Sauvignon from a vineyard at 800 metres on the Ceres Plateau, which is on the marginal side for such a late-ripening variety. Picked in April as a result, it’s certainly on the green and herbal side, but has appealing 25% new oak, flavours of rhubarb, blackcurrant leaf and dill, fine tannins and a racy finish.

n: BLANKbottle Confessions of a White Glove Chaser
d: Inspired by the pickers at the de-luxe 4G winery, who wear gloves in the vineyard, this is a Helderberg blend of Cabernet Franc and 40% Cabernet Sauvignon from five different vineyards. Serious, structured and built to last, it’s a youthful, vigorous cuvée with damson and blackcurrant leafy flavours, a hint of espresso coffee and a firm finish.

Don’t Look Back sounds like something that Pieter Walser would adopt as a motto for life, but it’s also the name of this Clairette Blanche from the Voor Paardeberg. Rich and creamy, yet tethered by bright, sappy acidity, this has impressive underlying structure, flavours of peach and crème fraîche and energetic underlying acidity.

Epileptic Inspiration is a reference to the fact that Pieter Walser suffers from the condition and claims to be at his most creative after an attack. The result is a superb varietal Semillon from Elgin, with subtle 40% new oak, layers of lime, citrus and lanolin and a taut, pithy, palate-cleansing finish. Good now but will develop further in bottle.

A wine that has achieved cult status among BLANKbottle’s many fans – the story behind it is the stuff of a good short story – Familiemoord is a varietal Grenache from sandstone soils in Piekenierskloof. Given a 50% saignée to deepen its concentration, it has good and intensity, flavours of pomegranate and blood orange and a refreshing, acid-driven finish.

Made with vine-dried grapes, which are pinched and left to pick up sugar and concentration for a month, this is a wine that combines intensity and a certain viscosity with flavours of honey, guava and pink grapefruit, good texture and weight and a subtle interplay between acidity and 170 grams of residual sugar.

Pieter Walser sources this bone-dry Riesling with grapes from the Eikendal farm in Elgin. Barrel fermented in older oak, it’s more Alsace than Mosel Valley, as it were, with white flower, jasmine and wet stone aromas and a chiselled, refreshing palate of lime and quinine supported by mouth-watering acidity.

Jimmy is an unblended Verdelho from Wille Mostert’s farm in the Voor Paardeberg, making the most of what Pieter Walser calls “very good grapes”. Deftly curated in older barrels, it’s all about precision and focus, with quince, yellow apple and waxed lemon flavours and a pithy, palate-cleansing finish.

A rare sighting of a stand-alone Fernão Pires in the Cape, this hails from a low-yielding block on the Darling side of Swartland, close to the Atlantic Ocean. Picked in three stages, it marries aromas of jasmine and honeysuckle with a palate of lemon and lime and touch of apricot sweetness.

Little William is one of Pieter Walser’s most iconic wines, made with ungrafted Syrah vines from Marguerite Macdonald’s vineyard on the high-altitude Ceres Plateau. Daringly fermented with whole clusters in a cool, marginal site, it has alluring clove, thyme and white pepper aromas, layers of beetroot, tobacco leaf and earth and some vanilla sweetness from 10% new oak.

Luuks uses grapes from the corner of the Helderberg, close to False Bay, where the ocean influence is marked. Fermented and aged in around 40% new oak, it’s a structured, mediumbodied style of Chardonnay with cinnamon and wet stone aromas, some lees-derived texture and a refreshing palate of pear, citrus and cumin.

Pieter Walser is one of only two Cape producers that I know who has two different Verdelhos in his range (the other being Longridge). Makstokkie hails from schist soils in RiebeekKasteel and is the more perfumed of the pair, with top notes of honeysuckle and saffron and a palate of pear, lemongrass and orange zest.

Master of None is Pieter Walser’s joke at his own expense, given how many different wines he makes. An off-the-wall blend of Cinsault, Grenache and 20% white grapes, it’s so pale it could almost be a rosé with sappy rooibos tea and goji berry flavours, fine tannins and a touch of Turkish Delight sweetness.

A constant presence in Pieter Walser’s shifting kaleidoscope of a range, Moment of Silence is BLANKbottle’s biggest production wine. Sourced from Wellington, it’s a cuvée of Chenin Blanc, 30% Grenache Blanc and 10% Viognier with the structure to age. Sappy, layered and refined, it has pear and tangerine fruit, hint of fennel and almond paste and a racy finish.

My Köffer has been part of the BLANKbottle range since 2011 and is always one of my favourite Pieter Walser reds. Sourced from Eight Gates in the Breedekloof it has layers of redcurrant, blood orange and wild strawberry, a hint of forest floor, some pepper spice from 30% whole clusters and appealing underlying grip.

Made with grapes from a vineyard in the Voor Paardeberg that was coaxed back from extinction, this is an unusual field blend of mostly Chenin Blanc with Chardonnay, Grillo, Grenache Blanc, Petit Manseng, Picpoul, Semillon and Viura, all of them picked on the same day. Layers of lime, greengage, sherbet and subtle skin phenolics are framed by nicely understated older oak.

It varies from year to year – “no rules” is Pieter Walser’s motto – but in 2025, this is a blend of 17 white varieties from 20 different vineyards, with Chenin Blanc, Clairette Blanche and Verdelho in the driving seat. Racy, layered and effortlessly complex, it’s a medley of lime, lemon and yellow apple flavours with some underlying phenolic grip.

Pierre Le Cois sounds like a dashing French three-quarter, but is actually a Helderberg blend of Cabernet Franc and 25% each of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. Coffee bean, mint and liquorice aromas lead you into a palate of dark chocolate, blueberry and blackcurrant pastille with a firm, earth and dried-herb finish.

PTSD is a new wine from the ever-inventive Pieter Walser, made with Hárslevelű grapes from the Lammershoek farm on the Paardeberg. Nutmeg and Turkish bazaar aromas segue into a palate of ginger, pear and lychee, supported by some underlying tannic grip. Promising stuff from the self-confessed “master of none”.

Retirement at 65 – no chance of that where I’m concerned, folks – is a brilliant pairing of Cinsault and 3% Syrah from Darling, making the most of one of the oldest red wine blocks in the country. Juicy, sappy and ethereal, it has some subtle whole bunch notes, hints of stem ginger and rose petal and tea-leaf tannins.

Saint Rand is a stand-alone Pinotage from Stellenbosch that’s deliberately made in a serious, age-worthy style. Curated in 20% new oak, it’s a full-bodied style with lots of plum, bramble and blackberry fruit, some Asian spice top notes and an undertow of tannin. One to tuck away for a while.

Chardonnay sometimes gets overlooked in the BLANKbottle range, such is the winery’s focus on Portuguese, Rhône and Mediterranean grapes, so it was a pleasure to taste this Stellenbosch example from Firgrove. Oak-fermented in Italian Mittelberger barrels, it has top notes of gunflint, coconut and sandalwood, citrus and tangerine flavours and energetic acidity.

Sewejaartjie – try saying, let alone spelling that after a few glasses of wine – is an amphorafermented and aged Grenache from Bot River. A red that has some grip and density, it has layers of rose petal, Campari spices and cranberry and a spine of firmish tannins. Needs more time in bottle.

While Pieter Walser made the wine, his son designed the label of Smaug the Magnificent. Dominated by Chenin Blanc, with a supporting chorus of Grenache Blanc, Marsanne, Roussanne and Verdelho, it uses components from Darling, the Swartland and the Voor Paardeberg. Quince, pear and passion fruit flavours are supported by fresh acidity.

The Bomb is appropriately named, as it weighs in at 15% alcohol. Sourced from Keermont at the eastern end of the Helderberg, it’s a cuvée of Cabernet Sauvignon and 30% Cabernet Franc with impressive concentration and backbone, layers of mint, cassis and black cherry and a waft of fynbos and mountain herbs.

The Spaniard is a pure Mourvèdre from schist soils at Kloovenburg in the Swartland, with ageing in 25% French and German oak from Mittelberger in Italy. (Should the wine be called The European?). Floral, stony and garrigue-perfumed, it’s sappy and refreshing for the variety, with bramble and redcurrant flavours and savoury tannins.

Ultra is a Chenin Blanc from the Swartland’s border with Malmesbury, owned by a grower who is likes to live life on the edge, according to Pieter Walser. Picked in different stages, it has layers of citrus and apple pie, plenty of steely minerality, a kiss of old oak and some subtle skin phenolics on the finish.

“It eats wood,” says Gottfried Mocke of this blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and 13% Cabernet Franc from Franschhoek, almost all of it sourced from vines around the cellar. Curated in 85% new oak, it has leafy, graphite and basil aromas, smooth tannins, racy acidity and flavours of capsicum, espresso coffee and blackcurrant.

Boekenhoutskloof’s Stellenbosch Cabernet Sauvignon comes from four different sites, with a focus on the Helderberg. Paired with 15% Cabernet Franc for extra complexity, it has lots of energy and structure, stylish 60% new oak, flavours of bramble, cedarwood, mocha and cassis and the concentration to develop further in bottle.

The Goldmine white is blended across the Cape, using components from Franschhoek, the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley and the Goldmine property itself. Chenin Blanc based with support from 6% Chardonnay, 5% Semillon and 5% Viognier, it’s tauter and more focused than the maiden 2024 release, with a nice medley of lime, waxed lemon and nectarine flavours, a hint of jasmine and nicely understated oak.

n: Boekenhoutskloof Helderberg Winery Cabernet Sauvignon Reserve

d: One of two world-class Semillons from the dream team of Marc Kent and Gottfried Mocke, this comes from vineyards that get botrytis every year because of the high water table. Fermented and aged for three years in new French oak, this is a complex delight, with layers of peach, pear tart and toast, a waft of baking spices, tangy acidity and a subtle volatile lift. Wonderfully textured and self-assured.

A wine that shows well young but develops wonderfully in bottle, this is a blend of old-vine Semillon from blocks planted between 1902 and 1942 and (a barely noticeable) 2% Muscat d’Alexandrie. Fermented and aged in 70% new wood, 28% concrete eggs and 2% amphoras, it’s a wine of effortless brilliance, with wet stone and saffron aromas, flavours of lemon and lime, subtle nutmeg spice and lots of underlying extract and concentration.

Gottfried Mocke makes this brilliant Syrah with grapes from the cooler, Wellington side of Porseleinberg, combining them with 10% from the Goldmine property. Subtly wooded in Stockinger foudres and 600-litre barrels, it’s enticingly scented and refined, with some spicy notes from 65% whole bunches, layers of violet, ginger, blackberry and fennel, fine, glossy tannins and a faintly ferrous undertone.

Volumes are not quite as high as they once were, but this ultra-successful premium South African red still sells more than a million bottles to 112 markets around the world. Combining Boekenhoutskloof’s own grapes with 30% purchased material, it’s a seamless, still youthful cuvée of Syrah, 12% Grenache, 10% Cinsault, 5% Cabernet Sauvignon and 1% Viognier. Showing the freshness and intensity of the 2025 vintage, it has violet and subtle aromatic spice top notes, fleshy tannins and layers of bramble, blackberry and summer pudding fruit. Good now and will develop further in bottle.

n: Boland Cellar A Hint of Litchi Sauvignon Blanc
Boland Cellar A Hint of Melon Chenin Blanc
Boland Cellar A Hint of Spice Shiraz
Boland Cellar A Hint of Vanilla Chardonnay
Boland Cellar Classic Selection Chenin Blanc
d: Impressive value from the reborn Boland Cellar, this mass-market Chenin Blanc uses grapes from shale and granite soils on the Paardeberg. Just off dry at 4.9 grams of residual sugar, it’s a very appealing quaffer, with peach, lemon and yellow apple flavours and appealing underlying grip.

n: Boland Cellar Classic Selection Sauvignon Blanc
Boland Cellar One Formation Chenin Blanc/Sauvignon Blanc/Grenache Blanc
d: One Formation is an intriguing cuvée of mostly Chenin Blanc with 20% Sauvignon Blanc and 15% Grenache Blanc, using grapes from Darling, Paarl and the Swartland. Smartly packaged, it’s an attempt to shift the dial at this former co-operative, showing subtle wood spices, flavours of passion fruit, greengage and cream soda and a racy, slightly salty finish. Bravo!

Part of what Ross Sleet calls “our wine history”, this is the kind of thing that good cooperatives can almost bottle in their sleep. Showing some nice evolution, it has flavours of fig and strawberry jam, a subtle balsamic undertone and a nice balance between residual sugar and fortifying spirit.

The Reserve Red showcases what the Boland Cellar team consider to be the best lots in any given vintage. In 2024, it’s a blend of 43% Pinotage, 24% Cabernet Sauvignon, 15% Grenache, 14% Syrah and 4% Cabernet Franc. Matured in new and second-fill barrels, it’s spicy, textured and deeply coloured, with bramble and blackberry fruit, a touch of clove and a frame of scented oak.

n: Boland Cellar Reserve Sparkling Chenin Blanc

d: If this were a white Port from the Douro Valley, it would sell at three times the price. Mature, nutty and full-bodied it has time-kissed flavours of fig, date and dried orange peel, wellintegrated 189 grams of sugar and a balanced, self-assured finish.

n: Bon Courage Jacques Bruére Blanc de Blancs CC
d: Jacques Bruére is a great-value bubbly made by Jacques Bruwer and Philip Viljoen. Still youthful as it enters its second decade, it’s an unwooded, all-Chardonnay Blanc de Blancs with citrus, toast and fennel flavours, fine bubbles and a faintly earthy undertone.

n: Bon Courage Jacques Bruére Brut Reserve CC
d: Bon Courage make some of the best-value fizzes in the Cape, typified by the quality of this Robertson cuvée of Pinot Noir and 40% Chardonnay from Philip Viljoen. Showing some appealing colour and palate development, it has layers of hazelnut and fresh cèpes, good extract and concentration and finely judged 5.3 grams of dosage.

n: Bon Courage Jacques Bruére Cuvée Rosé Brut CC
d: This appealing Robertson rosé is entirely made with Pinot Noir and is another example of how Bon Courage over-delivers in the glass. Malt and rose petal aromas are a scented introduction to a palate of raspberry coulis and Turkish Delight supported by racy acidity.

This is rare stuff – there is only one barrel for the world – so the price reflects the scarcity. Touriga Nacional based, with lesser contributions from Tinta Barroca, Touriga Franca and Souzão, it’s darker and more brooding than the 2025 release, with impressive structure and vigour, flavours of walnut, raisin and toffee and enough concentration to develop for another decade in bottle.

Picked in two stages for complexity, this Alvarinho – the spelling reflects Margaux Nel and Leon Coetzee’s love of Portugal – comes from a young block planted in 2020. Lagar fermented before ageing in older barrels and stainless steel, it has top notes of curry leaf and celery and a palate of pear, passion fruit and citrus underpinned by acidity and some skin tannin grip.

"These are lekker things to drink," says Leon Coetzee, and who am I to disagree with him? A flag-waving delight after three decades in barrel and bottle, it’s a classic Boplaas blend of Touriga Nacional and 10% Tinta Barroca and Souzão that’s perfect to drink now, with flavours of molasses, Christmas cake and North African spices, 110 grams of sugar and a lingering, layered finish.

Made every year (well, “almost”, according to Margaux Nel), this is a wine that can go toe to toe with the Ports of the Douro Valley. Made in a structured, slightly drier style – more Dow’s than Graham’s – it’s a happy cuvée of Touriga Nacional and 10% Tinta Barroca and Souzão, with damson, liquorice and dark chocolate, 93 grams of sugar and some fire in its belly. Complex, dense and built to age.

Planted in Carel Nel’s birth year, this fortified Muscat hails from a block planted close to the river that produced a lot of raisins in 2025. Sweeter than its 1932 stablemate, it also tastes a little older, with flavours of honey, green fig and aromatic kitchen spices, a bitter twist from overnight skin contact, 208 grams of sugar and well-handled grape spirit.

The Muscat vines responsible for this youthful fortified are nearly a century old, proving that Calitzdorp isn’t just about red grapes. This is a South African take on a Muscat de Rivesaltes, with citrus and orange marmalade flavours, good underlying structure and a slightly spirity finish. A little skin contact adds extra perfume.

Two clones on the Highfield farm – CY95 and lower-yielding CY548 – supply the raw material for this well-framed cool climate Chardonnay. The 31% new French oak is deftly handled here, adding perfume, structure and interest to a palate of pear, waxed lemon and vanilla supported by zesty acidity.

n: Boschendal Appellation Series Elgin Pinot Noir
d: A solo outing for the 777 clone in Elgin, this well-made Pinot Noir comes from the Eikenhof estate, like the Appellation Sauvignon Blanc. Refined, textured and aromatic, it has deftly handled 10% new oak, rose petal and peony aromas, red cherry and pomegranate flavours and a nip of savoury tannin.

n: Boschendal Appellation Series Elgin Sauvignon Blanc
d: The Eikenhof farm at a comparatively elevated 500 metres in Elgin is the source of this wooded Sauvignon Blanc from Charl Schoeman. Fermented in large foudres and 16% new barrels, it has toast and blackcurrant leaf flavours and a palate of elderflower, vanilla and coriander. Engagingly racy.

Black Angus is a comparatively small release of just 2,800 bottles, made with an Aussie-style blend of Syrah, 28% Cabernet Sauvignon and 12% Cabernet Franc. Smart for a 2023, it has stylish 33% new oak, flavours of cassis and blackberry, some meaty reduction and a dusting of thyme and fynbos.

Showing some of the firmness and tannic grip of the 2022 vintage, this is a serious, structured Cabernet Sauvignon that’s leavened with 10% Cabernet Franc from a vineyard at 450 metres next to Taaibosch. The 33% new oak is well handled, adding a coffee bean note to a palate of mint, cassis and dill.

Boschendal’s top bubbly comes from its own Highfield estate in Elgin and is a blend of Pinot Noir and 41% Chardonnay. Lees aged for 50 months, it’s still impressively fresh and tangy, with plenty of zip and acidity, some texture from 20% malolactic and flavours of citrus and subtle wild strawberry.

Grande Syrah comes from owner DGB’s expanding holdings on the slopes of the lower Helderberg. Deeply coloured, structured and intense, it has some stony reduction, plum and bramble fruit, refreshing granitic energy and negligible oak from ageing in foudres and older, smaller barrels.

An impressive feat of viticulture and winemaking in the challenging 2023 vintage, this is a Helderberg blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, 29% Syrah, 26% Merlot, 5% Cabernet Franc and 1% each of Malbec and Petit Verdot. Great at the price, this is a fine, seamless cuvée with layers of graphite, cut grass, blackcurrant red berries, subtle 30% new wood and graceful tannins.

Consistently among the highlights of the Boschendal range, Suzanne is one of the best white Bordeaux blends in the Cape, made with Semillon from Stellenbosch and 40% Sauvignon Blanc from Elgin. Lanolin, nutmeg and wet stone aromas are a perfumed introduction to an elegant, tangy palate of pink grapefruit and lemongrass framed by 30% new oak.

n: Boschendal Vin d'Or Noble Late Harvest
d: Continuing a rich recent run of form, the latest Vin d’Or is an assemblage of Viognier from Elgin with 15% Riesling from Stellenbosch. Made with the addition of 15% of the 2023 release, it’s an intense, botrytis-rich style with peach, apricot and pear tart flavours, some subtle patisserie spices and 157 grams of sugar. A sweet wine of impressive poise and palate length.

Conclusion is a red blend that’s improving with every vintage, made in 2024 with a blend of Cabernet Franc, 35% Cabernet Sauvignon and 20% Syrah. Described as a “farm blend” by Reenen Borman, it has graphite and rocket aromas, appealing focus and freshness, a palate of red berries and blackcurrant pastille and a tangy, herbal finish.

Epilogue is a world-class Syrah that deserves all the plaudits that come its way. Sourced from half of a 1.8-hectare parcel on a cooler, south-facing slope, it’s hauntingly perfumed and well balanced, with none of the extraction and tannic backbone of some of its peers. The 60% whole bunches add notes of incense and Indian spices to a palate of blackberry and liquorice and scented 40% new oak. A wine that you can buy every year with confidence.

Kottabos is made with purchased grapes from the Polkadraai Hills are and was given 40% skin contact for five days before fermentation in old wood to give it a bass note or two. Textured, refreshing and noticeably granitic, it has a descant of jasmine and white flowers and a citrus and lemongrass mid palate.

"The two varieties marry well", says Reenen Borman of this assemblage of Grenache and 22% Syrah from vineyards in and around the Polkadraai Hills. Scented and ethereal, it’s a refined, ocean-influenced style with layers of redcurrant, strawberry and plum, some clove spice from 78% whole bunches and a touch of stony reduction.

Pinotage is “easily not well done”, according to Reenen Borman, but he’s avoided any elephant traps here. A wine for Pinot Noir lovers, it was given a very short fermentation on skins of just three days to avoid excessive extraction, showing a perfumed, sappy, well-defined palate with plum and raspberry fruit and scented whole bunch spices.

One hesitates to describe this wine as a “mini-Epilogue”, but it’s pretty special at the price, offering a glimpse of what the Grand Vin will taste like when the 2025 is released. Sourced from two parcels on the Boschkloof estate. Fermented with 10% whole bunches, it has violet and fynbos top notes, textured tannins and a palate of clove, pepper spice and black cherry. Good now, but will improve.

Optenhorst comes from the third oldest plantings of Chenin Blanc in South Africa is generally the highlight of the extensive Bosman range. Showing the effortless concentration of its source in Wellington, it’s all about fruit and intensity rather than oak, with evident energy and acidity, pear, tangerine and apricot flavours and a racy, harmonious finish.

A comparatively rare example of a Chenin Blanc from the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, which is Chardonnay country, this is a stylish, if ambitiously priced white with good texture and weight, pear, quince and orange zest flavours and an undertone of boiled sweets on a just off-dry finish.

"I’m trying to make it less Bordeaux like", says Ginny Povall of her Cabernet Franc, but I’m not sure why, as it’s very tasty as it is. Curated in 15% new French oak, it has some subtle cigar box, violet and graphite aromas, refreshing acidity, some underlying grip and a core of cassis and black cherry. Good now, but should evolve further in bottle.

Big Flower – a nod to the estate’s dual role as a protea and wine farm – is a varietal Cabernet Sauvignon from vines planted in 2009 and 2010. Showing the structure and balance of the 2025 vintage, it’s a leafy, refreshing style with layered tannins, cassis and damson fruit flavours and top notes of cut grass and Asian spices.

n: Botanica Big Flower Petit Verdot Rosé
d: Made with the same grapes as Botanica’s sparkling Pet Nat, but obviously treated in a different way, this is a good-value, direct-pressed rosé that sees no oak at all. Racy and bone dry, it has layers of redcurrant and raspberry, racy acidity and a subtle herbal undertone. Just the thing to enjoy by the pool at the winery’s tourist lodge.

n: Botanica Flower Girl Petit Verdot Pet Nat
Botanica The Mary Delany Collection Chenin Blanc
d: One of those wines that’s easy – and a pleasure – to spot in a blind tasting, this brilliant, old-vine Chenin Blanc has been sourced from the Laing family’s farm on Citrusdal Mountain since 2009. Fermented and aged in older wood, it has layers of pear, yellow apple and aniseed, a waft of honeysuckle plenty of zip and energy and the faintest hint of passion fruit. Typically well balanced and self-assured.

n: Botanica The Mary Delany Collection Pinot Noir
d: Sourced from Ginny Povall’s picturesque home farm in the Devon Valley, this Pinot Noir showcases the quality of the 777 Dijon clone. Appropriately floral, given that she also grows proteas, it’s a vibrant, very lightly wooded style with aromas of mint, ginger and petrichor, pomegranate and redcurrant fruit and a savoury finish.

n: Bouchard Finlayson Aurum Riesling Straw Wine
d: Bouchard Finlayson is undergoing a rebranding at the moment, so this was the only wine I tasted from Chris Albrecht this year. Made with Riesling grapes that are dried on the vine in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, it’s mature and intensely sweet, with nectarine, honey and guava flavours, an appealing volatile undertone and enough acidity to lift and lengthen the finish.

Bradbourne uses grapes from a clay-based vineyard and is a carefully judged assemblage of Grenache Blanc, 23% Roussanne, 12% Marsanne, 4% Palomino and 2% Vermentino. Flavours of pear, quince and lime are complemented by some subtle tannic structure from partial skin contact, negligible oak and a waft of aniseed spice.

One of the best releases yet from Brookdale, which is part of an exciting new wave in Paarl, this comes from a north-facing site at 230 metres, close to the top of the farm. Fermented with 20% whole clusters, it’s ripe yet ethereal and well balanced, with graceful tannins, redcurrant, rooibos tea and pomegranate flavours some stony minerality and wafts of clove and tobacco leaf from 20% whole bunches.

Xander Sadie has taken over where Kiara Scott left off at Brookdale, making excellent wines at the price under the Mason Road label. This “GSM” combines Syrah, 24% Cinsault, 8% Grenache and 6% Mourvèdre, with 70% whole bunches, stylish granular tannins, raspberry and redcurrant fruit and a savoury, spicy finish.

The latest in a superb run of Mason Road Syrah releases from Brookdale’s painterly estate in Paarl, this is one of the best value reds in the Cape. Aged in older barrels and Austrian foudres, it has a waft of whole bunch spices, blackberry, thyme and subtle cooked meat flavours and a spine of serious tannins.

Made by the brilliant Kiara Scott before she left for Hazendal, but blended by Xander Sadie, this comes from a 1985 parcel on decomposed shale and granite soils. Exhibiting impressive old-vine concentration, it has a touch of struck match, flavours of green tea and sake, subtle oak integration and a stony, palate-cleansing finish. One the best Chenin Blancs in Paarl.

Following on from where Kiara Scott left off, Xander Sadie (son of Eben) is doing fantastic work at Brookdale. This is made with 14 Mediterranean grapes, complemented by Chenin Blanc and Chardonnay, and is suitably complex and layered, with greengage, citrus and grapefruit flavours, a hint of wet stone and a subtle volatile lift. Full malolactic adds some texture to the mid palate.

This is the second release of Brookdale’s flagship red blend, made with 20 different youngvine Rhône, Portuguese and Mediterranean grapes. Seamless, elegant and hauntingly perfumed, it has rose petal and candy floss aromas, layers of plum, pomegranate and summer pudding, filigree tannins, understated oak and a hint of good reduction.

Wade Sander is making some very tasty whites in remote, cool climate Sondagskloof, typified by the quality of this ocean-influenced Sauvignon Blanc. Fermented in older oak, it’s the kind of thing that wouldn’t look out of place in Sancerre, with intense oyster shell, elderflower and cardamom flavours and a nettley, briny finish.

Mixing components from Sondagskloof and the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, this is a comparatively full-bodied cool climate Syrah from Wade Sander. With 40% whole bunches adding perfume and texture, this has appealing pepper and fynbos aromas and a racy palate of redcurrant and black cherry complemented by tobacco leaf tannins.

Brunia’s White is a Bordeaux style blend of Sauvignon Blanc and 33% Semillon from Sondagskloof. Lightly wooded in 5% new oak, it’s a structured, pithy, palate-cleansing style with aromas of kelp and rock pools, flavours of green herbs, lime and cream soda and some underlying stony grip.

Haarlem to Hope pays tribute the first Dutch inhabitants of the Cape and is a blend of Chenin Blanc and 20% Semillon. Made in what Gavin Brewer calls a “fuller” style, it’s still pretty restrained at 12.5% alcohol, with white pepper and lanolin aromas, layers of white pepper, citrus and orange zest and an earthy note from a concrete egg component.

The kind of wine that would convert anyone to Pinotage – it still gets a bad rap from some quarters – this uses grapes from decomposed granite soils in the Polkadraai Hills. Fermented with 30% whole bunches, it has some underlying stony grip, racy plum and summer berry flavours and a hint of Negroni spices.

"I don’t think Cinsault should be a big wine," says Gavin Brewer and he’s true to his word on this bottling from a 1953 block on the Bellevue farm in the Bottelary Hills. Fermented with 95% whole bunches, it’s a racy, elegant, ethereal red with goji berry and Turkish Delight flavours and a nip of savoury tannin.

One of a distinguished line-up of Syrahs from the Karibib farm in the Polkadraai Hills, this was fermented with whole clusters before ageing in older oak. Cola, ginger spice and black pepper flavours segue into a palate of plum and red berries with some subtle reduction adding a further layer of complexity.

n: Durbanville Hills Collectors' Reserve The Castle of Good Hope Cabernet Sauvignon
d: The Collectors’ Reserve Cabernet Sauvignon is an unblended red from the Oatlands block which has now dispensed with any American oak in favour of 40% new French barrels. Minty, floral and nicely judged, it has classic capsicum, cassis and damson fruit, sinewy tannins and a sheen of mocha spice.

Combining grapes from Cap Maritime’s own vineyards with 10% from the nearby Bosman farm, this demonstrates Gottfried Mocke’s fine touch with Chardonnay. Made entirely with the 115 Burgundy clone, it has subtle lemongrass and tangerine flavours, top notes of honeysuckle and vanilla, fine 55% new oak and some mid-palate texture from full malolactic fermentation.

Cap Maritime’s value-for-money Pinot Noir uses grapes from the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge and Bot River, based on a mix of granite, quartz and sandstone soils. Lightly oaked in 10% new barrels, it has some clove spice from 25% whole bunches, good texture and grip and flavours of orange zest and black cherry.

Showcasing the 115 Dijon clone, this is a comparatively youthful Pinot Noir from the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley that was fermented with 30% whole clusters and aged in 40% new French oak. Tobacco leaf and gingerbread aromas are a prelude to a palate of plum and red cherry supported by firmish tannins that need time to integrate.

This superb, pan-Cape Chardonnay uses grapes from Stellenbosch, Robertson and the Overberg. Picked long before the rains in 2023, this is a seamless, self-confident cuvée from the well-travelled Graham Weerts, with wet stone and fennel aromas, stylish 33% new oak, good mid-palate weight and texture, flavours of citrus and tangerine and a lingering finish.

Capensis’ world-class Fijnbosch Chardonnay hails from the highest vineyard in Stellenbosch, overlooking the Simonsberg at 600 metres on decomposed granite and sandstone soils. Still very fresh after four years in barrel and bottle, it has perfumed 50% new oak, remarkable purity and focus, chiselled acidity, flavours of lime, vanilla and lemongrass and impressive energy and va-va-voom.

Silene is a well-judged assemblage of Cabernet Sauvignon, 8% Merlot and 2% Cabernet Franc, all sourced from the Helderberg. The 30% new oak is deftly integrated here, adding scents of coffee bean and cedarwood to a palate of tarragon and blackcurrant complemented by hints of graphite and green herbs. Good now but will reward a degree of patience.

The Silene Chardonnay is based on fruit from Capensis’ Fijnbosch Vineyard, but also uses components from four other sites in Stellenbosch. Fermented in 30% new wood, it’s a comparatively good value bottling with gunflint and baking spice aromas, lime, tangerine and passion fruit flavours and an undertow of racy acidity.

A new addition to Capensis’ mouth-watering line-up of Chardonnays, this was made as a one off from a seven-year-old vineyard in Ebenezer on the West Coast. Fermented in old barrels, without malolactic, it’s a savoury, umami-rich style with top notes of aniseed and brine and plenty of concentration, acidity and extract. Let’s hope Graham Weerts makes it again.

Always picked in four stages to maximise blending options, this comes from the Swartland Chenin Blanc from red clay soils near Malmesbury. Barrel fermented in older oak, it has some subtle reduction, good texture from full malolactic, citrus zest and yellow apple flavours and a zesty, medium-bodied finish.

Growers Hugo and Danie Carinus use the services of the brilliant Lukas van Loggerenberg to make this Colombard from the Rooidrai farm in the Swartland. Drier than the 2024, it has what Danie calls the “texture and tension” of the vintage, with greengage, lemongrass and apricot flavours, understated oak and a tangy, saline finish.

Most of the production of this Devon Valley Pinot Noir is destined for Scotland, where it will go down well with restaurant punters. Made with two clones grown on an east-facing slope at 220 metres, it has easy-drinking, winningly approachable flavours of strawberry and pomegranate and a whisper of oak.

A well-priced Syrah from the Polkadraai Hills, this comes from Danie Carinus’ Bluegum Grove farm and is made by Lukas van Loggerenberg, who knows a thing or two about the variety. Thirty per cent stems are added back to the blend here adding perfume and clove spice to a palate of incense, blackberry and black olive and a spine of granitic freshness.

One of a pair of top single-site Chenins from Danie Carinus, this was made with the help of the ludicrously talented Chris Alheit. Taut, tangy and stony, it’s lightly wooded in concrete and old oak, with jasmine and wet stone aromas, a palate of green apple and lime zest and a pithy, focused, mouth-watering finish.

Rooidraai uses grapes from Hugo Carinus’ farm of the same name near Malmesbury in the Swartland. Fermented and aged in older barrels, with Lukas van Loggerenberg at the helm, this has subtle top notes of pepper, bay leaf and aniseed, stony intensity, layers of lanolin, citrus and cardamom and impressive palate length.

n: Catherine Marshall Amatra Jono's Wave Chenin Blanc
d: Named after Cathy Marshall’s son, Jono, as it reminds her of a “free surf break”, this is a blend of Chenin Blanc and 7% Roussanne from the Bottelary Hills and the Voor Paardeberg. Fresh, stony and granitic, it’s an approachable, good value white with herbal top notes, flavours of citrus, fennel and passion fruit and a touch of oak.

Between Two Worlds is a superb Voor Paardeberg blend of Roussanne and 40% Grenache Blanc that does justice to its eye-catching label. Sadly only a never-to-be-repeated one off, it’s a small volume triumph from Doran Vineyards, with flavours of lemon, lime and gin botanicals, a touch of wood and a thrilling, palate-cleansing finish.

n: Catherine Marshall Fine Art Collection Finite Elements Pinot Noir
