d: Finite Elements combines Pinot Noir fractions from the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge (on shale) and Elgin (sandstone), which combine beautifully in the hands of such a talented winemaker. Matured in 17% new oak, it’s a youthful, intensely floral wine with the structure and intensity to age, flavours of black cherry, pomegranate and subtle toast and beautifully judged tannins.

Now on its second vintage, Ode to Arges comes from the South Hill Farm on the Bot River side of Elgin. Made with the original GD1 clone, it’s a subtle Semillon that looks towards Burgundy in a sense, with white flower and cumin aromas, some creamy mid-palate texture, notes of beeswax and lemon zest and nicely understated oak.

n: Catherine Marshall Pinot Noir on Clay Soils
d: Cathy Marhsall’s Bokkeveld shale-focused Pinot Noir uses grapes from Domaine des Dieux on the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, supported by 33% from Casey’s Ridge in Elgin. Showcasing the 115 and 667 Dijon clones, it’s a structured, almost Pommard style red with good grip and density, clove, vanilla spice and black cherry flavours, savoury tannins and a spine of racy acidity.

n: Catherine Marshall Pinot Noir on Sandstone
d: This stylish Pinot Noir uses grapes from two farms in Elgin – South Hill and Casey’s Ridge – and is a scented, cool climate expression of the 115 and 777 clones. Complex, layered and light on its feet, it has aromas of rose petal and Turkish bazaar spices, pomegranate, wild strawberry and tobacco leaf flavours, savoury tannins and appealing underlying grip.

Cathy Marshall’s love of German Riesling shines through on this floral, sweet and sour white from Vrede en Lust’s Casey’s Ridge farm in Elgin. Made with the 110 clone grown on slate and shale soils, it’s clean, crunchy and racy, with lime leaf and green apple fruit and beautifully integrated 8.7 grams of residual sugar.

Cathy Marshall uses three picks to make this Elgin Sauvignon Blanc, using raw material from South Hill Vineyards, all of it the 315 clone. Showing a hint of the “sweaty” character you find in Marlborough versions of the grape, this has appealing lime, blackcurrant leaf and gooseberry fruit and tangy, lip-smacking finish.

Rianie Strydom has always had a sure touch with Chardonnay and it’s evident in this youthful example from Cavali’s Stellenbosch estate. Featuring 30% new oak and 20% malolactic, it has appealing flavours of oatmeal, lemon zest and nutmeg spices, a spine of palate-cleansing acidity and the concentration and structure to develop further in bottle.

Like the 2024 release, this Stellenbosch Chenin Blanc was harvested in four stages to build layers into the wine. Fermented and aged in 15% new oak, this has top notes of toast and baking spices, racy, mouth-watering acidity and plenty of stony minerality.

Experienced winemaker Rianie Strydom, a comparatively recent arrival at Cavali, makes this layered white blend with Chenin Blanc, 28% Verdelho and 6% each of Chardonnay and Viognier. Subtly wooded on lees in 15% new oak, it has lots of underlying zip and acidity, layers of pear, greengage and grapefruit and a waft of aromatic spices.

It’s good to see Chamonix making great Chardonnay again, establishing itself once more among the best Cape producers of the grape. Made with a parcel on shale soils planted with the CY95 clone in Elgin, this is a refined, sculpted white with layers of salted almond, waxed lemon and vanilla spice and adroitly handled 50% new oak and 20% concrete eggs. Welcome back!

The Greywacke Chardonnay uses grapes from the new plantings at Chamonix for the first time, all of which are clone CY96. Subtly fermented in 10% new oak, with 30% malolactic adding some texture, this is a racy, pithy cool-climate style with flavours of dried coconut, lemongrass and nougat underpinned by palate-cleansing acidity.

n: Chamonix Estate Old Vine OVP Steen
d: Most of the vineyards on Chamonix were replanted in 2022 and 2023, but this block of 1965 Chenin Blanc escaped the cull. Naturally fermented in a combination of old barrels, an amphora and a concrete egg, this is an appealingly dry, racy style with impressive focus and purity, pear and yellow apple flavours and a steely, tucked in finish.

Bought from a neighbouring farm while Chamonix’s new plantings come on stream, this comes from a parcel planted with the 115 Dijon clone at 550 metres. Redcurrant and goji berry flavours are complemented by 20% whole bunches, well-handled 50% new French oak and savoury, dried-herb tannins.

Neil Bruwer makes this white blend with purchased Franschhoek grapes, combining Semillon and 42% Sauvignon Blanc. Fermented in 15% new 300-litre Stockinger barrels, it’s racy, herbal and complex with flavours of vanilla, citrus, cucumber and pink grapefruit and a sappy, chiselled finish. Has some more gas in the tank.

The best wine yet from Charla Haasbroek’s exciting solo venture, this is a medley of Chenin Blanc and 36% Semillon from Piekenierskloof and 21% Chardonnay from Tradouw. Racy, mouth-watering and beautifully balanced, it has some engaging gunflint reduction, flavours of pear, lime and grapefruit, understated oak and plenty of energy, zip and palate length.

Charla Haasbroek buys her Chenin Blanc grapes from Sijnn in Malgas, where she used to work as the winemaker. Basket pressed in a traditional style before ageing in neutral, 400-litre barrels, it has the grip and slightly ferrous edge that comes with the terroir, layers of saffron, beeswax, yellow apple and lemon zest and an appealingly phenolic undertow.

n: Charla Haasbroek Prince of Peace Syrah/Grenache
d: Now into its second release, Prince of Peace uses raw material from Tradouw and the Breedekloof Valley, rather than Malgas, and is a southern Rhône style cuvée of Syrah and Grenache, with nicely judged partial whole bunch notes. Rose petal, liquorice and Campari spice aromas segue into a palate of bramble, blackberry and redcurrant and a firm, aciddriven finish.

Rare Air comes from the Olivedale farm near Swellendam, an area that benefits from significant diurnal variation. Fermented and aged in older oak, this is an exciting release from Charla Haasbroek, with engaging fennel, lemongrass and oatmeal flavours, touches of beeswax and green herbs and a pithy, refreshing finish.

n: Perdeberg Wines OVP The Dry Land Collection Courageous Barrel Fermented Chenin Blanc
d: This is a best seller at Perdeberg Wines and you can see why. Sourced from a large, old vine block on the Eenzaamheid farm that was planted in 1985 on decomposed granite soils, this is a stunning value Chenin Blanc with subtle 10% new oak, stony intensity, pear, pink grapefruit and yellow apple fruit and a balanced finish.

Colmant’s Blanc de Blancs is an all-Chardonnay bubbly that marries components from Bonnievale, Elgin and Stellenbosch. Partnered with 20% reserve wine – part of the style here – it has aromas of jasmine and chamomile, lemon zest and juniper flavours and some understated nutty autolysis from 40 months on lees.

Absolu has been a Brut Nature in the past, but was bottled with 2.7 grams of dosage this time around, with the 2018 vintage providing the core of the wine. Showing commendable refinement and purity, it’s a beautifully balanced Blanc de Blancs from Bonnievale, Elgin, Franschhoek, the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge and Robertson, with layers of pear, waxed lemon and wet stones and a hint of dried mushroom on the finish.

Paul Gerber and Kalissa de Kok source this well-balanced bubbly from Bonnievale, Elgin, Franschhoek and Stellenbosch. Blending Chardonnay and 42% Pinot Noir, it includes a sizeable, barrel-aged reserve wine component for added complexity, offering aromas of white flowers and brioche and a palate of citrus and cashew nut.

Part of an intriguing new range from Daniel Colombo, this is true to his hands-off, mediumbodied style. Using old-vine Palomino from Piekenierskloof, one of the few places you find the variety in South Africa, this is earthy, savoury and stony, with some tannic structure, layers of fennel, lanolin and citrus zest and a well-balanced finish.

n: Colombo Family Wines There's Something About You
d: The kind of wine that wouldn’t look out of place in Chile’s Citrusdal Mountain, this is an intense, bronze-hued Muscat d’Alexandrie from promising young winemaker Daniel Colombo that was skin macerated for 14 days. Quince and blood orange flavours combine neatly on the palate here, farmed by subtle tannins and racy acidity. Nuanced, layered and refreshingly low in alcohol.

Always among the finest reds in the Constantia Valley, especially in a demanding vintage like 2023, this is a stylish, relatively full-bodied cuvée of the five red Bordeaux varieties, combining Cabernet Franc, 24% Cabernet Sauvignon, 22% Merlot, 15% Petit Verdot and 11% Malbec. Light, floral and herbal, it has aromas of mint, dill and vanilla spice, subtle forest floor tannins and well-honed 75% new oak.

Produced in what Justin van Wyk calls a “super vintage” for both reds and whites, this is an unwooded blend of four Sauvignon Blanc clones (10, 11, 316 and 317) and 7% Semillon. Nettley, racy and winningly herbal, it has granitic freshness, flavours of green asparagus and gooseberry and a tangy, mineral-etched core.

"I was grateful we had a sorting table,” says Justin van Wyk of the 2023 vintage, when 187mm of rain fell in March alone. But he succeeded in the tricky conditions. Combining Merlot, 32% Cabernet Franc and 13% Cabernet Sauvignon, it’s a fresh, medium-bodied style with red cherry, tobacco leaf and dried herb flavours and stylish 20% new oak.

Two is a consistently impressive Bordeaux-style white blend from the upper part of Constantia, combining Sauvignon Blanc and 30% Semillon. Oak, acacia and amphora-aged components add to the complexity here, bringing extra layers to a palate of greengage, grapefruit and cinnamon spice. Beautifully focused.

Year in, year out, the modest Roger Burton quietly gets on with producing one of the best blends of Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon in the Constantia Valley. Subtly wild yeast fermented in 500-litre barrels, it tastes as good as it looks, with engaging grip and minerality, crunchy flavours of cucumber, elderflower and wet stones and a whisper of aromatic wood spices.

As well as making the wines at Almenkerk, Cameron Corney makes a couple of different Chenin Blancs under his own family label. Stylishly packaged, this Swartland-sourced iteration has nuanced oak from fermentation in neutral 300 and 500-litre barrels, aromas of wet stones, thatch and gin botanicals and a palate of green apple, citrus and aniseed.

One of two region-specific Chenin Blancs from Cameron Corney, this is richer and slightly riper than its stablemate from the Swartland. The oak is understated and finely judged, adding some subtle aromatic spices to a palate of yellow apple, pear and apricot. A brand to keep an eye on, given the pedigree of the winemaker.

Emma, daughter of JC and Carolyn Martin, must be delighted to have her name on the label of this single vineyard Pinot Noir, sourced from one of the warmer parcels on the estate. Three clones – mostly 115 with a little 667 and 777 – contribute to the blend here, with haunting perfume from 30% whole bunches. Elegant, floral and well balanced, it has some underlying grip, black cherry, strawberry and baking spice flavours and a touch of good reduction.

Made by Glenn Martin, who is fast turning into one of the Cape’s rising stars, this comes from the same block at The Art of Chardonnay, which is made by his dad, JC. Fermented with wild yeasts before ageing in 30% new oak, it’s a savoury, slightly salty delight, with scented vanilla oak, flavours of waxed lemon and clementine and a tapering oyster shell finish.

Formerly sold as the Reserve Chardonnay, this comes from two blocks totalling 3.5 hectares on the farm. Showing the quality of what JC Martin calls a “spectacular year”, this is a wine that will develop further in bottle, with top notes of fennel and iodine and a palate of waxed lemon, tangerine and brown toast complemented by nice texture from full malolactic.

Still on the youthful side when I tasted it, this layered Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge Pinot Noir is a slightly meaty cuvée of the 115 and 777 clones, fermented with 30% whole bunches. Sappy, racy and toasty, it has assertive 30% new wood, flavours of plum, black cherry and coffee bean and a sinewy, well-structured finish.

This well-judged white blend comes from the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge and neighbouring Shaw’s Mountain, combining mostly Roussanne, 44% Grenache Blanc and 3% Viognier. Fermented and aged in concrete eggs and third-fill barrels, it has saffron, wet stone and honeysuckle aromas, pear and citrus fruit flavours and a touch of stone fruit sweetness.

JC Martin is best known for his work with Burgundian grapes, but he can turn his talents to Bordeaux varieties too. This is a lightly wooded cuvée of Sauvignon Blanc and 20% Semillon with lime, cream soda and gooseberry flavours and a hint of cinnamon spice from 20% new oak. Pithy and satisfying.

The Art is a bottling of the 23 best barrels from a 2.2-hectare parcel on the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, showing the most “tension and precision”, according to JC Martin. The 30% new oak is still quite assertive here, suggesting that the wine needs more time in bottle. Racy and intense, it has aromas of vanilla spice and cheese rind, a palate of nettle, lime and wet stone and a mouth-watering finish.

n: Creation The Art of Pinot Noir
d: Like its stablemate The Art of Chardonnay, this ambitious Pinot Noir needs more time in bottle to show at its best. Bold and intense, it’s more Gevrey-Chambertin than ChambolleMusigny, with toasty 30% new barrels, layers of earth, beetroot and black cherry, lots of oak spice and acidity and a sturdy backbone of tannin.

One of my go-to Chardonnays in South Africa - it’s well worth cellaring, too - this comes from a vineyard on the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge that was grafted on to Cabernet Franc in 2014. Textured, layered and effortlessly complex, it wouldn’t look out of place in a line-up Premier Cru Burgundies, with very subtle 20% new oak, layers of gunflint, beeswax, lemon zest and clementine and top notes of wildflowers and aromatic baking spices.

Cuvée Cinéma – after all these years, I still love the name – comes from the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, where Peter-Allan Finlayson also sources his Clay Shales Chardonnay. A blend of the 115 and 667 clones, it’s a Pinot Noir of depth, finesse and grace, with a frame of scented 25% new oak, alluring spice from 60% whole clusters, sappy redcurrant, hibiscus and wild strawberry fruit and a tapering finish.

Ferrum is a comparatively new addition to the Crystallum range, sourced, as its name suggests, from red clay soils on Shaw’s Mountain. Fermented with full malolactic – a PeterAllan Finlayson preference – this has deftly integrated 20% new oak, notes of fennel, juniper and lemongrass and a waft of vanilla spice.

Made in what Peter-Allan Finlayson calls a “more serious style”, Litigo comes from the clay shale soils of Shaw’s Mountain, adjacent to the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge. Planted with the 155 clone (and 20% 667), it has clove and tobacco leaf notes from 75% whole clusters, fynbos and rose petal aromas and a core of black cherry and subtle vanilla spice from 20% whole clusters.

Some of the grapes for this brilliant Pinot Noir come from vines at 700 metres, which is why Peter-Allan Finlayson eschews the use of whole bunches because of unlignified stems. The result is a layered, savoury delight, with a hint of reduction, lots of zip and acidity, sinewy tannins and lip-smacking wild strawberry and redcurrant fruit. The 20% new oak is right on point.

Peter Max uses grapes from seven sources – six of them close to the coast, the other in Elandskloof. The result is a supremely drinkable Pinot Noir at an affordable price, with a spicy lift from 50% whole clusters, flavours of goji berry and raspberry coulis, graceful tannins and some underlying zip.

The Agnes uses components from the Ceres Plateau, the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge and Shaw’s Mountain and is always one of the most consistent wines in the Crystallum range. Fermented in older oak with full malolactic, it’s a balanced, self-assured bottling with citrus, oatmeal and vanilla spice flavours and a zesty, tapering finish.

Songbird is a Sauvignon Blanc with good complexity for a sub R200 white, using eight hours of skin contact, 25% new oak fermentation and a concrete egg component to build layers into the wine. Flavours of greengage, celery and white pepper combine on the palate here, embellished by some subtle patisserie spices.

Graham Weerts is a Chardonnay wizard, but he can also apply his considerable talents to Chenin Blanc. This comes from three old-vine parcels on Adi Badenhorst’s Kalmoesfontein farm, with fermentation and ageing in concrete eggs, ceramic pots and older wood. Leesy and intense, has layers of thatch, yellow apple and citrus, a hint of subtle reduction and some underlying granitic grip.

Jean Smit is best known as a Syrah producer, but he can turn his talents to any variety. This comes from pure granite soils on the Mooiplaas estate in the Polkadraai Hills and is a serious, layered, well-structured expression of Cabernet Franc, with fynbos, violet and liquorice aromas, notes of graphite and black cherry and below-the-radar oak.

Produced in a vintage that “tested focus and adaptability”, in Jean Smit’s words, this 2023 Cabernet Sauvignon is something of a triumph over the elements, using grapes from two sites in Stellenbosch that were picked before the heavy rains. Minty and leafy with plenty of underlying grip and backbone and a black-fruited core.

Three old vines sites in Bottelary and the Polkadraai Hills, planted between 1972 and 1981, supply the grapes for this brilliant Chenin Blanc. Impressively complex and concentrated, especially for a wine with just 12.7% alcohol, it’s a foudre-aged delight, with aromas of beeswax, fennel and hay, flavours of citrus and yellow apple and impressive tension, focus and palate length.

The Paardeberg – Chenin central as far as the Swartland is concerned – is the source Jean Smit’s impressive white, combining grapes from three blocks planted between 1971 and 1986. Granitic to its core, it’s racy, focused and mouth-wateringly fresh, with a sheen of subtle baking spices, flavours of waxed lemon, green apple and juniper and a tapering finish.

Franschhoek has a greater percentage of South Africa’s best Semillons than any other region. This comes from the La Châtaigne vineyard, planted in 1932 and 1962, and includes 15% Semillon Gris. Pithy, focused and refreshing, it has very understated oak from Stockinger foudres, aromas of fennel and mustard seed, hints of musk, custard and lemon zest and a chiselled finish.

A member of a trio of world-class Syrahs from the self-effacing Jean Smit, this comes from the Karibib farm in the Polkadraai Hills. Intense, meaty and a little ferrous, it’s a wine for Cornas lovers, with top notes of incense and thyme and a palate of tapenade, damson and black olive. Dense and deeply coloured, it has subtle oak and a sturdy backbone of tannin.

“What you put in the bottle needs to shout,” says Jean Smit, and this Swartland Syrah certainly does that, albeit in a mellifluous voice. Sourced from the schist soils of the Elim farm, it’s a perfumed, layered style, with 75% whole bunches, typically understated oak, violet and potpourri aromas and a graceful core of plum, paprika and red berries. A wine for Côte Rôtie fans.

The Ceres Plateau is “one of the most exciting regions in the country”, according to Jean Smit and I, for one, would agree. This layered, nuanced, world-class Syrah comes from an east-facing site at 1,000 metres on Bokkeveld shale and is correspondingly pure, racy and refreshing, with a medley of blood orange, red cherry and pink grapefruit and some clove spice from 60% whole clusters.

The sort of wine that you’d more commonly find in Constantia or Darling, this is an equal blend of Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon. Gracefully fermented in subtle new French oak, this is something of a bargain, with enticing layers of vanilla cream, cardamom, beeswax and pink grapefruit and a green pepper undertone.

Crazily good at the price, this shows you why Darling Cellars is one of the most respected (ex) co-ops in the Cape. Entirely fermented in stainless steel, it has some subtle, flinty reduction, tangy, mouth-watering flavours of lime, green apple and greengage and some mid-palate texture from ageing on lees.

n: Darling Cellars Old Bush Vines OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Two old-vine parcels in Darling – one on Hutton soils, the other on weathered granite – supply the grapes for this impressive Chenin Blanc from Andre Scriven. Showing some appealing, flinty reduction, this is a focused, acid-driven style with vanilla spice from 30% new oak, tangy citrus and green apple flavours and a sappy, mouth-watering finish.

n: Darling Cellars Singal Tower Sauvignon Blanc
d: Very tasty stuff from Andre Scriven, this is the kind of thing that will make Sauvignon Blanc drinkers on a budget very happy. Aromas of white flowers and cut grass segue into a palate of elderflower, passion fruit and green pepper, complemented by a racy, sea salty finish.

n: Darling Cellars Sir Charles Darling Heritage Collection
Darling Cellars The Old Grain Silo Heritage Collection Shiraz
Darling Cellars The Old Tractor Heritage Collection Pinotage
d: Grown on decomposed granite soils, this Darling Pinotage comes from unirrigated 37-yearold bush vines close to the Atlantic Ocean. Subtly wooded in a combination of French and American oak, this is smooth and attractive, all bramble, banana and summer pudding flavours, textured tannins and a fresh finish.

Using grapes from a 0.3-hectare vineyard that dates back to 1977, this is a wine that gives under-rated Clairette Blanche its moment in the spotlight. Complex, zesty and tangy, it has a nice undertow of oak, layers of yellow apple, aniseed and lemon juice and a hint of tangerine on the finish. Appealingly refreshing.

Hanepoot, also known as Muscat d’Alexandrie, has been grown in the Cape for a long time and still makes a number of outstanding sweet wines. This one comes from a 0.18-hectare parcel planted in 1883 and is suitably sweet and intense, with 220 grams of residual sugar, layers of orange zest, honey, peach and dried fruits, well-integrated spirit and supporting acidity.

Mossiesdrift uses grapes from the oldest Chenin Blanc block in the Breedekloof, planted in 1962, and offers a lot of flavour at a reasonable price. Bearing the OVP seal, it’s racy, pithy and refreshing, with plenty of natural acidity, some texture from lees stirring, flavours of oatmeal, aniseed and citrus and negligible oak.

Tasted as a tank sample just before bottling, this is lighter and less extracted than the 2025 release, this is a skin contact white that will bring new consumers to the category. Blending Chenin Blanc and 20% Muscat d’Alexandrie, it has quince and clementine flavours and a hint of earth on the finish.

First made in 2010 – tempus fugit and all that – this remains a textbook Cape white blend, marrying Chenin Blanc, 12% Semillon, 10% Marsanne, 9% Roussanne, 8% Clairette and 6% Colombard in a seamless whole. Concentrated, dense, yet also light on its feet, it has granitic energy, flavours of pear, citrus and lime and a hint of white peach sweetness.

Elpidios shows David Sadie’s talent as a blender, featuring Grenache, 19% Syrah, 13% Carignan, 12% Pinotage and 8% Cinsault. Made in a semi-carbonic style, it has some subtle stony reduction, plenty of grip and intensity, flavours of plum, blackberry and blood orange and a focused, acid-driven finish. Fruit rather than oak dominated.

Three sites in the Swartland contribute to this stylish Grenache – two from the Paardberg and one in Malmesbury – with granite the predominant soil type. Lightly wooded in concrete and older, neutral barrels, it’s a tangy, bright, acid-drive style with cranberry and redcurrant flavours and sinewy tannins.

n: David & Nadia Hoë-Steen OVP Chenin Blanc
d: If you love Hoë-Steen as much as I do, get your order for the 2025 in now, as only 700 bottles were produced. Sourced from a two-hectare block of the CN1 clone planted on decomposed granite in 1968, this shows the focus and elegance of its cooler, south-facing site, with aniseed, citrus zest and green apple flavours and a lingering finish.

n: David & Nadia Langland OVP Chenin Blanc
d: This is the second vintage of Langland – long valley in Afrikaans – sourced from a shaded, east-facing site on the classic sandy, decomposed granite soils of the Paardeberg. Fermented and aged in older oak, this is sappy, mouth-watering and nicely understated, with stony minerality, lime, aniseed and lemon juice flavours and a subtle, juniper-like bitter twist.

This is “only” the basic Chenin Blanc from David and Nadia Sadie, but it’s still a very impressive iteration of the variety, sourced from six old-vine sites on the Paardeberg and two in Malmesbury. Aged in concrete and 75% older barrels, it has stony intensity, flavours of yellow apple, citrus zest and wet stones and a mouth-watering finish.

n: David & Nadia Plat'bos OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Plat’bos is a Chenin Blanc that can be reserved in its youth but rewards patience. Sourced from bony soils with lots of decomposed granite but very little clay, it’s early picked for extra freshness and zing, with white flower and gin botanical aromas, some stony reduction, considerable extract and intensity for a wine with just 11.5% alcohol and a core of cardamom and green apple.

n: David & Nadia Skaliekop OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Skaliekop is a warmer 1.4-hectare site that is nearly always picked first of the single vineyard Chenin Blancs at David & Nadia. Located on shale and clay soils, with no decomposed granite, it’s a dense, layered, compact white with good texture and grip, a layer of skin tannins and flavours of pear, lemongrass and wet stones and a fynbos top note. Part of a brilliant line up of 2025s.

Now aged in 20% new French oak – the 2023 had an American component too – this demonstrates, not for the first time, how well-suited Pinotage is to Durbanville. Savoury, spicy, textured and poised, it has appealing bramble, plum and raspberry fruit, fine tannins and a slightly ferrous finish.

This is only the second vintage of De Tijger, following on from the 2022 after a rain-induced break in 2023. Sourced from a single, 24-year-old vineyard, it combines aromas of mint, mocha and tarragon with a palate of cassis and summer berries, scented one-third new oak and a firmish, dried herb finish.

Wooded since the 2023 vintage, this impressive Sauvignon Blanc is entirely sourced from Darling. Fermented in an equal combination of stainless steel and second and third-fill oak, it has some subtle nutmeg and vanilla spices, sea breeze acidity and layers of kiwi fruit, lime and cardamom.

Ripe, fleshy and nicely textured for a 2023 Merlot, this comes entirely from De Grendel’s own vines in Durbanville, where Morgan Steyn did a degree of crop-thinning to encourage ripeness. Framed by 10% new oak, it’s a subtle, herbal wine with plum, mocha spice and paprika flavours and a twist of capsicum.

n: De Grendel Op Die Berg Chardonnay
d: De Grendel’s pioneering Chardonnay comes from vineyards at 1,000 metres on the Ceres Plateau. Made with 90% malolactic to reduce the pithy, lip-smacking acidity, this has a sheen of toasty 38% new oak, appealing pear, citrus and clementine fruit flavours, some texture from time on lees and a sappy, mineral-rich core.

n: De Grendel Op Die Berg Pinot Noir
d: The red companion to the Op Die Berg Chardonnay, this Pinot Noir comes from two different properties on the Ceres Plateau, located between 960 and 1,000 metres. Earthy, savoury and complex, with a top note of tomato leaf and dill, this has red berry and forest floor flavours and a nicely savoury, sinewy finish.

n: De Grendel Op Die Berg Syrah
d: It takes guts to grow Syrah at 1,100 metres on the cool Ceres Plateau, let alone ferment the result with 60% whole clusters, but this wine from the Rietfontein farm justifies both choices. The 15% new oak is well handled, adding some patisserie spice flavours to a palate of redcurrant, raspberry and white pepper.

The Cabernet Sauvignon core of this Bordeaux-style red blend comes from Stellenbosch, but the other components –37% Petit Verdot and 9% each of Cabernet Franc and Merlot are from Durbanville. This is a firm, well-structured cuvée with stylish 40% new French oak, age-worthy tannins, cassis, bramble and cedarwood flavours and the freshness that’s a feature of the 2021 vintage.

Morgan Steyn has toned down the influence of Viognier here, allowing the 50% Semillon and 30% Chardonnay a more prominent role. Using older oak, amphoras and ceramic eggs, it’s a more complex wine as a result, with citrus, pear and apricot fruit, a petrichor top note and some texture from lees stirring.

n: De Krans Cape Tawny Limited Release
d: Boets Nel uses barrel-matured components with an average of 15 years of age to make this blend of five Portuguese varieties – Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Souzão and Tinta Amarela. Light, elegant and ethereal, it has a subtle 100 grams of residual sugar, flavours of fig, date and dried fruit and a rose petal top note.

While we await the release of the 2024 Vintage Reserve, we can content ourselves with a bottle of this intense, still youthful 2015. Combining Touriga Nacional, Tinta Barroca and Tinta Roriz, it’s a structured, comparatively dry style with fig, blackberry and dark chocolate flavours, muscular tannins and 93 grams of sugar.

n: De Krans Garden Route Sauvignon Blanc
d: Tasted from tank before bottling, this stony, racy Sauvignon Blanc comes from the six-yearold Soldaatskraal vineyard at 650 metres. Gunflint and white pepper aromas segue into a palate of elderflower and padrón peppers and a pithy, mouth-watering finish.

"It looks like caviar," says Boets Nel of the Verdelho bunches he harvests from Calitzdorp. Subtly wooded in older barrels, it has layers of lanolin, greengage and fresh herbs, some texture from lees ageing and a racy, mineral-etched finish.

Book XVII had often seemed a wine that was dominated by style and marketing rather than substance, but the 2023 lives up to the hype. Tasted both sighted and blind, it’s a very impressive rendition of a tricky vintage, combining Cabernet Sauvignon and 20% each of Cabernet Franc and Malbec. Matured in 70% new oak, it’s structured, textured and very well balanced, with layers of potpourri, cedarwood, cassis and summer berries, bright acidity and deftly integrated Asian spices.

Further evidence of the impact that Martin Fourie has had at De Toren, this is now a blend of Merlot and 29% Cabernet Franc – it had five varieties until 2018 – made in what he calls a “Pomerol style”. Subtly wooded in 50% new oak, it combines aromas of graphite, toast and basil with a palate of sweet red fruits, granular tannins and a leafy finish.

Definitely among the better 2023 Stellenbosch releases, this is a well-structured cuvée of Cabernet Sauvignon, 16% Merlot, 14% Malbec, 13% Cabernet Franc and 3% Petit Verdot from the Polkadraai Hills. Savoury, leafy and appealing, it has layers of dried herbs and red berries and more concentration and backbone than you think at first. Fresh, yet appealingly balsamic, with stylish 40% new French oak.

Produced in small quantities - there are just 1,084 bottles of the 2023 - Patronus is a varietal Malbec that’s sourced from three low-yielding sites in the Polkadraai Hills. Barrel-fermented in 65% new oak, it has appealing top notes of violet and stem ginger, glossy bramble and blackberry fruit, supporting acidity and some underlying granitic grip and structure.

The price tag is a little on the ambitious side, but there’s no denying the quality of this Syrah, made with an 85/15 blend of grapes from the Swartland and Stellenbosch. Very much a granite-based wine, it has aromas of sage and lavender and a palate of liquorice, damson and blood orange. The 65% new oak needs more time to integrate.

Allister Kreft’s vineyard is the source of this nuanced cuvée of Cabernet Sauvignon and 13% Merlot, which is the only wine from outside Stellenbosch in the De Trafford range. Light on its feet, but far from insubstantial, it’s restrained, floral and detailed, with fine red berry, tomato leaf and blackcurrant flavours and graceful tannins.

Sourced from neighbouring Keermont in 2023 because De Trafford’s own vines burnt in 2022, this uses fruit from three excellent single vineyards picked on the same day. Fermented with 15% whole bunches, it has impressive depth and concentration for the vintage, with layers of tapenade, blackberry, fig and steak tartare and a top note of iodine.

Not for De Trafford wines that lack substance, structure and intensity, even in a lighter, wetter vintage like 2023. Sourced from three contrasting sub-regions – the Helderberg, Raithby and the Polkadraai Hills – it has some coffee bean and cedarwood aromas from 30% new wood and a core of blackcurrant pastille, mulberry and plum.

David Trafford sources grapes from a trio of Stellenbosch vineyards to make this finely judged Chenin Blanc. The 8% new oak is very well integrated here, complemented by 40% malolactic, some wild yeast notes of umami and almond, a nice interplay between passion fruit and green apple and a slightly salty finish.

Elevation 393 comes from one of the highest blocks on the De Trafford farm and is a tenbarrel blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, 20% Merlot, 17% Shiraz and 9% Cabernet Franc. Showing the fine oak integration that’s a feature of the winery’s style, this is floral, minty and black fruited, with the concentration to age.

De Trafford is right up there with the best Merlot producers in the Cape, a place where the variety doesn’t always give of its best. This comes from two blocks at 370 metres and is a bold, ripe yet well-balanced expression of the variety with a waft of mint and fynbos, textured savoury tannins and flavours of fruit cake, blackberry and dark chocolate.

A regular fixture among the Cape’s best sweet wines, this brilliant straw wine Chenin Blanc uses grapes from Malgas, the Helderberg and Raithby. Dried on racks in the shade for three weeks for intensity and concentration, with cinnamon-scented 33% new oak, flavours of honey, tangerine, pear and pineapple and a refreshing finish.

n: De Wet Cellar Leyland Single Vineyard Chenin Blanc
De Wet Cellar Mashup Sauvignon Blanc/Chenin Banc/Semillon

d: My pick of the current range of De Wetshof Chardonnays – I must have expensive tastes – Bateleur uses fruit from the oldest parcel of the variety in South Africa, established in 1986. Fermented in new French oak, without malolactic, it has top notes of toast, oatmeal and sourdough bread, lemon, lime and tangerine flavours and impressive drive, energy and freshness.

n: De Wetshof Blanc de Blancs CC
d: The De Wet family have Chardonnay in their veins, so it’s no surprise that their bubbly is a Blanc de Blancs. Using grapes from 29-year-old vines on limestone-rich soils, it’s a steely, racy, mineral-etched style with citrus, aniseed and wet stone flavours and a just off-dry finish of 4.7 grams of dosage.

Bon Vallon comes from a cooler, north-facing site on rocky soils. Stainless steel fermented, followed by 100 days on lees, it’s an approachable, crowd-pleasing Chardonnay from Loïc du Toit that has stone fruit flavours of peach and apricot and enough acidity and minerality to lift and freshen the finish.

Part of a group of Roberston Chardonnays under the Calcrete banner, all of them made in an unwooded, so-called Chablis style, this comes from an early picked block with plenty of limestone. Racy, sappy and pure, it has oyster shell and freshly squeezed lemon flavours and chiselled, razor-sharp acidity.

Named after matriarch Lesca de Wet, this comes from slightly younger, north-facing vines on this 210-hectare estate in Robertson. Lightly wooded in older oak, it has racy, palatecleansing acidity, lots of chalky intensity and undertones of toast and vanilla spice. Still young, with the fruit concentration to age.

The Shard is a new Chardonnay from De Wetshof that uses the same grapes as The Site but ferments and ages them in glass globes. Lees-aged for eight months, it has layers of beeswax, passion fruit and greengage, good weight and texture and a refreshing, tangy finish.

The Site is one of a pair of top Chardonnays from De Wetshof sourced from a parcel planted in 1993. Fermented and aged in new 300-litre barrels, this has aromas of petrichor and wet chalk, impressive concentration from vines planted in 1993, lime and lemongrass flavours and a toasty, patisserie spice finish.

n: Deep Rooted Wines Centre of the Universe Blanc Fumé
d: Centre of the Universe is a Bordeaux style white blend that partners Sauvignon Blanc and 10% Semillon, using three vineyard sources on different soil types. Fifteen per cent skin contact adds some structure here to a low-intervention palate with layers of grapefruit, orange peel, black tea and umami and a waft of aromatic herbs. Unusual.

n: Deep Rooted Wines Free The Bubble
d: Free The Bubble is a characteristically playful Pet Nat from viticulturist-turned-winemaker, Mark Stephens. Marrying equal parts Chardonnay and Pinotage, it’s a creamy, just off-dry style with pear, fennel and citrus fruit flavours and a tangy refreshing finish.

By his own admission, Mark Stephens screwed up his 2024 Syrah, so it’s good to see the wine back on the market in 2025. Sourced from a trio of vineyards in the Stanford foothills, where the ocean influence is significant, this is a refreshing style with a savoury note from 15% whole bunches. Clove, sage and white pepper aromas are complemented by a palate of plum, bramble and cola.

n: Deep Rooted Wines Touch Me Verdelho
d: With its provocative nipple label, Touch Me is a Verdelho that never fails to raise a titter on Instagram. Fermented on skins with carbonic maceration for 16 days without added sulphites, this has ample colour and concentration, some tannic backbone and flavours of quince, sourdough bread and patisserie spices.

Morné Vrey’s Banghoek Chardonnay comes from five hillside sites between 350 and 550 metres that are planted with the 96 and 277 clones. Creamy, textured and full of flavour, it has layers of orange peel, patisserie spices and stone fruit, stylish 40% new oak and some underlying freshness from decomposed granite soils.

“We can shine in bad vintages,” says Morné Vrey of this virus-free block planted in 1999. This is certainly impressive, with Cabernet Franc-like aromas of pencil shavings and cut grass, flavours of plum, mint and red berries and finely integrated 80% new oak. Very impressive for a 2023 Merlot.

For the first time ever, the 2023 Botmaskop had less than 50% Cabernet Sauvignon, with the variety’s 45% complemented by 37% Cabernet Franc, 10% Petit Verdot and 8% Merlot. Picked before the heavy rains, it’s a glossy, refined Bordeaux-style blend with appealing liquorice, mint, mocha and blackcurrant flavours, sinewy tannins and on point 40% new oak.

"I’m a purist", laughs Morné Vrey when asked why he didn't blend this Cabernet Sauvignon. Serious stuff in a demanding vintage, this showcases the pedigree of the 169 clone, with ample structure and concentration, layers of damson, dried herbs and blackcurrant pastille and a sheen of toasty dark chocolatey oak.

Morné Vrey grew up in Calitzdorp, so he has a soft spot for fortified wines. This is a classic Vintage style that blends Touriga Nacional and 31% Tinta Barroca, with the emphasis on power, concentration and tannic structure. Curated in older barrels, it has intense violet and Asian spice aromas, layers of blackberry and fig, compact tannins and deftly integrated 87 grams of residual sugar.

n: Delaire Graff Coastal Cuvée Sauvignon Blanc
d: A pairing of Sauvignon Blanc and 8% Semillon from Banghoek and Durbanville, this is a very lightly wooded Bordeaux-style blend that over-delivers at its price point, with top notes of kelp and vanilla spice, flavours of cream soda and pink grapefruit, a hint of custard and a racy, well-balanced finish.

The Laurence Graff Reserve is the estate’s icon red, priced accordingly and aimed at the kind of people who buy diamonds here too. Made from Cabernet Sauvignon planted on Block Eight, it’s a bold, concentrated red with both eyes on the future, with mocha-scented 80% new oak, intense liquorice, damson and blackberry flavours and the concentration to develop well in bottle.

n: Delaire Graff Terraced Block Reserve Chardonnay
d: Volumes are comparatively small here, as the source is a one-hectare parcel at 400 metres, planted on a series of small terraces. More Meursault than Puligny-Montrachet, as it were, this has good texture and weight, aromas of saffron and vanilla spice and a palate of citrus, crème fraîche and butterscotch complemented by stony minerality.

The Banghoek is the second label of the Laurence Graff Reserve, but I slightly prefer it to the Grand Vin in 2022, at least for current drinking. Partnering Cabernet Franc, 31% Cabernet Sauvignon and 5% Petit Verdot, it’s a focused, refined cuvée with granular tannins, plenty of zip, energy and acidity and a core of black cherry, capsicum and espresso coffee.

Banghoek, Durbanville and Elgin supply the components for this self-assured blend of Sauvignon Blanc and 32% Semillon. Barrel-fermented in 10% new “cigars”, it’s a worked, textured style with subtle oak, layers of blackcurrant leaf, cream and pink grapefruit, racy acidity and a pleasing bitter tang.

Sourced entirely from the Vera Cruz vineyard, planted with bush vines between ten and 20 years’ old, this was made with modern, virus-free clones and it shows. The 45% new French oak is well integrated here, adding a touch of mocha and vanilla spice to a palate of mint, dill and blackcurrant complemented by fine tannins.

The latest in a run of very smart, botrytis-affected Rieslings from a parcel planted in 1984, Edelspatz is a labour of love. Carrying its 130 grams of residual sugar lightly, it’s one of the less exotic expressions of the site, with citrus, nectarine, cherimoya and passion fruit flavours, a touch of older oak and impressive structure, freshness and acidity.

Expressing the Simonsberg at it best, this is a still youthful blend of mostly Cabernet Sauvignon, 8% Merlot and 6% each of Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot. Subtly wooded in 40% new oak, it has lovely bramble and blackcurrant fruit purity, textured, layered tannins, vibrant acidity for a 2022 and the effortless concentration to develop in bottle.

The Iconoclast range is normally reserved for one-off wines, but this varietal Cabernet Franc from the Vera Cruz vineyard is back for the second time in 2022. Matured in 40% new oak, it has notes of earth, graphite and subtle reduction on the nose and a palate of black cherry and marjoram, toasty wood spices and a slight volatile lift.

Delheim has a richly deserved reputation for the consistent quality of this single-site Pinotage from the best block on the Vera Cruz estate. Stylishly wooded in 40% new oak, it’s a ripe, textured, alluringly well-balanced iteration of the grape with liquorice and cinnamon aromas, juicy bramble and black cherry fruit, refreshing acidity and sculpted tannins.

n: Delheim Wild Ferment OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Delheim’s old-vine Chenin Blanc hails from blocks planted in 1986 between 240 and 300 metres on the Delvera farm. Made in a modern, refreshing style with fermentation and ageing in concrete and older barrels, it’s tangy and refreshing, showing citrus and yellow apple flavours, ample zip and minerality and a balanced finish.

Two different clones – 169 and 338 – on clay soils supply the fruit for this unblended Cabernet Sauvignon. Showing the density and tannic backbone that are a feature of many 2024s, this is a bold, modern red with adroitly integrated 50% new French oak, with layers of cassis, damson and bramble and a firm, grippy finish.

The top DeMorgenzon hails from a single vineyard on the estate, where it is serenaded by classical music. Dominated by the CY95 clone, which is behind many of the Cape’s top Chardonnays, this is tangy, sappy and engagingly refreshing, with 30% new oak and 5% amphora-ageing adding extra nuances to a palate of pear tart and waxed lemons and a waft of struck match reduction.

After a few changes of personnel in recent years, DeMorgenzon appears to be finding its feet again. This bubbly is made with early picked Chenin Blanc from Block 24 on the farm and is effectively an Extra Brut, with 4.2 grams of dosage, sappy green apple, citrus zest and aniseed flavours and a cushion of bubbles.

Another wine that’s back on form at DeMorgenzon, this Chenin Blanc has dialled back on the new oak (to 20%) in 2024. Combining components from different altitudes on the farm, it has engaging quince and pink grapefruit flavours, a hint of apricot sweetness, lovely focus and zip and a petrichor undertone.

New to the DMZ line up, this is a well-judged Cabernet Sauvignon from an estate that specialises in red Rhône varieties. Sourced from a warmer, north-facing slope, it’s a modern, virus-free expression of the variety, with plum and blackcurrant pastille flavours, scented 25% new oak, sinewy tannins and a mineral core.

The DMZ Chardonnay uses grapes from south-east facing vines at 200 metres and is classic by-the-glass material. Fermented in aged in 8% new oak, it’s a textured, well-balanced white that combines flavours of citrus, pear and stone fruit with a touch of struck match reduction.

Anthony Sanvido makes this well-priced Chenin Blanc with younger blocks in Stellenbosch Kloof. Matured in foudres and concrete eggs, it’s a pithy, tangy, refreshing iteration of the grape, with citrus and greengage fruit and a nicely understated bitter twist. Eminently drinkable at well under R200.

South Africa’s equivalent of a good Crozes-Hermitage, this is a wine for Syrah lovers on a budget. Inky and aromatic, it has wonderful granitic freshness, some clove spice from 10% whole bunches, layers of blackberry, liquorice and black olive and skilfully integrated 15% new oak. Hard to beat at the price.

The best release of Maestro White yet, this is a beautifully judged blend of Roussanne, 17% Grenache Blanc and 12% Marsanne from Anthony Sanvido. Using a little skin contact for what he calls “phenolic pith”, it’s racy, focused and finely layered, with aromas of fennel, mustard seed and gin botanicals, understated 15% new oak and a core of pear, pink grapefruit and lemon zest.

Picked in two stages – pre- and post-rain – in 2023, this tastes lighter and more refreshing than its 14.5% alcohol would suggest. Fermented with 20% whole bunches for what Anthony Sanvido calls “stem spice”, this has fennel, black pepper and violet aromas and a palate of black cherry, summer berries and perfumed 30% new oak.

n: Diemersdal Noble Late Harvest Sauvignon Blanc
d: Diemersdal’s Noble Late Harvest is made with Sauvignon Blanc – what else? – and was picked with 50% botrytis. More Barsac than Sauternes in style perhaps, it’s a racy, refreshing sweet wine with a nice duet between acidity and 129 grams of residual sugar, flavours of citrus, apricot and honey and an elegant, tapering finish.

At 39 years of age, these are among the oldest Chardonnay vines in South Africa. Fermented and aged in 25% new 600-litre barrels and 1,200-litre foudres, this has appealing pear, waxed lemon and patisserie spice flavours, good mid-palate weight and a touch of white peach sweetness.

"Pinotage as a category is dying," says Thys Low, and this is his attempt to reverse that decline, Fermented with 70% whole clusters, using old oak and concrete rather than new barrel ageing, it’s a subtle, refreshing, by-the-glass style with rose petal and rosehip aromas and a palate of strawberry, goji berry and tobacco leaf.

Diemersdal may be better known for its Sauvignon Blancs, but it is also one of the best Pinotage producers in Durbanville. Juandré Brewer and Thys Low have toned down the new oak to 40% in 2024, but this is still a bold, well-structured expression of the variety, with layers of bramble, raspberry and black cherry fruit, top notes of vanilla and cedarwood and the concentration to develop in bottle.

Private Collection is a serious, very well-priced assemblage of Cabernet Sauvignon, 27% Merlot, 14% Petit Verdot and 2% Cabernet Franc. Intense, firm and deeply coloured, it has mocha, rose petal and cut grass aromas, cassis and blueberry fruit flavours, textured tannins and the backbone to age in bottle. Serious stuff in a challenging vintage.

Something a little different from Diemersdal, a winery that likes to push a few boundaries, this comes from a two-hectare block of seven-year-old vines on the farm. Mint, plum and dried herb flavours combine nicely on the palate here, with savoury tannins and toasty, mocha-scented 20% new oak.

Prospect is a new Sauvignon Blanc from Thys Low, made entirely with the 316 clone and sourced from dryland vineyards on the ocean side of farm. Leafy, herbal and at the greener end of the variety’s spectrum, it has layers of gooseberry, asparagus and padr0n peppers and a pithy, just off-dry finish.

Does any winery in the world make more styles of Sauvignon Blanc than Diemersdal? I seriously doubt it. This is an off-the-wall solera style white made from six different vintages. Made in an oxidative style, without topping, it has 15.5% alcohol from fortification, flavours of molasses, brown sugar and hazelnut, a touch of dried orange peel and well-integrated 176 grams of residual sugar.

Diemersdal’s Syrah comes from a single block on a farm that is more focused on white grapes than red. Fresh, herbal and still very youthful when I tasted it at the winery, it needs more time to integrate its 20% new French oak, but has some clove spice from 50% whole bunches and an earthy palate of blackberry, redcurrant and dark chocolate.

An impressive follow up to the maiden 2023 release, this Sauvignon Blanc was fermented and aged in 220-litre glass globes that were inspired by the late Loire Valley winemaker, Didier Dagueneau. Complex, pure, direct and beautifully balanced it has stony intensity, layers of lime, gooseberry and petrichor and impressive palate length.

Just like The Journal Pinotage, its Cabernet Sauvignon equivalent is a wine that’s built for the long haul with ageing in 100% new French oak. Showing the underlying freshness that you expect from a cool climate, it’s a Bordeaux-meets-the-Cape style with aromas of mint, dill and plain chocolate, blackcurrant, cranberry and damson flavours and a spine of chewy tannins.

The top-of-the-range Pinotage at Diemersdal comes from a vineyard planted in 1974 and was given the full 100% new oak treatment in 2024. Whether it needs it depends on your taste. Made in a Bordeaux rather than Burgundy style, this is bold, firm and compact, with damson and blackberry fruit, serious tannins and supporting acidity.

The Journal is a complex, layered blend of Sauvignon Blanc and 7% Semillon from a vineyard planted in 1994. Naturally fermented in Stockinger barrels and foudres and 10% clay amphoras, it’s a sappy, tangy and complete with gooseberry and pink grapefruit flavours, scoop of cream and a waft of vanilla spice.

Using grapes from the same 1994 block as The Journal, this is a low-intervention style of Sauvignon Blanc that was given 96 hours of skin contact. Showing a subtle oak undertone, it has appealing greengage and green fig flavours, a touch of tannin and a savoury note from 50% wild yeast fermentation.

n: Domaine des Dieux Claudia Brut CC
d: A Cap Classique with intensity to spare, the 2021 release of Claudia spent four years on lees before disgorgement. Chardonnay-based with 24% Pinot Noir, it’s rich, savoury and intense, showing layers of malt, patisserie spices and wild strawberry, a dab of cream and a tangy, well-balanced finish.

n: Domaine des Dieux Claudia Brut R.D. CC
d: R.D. – short for Recently Disgorged – is a brilliant new bubbly from Megan Mullis, made with Chardonnay and 20% Pinot Noir from Elgin. Matured on lees for a remarkable 12.5 years, this is an intense, layered cuvée with time-aided complexity, flavours of toast, wild mushroom, fennel and red berry fruit and subtle 6.9 grams of dosage.

n: Domaine des Dieux Rosé of Sharon CC
d: Part of an excellent current sparkling wine range from Domaine des Dieux, this is a Cape South Coast bottling of Pinot Noir and 13% Chardonnay. Showing noticeable intensity of colour for a rosé, it’s a full flavoured style with raspberry, toast and Negroni spice flavours, creamy bubbles and a tapering finish.

The talented Rüdger van Wky sources this Limietberg Chenin Blanc from three different parcels on the estate between 170 and 280 metres. Scented, poised and refreshing, it’s has stylishly integrated 33% new oak, a waft of stony reduction, pear, quince and lemongrass flavours and a lightly salty finish.

Morestond is a self-assured Chardonnay, made with grapes from a cool parcel that’s shaded in the afternoon. Skilfully fermented in 35% new oak, it has impressive structure and tension, subtle patisserie spice sweetness and a core of tangerine and fresh lemon flavours. Good now and should develop in bottle.

Taking up where the award-winning Xclusiv Rosé left off, this is a finely judge cuvée of Syrah and 49% Grenache from Limietberg. Whole bunch pressed before ageing in stainless steel, it’s very pale in style, with a hint of boiled sweets, peach, citrus and watermelon flavours and a pure, tangy, acid-driven finish.

n: Du Bois Vineyards Sonop Chenin Blanc
d: The du Bois family grow some of the best grapes in Stellenbosch, so it was only a matter of time before Gabriel du Bois released his own wine. Barrel fermented in older oak, with complete malolactic, this has layers of fennel, thatch, earth and almond paste, citrus and green apple flavours and a subtle bitter twist.

Granite Pinotage comes from Malmesbury in the Swartland and has good supermarket distribution in South Africa. Lightly wooded in 25% new barrels, it has good structure and intensity, plum, bramble and wild strawberry flavours and some underlying tannic grip.

n: Du Toitskloof Quest OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Du Toitskloof’s stylish OVP Chenin Blanc is a bargain, sourced from a small, 0.8-hectare vineyard planted in 1985. It’s a fresh, acid-driven style with no malolactic and negligible oak, offering green apple and waxed lemon flavours and an earthy undertone from 20% amphoras. Delicious at the price.

Fortified wines don’t enjoy the popularity they once did in the Cape, but this is perfect by-theglass material at the end of a long lunch. Rose petal and Turkish Delight aromas are a scented introduction to a palate of Asian spices, orange peel and candied fruit and a rancio top note. Carries its 240 grams of residual sugar lightly.

Breedekloof might seem too warm to grow good Viognier, but that’s not the case on the evidence of this example from Shawn Thomson. Deftly oaked in 20% new barrels, it comes from a single 25-year-old block, benefitting from three months on lees, subtle acid adjustment and a palate of crème fraîche, pear and apricot.

n: Durbanville Hills Collectors' Reserve The Cableway Chardonnay
Durbanville Hills Collectors' Reserve The Cape Garden Chenin Blanc
d: Put together “like a puzzle”, according to Pieter-Niel Rossouw, this uses five different components, with amphora, stainless steel and older barrels all featuring. Another wine that has made a makeover, it has lots of zip, energy and acidity, layers of quince and orange peel and a pithy, stony, oyster shell finish. Chenin meets Sauvignon Blanc.

n: Durbanville Hills Collectors' Reserve The Cape Mist Sauvignon Blanc
d: Exciting times at Durbanville Hills now that Pieter-Niel Rossouw is in charge as cellarmaster. This is very impressive given the volumes involved, with amphora and wooded components adding layers to the blend. Stony, pithy and much drier than it has been, this has greengage, kiwi and fresh lime flavours and a steely finish.

n: Durbanville Hills Collectors' Reserve The High Noon Shiraz
Durbanville Hills Collectors' Reserve The Lighthouse Merlot
d: More textured and approachable than it used to be, with less tannic grip, this is a lot of wine at just R175. Matured in 40% new wood, it’s a smooth, graceful, textured Merlot with green herb and pencil shaving aromas, cassis and red cherry flavours and plenty of underlying zip and freshness.

n: Durbanville Hills Collectors' Reserve The Promenade Pinotage
d: Very drinkable at the price, this is another Durbanville Hills red that has backed off on the new French and American oak. Bramble and red berry flavours are complemented by smooth, palate-coating tannins here, with top notes of vanilla and cinnamon and supporting acidity. Commendably drinkable.

n: Durbanville Hills The Tangram Red Blend
d: Tangram used to be a wine that seemed to be trying too hard to impress, but this is much more restrained and on point. A five-way Bordeaux-style blend of Merlot, 21% Cabernet Sauvignon, 11% each of Cabernet Franc, Malbec and Petit Verdot, it has stylish espresso coffee notes from 100% new oak, flavours of cassis, plum and fresh herbs and enough tannin to evolve and develop in bottle.

The Tangram White has always been one of the best wines at Durbanville Hills, but this is a breakthrough vintage in 2024 under Pieter-Niel Rossouw. Featuring 77% Sauvignon Blanc and a highest ever Semillon component, this is a beautifully refined, subtly wooded white Bordeaux-style blend with layers of vanilla, cream soda, grapefruit and lime and a pure, palate-cleansing finish.

Up a point since I tasted it last year, the Durbanville Pinotage is a joint effort between De Grendel, Durbanville Hills, Meerendal and Klein Roosboom that is only sold in magnums. Succulent, textured and smooth, it has well-integrated oak, flavours of plum and bramble and plenty of supporting acidity.

Sauvignon Blanc is part of the renewed focus, alongside Syrah, at Eagle’s Nest. Made with the French 314 clone, using six different pickings for complexity, it has subtle wood from stainless steel and 5% new oak fermentation citrus, greengage and kiwi fruit flavours and a salty, mineral-etched finish.

Named after her grandmother, Edith May, the first vintage of Nikki Weerts’ Karoo-Hogland Chardonnay was one of the highlights of this year’s discovery tasting. Barrel fermented in second and third-fill oak, with no malolactic, it’s a tangy, stony, chiselled style with layers of gunflint, fynbos, citrus and vanilla spice and a mineral-etched core.

One of a pair of exciting new wines from Nikki Weerts under the Edith May label, this is a youthful, floral, nicely balanced Elgin Pinot Noir with rose petal and tobacco leaf aromas, a touch of clove, succulent raspberry and red cherry flavours, scented 20% new oak and a lightly savoury finish.

Carlo Suter supplies grapes to other top producers, as well as making wines under his own Eight Gates label, some of which are sourced from other vineyards. This tasty Chenin Blanc comes from Opstal’s Bergsteen parcel and is appealingly racy and well balanced, with deftly handled 40% new oak, saffron and fynbos aromas and layers of citrus, greengage and wet stones.

n: Eight Gates Chenin Blanc De Liefde
d: De Liefde is a one-off release from ex-cabinet maker Carlo Suter. Fermented and aged in 50% new oak, it’s a subtle, bijou Chenin Blanc that shows the less exotic side of the grape’s personality, with subtle baking spice and gunflint aromas, flavours of pear and lemongrass, a waft of white flowers and a spine of racy acidity.

Held back for a while in barrel and then bottle, this uses grapes from the Eight Gates’ farm in the Breedekloof. A wine for Pinot Noir lovers, it’s scented, subtle and refined, with 10% whole clusters, rose petal and ginger aromas and a core of pomegranate and wild strawberry embellished by 20% new oak and fine-boned tannins.

The in-demand Karibib farm in the Polkadraai Hills supplies the grapes for this 50% whole cluster-fermented Syrah from Breedekloof-based Carlo Suter. Matured in 60% new wood, it’s an intense, slightly earthy style that marries a nose of pepper, sage and wild herbs with black cherry and liquorice flavours supported by grippy, sinewy tannins.

2023 wasn’t the easiest vintage in Stellenbosch, but this Cabernet Sauvignon has good ripeness and intensity. Curated in 20% new oak, it marries aromas of mint and dried herbs with a palate of mulberry, cassis and red berries supported by a firm spine of tannins.

Eikendal has a deserved reputation for the quality of its Chardonnays using grapes from the lower slopes of the Helderberg. Aldert Nieuwoudt has used the 20% new oak well here, with 30% malolactic providing some extra texture. Vibrant, focused and well balanced, it’s a layered white with lemongrass and patisserie spice flavours, a spine of acidity and a salty finish.

n: Electric Mud Old Bush Vines Grenache
d: The grapes from this 1.4-hectare parcel of 1966 vines used to go to the late Jan Boland Coetzee, and I think he’d be delighted by their new home. Showing the freshness of a site at 670 metres, this was fermented with 80% whole bunches in concrete tanks, producing a stunning wine with rose petal and rooibos tea aromas, sinewy tannins and layers of red cherry, raspberry and clove. What a début!

Demonstrating his experience with Chardonnay, first developed in Beaune, Gus Dale ferments this wine with natural yeasts, allowing it to go through 60% malolactic. Honeysuckle and subtle aromatic spice top notes from 10% new oak guide you into a palate of citrus, beeswax and subtle stone fruit and a lightly salty finish.

Gus Dale trained in Burgundy rather than the Loire Valley, but he brings a French sensibility to this Sauvignon Blanc too. Subtly wooded in second and third-use oak, it has a sheen of vanilla spice, flavours of elderflower, pink grapefruit and smoked lemon and some mid-palate texture from 50% malolactic.

Silver Lining is Zevenwacht winemaker Hagen Viljoen’s personal project, made with grapes from two blocks of contrasting ages in Piekenierskloof. Fermented with 80% whole bunches, it’s a sappy, scented red with layers of pomegranate, wild strawberry and tobacco leaf, sculpted tannins and a mineral core.

A tribute to the smoothness of Ernie Els’ golf swing, the Big Easy is a blend of mostly Cabernet Sauvignon with 30% Syrah and 5% each of Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Merlot and Petit Verdot. Reflecting the art of blending in a rainy year, it’s a supple, fruit-forward style with vanilla, cumin and red berry flavours and some added weight from 15% of the 2024 vintage.

n: Ernie Els Cabernet Sauvignon (Ten Year Release)
d: Enjoyable enough in its way, but this was made before Ernie Els made a welcome shift in style in 2021. Compact, dense and well structured, even after a decade in barrel and bottle, this is a dense Helderberg Cabernet Sauvignon that combines aromas of graphite and dried herbs with a palate of blackberry and cigar box, savoury tannins and enough acidity to lift and freshen the finish.

n: Ernie Els Major Series Cabernet Sauvignon
d: Louis Strydom is a big fan of the “cooler, perfect” 2024 vintage in Stellenbosch, and you can see why. Made with a quartet of different Cabernet Sauvignon clones, this is dominated by grapes from a fresher site, and it shows. Bright and sensitively wooded, it has subtle aromatic spices, granular tannins, layers of plum and blackcurrant leaf and a whisper of oak sweetness. Bravo!

n: Ernie Els Major Series Double Red
d: Double Red marries Cabernet Sauvignon and 45% Merlot, with ageing in 20% new oak and (for 5% of the blend) terracotta amphoras. New to the Ernie Els range, it reflects the move away from new oak at the winery, revealing layers of bramble and red fruits, nuanced aromatic spices, detailed tannins and a finely balanced finish. Drinkable now but will evolve further in bottle.

Showing Louis Strydom’s skills as a blender and his deep knowledge of Stellenbosch’s terroirs, this is a triumph over the elements in 2023. Cabernet Sauvignon takes the lead here, supported by 30% Syrah and 10% Merlot. Aged in concrete, amphoras and 40% new wood, it’s a racy, refined cuvée with tangy bramble and red cherry fruit, fresh acidity and finegrained underlying tannins.

“I surprised myself,” says veteran winemaker Louis Strydom of his 2023 Syrah, picked before the later season rains in Stellenbosch. Fermented with 40% whole clusters and aged in 30% new oak and terracotta amphoras, it’s a floral, enticingly perfumed expression of the grape, with wafts of clove and pepper flavours of black cherry and summer berries and some underlying grip and a balsamic twist.

The 2023 Signature release from this increasingly impressive Helderberg property was blended with 15% of 2024 to give it a bit more weight in a tricky vintage. Pairing Cabernet Sauvignon, 25% Merlot and 5% each of Cabernet Franc, Malbec and Petit Verdot, it’s an elegant, refined blend with notes of potpourri, tobacco leaf and red berries, granular tannins and stylishly handled 50% new oak.

Something of a throwback to the red wine style that Ernie Els was making a decade ago, this is a mature, structured cuvée of Cabernet Sauvignon, 25% Merlot ad 5% each of Cabernet Franc, Malbec and Petit Verdot. Eucalyptus and dried herb aromas are complemented by firmish tannins, toasty 70% new wood and a savoury finish.

Beryl Black is tribute to Charles Back’s mother and is one of those Cape white blends that is much easier to taste and score than it is to sell to a public obsessed with Sauvignon Blanc. Made as a three-way blend of Chenin Blanc, 25% early picked Viognier and 16% Grenache from Paarl. Floral, textured and complex, it has aromas of thatch, ginger and aniseed, lots of supporting acidity, subtle oak a palate of quince, apricot and yellow apple.

Bloemcool is the best dry white at Fairview, made with old-vine Chenin Blanc, 39% Palomino and 13% Grenache Blanc, all from Piekenierskloof. Layered, complex and beautifully balanced, it has intriguing layers of oatmeal, beeswax and umami, impressive mid-palate texture, pear and citrus fruit and an earthy undertone.

Priced just above Goats Do Roam, this is a varietal expression of Cinsault from a 1994 vineyard in Paarl. Matured in seasoned oak, it’s a good-value introduction to the variety, redcurrant and cranberry fruit flavours, savoury tannins and a touch of meaty reduction.

Cyril Back is named after the father of Fairview’s owner, Charles Back, and is a well-judged blend of Syrah and 30% Cabernet Sauvignon. The 30% new oak is adroitly handled here, adding some structure and wood spices to a palate of cassis, blackberry and Mediterranean herbs supported by chewy tannins and racy acidity.

Eenzaamheid comes from a 1996 block on red shale soils close to the winery in Paarl. Denser and firmer than the Lanner Hill Syrah, it’s more Cornas than Côte Rôtie with lots of bloody, ferrous intensity, grippy, chewy tannins, blackberry and damson fruit flavours and the concentration and focus to develop further in bottle.

Vines in Paarl and higher altitude Piekenierskloof supply the raw material for this good value Western Cape Grenache. Fermented with some whole bunches for perfume and texture, it’s an appealingly ethereal wine, with notes of rose petal, red cherry and goji berry, negligible oak and a savoury finish.

n: Fairview La Beryl Blanc Straw Wine
d: La Beryl, not to be confused with Fairview’s dry Beryl Black, is a straw wine made from Chenin Blanc and 25% Muscat Blanc. Showing the concentration of grapes that were dried on mats for three weeks, it has layers of peach, guava and orange zest, a nice interplay between high acidity and 210 grams of sugar and a subtle volatile lift.

Lanner Hill is a brilliant expression of cool climate Syrah, underlining Darling’s suitability for the grape. With medium body and pepper spice and tobacco leaf notes from 20% whole bunches, it has good grip and intensity, layers of wild herbs, black olive and cooked meat, racy acidity and beautifully integrated oak.

Two old-vine blocks in Paarl and Piekenierskloof, planted in 1974 and 1962, respectively, are the source of this Chenin Blanc, or Steen, from Anthony de Jager and Annette van Zyl. Barrel fermented in older oak and 15% concrete eggs, it combines aromas of jasmine and chamomile with a palate of greengage, citrus peel and fennel.

One of three line-priced Syrahs, or Shirazes, in the Fairview range, this uses Leeuwenkuil Family Vineyards’ dry-farmed grapes in the Swartland. Yields were tiny in 2023, but this block benefitted from the work of old-vine guru, Rosa Kruger. Rosemary and thyme aromas provide a scented introduction to a palate of blackberry and damson complemented by savoury tannins and a ferrous finish.

Chris Alheit has stopped producing red wines under his own label, alas, but you can still buy his Fogwell Syrah. This comes from two top sites – Karibib in the Polkadraai Hills and the Ava vineyard in the Swartland, both dry farmed. Clove, sage and Turkish bazaar spices are a scented introduction to a palate of blackberry, liquorice and tapenade, with a spine of sinewy tannins and the concentration and intensity to develop further in bottle.

Pinotage specialist Francois van Niekerk may have branched out into other wines, but this remains his calling card and focus. Serious, dense, concentrated and built to last, it has deftly handled 40% new oak, subtle gingerbread and patisserie spices, flavours of plum, bramble and wild strawberry and a spine of firm, age-worthy tannins.

n: Francois Van Niekerk Sonland Chenin Blanc
Fryer's Cove Bamboes Bay Sauvignon Blanc
d: The straight Bamboes Bay Sauvignon Blanc is what made Fryer’s Cove reputation under previous owner Jan Ponk. A wine for lovers of pyrazine-dominated styles, it has green asparagus and cucumber flavours, some lees-derived texture and a briny, oyster shell finish.

Something of an outlier in the Freyer’s Cove portfolio, as it’s made from Chenin as opposed to Sauvignon Blanc, this comes from Koekenaap and, for the first time, Natasha Love’s parcel in Ebenezer. Using a combination of ceramic pots and older oak, it has plenty of West Coast acidity and pear, nectarine and citrus fruit flavours.

n: Fryer's Cove Hollebaksstrandfontein Bamboes Bay Sauvignon Blanc
d: Hollebaksstrandfontein is the top-of-the-range Sauvignon Blanc from Fryer’s Cove, sourced from the winery’s own vines in Atlantic-influenced Bamboes Bay. Fermented in pricey Stockinger 500-litre barrels, it’s a Blanc Fumé style with 30% new oak, layers of kelp, rock pool and mange tout and a sappy, palate-cleansing finish.

Essence of the West Coast, this textbook, sea breeze Sauvignon Blanc uses grapes from Bamboes Bay and Koekenaap. Less green than the more expensive Hollebaksstrandfontein bottling, it’s a racy, floral, lime, passion fruit and gooseberry number with a salty tang.

n: Fuselage Wines Staggerwing Old Vines Chenin Blanc
d: The pick of Danie Morkel’s range, this shows how good Paarl Chenin Blanc can be when it comes from the right site. Fermented and lees-aged in neutral barrels, it’s a sappy, racy expression of the variety, with layers of fennel, oatmeal, citrus and petrichor and a savoury finish. Complex stuff.

n: Fuselage Wines Staggerwing Old Vines Cinsault

d: Oxalis is the icon Syrah from Gabriëlskloof, released for the second time in 2024. Using grapes from three vineyards, with an equal mix of sandstone and shale, this is bold, dense and compact, with impressive intensity for a wine with only 12.8% alcohol, layers of damson, blackberry and white pepper and a firm, age-worthy finish.

n: Gabriëlskloof Project Series Amphora Sauvignon Blanc
d: Amphora uses grapes from three farms in Olifantsriver and Bot River, fermenting and ageing the result in clay amphoras. Herbal, stony and intense, it has appealing briny aromas, lots of tangy minerality, layers of petrichor, lime and nettle and a subtle, earthy finish.

n: Gabriëlskloof Project Series Whole Bunch Syrah
d: Fermented with 100% whole clusters, as per the label, this uses grapes from mostly shale soils, with a 20% sandstone component. Spicy, tangy and lightly wooded in older barrels and stainless steel, it has layers of clove, black olive and redcurrant, a hint of vinyl and some underlying tannic grip.

Synonym is a rebrand of Gabriëlskloof’s entry-point Chenin Blanc, made with components from Bot River and the Swartland. Aged older barrels and stainless steel, with 50% malolactic, it’s a sappy, racy, slightly savoury style with some underlying grip and flavours of aniseed, citrus and green apple.

n: Gabriëlskloof The Landscape Series Cabernet Franc
d: First made in 2015, this was a key wine in the development of Cabernet Franc in the Cape. Entirely destemmed before ageing in newer 500l-litre barrels, it’s a firm, compact, slightly chewy expression of the variety, with top notes of green herbs and vinyl, flavours of black cherry and tarragon and the concentration to age. Not quite the wine it once was perhaps?

n: Gabriëlskloof The Landscape Series Elodie Chenin Blanc
d: Elodie uses grapes from two top sites in the Swartland - Jakkalsfontein and Nuwedam – and has the granitic intensity to prove it. Naturally fermented in older oak, it’s a leesy, savoury style with some subtle reduction, layers of citrus and wet stones and a kerosene undertone.

n: Gabriëlskloof The Landscape Series Era René Chenin Blanc
d: This is the third vintage of Era René, sourced from Gabriëlskloof’s home blocks in Bot River. Broader and a little more textured than the Elodie release, it has an earthy, Xarel-lo like top note, subtle patisserie sweetness from 20% whole bunches, flavours of crème fraîche, quince and yellow apple and supporting acidity.

Magdalena is an unusual, separately fermented cuvée of Chenin Blanc, 34% Semillon, 22% Sauvignon Blanc and 3% Muscat d’Alexandrie from a variety of Western Cape sources. Naturally fermented in older wood, it’s sappy and restrained, with beeswax, fynbos and honeysuckle aromas and a palate of grapefruit and citrus and a stony finish.

n: Gabriëlskloof The Landscape Series Syrah on Sandstone
d: Anmar van Niekerk and Peter-Allan Finlayson use a smaller whole bunch component of 30% on their Sandstone Syrah, believing that the wine has ample zip of its own. Showing some subtle, faintly earthy reduction, this has good grip, density and extraction, flavours of blackberry, clove and liquorice and nicely understated oak.

n: Gabriëlskloof The Landscape Series Syrah on Shale
d: Now made with 60% whole bunches, this is a Bot River Syrah that only uses grapes grown on shale soils. Not quite as thrilling as it used to be perhaps, but this is still racy, focused and chiselled, with flavours of blood orange and red cherry, a touch of cola and an earthy finish. Needs more time in bottle.

The kind of big-volume white that I’m always happy to find on a wine list, this has morphed in style in recent vintages and now has no malolactic whatsoever. Fermented in 25% new wood, it’s all about freshness and focus, with lots of zip and acidity, citrus and melon flavours and subtle oak spices. A very good drink at the price.

New to the rejuvenated range at Glen Carlou, this is an impressive, unblended Petit Verdot from decomposed granite soils in Simonsberg-Paarl. Fermented and aged in new 400l-litre barrels, it has aromas of mint and dark chocolate, glossy tannins, plenty of tangy acidity and pristine fruit flavours of blueberry and black cherry and a waft of Asian spices.

Part of a revamped range at Glen Carlou under long-term winemaker Johnnie Calitz, Grand Classique is a Bordeaux-style blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, 20% Merlot, 14% Malbec, 4% Cabernet Franc and 2% Petit Verdot from various sites across the Cape. Refreshingly medium bodied, with subtle oak, it has textured tannins, flavours of mint, plum and blackcurrant and good concentration for a 2023 release.

n: Glen Carlou Gravel Quarry Cabernet Sauvignon
d: Gravel Quarry is the top-of-the-range Cabernet Sauvignon from Glen Carlou, sourced from Simonsberg-Paarl and Deon Joubert’s farm in Stellenbosch. Modern, pure, scented and effortlessly focused, it’s a wine that wears its 100% new oak lightly, with top notes of graphite and mint and a palate of plum, dark chocolate and blackcurrant pastille.

Quartz Stone comes from two sites in Stellenbosch and Simonsberg-Paarl and is the winery’s super premium Chardonnay. Fermented and aged in new oak and 10% concrete eggs, it has eschewed malolactic in favour of greater freshness and focus. Lime, citrus, white peach and baking spice flavours combine appealingly on the palate supported by racy acidity.

n: Glen Heatlie The Frontier Grenache Blanc
d: Refreshingly pithy and low in alcohol at 12.5%, this has the precision and racy acidity that are part of Grenache Blanc’s DNA. Stony, pithy and refreshing, it has greengage, citrus and subtle vanilla spice flavours and a chiselled, palate-cleansing finish.

Appealingly low in alcohol, this comes from one, early picked parcel on the Simonsberg. Combing foudre, 18% new wood and Flexcube components, it’s a floral, easy-drinking style of Chardonnay with citrus, peach and cardamom flavours, some subtle patisserie spices and an intriguing bitter twist.

Released with some bottle age, the Estate Reserve Red is the second wine of Glenelly’s icon bottling, Lady May. Still youthful at seven years of age, it’s an expression of what Dirk van Zyl calls our “Bordeaux roots”. Combining Cabernet Sauvignon, 17% Merlot, 15% Syrah, 13% Cabernet Franc and 8% Petit Verdot it has top notes of dried herbs, cedarwood and graphite and a palate of plum and blackcurrant pastille.

Made by Luke O’Cuinneagain but blended by Dirk van Zyl, this is the latest in a superb run of releases of Glenelly’s top red. Cabernet Sauvignon dominates the blend, with back up from 7% Cabernet Franc and 6% Merlot. Curated in 70% new oak, it’s full-bodied yet refreshing, with lots of texture, concentration and backbone, sinewy tannins and flavours of blackcurrant, bramble and black fig.

The Glass Collection is a range that almost over-delivers at the price. This Merlot uses grapes from one of the cooler parts of the estate, and it shows in the wine. Matured in foudres and 10% new oak, it marries aromas of coffee bean and basil with a palate of plum and cassis framed by subtle wood spices. Smooth and approachable.

A new addition to the Glass Collection range – 2023 was not the easiest of début vintages – this is a stylishly rendered assemblage of Cabernet Sauvignon, 17% Syrah, 15% Cabernet Franc, 14% Merlot and 4% Petit Verdot. Effectively the third wine of Lady May, it’s appealingly floral and aromatic, with deftly integrated 30% new oak, bramble, mint and blackcurrant leaf flavours and some underlying grip.

Very impressive given its sub-R200 price, this comes from four blocks on the farm and draws on Dirk van Zyl’s experience with Syrah at Saxenburg. Clove, fynbos and white pepper aromas segue into a palate of red cherry, bramble and liquorice complemented by 25% whole bunches and fine-grained tannins.

Grand Duc is something of a throwback in style to the wines that the New World, especially California, made in the 1990s, but there’s nothing wrong that, which is why this Chardonnay has its fans.
