Fermented in first-use barrels, followed by full malolactic, it’s a rich, textured wine with ample concentration, sweet spices and layers of butterscotch and apricot underpinned by acidity.

The Grand Duc Semillon gets eight hours of skin contact before fermentation and ageing in third-fill barrels. Wild yeast fermented with full malolactic, it has layers of beeswax, fennel and toast, impressive underlying structure and a hint of oak spice.

The cheaper of Glenwood’s two Chardonnays, this has reduced the amount of new oak to 30% in 2021. Wild yeast fermented, with 20% malolactic, it’s floral and refreshing, marrying aromas of baking spices and white flowers with a palate of oatmeal, citrus and macadamia nut and a hint of stone fruit sweetness.

n: Goedverwacht Family Wines Great Expectations Chenin Blanc
Goedverwacht Family Wines Great Expectations Sauvignon Blanc
d: New Zealand Sauvignon Blancs from Marlborough are often said to have a slightly “sweaty” character – nicer than it sounds, I promise you - and there’s a bit of that here, complemented by flavours of gooseberry and passion fruit and a tangy, refreshing finish.

n: Goedverwacht Family Wines Great Expectations Triangle
Goedverwacht Family Wines Maxim Cabernet Sauvignon
d: Sourced from Goedverwacht’s substantive estate near Bonnievale, this is a well-defined Cabernet Sauvignon from third-generation vintner Robert du Toit that carries its oak lightly. Showing some subtle minty reduction, it has plum, red cherry and blackcurrant fruit flavours, fine tannins and a floral top note.

n: Graham Beck Artisan Collection Blanc de Meunier Magnum CC
d: Pierre de Klerk reckons this is the only pure Pinot Meunier bubbly in the Cape and he should know. Made with a 70/30 blend from Robertson and Elgin, it’s a bone-dry style that spent four years on lees before disgorgement, showing a pinkish tinge, fine, textured bubbles, flavours of malt, citrus and raspberry and an appealing bitter twist.

n: Graham Beck Blanc de Blancs CC
d: Produced in what Pierre de Klerk calls a “voluptuous vintage”, when picking started on January 3rd, this lightly wooded all-Chardonnay Blanc de Blancs is a delight. Aromas of hazelnut, aniseed and petrichor segue into a palate of brioche, macadamia nut and citrus zest complemented by texture from 60 months on lees. Slightly tighter and more focused than it was a year ago.

n: Graham Beck Blanc de Blancs CC Magnum
d: Evolving more slowly than the 75cl bottling, as you’d expect, this magnum release was fermented in a combination of stainless steel and older barrels. It’s another superb expression of Robertson Chardonnay, with impressive structure and majesty, layers of patisserie, lemongrass and Digestive biscuit and a dry finish of just 3.5 grams of dosage.

A Cap Classique that has opened lots of doors for South African sparkling wines, this is a commendably reliable 1.5-million bottle cuvée of Chardonnay and 41% Pinot Noir. Blended with 20% of what Pierre de Klerk calls “perpetual reserve”, it uses grapes from 19 regions, showing pear and fresh lemon flavours, a touch of peachy sweetness and 7.6 grams of dosage.

One of a pair of large-volume wines from Graham Back that showcase the blending skills of Pierre de Klerk, this uses grapes from ten growers and 12 regions. Pairing Pinot Noir, 48% Chardonnay and 2% Pinot Meunier, it has appealing redcurrant, candy floss and pink grapefruit flavours, nice texture from 15 months’ autolysis and a racy, just off-dry finish.

Sparkling wine lovers in the know have long appreciated the quality of Cuvée Clive, which deserves to share the limelight with the very best Champagnes. Sourced from Durbanville and Robertson, it’s a seamless blend of wooded Chardonnay and 19% Pinot Noir of remarkable depth and complexity. Savoury, spicy and toasty, it has layers of lemon zest, strawberry, malt and shiitake mushrooms, effortless structure and focus and perfectly judged autolysis from 67 months on lees. The new disgorgement is another winner.

Bottled with just three grams of dosage, Ultra Brut is effectively dry. Sourced from Darling, Robertson and Stellenbosch, it’s a well-judged cuvée of Chardonnay and 35% Pinot Noir, with fermentation of the base wine entirely in stainless steel for the first time. Stony, intense and focused, it’s still young for a wine that spent 80 months on lees, with aniseed and citrus zest flavours and a sheen of patisserie spices.

n: Graham Beck Ultra Brut CC Magnum
d: The magnum bottling of Graham Beck’s Ultra Brut has slightly higher residual sugar at 4.85 grams and is developing beautifully. Pairing Chardonnay and 35% Pinot Noir, it spent eight years on lees before disgorgement and is commendably well balanced, with savoury intensity, racy acidity and citrus, nougat and wild strawberry flavours.

n: Graham Beck Vintage Pinot Noir Rosé CC
d: Sold as a Western Cape blend because it combines Durbanville Pinot Noir with 11% Chardonnay from Robertson, this is an appealingly dry rosé with pomegranate, malt and juniper flavours, a touch of Negroni spices, an earthy note from an amphora-fermented portion and a savoury, lingering finish.

n: Graham Beck Vintage Pinot Noir Rosé Magnum CC
d: Reviewed last year in a single bottle format, the 2019 is back at twice the size. Aged for six years on lees, it’s a seamless cuvée of Pinot Noir and 13% Chardonnay from Durbanville and Robertson, with some added complexity from a 10% amphora component, redcurrant, toast, juniper and strawberry flavours and an elegant finish.

n: Grande Provence The Grande Provence Red
Grande Provence The Grande Provence White

d: Naturally fermented, with minimal intervention in the winery, this is a textbook expression of Cabernet Franc from Franschhoek. Lightly wooded in older oak, it’s grassy and refreshing, with plum, capsicum and black cherry flavours and graceful, layered tannins.

Exciting young winemaker Gynore Hendricks sources her Great Heart Chardonnay from a single site in the Polkadraai Hills. Lees aged in older French wood, it’s a comparatively exotic style, with pineapple and nectarine flavours, understated oak and a citrus-driven finish.

De Grendel’s cool climate Op die Berg vineyard on the Ceres Plateau is the source of this youthful, vibrant Pinot Noir, which used to be sourced from Elgin. Redcurrant, pomegranate and goji berry flavours are complemented by plenty of zip and acidity and a touch of savoury tannin.

Now back at Groot Constantia after a ten-year absence, Danie Keulder is having a noticeable impact at this historic estate. Fermented with full malolactic in one-third new oak, this has lovely lime and lemon zest fruit, a subtle juniper undertone, good, buttery texture and a patina of baking spice sweetness.

"You’re better off waiting in Constantia," says Danie Keulder, “unless it’s 2023.” For all that, this is a well-judged, cool climate assemblage of Cabernet Sauvignon, 33% Cabernet Franc and 23% Merlot that handles its 75% new oak comfortably, with flavours of cassis, red cherry and mint, undertones of tobacco leaf and fresh earth, plenty of tangy acidity and subtle coffee bean oak.

Drawing on the time he spent in Durbanville, Danie Keulder has made a masterful Gouverneur’s Reserve in Constantia in 2025. The new oak has been reduced to 25% (from twice that amount), giving the fruit more room to express itself. An equal blend of Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon, this is racy, flinty and intense, with layers of oyster shell, wet stone and pink grapefruit, subtle wood spices and a herbal tang.

Grand Constance is the other famous sweet wine from Constantia and is very different in style from Klein Constantia’s Vin de Constance. Made with an equal mix of red and white Muscat de Frontignan clones, it has rose petal and Christmas cake spice aromas, flavours of orange peel, dried fig and raspberry coulis, well-integrated 165 grams of residual sugar and supporting acidity.

Picked on taste rather than analysis, according to Danie Keulder, this is a very well-judged blend of Sauvignon Blanc and 11.5% Semillon that’s worth paying a little extra for. Very lightly wooded, it’s a pithy, tangy Constantia white with layers of beeswax, cream soda, lime and oyster shell and an appealing herbal undertone.

n: Groot Parys Die Tweede Droom Chenin Blanc
Groot Parys Die Tweede Droom Chenin Blanc Demi Sec
Groot Parys Die Tweede Droom Colombard
Groot Parys Die Tweede Droom Mengelmoes
d: This historic property in Paarl is now using the services of talented young consultant, Angus Paul, who makes this low-intervention white with Chenin Blanc and 40% Colombard. Showing an earthiness that’s a little Xarel-lo-like, it’s a savoury, tangy, high acid white with some texture from full malolactic and an appealing bitter twist.

n: Groot Parys Die Tweede Droom Rooklippe Chenin Blanc
d: Grown on a 37-year-old parcel of red, rocky soils, as its name indicates in Afrikaans, this an expression of place and fruit, rather than oak, with fermentation in very old barrels. Racy, bready and appealingly dry, it has aromas of hay and fennel, some phenolic grip and a textured palate of citrus, cardamom and turmeric.

n: Groot Parys Die Tweede Droom Sandkol
d: Sandkol comes from a 40-year-old vineyard on sandy soils in Paarl and is a very lightly wooded, minimum intervention expression of the site, with lots of weight, texture and intensity for a wine with only 12.6% alcohol. Aromas of beeswax, white flowers and lanolin guide you into a palate of aniseed, pear and lemongrass and a salty finish.

n: Groot Parys Die Tweede Droom Straw Wine
d: Made with bunches that were dried in the shade – essential in Paarl – for a fortnight, this is a straw wine that combines Chenin Blanc and Colombard, two of the Cape’s most planted grapes. Luscious yet refreshing at the same time, it has a nice interplay between racy acidity and 205 grams of residual sugar, with flavours of molasses, orange zest and guava and a waft of aromatic spices.

n: Groot Phesantekraal Anna de Koning Chenin Blanc
d: Proof that Durbanville can make great Chenin Blanc as well as Sauvignon, this is a superb single-vineyard example from Richard Schroeder. Fermented in 10% new oak, amphoras and concrete eggs, it’s a wine of impressive texture and focus, with lots of racy acidity, layers of lime and grapefruit and a stony, tapering finish.

A sworn enemy of the Vin 7 yeast, which tends to produce tutti-fruity whites, Richard Schroeder has produced an elegant, refined cuvée of Sauvignon Blanc and 11% Semillon. Eschewing new oak entirely, it has some subtle reduction, flavours of lemongrass, green fig and grapefruit and a petrichor note from partial ageing in amphoras.

n: Groot Phesantekraal Noble Late Harvest Muscat d'Alexandrie
d: Produced with a combination of botrytis-affected and vine-dried grapes, this is more Jurançon than Sauternes in style, as it were, with comparatively low alcohol, 146 grams of residual sugar, pear, peach and pink grapefruit flavours and a sheen of oak spice.

"I don't own a crusher, just a destemmer," says Richard Schroeder, who uses 20% whole clusters in the final blend here. Spicy, sappy and refreshing, this is an appealing cool climate style, with clove and white pepper aromas, understated oak and a core of tangy plum and red berry fruit. Very drinkable.

n: Groote Post Pinch of Salt Chardonnay
d: Not quite as “salty” as Lukas Wentzel’s Sauvignon Blanc, this layered Chardonnay uses three different fermentation vessels – stainless steel, older French oak and amphoras – to create layers of complexity. Refreshing, nuanced and low key, it has nice texture and weight, flavours of cardamom, lemongrass and pear tart and a sappy finish.

Riesling lovers should be forming a queue to buy a bottle of this incredible wine, which is crazily under-priced for its quality. The interplay between tangy acidity and 11.2 grams of residual sugar is beautifully done, with a medley of lime, peach and passion fruit and remarkable balance and palate length.

n: Groote Post Salt of the Earth
d: The best of the Groote Post reds, this is a medium-weight blend of Cinsault and 40% Syrah that speaks of its cool climate. Taut, crunchy and refreshing, it has a waft of oak spices, tangy red cherry, bramble and pomegranate flavours, tobacco leaf tannins and an ocean-influenced, acid-driven finish.

Seasalter is a reference to Groote Post’s proximity to the Atlantic Ocean and is also a partial description of this wine. Showing aromas of kelp and brine, it’s a stylish, lightly wooded blend of Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon, with flavours of padrón peppers and grapefruit, mouth-watering acidity and a struck match undertone.

n: Groote Post The Inheritance Pinot Noir
Groote Post The Inheritance Sauvignon Blanc
d: The Inheritance is a Fumé Blanc style of Sauvignon, picked with a little more ripeness to balance the barrel fermentation. Toast, sea breeze and cinnamon aromas are a scented introduction to a palate of lemongrass, pink grapefruit and green herbs and a scoop of crème fraîche to tie the whole thing together.

“Forward fruit flavours don’t come easily here,” says Anthony Hamilton Russell, whose Pinot Noir can often be backward and slightly earthy in its youth. This is a blend of the 113, 115 and 667 clones, showing deftly handled 25% new oak, slightly ferrous top notes of blood and root vegetables, layers of plum and black cherry and complex, savoury, well-integrated tannins.

"Lovely and pristine" is how Emul Ross describes the 2025 vintage in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley. This Chardonnay is correspondingly bright and refreshing, with scented 24% new oak, a savoury undertone from wild fermentation, mid-palate texture from 30% malolactic and flavours of lemongrass and tangerine.

Ten different sites, planted with the CS46 and 338 clones, contribute to the blend here. It’s another impressive red from the Hartenberg team, with alluring graphite, parsley and fresh mint aromas, scented 35% new oak, textured tannins and a core of plum and cassis.

An appealing, well-priced alternative to The Eleanor, this Chardonnay comes from six regeneratively farmed blocks, with different pickings for added complexity. Fermented and aged in 30% new oak, with the same amount of malolactic, this has appealing layers of toast, tangerine and fresh lemons, a scoop of cream and some subtle nutmeg spice.

Gravel Hill, as its name suggests, is located on an east-facing parcel of stony, red clay soils and tends to produce a deeper, denser, darker expression of Syrah that’s rich, powerful and built to age. Ferrous and intense, it has ample concentration and structure, layers of toast, blackberry, damson and barbecued meat and a waft of incense and iodine. A wine to tuck away for a while.

A Merlot that emerged relatively unscathed from the wet conditions of the 2023 vintage in Stellenbosch, this is an elegant, layered expression of the variety. Granular tannins frame a palate of red cherry, plum and paprika, with a hint of tobacco leaf, subtle 20% new oak and supporting acidity. Always impressive at the price.

Hartenberg’s well-priced Riesling comes from two 28-year-old blocks on the farm and has always been made in a defiantly dry style without botrytis or residual sugar. Lees aged for six months, it has lime blossom aromas, chiselled acidity, flavours of citrus and stone fruit and an appealing bitter twist.

Sacred Soil is a new wine from the Hartenberg, referencing the regenerative farming that’s used in its vineyards. A Bordeaux style blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, 35% Merlot and 11% Cabernet Franc, it has good structure for a 2023, with 20% new coffee bean oak, flavours of red cherry, plum and dried herbs and a firm, robust finish.

Shiraz is something of a specialism at Hartenberg, so it’s no surprise that this estate blend used grapes from 11 different blocks planted with a quartet of different clones. Engagingly perfumed, it marries aromas of cola, lavender and thyme with a palate of blackberry and cooked meat supported by sinewy tannins.

The Eleanor, named after a previous owner of Hartenberg, this excellent Chardonnay comes from Block 33, which is entirely planted with the in-demand CY95 clone. The 30% new oak is deftly integrated here, with appealing lees and subtle malolactic characters, lots of zip and structure, a patina of patisserie spices and flavours of toast, pink grapefruit and wet stones.

Made by Carl Schultz before he left Hartenberg to pursue his own project, this is even better than the impressive 2021 release of The Mackenzie. Elegant and nuanced for a 2022, it’s a seamless cuvée of Cabernet Sauvignon, 27% Merlot and 4% each of Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot. Curated in 50% new oak, it has a frame of fine tannins, enclosing textured layers of cassis, plum and summer berry fruit and a waft of fynbos and cedarwood. Very classy.

Generally the lighter of the two single vineyard Syrahs at Hartenberg, this comes from a later-picked site on cooler, clay-rich soils. Matured in 40% new 500 litre-barrels, it has some of the variety’s tell-tale reduction, a waft of clove, vanilla and fynbos, bramble and blackberry fruit, firmish tannins and a subtle volatile lift.

n: Hasher Family Wines Ernest Pinot Noir
d: Ernest is made with the older-vine parcels at Hasher, planted in the early 2000s. Showcasing the 115 Burgundy clone, with 10% 113, it’s elegant, floral and very attractive, demonstrating Natasha Williams fine touch with Pinot Noir. Deftly wooded in 25% new oak, it has rose petal and ginger spice aromas and a palate of plum and red cherry.

Marimist is a new Chardonnay from Hasher, sourced from six different parcels in the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley. Fermented in 23% new oak, with full malolactic, it has saffron, white flower and vanilla spice top notes, a dab of crème fraîche and a nice medley of pear, citrus and orange water flavours.

n: Hasher Family Wines Nauticus Sauvignon Blanc
d: Nauticus comes from three sites in the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, picked in four different stages for complexity. Combining older barrel and concrete egg components, it’s a racy, subtly wooded, semi-Fumé style with appealing restraint, nettle, rock salt and gooseberry flavours and a herbal twist.

Part of a rapidly improving range at Hasher Family Wines, made by Natasha Williams, this Pinot Noir comes from the older vines on the property and is a blend of the 115 and 113 clones. Elegant, lithe and ethereal, this is a textured, sappy, well-balanced red with pomegranate and wild strawberry flavours and fine-grained tannins.

n: Haute Cabrière Haute Collection OVP Amphora Chardonnay
d: Tim Hoek uses grapes from the second-oldest Chardonnay block in South Africa, planted in 1983, to make this wine, with fermentation and ageing in terracotta amphoras. Wet stone and petrichor aromas are a scented introduction to a palate of pear, citrus and fennel, complemented by leesy texture and an earthy undertone.

n: Haute Cabrière Haute Collection OVP Chardonnay
d: This Old Vine Project Chardonnay comes from a 0.5-hectare parcel in Franschhoek that was established in 1983. Fermented and matured in an equal combination of one-third new barrels and amphoras, it has aromas of nougat and baking spices and a racy, mineral-etched palate complemented by a subtle bitter twist.

n: Haute Cabrière Haute Collection Pinot Noir
d: A quartet of different Burgundy clones – 115, 116, 667 and 777 – contribute to this welljudged Franschhoek Pinot Noir, which used to be a single vineyard wine but now comes from four blocks. Rose petal, rooibos tea and dried herb aromas are a scented portal to a palate of rhubarb and redcurrant complemented by understated oak spices.

n: Haute Cabrière Pierre Jourdan Achim OVP Amphora Blanc de Blancs CC
d: Named after the late Achim von Arnim, one of the key figures in the history of the Franschhoek Valley, this all-Chardonnay bubbly used terracotta amphoras for the fermentation of its base wine. Lees aged in bottle for 36 months, it’s a pithy, savoury, slightly salty bubbly with old-vine concentration that tastes drier than its seven grams of dosage would suggest.

n: Haute Cabrière Pierre Jourdan Blanc de Blancs CC
Haute Cabrière Pierre Jourdan Brut CC

d: Trust Kiara Scott to shoot the lights out with her first vintage of Carignan from the Bottelary Hills. Sourced from just five rows of the variety, this impressive début is only sold in magnums. Showing some clove spice and tobacco leaf from 15% whole bunches, it’s a savoury, stony style with bramble and redcurrant flavours, sinewy tannins and wonderful complexity. Bravo!

Part of a massively improved range under the talented Kiara Scott, this estate Chenin Blanc was picked in five stages for added layers of complexity. Peach, citrus and subtle orange zest flavours are complemented by well-integrated older oak and a lip-smacking mineral core. Promising stuff.

Like all the new Hazendal releases, this reflects the change in direction for the better at the property. The 15% whole bunch fermentation is adroitly used here adding perfume and texture to a wine with rose petal aromas, strawberry, plum and black cherry flavours and a kiss of spicy oak.

A very solid first release from Kiara Scott, this is a Sauvignon Blanc with layers, thanks to partial skin contact and components that saw concrete eggs, seasoned oak and stainless steel. Salty, tangy and sappy, it has an appealing medley of greengage, gooseberry and kiwi fruit and a taut, tapering finish.

Proving that Hazendal has “great potential for Syrah”, as Kiara Scott puts it, this is a lightly wooded, medium-bodied style that was fermented with 22% whole clusters. Wonderful value at R139, it has red berry, black cherry and tapenade flavours, layered tannins and a savoury finish.

Drawing on the experience she developed at Brookdale with white Rhône varieties, Kiara Scott’s new blend marries Roussanne and 42% Marsanne from a total of 0.4 hectares. Subtle wet stone, cardamom and allspice aromas segue into a palate of citrus, musk and angelica root framed by subtle oak and driven by fresh acidity.

Artjesvlei comes from the top part of the Sanford vineyard, showcasing the 777 clone. Tobacco leaf, rose petal and North African spice aromas segue into a detailed, layered, enticingly perfumed palate that wouldn’t look out of place in Chambolle-Musigny. The 30% new oak is superbly done, framing a palate of red cherry, pomegranate and pink grapefruit and savoury tannins.

Swinsian is one of a pair of excellent wines under Nadia Newton Johnson’s Hearth label. Made with grapes from the cooler, south-facing Siberia vineyard, it’s a self-assured Chardonnay with full malolactic and 30% new wood, offering layers of oatmeal, lemon butter and subtle patisserie spices and a touch of flinty reduction.

Up three points with an extra year in bottle, this is a scented, comparatively light-bodied Pinot Noir that’s all about perfume and fruit rather than oak. Forward, floral and lightly balsamic, it has layers of sweet aromatic spices, goji berry and pomegranate, a nip of tannin and a forest floor undertone.

n: Highlands Road Sauvignon Blanc White Reserve
d: Using grapes that deliver “pyrazine character, not thiols”, according to Vanessa Simkiss, this is a stylish, barrel-fermented Sauvignon Blanc from Elgin’s cool climate. Sappy, tangy and lightly savoury, it carries its oak lightly, with layers of parsley, cucumber and pink grapefruit, a hint of cream and some subtle vanilla spice.

n: Hillcrest Estate Atlantic Slopes Quarry Merlot
Hillcrest Estate Atlantic Slopes Sauvignon Blanc

d: Jocelyn Hogan sourced this superb Chenin Blanc from two east-facing blocks on the granite soils of the Paardeberg. Refreshingly low in alcohol at 12%, this has appealing texture and weight from full malolactic in a low-acid year, understated oak, wonderful purity and focus, some stony freshness and flavours of citrus and fennel.

Among the Cape’s more individual reds, this is a blend of equal parts Cabernet Sauvignon from Stellenbosch and Cinsault from Somerset West with 28% Carignan from Wellington. The oak is nicely understated here framing a palate that’s much more than the sum of its parts. Racy and refreshing, it has layers of cassis, blood orange and Campari spices, and a hint of clove from 10% whole bunches.

n: Hogan Wines Mirror for the Sun Cabernet Franc
d: Sourced from the Steyn family’s Eendrag farm overlooking False Bay, this is consistently among the best Cabernet Francs in the Cape. Matured in 20% new wood, this has a cool elegance that’s reminiscent of some Loire Valley reds, with red plum, bay leaf and red pepper flavours, a waft of graphite and ocean breeze and beautifully understated tannins.

"My most Chablis-like Chardonnay yet," is how Jocelyn Hogan describes her 2025 release, made with grapes from Banghoek and a 20% component from the Helderberg. Barrel fermented with full malolactic in older barrels, this has subtle wood spices, a white flower top note, racy acidity and flavours of lemon zest and dried honey.

n: Holder Vineyard and Wines Dorper Cabernet Franc
d: A new wine from Reg Holder is always something to celebrate, given the quality of his existing range. This small-volume Cabernet Franc comes from ferricrete soils on the Mulderbosch farm and is a promising début. Matured in fourth-fill oak, it’s a scented, aciddriven style with graphite and basil aromas, racy plum and black cherry flavours and the succulent tannins that are part of the house style here.

n: Holder Vineyard and Wines Dorper OVP Chenin Blanc
d: This is Reg Holder’s sixth vintage from a 1981 block of Chenin Blanc on the Sterhuis farm in the Bottelary Hills. Picked in four stages for complexity, it comes from a cooler, south-west facing slope and shows delightful granitic freshness, with savoury, umami-like intensity, pear and citrus fruit and a hint of melon sweetness.

n: Holder Vineyard and Wines Dorper Pinotage
d: One of the Cape’s best – and most reliable Pinotages – this marries components from the Bottelary Hills, the Polkadraai Hills and the Lower Helderberg. Enticingly floral and ethereal, it’s a Pinotage for Pinot Noir lovers, with bramble, plum and summer pudding flavours, very subtle oak, granular, palate-coating tannins and engaging freshness.

n: Holder Vineyard and Wines Dorper Rosé
d: Sourced from two different farms – Sterhuis and Sonop – this is a pale, direct-pressed rosé made with Pinotage and 1.5% Viognier. Showing nice texture and mouthfeel, it has a savoury undertone from older oak and a palate of redcurrant, raspberry and gin botanicals.

Rhino Tart ferments this cooler climate Stellenbosch Sauvignon Blanc in older barrels to give it a little more texture and nuance. Tangy, crisp and well-defined, it has intriguing layers of celery, elderflower and tarragon, racy acidity and a dab of cream.

The highlight of the current Idiom range from the Bottega family’s estate overlooking False Bay, this is a delicious expression of Semillon that ticks all the right boxes. Lightly wooded in 15% new barrels, it has enticing aromas of fennel and dill, a textured palate of custard and citrus fruit and a complex, lingering finish.

Lucinda Heyns’ Cinsault is a wine that whispers rather than shouts at you and is even more enticing for it. Fermented with 100% whole bunches, it has the elegance that comes with the territory in Darling, flavours of strawberry, rooibos tea and Negroni spices and savoury, fine-grained tannins.

Two blocks on the same farm in Wellington supply the grapes for this characteristically refined, restrained Grenache from Lucinda Heyns. Fermented with 80% whole clusters, it’s pale and ethereal, with understated oak spices, goji berry and redcurrant fruit and detailed, fine-grained tannins.

The Karibib farm in the Polkadraai Hills is the source of Lucinda Heyns’ subtle, 80% whole bunch-fermented Pinotage, a grape that she handles like one of its parents, Pinot Noir. Rose petal, paprika and potpourri aromas segue into a palate of wild strawberry, hibiscus and watermelon complemented by savoury tannins.

Paarl is better known for full-bodied reds than it is for wine like this subtle, elegant Syrah, which weighs in at just 12.2% alcohol. Rose petal and white pepper aromas are a scented introduction to a palate of summer berries, rooibos tea and ginger and a refreshing, almost ethereal finish. Every bit as good as the 2023 from Janno Briers-Louw.

n: Iona Beeskamp Single Vineyard Pinot Noir
d: Beeskamp is a brilliant new Pinot Noir from Iona, sourced from comparatively young vines planted at 415 metres with the 115 and 667 clones. Elegant, floral and ethereal, it has a nice frame of granular tannins, a succulent palate of goji berry and summer pudding, plenty of zip and energy and scented 25% new oak. Quite the début.

One of a very impressive range of Chardonnays from Werner Müller, this uses raw material predominantly from the Kloof, Kraal and Fynbos vineyards. Wild yeast fermented in 20% new oak, it has some mid-palate texture from 20% malolactic, appealing pear, citrus and stone fruit flavours, tangy acidity and a waft of oyster shell.

Made with a trio of Burgundy clones – 115, 667 and 777 – this is an appealing, cool climate Pinot Noir that was fermented with wild yeasts and bottled unfined and unfiltered. Stylishly wooded in 25% new oak, it has aromas of rose petal and tomato leaf, racy cranberry and red cherry fruit, fine tannins and plenty of supporting acidity.

Much more than your run-of-the-mill Sauvignon Blanc, this is a blend with 8% Semillon that benefitted from a touch of barrel fermentation. Herbal, flinty and appealingly complex for a wine that’s widely available, this marries flavours of greengage, lime and passion fruit with plenty of sappy, palate-cleansing acidity and a hint of vanilla spice.

n: Iona Elgin Highlands Wild Ferment Sauvignon Blanc
d: Barrel fermented in older oak, with 12% Semillon for company, this is a smaller volume Sauvignon Blanc release from quartz, clay and sandstone soils on the Iona farm. Savoury and appropriately “wild”, it has some subtle wood spices, flavours of umami and pink grapefruit and a racy, stony, mineral-etched core.

It’s always a treat to taste the top, site-specific Iona Chardonnays alongside each other and compare and contrast them. Fynbos is the broader of the pair, sourced from a 1.12-hectare block on north-facing clay soils. Textured, yet focused, it’s an effortlessly complex wine from Werner Müller, with kumquat, citrus and pink grapefruit flavours, a dab of crème fraîche and an appealing bitter twist.

Kloof comes from a cool 1.18-hectare site at 410 metres with quartz-based, rocky soils. Produced with the CY96 and 277 clones, it’s an appropriately focused, pithy style of Chardonnay with nuanced 20% new oak, a hint of malolactic, mouth-watering acidity and minerality, hints of brine and kelp and a flinty top note. Elgin meets Grand Cru Chablis.

n: Iona Kroon Single Vineyard Pinot Noir
d: Kroon is planted with the 115 and 777 clones on iron-rich red clay soils at Iona and often has a slightly ferrous undertone. Notes of earth and beetroot are complemented by red cherry and wild strawberry fruit, stylish 25% new French oak, textured tannins and a waft of tomato leaf. Needs a little more time in bottle.

Produced as what owner Andrew Gunn calls a “bit of an indulgence”, this smells and tastes like Nebbiolo, which isn't always easy outside north-west Italy. Using grapes from seven-yearold vines, it has aromas of tar and pressed rose petals, savoury tannins, fresh supporting acidity and a core of plum, red cherry and dried herbs.

n: Iona Pax Aut Bellum Brut CC
d: A new bubbly from Iona, this is an all-Pinot Noir Blanc de Noirs made with the help of consultant Pierre de Klerk. Showing some attractive, autolysis-derived aromas of toast and malt, it has appealing aniseed and wild strawberry flavours and a racy, tangy, acid-driven finish.

Consistently offering good value for money, Louis van de Riet’s range has something for (almost) everyone. Modern, glossy and self-assured, this Western Cape Cabernet Sauvignon combines grapes from Herbertsdale on the Garden Route and Langeberg-Garcia. Curated in third and fourth-fill oak, it has appealing flavours of mint, plum, cassis and dried herbs and finely integrated tannins.

A strong candidate for the title of best Barbera in the Cape, this wouldn’t look out of place in Piedmont. Matured in older oak barrels, it has tobacco leaf and leather aromas, sweetly fruited flavours of wild strawberry and red cherry and the savoury tannins that are so often part of the DNA of Italian wines.

n: Jakkalsvlei Lord Jackal Cape Vintage Reserve
d: The best Cape Vintage release yet from Louis van der Riet, this small volume fortified was made from just two tons of Touriga Nacional. Using a saignée of 20% of the juice to concentrate what’s left behind, this is beautifully balanced and refined, with lovely aromas of violet and liquorice, finely integrated tannins, glossy fig and blackberry fruit and wonderful accord between acidity and 92 grams of residual sugar.

The Klein Karoo is starting to develop a reputation for Chardonnay, thanks to wines like this one from Louis van der Riet. Subtly fermented in third use, 300-litre barrels, this a touch of struck match reduction, lots of energy and tension, lemongrass, cardamom and wet stone flavours and a waft of patisserie spices.

Sourced from the Jakkalsvlei in Mossel Bay and Langeberg-Garcia, this is an unusual red blend from Louis van der Riet, made with Pinotage and 49% Syrah. Subtle gingerbread and rose petal aromas segue into a palate of bramble, raspberry and wild strawberry, a hint of wild mountain herbs and a textured finish.

Chenin Blanc is the Breedekloof Valley’s secret weapon, especially at an affordable price like this one from Ivy du Toit. Wild yeast fermented in amphoras and Hungarian oak, it’s a fresh, medium-bodied style with quince and tarte tatin flavours, subtle wood spices and a spine of fresh, tangy acidity.

n: Jasper Raats Cuvée Rika Pinot Noir
d: Cuvée Rika is a fresh, savoury, very lightly wooded Pinot Noir from Jasper Raats, blended with 14% Cinsault for added complexity. (No wonder it tastes a little Pinotage-like.) Peppery and herbal, it has layers of raspberry, tomato leaf and wild strawberry and a spine of sinewy tannins.

Produced in a low-intervention style, with natural yeast fermentation and no filtration, this comes from a single parcel on the Stellenzicht farm. Comparatively well-structured and serious for a Cinsault, it has a rose petal and forest floor nose and a palate of redcurrant, tobacco leaf and hibiscus supported by savoury tannins.

It doesn’t advertise the fact on the label, but this is a varietal Sauvignon Blanc, picked in two stages for extra complexity. Wild fermented in older oak barrels, this was bottled unfined and unfiltered, showing layers of nettle, lime and elderflower and a refined, alluringly flinty finish. A South African Pouilly-Fumé.

Skebenga has one of my favourite labels, paying tribute the Cape Town underworld. Marrying Cinsault, 39% Pinotage and 10% Pinot Noir, using grapes from the two ends of the Helderberg, it has appealing flavours of rooibos tea, wild strawberry and red cherry and a firmish, appealingly savoury finish.

n: Jasper Raats The Silk Weaver Sangiovese
Joostenberg Die Agteros OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Three different blocks, all of them planted in 1989, supply the raw material for this dryfarmed OVP Chenin Blanc. Leesy and intense, it’s an unfiltered, full malolactic style with understated oak, impressive zip and energy and flavours of pear, citrus and yellow apple. Refreshingly low in alcohol at 12.7%.

Tyrrell Myburgh was ahead of the game with Fairhead, producing a highly original blend of Roussanne, 35% Chenin Blanc, 12% Albariño and 9% Viognier. Saffron, fynbos and aromatic baking spice aromas segue into a palate of pear, peach and quince with a waft of ginger and a smooth, palate-coating finish.

Always prepared to try something different Tyrrel Myburgh makes this Rhône-meetsPortugal blend with Syrah, 24% Mourvèdre, 10% Grenache and 5% Touriga Nacional. Thirty per cent whole bunches add some structure and perfume here, complementing a palate of bramble, red cherry and tobacco leaf.

Klippe Kou – great name – uses Syrah grapes from seven different block on the farm. Low in alcohol for a Paarl red, it has subtle 30% whole bunch notes of pepper and allspice, plenty of depth and structure, damson and black olive flavours and a violet top note. Good now, but will develop further in bottle.

This is the third release of a bubbly from Tyrrel Myburgh, made in partnership with Cava producer Alta Alella in Catalunya. Produced with early picked Chenin Blanc from the farm in Paarl, it’s a pithy, tangy, bone-dry style with flavours of lemon, fennel and sourdough bread and a slightly earthy finish.

n: Joostenberg Noble Late Harvest Chenin Blanc
d: A distinguished part of the range since 2001, this 100% botrytis-affected Chenin Blanc is made almost every year and is an engagingly drinkable sweet wine. Marrying 198 grams of residual sugar and plenty of supporting acidity, it has appealing pear tart, honey and grapefruit flavours and nicely restrained volatility.

Philip Albert combines Cabernet Sauvignon and 8% Merlot from Joostenberg’s estate close to the border between Stellenbosch and Paarl. Elegant, refreshing and well balanced, it has bright, racy natural acidity, subtle 15% new wood, aromas of mint and blackcurrant leaf and a palate of redcurrant and cassis.

One of a handful of great Assyrtikos produced outside Greece, this is a wine that gets better with every vintage. Planted on a windy site at the top of the farm, next to the Polkadraai Hills, it’s vibrant, stony and energetic, with flavours of citrus and greengage, good structure and grip and chiselled, mouth-watering tannins. Very exciting.

The oak is arguably a little too assertive, but it’s part of the Jordan style and has many fans. Fermented with 50% malolactic to “tie it all together” in the words of Sjaak Nelson, this has flavours of tangerine, lemon zest and cinnamon spice and a creamy, palate-caressing midpalate. Getting fresher by the vintage.

Cobblers Hill - a reference to the Jordan family’s time in the shoe trade - is a seamless assemblage of Cabernet Sauvignon, 22% Petit Verdot and 9% each of Cabernet Franc and Merlot. Aged in older French and 9% American oak (the latter on the Merlot component), it’s a modern, virus-free blend with impressive structure, balance and freshness, cassis and bramble fruit, fine-grained tannins and a balsamic undertone.

Great value from Sjaak Nelson, this rosé combines Merlot with 13% Syrah and is the best seller on the farm. Benefitting from fruit that used to go into the Black Magic red, it’s a serious, unwooded, direct-pressed style that tastes as good as it looks, with raspberry and wild strawberry fruit and a savoury, lightly spicy finish.

Showcasing the quality of the Montpellier clone, this uses grapes from an old-vine block planted in 1983. Fermented with full malolactic in a combination of older oak and stainless steel, it has appealing pear and apricot flavours, a dab of cream, toasty, vanilla spices and plenty of underlying zip, focus and acidity.

Surprisingly light in alcohol at just 12.5%, this is a Chardonnay that looks towards the United States rather than Burgundy in style, with lots of flavour, texture and intensity. Toasty 51% new oak is a bit part of the wine’s appeal, complemented by layers of popcorn, citrus and patisserie spices and a buttery undertone from 50% malolactic.

I tasted this remarkable wine twice – once sighted and once blind – and I’m convinced it’s one of the wines of the vintage. Floral, nuanced and enticingly balanced, it’s a seamless mix of Cabernet Sauvignon and 33% Merlot that was aged in French and 33% American oak. Rose petal, violet and espresso coffee aromas segue into a palate of cassis, blackberry and Asian spices with filigree tannins and a balsamic twist. World class.

n: Jordan The Long Fuse Cabernet Sauvignon
d: The Long Fuse is an unblended Cabernet Sauvignon that uses raw material from different blocks on the farm, the oldest of which dates back to 1996. Made in a cooler climate style, it marries aromas of violet and mint with a palate of plum, green herbs and blackcurrant pastille, scented French and 10% American oak and a spine of sinewy tannins.

The Outlier comes from a single block planted in 1982 – Old Vine Project status beckons – and is one of the more complex Cape Sauvignon Blancs. Fermented in mostly new French and 38% American oak, it’s a rich, textured, intense white with leesy weight, full malolactic and flavours of cream and pink grapefruit. One for Chardonnay lovers.

It’s good to see the Jordans persisting with Riesling, which remains a comparatively difficult sell in the Cape. This hails from a vineyard planted in 1986 and is just off dry at 7.1 grams of residual sugar. Tangy, refreshing and self-assured, it has notes of quince, lemon and lime, a hint of sherbet, palate-cleansing acidity and engaging, apposite sweetness.

Timepiece comes from the oldest registered Cabernet Sauvignon vineyard in South Africa, planted in 1987. (That’s the effect of leaf roll virus for you.) Curated in 38% new French and American oak, it has aromas of coconut, eucalyptus and baking spices, impressive underlying structure, intense blackcurrant and damson fruit, savoury tannins and plenty of youthful vigour and concentration.

One of a trio of Chardonnays in the Jordan range, this is the most complete and well balanced of the lot in my view. Tank, new and older oak and concrete components add to the complexity here, with impressive old-vine concentration, layers of quince, stone fruit and lemongrass, spicy oak and a subtle bitter twist.

Fermented and aged in concrete eggs, stainless steel and older barrels, this is part of an excellent line-up of whites from Jordan. Drier and more focused than the Inspector Péringuey bottling, it’s a tangy, stony expression of the grape, with underlying old-vine concentration, flavours of lemongrass and green apple and a hint of wood spice.

One of a pair of brilliant Sauvignon Blancs from Sjaak Nelson and the Jordan team, this is the pithier of the pair, showing petrichor and rocket aromas, some subtle wood spices from a combination of 11% new barrels, older oak and amphoras, layers of wet stone, elderflower and lime and a tangy, tapering finish. Wonderful, complex stuff.

An excellent follow up to the 2023 release, this Bordeaux-style white blend draws on Michael Dawson’s experience in the Constantia Valley. Pairing Sauvignon Blanc and 17% Semillon, it has some subtle struck match reduction, a palate of citrus, lanolin and custard and a tangy pink grapefruit finish.

Chardonnay is a signature variety at Journey’s End, making the most of the winery’s cool slopes close to False Bay. Neatly fermented in 15% new oak, with plenty of lees stirring in barrel, this is a creamy, textured style of Chardonnay with citrus and tangerine flavours, some scented baking spice sweetness and a fresh finish.

Tasted pre-release at the winery, this is a new, top-of-the-range Chardonnay from Journey’s End, made with a barrel selection from a single 5.5-hectare parcel on the estate. Fermented in new French oak, it’s a rich, full-flavoured style with notes of orange peel, citrus and toffee fudge, toasty oak and a hint of stony reduction.

Merlot is well suited to the cooler parts of Stellenbosch, where the influence of False Bay is at its most marked. Appealingly perfumed, with wafts of capsicum and tomato leaf, this has a palate of black cherry, paprika and dark chocolate and supple, glossy tannins.

Among the highlights of the Journey’s End range, this comes from a single, one-hectare parcel within sight of False Bay. Plush, smooth and textured, it’s a comparatively supple, forward expression of the variety, with violet and laurel aromas, nicely integrated seconduse oak and a Syrah-like palate of tapenade and blackberry.

Mike Dawson uses grapes from two vineyards on the farm to make this unblended Cabernet Sauvignon. It’s a well-made, medium-bodied red with textured tannins, some cool climate freshness, top notes of mint and pencil shavings, plum and cassis fruit and 30% new wood.

Rooi – red in Afrikaans – is a Bordeaux-meets-the-northern-Rhône-meets-the-Cape blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, 33% Merlot, 20% Syrah, 10% Grenache and 5% Pinotage. Part of a new range at Kaapzicht, it has subtle oak, bramble and summer berry flavours, fine-grained tannins and good texture for a 2023 release.

Hard to beat for value in South Africa, this is a very lightly wooded Chenin Blanc that reflects extremely well on winemakers Danie Steytler and Kayleigh Hattingh. Racy, sappy and just off dry at 4.7 grams of residual sugar, this has a touch of oak, pear, citrus and cherimoya fruit and tangy underlying minerality.

Kliprug comes from a bush vine parcel that was planted in 1982 on decomposed granite and ferricrete soils close to the winery in the Bottelary Hills. Fermented in 20% new oak and (for the first time) Austrian foudres, this has appealing yellow apple, lemongrass and baking spice flavours, some nectarine sweetness and subtle wood integration.

Outstandingly good value for a Chenin Blanc from an Old Vine Project vineyard planted in 1985, this is a textbook expression of the grape from the Bottelary Hills. Three days of skin contact add a little grip here, bringing some texture to a palate of peach, pear and green apple complemented by a waft of oak.

Year in, year out, the 1947 block delivers exceptional quality and fruit concentration. Naturally fermented and appealingly dry, this has some subtle vanilla spice from 15% new 500-litre Stockinger barrels, flavours of passion fruit, nectarine and lime, a top note of honeysuckle and white flowers and a poised, lingering finish. One of the world’s great Chenin Blancs.

Picked early in a warm year, this is a fitting tribute to the end of Abrie Beeslaar’s distinguished tenure at Kanonkop. Sourced from a single block planted in 1953, it’s always one of the most structured, age-worthy Pinotages on the market, with a proven track record. The new Burgundian oak is very well-integrated here, adding some subtle aromatic spice notes to a palate of blackberry, fig and liquorice supported by grippy, nicely integrated tannins.

I’m not convinced this will age as well as the more recently released 2021 Cabernet Sauvignon, but it shows that Kanonkop’s reputation for producing long-lived wines is well deserved. Mint, dried herb and wet earth aromas lead you into a palate that’s savoury and well structured, with layers of leather and cassis and a balsamic twist. The cooler vintage is apparent on the palate.

One of those wines that helps to pay the bills at Kanonkop, this is a 240,000-bottle blend that mostly comes from the Helderberg. Well priced for a Cabernet Sauvignon of this quality, it has a frame of toasty spicy oak, good structure and depth, a spine of tannin and flavours of mint, fynbos and blackcurrant pastille.

A wine that carries the Pinotage flag worldwide, offering a textbook example of the variety at a very affordable price. Sourced from younger blocks, it has appealing second and third-fill barrels, granular tannins, liquorice, black cherry and raspberry fruit and a sheen of patisserie sweetness. Hard to beat at the price.

Made in what owner Johann Kriege admits was a “sorting table year”, this is one of the less exciting Paul Sauers. I tasted it twice – once sighted, once blind – and reached the same conclusion: Kanonkop should have considered skipping the vintage. Made in smaller quantities than usual, it’s a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, 23% Cabernet Franc and 16% Merlot, with assertive new oak, redcurrant and blackcurrant leaf flavours, firmish, savoury tannins and a slightly thin finish. Drinkable enough, but not a wine to keep.

Re-released with ten years in barrel and bottle, this is your chance to try a Kanonkop Pinotage with a decade under its belt. Still showing plenty of grip – it was made at the start of the drought – it has lots of mocha and dark chocolate from 80% new oak, bramble, fig and black cherry fruit, a hint of forest floor and a balsamic undertone.

Serious stuff from one of the best Pinotage producers on the planet, this was made by Abrie Beeslaar before he left Kanonkop to do his own thing. Made with grapes from five older blocks, it’s structured, intense and very aromatic, with toasty 80% new oak, layers of bramble, summer berries and ginger spice and plush, palate-coating tannins. Good now and will improve in bottle.

Kara-Tara uses grapes from Elgin, the Overberg and Stellenbosch and is all about fruit and focus rather than oak. Fermented in 10% new barrels, it has appealing pear, citrus and greengage flavours, palate-cleansing acidity and a subtle bitter twist. More than the sum of its parts.

José Conde’s skills as a blender are apparent in this pan-Cape cuvée of Pinot Noir grapes from Breedekloof, the Ceres Plateau, Elgin and Overberg. Deftly fermented with 20% whole bunches, it has juicy pomegranate and wild strawberry fruit, a dab of oak and a mineral core.

Broad Valley in the Overberg supplies the fruit for this well-judged Pinot Noir from Jaen Lochner and José Condé, combining the 113, 115 and 777 clones. Twenty per cent whole clusters add a savoury note here to a palate of raspberry and goji berry embellished by scented oak.

Graham Weerts of Capensis is the winemaker here, so it’s no surprise that this high-altitude Chardonnay is so good. Volumes are small, alas, but this is a stylish, refined expression of the grape, with some gunflint reduction, nicely understated oak, citrus, fynbos and cardamom flavours and a spine of racy acidity.

Sourced from vines at a lofty 1,100 metres in the Northern Cape, this is an impressive single-parcel Shiraz from Lourens van der Westhuizen. One for fans of cooler climate styles, it has engaging sage, kelp and white pepper aromas, good intensity and structure, a palate of cooked meat and black olive and an earthy, ferrous undertone.

Amphitheatre is a catch-all blend of five different varieties, partnering equal parts Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah with 17% Merlot and 8% Petit Verdot. Subtly wooded, it’s a grippy, full-bodied style with flavours of paprika, green herbs, red cherry and woodsmoke, a touch of tomato leaf and a firm finish.

Two vineyards on a crest of a hill in the Blaauwklippen Valley are the source of this varietal Cabernet Sauvignon from Alex Starey. Matured in older barrels – part of the style at Keermont – it’s a floral, graphite-scented red with racy acidity, cassis and bramble fruit flavours and smooth, palate-caressing tannins. Understated, as ever.

Whatever the vintage conditions throw at him, Alex Starey always seems to make a superb sweet wine under the Fleurfontein label, combining Sauvignon Blanc and 17% Roussanne. Dried on the vine, it has a remarkable 242 grams of residual sugar, exotic flavours of mango, honey and peach syrup, plenty of volatile acidity, subtle wood and enough acidity to lift and freshen the finish.

Alex Starey is often regarded as a Syrah specialist, but he can turn his hand to Bordeaux grapes too, not least Merlot. Sourced from two blocks and blended with 2% Malbec, it’s leafy, elegant and refined with potpourri and marjoram aromas adding perfume to a palate of paprika, capsicum and summer berries.

n: Keermont Single Vineyard Series Pondokrug Cabernet Franc
d: Showing plenty of freshness and natural acidity, Pondokrug hails from a cooler, west-facing site that has a lot in common with Topside. Fermented with 15% whole bunches, it has classic flavours of paprika, green pepper and black cherry, firmish tannins, nuanced oak and plenty of grip and concentration.

n: Keermont Single Vineyard Series Riverside OVP Chenin Blanc
d: The only one of Alex Starey’s Single Vineyard wines that comes from an Old Vine Project parcel, planted in 1971, this is a low-yielding Chenin Blanc from the valley floor. Dry but not short of fruit it segues from aromas of thatch, aniseed and nutmeg to a palate of citrus, greengage and a touch of cherimoya sweetness.

n: Keermont Single Vineyard Series Steepside Syrah
d: This superb Syrah comes from a north-facing block on loam and quartz soils that was planted with the SH470 clone in 2005. Showing the intensity of a hot site in a cooler vintage, it has lots of ferrous grip and concentration, a hint of stony reduction, layers of garrigue, graphite, blackberry and black olive and understated oak.

n: Keermont Single Vineyard Series Topside Syrah
d: Just nosing ahead of Steepside in 2021, which is a superb wine in its own right, this is a world-class Syrah from a cooler, west-facing slope at Keermont. Fifteen per cent whole clusters add some clove and tobacco leaf notes, bringing another layer of complexity to a palate of liquorice, white pepper and black cherry and summer berry fruit complemented by savoury, filigree tannins.

Combining fruit from Keermont’s three single sites, this is a blend of equal parts Steepside and Topside with 10% Sweetwater. Engagingly aromatic, with layers of rose petal, lavender and North African spices, it’s smooth, detailed and refined, with a palate of clove, strawberry and white pepper framed by finely judged tannins.

Effortlessly superseding the sum of its parts, this is a unique white blend from Alex Starey, based on Chenin Blanc with 16% Chardonnay, 15% Sauvignon Blanc, 7% Viognier and 3% each of Marsanne and Roussanne. Jasmine, thatch and honeysuckle aromas segue into a palate of citrus, pear and apricot complemented by subtle wood spices.

Kelvin Feku is the talented young assistant winemaker at Natte Valleij, working alongside Alex Milner. After producing a Rhône blend in 2023 and 2024, he’s gone back to a varietal Grenache in 2025. Modern, floral and appealing, it has plum and red berry flavours, layered, fine-grained tannins and a spicy finish.

n: Ken Forrester Dirty Little Secret Chenin Blanc Six
d: "Our most cerebral wine," is how Ken Forrester describes Dirty Little Secret. Made with a solera of eight vintages between 2016 and 2024, blended with 40% of the 2025 and 2026 harvests, this is the sixth release and it’s the best yet. Leesy, layered and extremely complex, it’s a superb expression of a 1959 vineyard in Piekenierskloof, with layers of umami, lanolin and almond paste and a savoury finish.

n: Ken Forrester Fairy Dust Field Blend
d: Fairy Dust is a new wine from the ever-creative Ken Forrester, made with a blend of Palomino and 48% Chenin Blanc from a single 1959 block in Piekenierskloof. Mealy, nutty and savoury, it’s a layered, high-altitude white blend with flavours of citrus, greengage and blanched almonds, understated oak, a waft of petrichor and mountain herbs and a mineral-etched core.

Previously made as an exclusive wine for the chef Franck Dangereux of The Foodbarn restaurant, this is now available to a wider audience. Sourced from the same Stellenbosch vineyard as Ken Forrester’s FMC, it’s a drier, more restrained style of Chenin Blanc with a nice interplay between baking spices, citrus and yellow apple flavours and racy, palatecleansing acidity.

n: Ken Forrester Old Vine Reserve Chenin Blanc
d: Under screwcap since 2005 – Ken Forrester is often ahead of the game – this large-volume Chenin Blanc combines quantity and quality, doing a lot to introduce consumers to variety’s delights. Flavours of pear, green apple and tangerine are complemented by lime-like acidity some subtle baking spice notes from oak fermentation and a tangy, just off-dry finish.

Ken Forrester sources his well-made, stand-alone Roussanne from a pair of vineyards in Stellenbosch. Stylishly fermented in 10% new oak, it’s a nicely tethered style that avoids the trap of exotic fruit flavours. White flower and patisserie spice aromas lead you into a palate of peach, pear and lemon zest and a taut, pithy finish.

n: Ken Forrester Silver Rose Grenache Rosé
Ken Forrester Terre Noire Chenin Blanc
d: Terre Noire uses grapes from two sites in the Swartland – in Piketberg and the Paardeberg – and is the French translation of the Afrikaans name for the region. Barrel fermented in older oak with wild yeasts, it segues from aromas of vanilla spice, fennel and wet stones to a palate of green apple and waxed lemons and some appealing weight and texture.

"I wanted to avoid those chopped liver flavours," says Ken Forrester of this new varietal Mourvèdre from Stellenbosch. Aged in 50% new American oak to add a little vanilla and coconut sweetness, this has plenty of backbone and grip, damson, plum and red cherry flavours, some dried herbs and a firm, sinewy finish.

Part of what’s known as the Icon Range at Ken Forrester, this is a wine that never fails to delight its many fans around the globe. Sourced from two Stellenbosch vineyards planted in 1974 and 1975, it’s one of the driest FMCs in a while at just 5.2 grams of residual sugar and no botrytis in sight. Wild fermented in 30% new oak, it’s made with 22 different components, combining some subtle cinnamon and nutmeg aromas with a palate of yellow apple, pear and peach and a crisp, tapering finish.

Ken Forrester deserves the credit for seeing the potential for a renaissance of Grenache in South Africa in the mid-1990s, when the variety had fallen into disfavour. This is a racy, perfumed Piekenierskloof example with redcurrant, raspberry and pink grapefruit flavours and a touch of oak spices.

Three Halves is a Mediterranean style red blend of Mourvèdre and 23% Syrah from Stellenbosch and 19% Grenache from higher altitude Piekenierskloof. Finer and less extracted than it has been in the past, the 2024 release has aromas of white pepper, thyme and cola, plum, bramble and red berry flavours, graceful tannins and understated oak.

n: Kershaw Chardonnay Deconstructed Kogelberg Sandstone CY76
d: The broadest and most exotic of the three Deconstructed whites, this comes from three vineyards planted with the CY76 clone. Fermented and lees aged for 11 months in 50% new oak, this has appealing quince, citrus and white peach flavours, a patina of vanilla and cinnamon spice and enough zip and acidity to lift and freshen the finish.

n: Kershaw Chardonnay Deconstructed Lake District Bokkeveld Shale CY95
d: CY95 is the most widely planted of the so-called Dijon clones in South Africa, partly because it has a bit of everything about it. Showing some subtle ferrous grip from Bokkeveld shale soils, this has appealing texture and freshness, notes of beeswax and lanolin, scented 50% new oak and flavours of citrus zest, peach and lemon butter.

n: Kershaw Chardonnay Deconstructed Lake District Bokkeveld Shale CY96
d: Showcasing the qualities of the CY96 clone, which tends to have more structure, focus and minerality, this is the most “Burgundian” of Richard Kershaw’s mouth-watering line up of Deconstructed Chardonnays, with some subtle struck match reduction, aromas of petrichor and white flowers, appealing patisserie spices and ac core of lemongrass, macadamia nut and lime.

A wine for Chardonnay geeks, this wine uses four different Burgundy clones – CY95, 96, 76 and 548 – all of which are grown in Elgin. Deftly wooded in 30% new barrels, it’s tight, focused and refreshing, with impressive structure, a waft of nutmeg and vanilla, lemongrass and subtle stone fruit flavours and a tangy finish.

Four Pinot Noir clones contribute here - predominantly 115 and 777 with 10% each of 113 and 667. Racy, tangy and well structured, it’s a pithy, acid-driven style with a touch of tomato leaf on the nose, flavours of cranberry and redcurrant and a pure, focused finish complemented by 32% French oak. Needs another year or two in bottle.

Effectively a blend of two blocks that are normally bottled alone as Deconstructed Syrahs, this is a tribute to the work that Richard Kershaw and his team did in the vineyard and cellar in 2023. Combining the SH9c and SH22 clones, it has some subtle whole bunch spices, flavours of tapenade, steak tartare and dried herbs, an undertone of meaty reduction and a frame of scented 40% new oak.

n: Kershaw GPS Chardonnay Lower Duivenhoks River Chardonnay
d: Grown on limestone soils close to the ocean and the tip of Africa, this cool climate Chardonnay is entirely made with the CY95 Dijon clone. Showing aromas and flavours that owe something to Albariño and Sauvignon Blanc, it has layers of coriander, lemongrass, fresh herbs and wet stones, a hint of oyster shell and beautifully integrated 30% new oak.

There were no 2023 Deconstructed Syrahs because of the very wet growing season in Elgin, so fans of Richard Kershaw’s reds will have to be content with this wine from Klein River instead. Made with clone SH1, it’s a delicate, almost Pinot Noir-like number that reflects its cooler, south coast climate, with plenty of racy acidity, red cherry, clove and fynbos flavours, filigree tannins and subtle 33% new oak.

You wouldn’t need a GPS to find the well-frequented Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge and this is a very faithful expression of the sub-region. Showing a hint of meaty reduction, this has appealing rooibos tea, hibiscus and red berry flavours, scented 25% new oak and some underlying ferrous grip.

Now sourced entirely from the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, this is a stylish, separately fermented cuvée of Sauvignon Blanc and 39% Semillon that sees 10% new oak. Subtle vanilla spice and fynbos aromas segue into a palate of toast, grapefruit and coriander. The finish is racy, bright and mouth-wateringly fresh.

n: Kershaw Pinot Noir Deconstructed Kogelberg Sandstone PN115
d: One of a pair of impressive, sandstone-based Pinot Noirs from perfectionist Richard Kershaw, this is a comparatively grippy, intense expression of the normally more ethereal 115 clone. Showing a touch of good reduction, it’s more tannic than its pale colour would suggest, with plum, bramble and redcurrant flavours, appealing structure and well-integrated 50% new wood.

n: Kershaw Pinot Noir Deconstructed Kogelberg Sandstone PN777
d: Sourced from the same vineyard in Elgin as the 2023 release – it was absent from the range for four years before that – this is a floral, enticing expression of the widely planted 777 clone, with some clove spice from 30% whole bunches, flavours of redcurrant, wild strawberry and gingerbread and a racy, acid-driven finish.

Chardonnay specialist Richard Kershaw makes this impressive white with grapes from Elgin, with 15% from the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge and Lower Duivenhoks River. Fermented in 10% new oak, it’s a floral, restrained, tucked in style with a flinty top note, flavours of lemon butter, citrus peel and salted almond and a mineral core.

Based on fruit from Elgin, with a smaller component from the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, this is Richard Kershaw’s entry-point Pinot Noir. Fermented with 15% whole bunches and aged in 15% new oak, it has appealing cool climate flavours of redcurrant and pink grapefruit, a nip of tannin and a savoury finish.

"Raw and real" is how Charl du Plessis describes the style of this medium-bodied Grenache from the Swartland. Concrete fermented before ageing in older oak, it’s a floral, charming expression of the variety with some underlying savoury grip, plum, pomegranate and redcurrant flavours and a spicy finish.

Die Nagmuis is a medium-priced Syrah from koffieklip soils in the Swartland that was naturally fermented in concrete before ageing in older barrels. Serious, compact and appropriately ferrous, it has grippy tannins, flavours of steak tartare, damson and black olive and a chewy age-worthy finish.

Inspired by the qvevri wines of Georgia, this is a separately fermented cuvée of Grenache Blanc and 25% each of Semillon and Chenin Blanc, each of which spent seven months on skins. Earthy, complex and savoury, it has aromas of rose petal and rooibos tea, flavours of quince and dried orange peel and some underlying tannic grip.

Clara is all about sandstone, using grapes from four, cooler, east-facing slopes on the estate. Deftly fermented and aged in 50% new wood, which enhances rather than detracts from the wine, this is appealingly bright, tangy and refreshing, with a palate of lemongrass and green fig and a briny, oyster shell finish.

Perdeblokke is in a rich vein of form right now and is consistently among the best Sauvignon Blancs in the Cape. Sourced from a single site on sandstone, which mostly faces south, this is South Africa’s answer to a Pouilly-Fumé, showing lots of energy, layers of white pepper, lime and kiwi fruit, obsidian acidity and subtly integrated 20% new oak.

Matt Day is planning to blend 15% Pontac into this wine in future, but for now it remains an assemblage of Cabernet Sauvignon, 31% Syrah, 15% Petit Verdot and 12% Malbec. Light, fresh and well balanced, despite its 14.6% alcohol, it has scented 50% new French oak, flavours of mint, cassis and summer berries and fine-grained tannins.

Formerly labelled as the estate Chardonnay, this comes from two blocks on the farm. Fermented in 50% new barrels before being transferred to Stockinger foudres, it’s a textured, medium-weight style with pear and banana fruit, some supporting acidity from granite soils and deftly handled 30% malolactic.

Matt Day’s focus on Sauvignon Blanc has trickled down from the top wines to this entry-point bottling. Sourced from the Glendirk and Klein Constantia estates, this has a touch of oak, lots of granite-derived freshness, flavours of greengage, lime and pear and a tangy, palatecleansing finish.

The wet 2023 vintage in Constantia resulted in 10% botrytis, the highest proportion since 1997, giving the resulting wine a slightly more exotic feel. Macerated on skins for two weeks before fermentation, followed by ageing in 50% new Austrian, French and Hungarian oak, it has layers of guava, peach and tarte tatin, 162 grams of residual sugar, a plush, ample palate and enough acidity to lift and freshen the finish. Broader than the 2022.

n: Klein Roosboom Limited Release Blanc Fumé
d: A wine that’s influenced by the whites of Pessac-Léognan, this varietal Sauvignon Blanc was fermented in 50% new oak and underwent full malolactic. Savoury and complex, it has good extract and concentration, layers of blackcurrant leaf, lime and grapefruit and a sheen of vanilla and nutmeg spice.

n: Klein Roosboom Limited Release Cabernet Sauvignon
d: Showing more structure and depth than many of its competitors from Durbanville, this is a deeply coloured Cabernet Sauvignon that was aged in 40% new French and American oak. Mint, dill and cigar box aromas segue into a palate of damson and cassis supported by granitic minerality.

Barrel-fermented and lees aged in second use barrels, this Chardonnay from Piti Coetzee has some mid-palate texture from full malolactic, subtle toasty oak, flavours of melon, citrus and tangerine and a refreshing, well-balanced finish.

n: Klein Roosboom Limited Release Chenin Blanc
d: The oak is all new here, but it’s skilfully folded into the wine, with six days of skin contact adding some welcome structure. Pithy and refreshing, it has appealing quince, pear and green apple fruit, plenty of supporting acidity and some added texture from 15% malolactic.

n: Klein Roosboom My Way Brut CC
Klein Roosboom My Way Brut Rosé CC
d: My Way is an equal cuvée of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir that uses 10% barrel fermentation on the base wine. Aged on lees for 43 months, it’s a pale, ethereal style with rose petal and sourdough bread aromas and a palate of lemon zest and wild strawberry.

n: Klein Roosboom My Way Petit Verdot
Kleine Zalze Family Reserve Cabernet Sauvignon

d: A Chardonnay that has gained in complexity in recent vintages, thanks to the use of amphoras and concrete eggs alongside 26% new French oak barrels. Refreshingly low in alcohol at just 12.6%, it has peach, citrus and lemongrass flavours, a waft of cinnamon spice and some mid-palate texture from partial malolactic fermentation.

n: Kleine Zalze Family Reserve OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Hats off to RJ Botha and his team for making 20,000 bottles of Old Vine Project Chenin Blanc of this quality. Fermented in older barrels, amphoras and concrete eggs, it uses grapes from three vineyards on the False Bay side of Stellenbosch, producing a wine that has quince, apricot and patisserie spice flavours and a fresh, stony finish.

n: Kleine Zalze Family Reserve OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Fresher and brighter than the 2024 release, which is also still on the market, this 2025 made in what RJ Botha calls a “much easier vintage”. Using concrete eggs, amphoras and older 400-litre barrels, it’s a drier, more focused Chenin Blanc with pear, greengage and wet stone flavours and a tangy, lemongrass finish.

n: Kleine Zalze Family Reserve Sauvignon Blanc
d: Family Reserve is a 60/40 cuvée from Durbanville and Darling that was fermented and aged in a medley of barrels, concrete eggs and stainless steel. Herbal and intense, it has top notes of parsley and padrón peppers, a palate of pink grapefruit and cream soda and a waft of sweet vanilla spice.

Different vineyards in Stellenbosch most of them on the western end of the Helderberg and in Faure, supply the grapes for this 25% whole bunch-fermented Syrah. The alcohol is on the high side perhaps, but this has plenty of concentration, flavours of blackberry, fig and Asian spices and toasty 50% new French oak.

n: Kleine Zalze Heritage Vineyards OVP Chenin Blanc
d: "It helps to get the message out," says RJ Botha, commenting on the bargain price of this Old Vine Project Chenin Blanc. Fermented and aged in stainless steel and older oak barrels, it has white flower and baking spice aromas, peach, honeydew melon and citrus zest flavours and a fresh, acid-driven finish.

n: Kleine Zalze Heritage Vineyards OVP Cinsault/Pinotage

d: Part of the left-field Project Z range at Kleine Zalze, this is a separately fermented cuvée of Alvarinho and 15% Riesling fermented in an amphora and old wood, respectively. Floral, racy, pithy and still on the youthful side, it has lime, lemon and juniper flavours and a sappy, mouth-watering finish.

n: Kleine Zalze Project Z OVP Chenin Blanc
d: The heart of this wine comes from Durbanville, paired with a 20%, skin-fermented component from the Rustenhof farm in Stellenbosch. The combination is intriguing, with quince, tangerine and baking spice flavours, a nip of tannin and a pithy, medium-bodied finish.

n: Kleine Zalze Project Z Red Blend
d: A tribute to the Cape blends of old, this is the kind of thing that was popular in the 1950s and 1960s, partnering Cinsault from the Bottelary Hills and 40% Cabernet Sauvignon from Stellenbosch Mountain. Serious and well structured – some of the Cinsault was bled off to make rosé – it has layers of mint, redcurrant and blackcurrant and the concentration to develop further in bottle.

n: Kleine Zalze Vineyard Selection Cabernet Sauvignon
d: The kind of Cabernet Sauvignon that I'd be happy to find in a wine bar or restaurant, this over-delivers at the price. It’s a full-bodied, textbook expression of Stellenbosch with toasty 24% new wood, layers of mint, dark chocolate and blackcurrant and a spine of tannin. Plush and well made, it will develop further in bottle.

n: Kleine Zalze Vineyard Selection OVP Chenin Blanc
d: The heart and soul of what we do, says Anri Botha of this large-volume Old Vine Project Chenin Blanc from 20 different sites in Stellenbosch. Commendably concentrated at the price, it has flavours of boiled sweets, pear and stone fruit, subtle aromatic spices from older oak and a racy, green apple finish.

Made with purchased grapes from the Upper Blaauwklippen Valley, close the Kleinood cellar, this is a well-made, medium-bodied Chenin Blanc that handles its 33% new oak comfortably thanks to some concrete eggs in the mix. Pithy, focused and refreshing, it has flavours of yellow apple, pear and citrus and a tangy mineral core.

One of a growing band of stand-alone Grenache Blancs, this comes from the variety’s South African home from home in Piekenierskloof. Fermented and aged in concrete eggs and old barrels, it’s racy, chiselled and energetic, with lime blossom and wet stone aromas and a palate of quince and lemon zest complemented by an appealing bitter twist.

Kleinood’s enjoyable Syrah is made with Syrah grapes from Banghoek and the Upper Blaauwklippen Valley. Showing some subtle reduction, it’s a lightly wooded style with rosehip and redcurrant fruit flavours, a light-bodied palate and a crisp, bone-dry finish.

Blended with 9% wine from the 2024 vintage, this unusual Mourvèdre is made with purchased grapes from Zorgvliet’s vineyards in Banghoek. Fermented with 40% whole clusters, it’s a lighter, comparatively approachable iteration of the grape with bramble and red cherry flavours, savoury tannins and lots of underlying zip and energy.

Fermented with 20% whole bunches, Kleinood’s well-judged Syrah uses grapes from 23 different parcels in the Upper Blaauwklippen Valley. Textured, savoury and spicy, it has subtle tobacco leaf and clove aromas, a touch of meaty reduction, firmish tannins and a palate of blackberry, red cherry and Negroni spices.

Sourced from vines in the Banghoek Valley, this is an appealing, comparatively restrained Viognier that displays freshness and subtle oak integration. Jasmine and honeysuckle aromas guide you into a palate of pear and white peach supported by refreshing acidity and a top note of aniseed spice. A more than one glass wine.

A Swartland red that wouldn’t look out of place in a line up from the Languedoc. Dominated by Syrah, with a supporting crew of 19% Mourvèdre, 7% Grenache and 5% Carignan, this is a blend with plenty of gas in the tank, with savoury, meaty intensity, negligible oak, sinewy tannins and a medley of black olive, fig and red plum complemented by aromas of fynbos and garrigue.

Cape white blends deserve to be much better known as these are some of the country’s highlights. This is based on Grenache Blanc, with 24% Roussanne and 12% each of Chenin Blanc and Verdelho. Fermented and aged in second-fill barrels, it has a touch of flinty reduction, good texture and intensity, a medley of greengage, lime and waxed lemon flavours and a dab of oak spices.

Two Garnachas for the price of one, as it were, this is part of a very smart range from the talented Duncan Stuart. Fermented with 30% whole bunches, it’s remarkably detailed and precise, with layers of red cherry, pomegranate and tobacco leaf, a waft of mountain herbs and an undertone of Campari spices.

Watch out, Bandol! Following in the footsteps of the maiden 2024 vintage, this is another triumph from this increasingly impressive producer. Meaty, savoury and intense, it’s a wine that’s good now but will improve in bottle, with nicely understated wood, flavours of allspice, blackberry and blood orange and sinewy, finely judged tannins.

A wonderful Syrah that deserves to be considered alongside the best examples of the variety in the Swartland, this is a wonderful expression of a very special vintage. Using grapes from the oldest block on the farm, planted in 2001, it’s intense, layered and concentrated, with scented 40% new oak, some clove and tobacco leaf notes from 35% whole clusters, layers of liquorice, incense, damson and blackberry and finely judged, sturdy tannins.

There are so many good reds at Kloovenburg these days, that it’s difficult to choose between them. Up there with the best value Syrahs in the country, this comes from four, schistdominated blocks on the estate in Riebeekberg, showing some stony, meaty reduction, vibrant blackberry and tapenade flavours, beautifully integrated tannins and wafts of thyme and black pepper.

The kind of wine you want to purchase by the case as well as tell your friends about, this is a seamless, ridiculously good-value Rhône style blend of Grenache, 47% Syrah and 3% Mourvèdre. Aromas of clove, rose petal and fynbos lead you into a sappy, juicy palate of bramble, redcurrant and tobacco leaf framed by neutral oak.

Impressive value from Duncan Stuart, this is a second release of Village White, featuring Chenin Blanc, 26% Grenache Blanc, 20% Verdelho and 12% Roussanne. Entirely unwooded, it’s a layered, easy-drinking cuvée with yellow apple, lemongrass and subtle stone fruit flavours and some mid-palate weight from time on lees.

n: Krone Amphora Blanc de Blancs CC
d: An all-Chardonnay bubbly that has changed origin in the last year, this now comes from Tulbagh rather than Elandskloof. Pale, unfiltered and intriguing, it is one of very few Cap Classiques that ferments its base wine in amphoras. Bone dry, racy and refreshing, it has texture from 24 months on lees, an earthy undertone and a crisp palate of aniseed and lemon zest.

Stainless steel, foudre and amphora-fermented components all contribute to this stylish, more fruit forward style of Blanc de Blancs from Stephan de Beer. Stone fruit, citrus pith and subtle baking spice flavours are complemented by five grams of dosage and a toasty finish. A tasty, mid-tier bubbly.

Stephan de Beer uses equal components from Tulbagh and Robertson to make this good value bubbly, marrying Chardonnay and 30% Pinot Noir. With a 10% wooded component and full malolactic, it’s a smooth ride, with layers of lemon zest and crème fraîche and well-integrated 7.5 grams of dosage.

n: Krone Kaaimansgat Blanc de Blancs CC
d: Kaaimansgat is one of the best places to grow Chardonnay in the country, so it’s no surprise that this is such a brilliant fizz. Steely, chiselled and very intense, it has 40% malolactic for extra, mid-palate texture, some subtle oak from foudre fermentation, layers of brioche and lemon juice and a stony, palate-cleansing finish.

n: Krone Koelfontein Blanc de Blancs CC
d: The high-altitude Ceres Plateau is increasingly coming into its own as a sparkling wine area. This stylish Chardonnay hails from vines at 700 metres and has the focus and intensity you’d expect with lovely, nutty autolysis from four years on lees, tiny bubbles, mouth-watering acidity and a salted lemon finish.

Showcasing the first ever vintage of a Krone bubbly from Elandskloof, this is a very stylish, layered, late-released Blanc de Blancs. Developing beautifully after a decade on lees, it has wonderful concentration and depth, aromas of iodine and fresh cèpes, a savoury undertone and a lingering, bone-dry finish.

n: Krone Twee Jonge Gezellen Blanc de Blancs CC
d: Part of a stylish and varied range of Blanc de Blancs from Stephan de Beer, this one comes from vineyards close to the winery in Tulbagh. Fermented in foudres before ageing on lees in bottle for four years, it has tangy, pin-head bubbles, layers of lemon juice, rock salt and white pepper and a brisk, palate-cleansing finish.

Made with grapes from the Bosmans’ farm in the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, this is a confident second release from Johan Kruger. Fermented in 10% new oak, it’s a racy, refreshing Chardonnay with lime, citrus and nectarine flavours and a chiselled, refreshing finish. The wood adds a sheen of patisserie sweetness.

If you love this wine as much as I do, stock up, because the 2026 vintage was wiped out by frost. Made with grapes from vines at 1,370 metres in Sutherland, it’s scented, saline and wonderfully focused and precise, with understated 15% new oak, flavours of peach and citrus, stony intensity and a hint of lanolin. One of the Cape’s very best Chardonnays.

The Karoo Syrah hails from Abrie du Plessis’ farm at 1,370 metres in Sutherland, located on the granite soils that the variety loves so much.
