Aromas of fennel, kelp and mountain herbs segue into a palate of rosemary, fig and black olive supported by thrilling energy, a hit of oak spice and a spine of sinewy tannin. One for Hermitage lovers.

Sourced from a 31-year-old vineyard that’s on the verge of Old Vine Project status (the minimum is 35), this Chardonnay comes from sandstone and granite soils in Piekenierskloof. Rocky, stony and mouth-wateringly fresh, it has effortless poise and concentration, lots of zip and energy, layers of citrus zest and wet stones and nuanced 10% new oak.

n: Kruger Family Wines Old Vines Chardonnay
d: The Du Bois family’s highly sought after farm in Stellenbosch supplies the raw material for this impressive old vine Chardonnay. Complex, focused and showing the energy of the 2025 vintage, it marries aromas of fennel and wet stones with a saline, mouth-watering palate of citrus and lemongrass supported by effortless concentration.

n: Kruger Family Wines Old Vines OVP Chardonnay
d: Bush vines on the granite soils of the Paardeberg – Chenin Blanc rather than Chardonnay country as a rule – are the source of this rich, textured Chardonnay from Johan Kruger. Showing the concentration of its old-vine source, it has layers of pear and passion fruit, subtle wood and nicely understated oak from ageing in barrels, foudres and concrete.

n: Kruger Family Wines Old Vines OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Crystal clear is how Johan Kruger describes the 2025 whites, and I know what he means. This Chenin Blanc comes from a pair of old-vine parcels on decomposed granite soils in Darling and Wellington, with ageing in older oak and concrete eggs, and has impressive weight, intensity and dry extract, citrus and wet stone flavours and an appealing, quinine-like bitter twist.

n: Kruger Family Wines Old Vines OVP Cinsault
d: A parcel of dryland bush vines in Wellington, planted back in 1952, is the source of this superb Cinsault from Johan Kruger. Pure, scented and perfumed, it’s a red with more structure and grip than you think, with negligible oak, redcurrant, hibiscus and wild strawberry flavours and a dusting of Negroni spices.

The vines are still young at nine years of age, but this is a scented, nicely defined Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley Pinot Noir made from the 777 clone. Plum, orange zest and red berry flavours are complemented by tangy natural acidity, a kiss of wood spices and savoury underlying tannins.

n: Kruger Family Wines Sans Chêne Chardonnay
d: Sans Chêne – unwooded in French – is a concrete egg-fermented Chardonnay from Piekenierskloof of all places. Showing appealing freshness, intensity and personality, it has pear and melon fruit flavours, a thread of racy minerality and a focused, well-balanced finish.

A wine that's big in Canada, apparently, this suggests that local consumers know how to spot a bargain. Sourced from vineyards in Darling, Stellenbosch, the Paardeberg and Wellington, this is firm, dense and commendably serious, with classic damson, graphite and blackcurrant notes and a slab of dark chocolate.

Sourced from the Helderberg – one of the best areas for the variety – and Firgrove, this is a Chardonnay that massively over-delivers in the bottle. Barrel-fermented, with a partial wild yeast component, it has a hint of struck match, nicely combined flavours of pear, waxed lemon, tangerine and aniseed spice and very subtle oak.

At just over R100 for a wine from Groenekloof, this is stonking value for money from the KWV. The use of 10% older wood adds an extra nuance to a palate of padrón peppers, kiwi fruit and gooseberry and a subtle volatile lift. Very drinkable.

Drawing on vineyards in Darling, Paarl and the Swartland, this is a good-value Syrah with a lot of structure and intensity at the price. Smartly wooded in 35% new oak, it has a spine of granitic intensity, plenty of colour, blackberry and tapenade flavours and a touch of meaty reduction. Another winner at the price.

Triptych is a three-way blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, 16% Petit Verdot and 13% Malbec that delivers a lot of concentration and flavour for just R159, using grapes from Stellenbosch and the Swartland. Toasty, inky and compact, it has flavours of mint, dark chocolate, cassis and blackberry and the concentration to develop further in bottle.

I’ve no idea what stocks the KWV has left of its Cape Tawny fortified, slumbering in old casks, but my advice is to buy some before it runs out. Representing incredible value for money, it’s a hauntingly ethereal blend of Chenin Blanc, Tinta Barocca, Touriga Nacional, Syrah, Souzão and Tempranillo with layers of date, toffee and almond, a rose petal top note and a gloriously balsamic finish.

n: KWV Laborie Blanc de Blancs CC
d: The KWV’s all-Chardonnay Blanc de Blancs offers very impressive quality at the price. Sourced from a single parcel in Wellington of all places, picked in four stages, it has added complexity from 15% barrel fermentation and 10% reserve material, appealing flavours of liquorice, lemongrass and patisserie spices and 5.87 grams of dosage.

Impressive at the price, this is an easy-drinking Cap Classique, combining Chardonnay and 48% Pinot Noir. Lees-aged for 18 months, it’s just off-dry at 7 grams of dosage, flavours of malt, wild strawberry and citrus zest and a balanced, refreshing finish. The kind of fizz that I’d be happy to pour at a party.

An ambitious wine that needs more time in bottle to soften, this is a pan-Cape cuvée of Syrah, 30% Cabernet Sauvignon, 20% Malbec and 10% Petite Sirah. Big, bold, ripe and concentrated, with fig, damson and blackberry fruit, some Asian spices and a whack of 100% new oak. Fewer first-used barrels would improve the wine in my view.

Still going strong as a brand after 75 years, Roodeberg continues to deliver the goods at less than R100 a bottle. Aged with staves and 5% real barrels, it’s a catch-all blend of Syrah, 25% Cabernet Sauvignon, 15% Petit Verdot, 9% Tannat, 8% Durif, 7% Malbec and 2% Tempranillo, showing layered flavours of bramble, blackcurrant and summer pudding and a patina of North African spices.

The Culturist is a classic, five-way Bordeaux-style assemblage from Izele van Blerk, combining Cabernet Sauvignon, 31% Petit Verdot, 23% Malbec, 8% Cabernet Franc and 5% Merlot. Skilfully wooded in 40% new oak, it’s a bold, glossy Western Cape red with aromas of gingerbread, allspice and mint and a palate that’s structured, layered and black-fruited.

Two sites in Stellenbosch – one on the Simonsberg, the other in Sir Lowry’s Pass – supply the grapes for this impressive Cabernet Franc. Curated in 40% new oak, this is fresher than its 14.5% alcohol would suggest, with leafy, espresso coffee aromas and a palate of tarragon, black cherry and basil.

The Canvas is what we might call a “Mediterranean style blend”, with components from the warmer areas of Paarl, the Swartland and Wellington. Dominated by Syrah, with a supporting cast of 29% Petite Sirah, 12% Mourvèdre and 10% each of Tempranillo and Carignan, it’s a chewy, intense, lavishly wooded cuvée with sinewy tannins, top notes of garrigue, lavender and fig and damson fruit.

Lovers of Chenin Blanc should be queueing at the cellar door to buy a case of this wine, especially given its price. Sourced from the Rooidraai farm in Malmesbury, it has the concentration of its 43-year-old vines, subtly integrated 33% new oak, flavours of custard, lemongrass, green apple and wet stones and a tapering finish.

Always among the high points of any tasting at the KWV, this is a brilliant Grenache Blanc from a single block in Wellington. Made with five different techniques in a single bottle, it has Riesling-like acidity and focus, chiselled acidity, subtle 40% new wood integration, lime, earth and aniseed intensity and a bone-dry finish.

Orchestra is the KWV’s top-of-the-range Bordeaux red blend, made as a five-variety blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, 28% Petit Verdot, 19% Malbec and 9% Cabernet Franc. The 70% new French oak is well marshalled here, adding some perfume and complexity to a palate of cassis, capsicum and mulberry complemented by firm tannins and refreshing acidity.

A tribute to the man who invented Pinotage, the grape that dominates the blend here, this icon red has support from 30% Syrah, 15% Cabernet Franc, 8% Malbec and 7% Petite Sirah. The 100% new oak might be a little too much for some, but this has the concentration and profundity to cope, marrying aromas of liquorice, incense and mocha spice with a compact palate of fig, damson and blackberry. Needs more time in bottle to soften.

A single Stellenbosch Mountain block on sandstone soils is the source of this serious, inky, ambitious Petit Verdot from Izele van Blerk. Structured, dense and black-fruited it has damson and blackberry flavours, lashings of toasty oak and a lot of underlying grip and ageing potential. One to tuck away for a while.

The Mentors Pinotage comes from the Bottelary Hills, described as the grape’s “spiritual home” by viticulturist Marco Ventrella. This uses raw material from bush vines at 250 metres and has some spice and texture from 15% whole bunches. The wood is a little assertive, but this has attractive plum and summer berry flavours and a spine of tannin.

Le Sommet comes from the Amperbor vineyard in the Bottelary Hills, where the decomposed granite soils are a significant factor. It’s an ambitious first release with a price to match, 25% new oak, layers of plum bramble and summer pudding fruit, some aromatic patisserie spices, fresh acidity and layered, fine-grained tannins.

Dirk Coetzee uses grapes from eight different blocks at L’Avenir to make this large-volume Chenin Blanc, staggering picking to build layers into the wine. Made in a fresh, bright, modern style, it has an appealing medley of pear, yellow apple and passion fruit, a dab of 5% new wood and a tangy, well-balanced finish.

Part of a good-value range under the Provenance label, this is the wine that keeps the lights on at L’Avenir. Sourced from 11 different blocks on the farm, it has a sheen of subtle oak spices, plum and raspberry fruit, supple, granular tannins and nice texture and weight. Textbook stuff.

Among the more ambitious rosés in South Africa, this wouldn't look out of place on the Côte d’Azur. Made with free-run Pinotage juice from a single parcel on the estate in Stellenbosch, it’s a refined, elegant, lightly wooded pink with raspberry and rooibos tea flavours, a hint of cotton candy and a fresh, bone-dry finish.

n: L'Avenir Single Block OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Picked in two stages, one of which contained 3% botrytis, this layered Chenin Blanc comes from an OVP block planted in 1973 on gravel and clay soils. Barrel fermented in older wood, it’s a textured style with an exotic undertone, all peach, pear, quince and beeswax with a drizzle of honeyed sweetness and supporting acidity.

n: L'Avenir Single Block OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Tasted just before release, this makes an interesting contrast with the riper, richer 2024 bottling, with less evident botrytis in the blend. Fermented and aged in older oak, it has lots of energy and zip, flavours of lemon, peach and vanilla spice and a hint of honeyed sweetness on the finish balanced by bright acidity.

L’Avenir has a well-deserved reputation for the quality of its Pinotages. This comes from the 33-year-old Block Two on the farm and shows the concentration of the 2022 vintage, revealing layers of bramble, plum and summer berries, embellished by 30% new oak and a touch of liquorice on the finish.

A comparatively rare example of a red Bordeaux blend from Franschhoek, Affinity is Cabernet Sauvignon based with support from 29% Merlot, 10% Cabernet Franc and 2% Petit Verdot. Produced in a fresh, even ethereal style, it has plum, basil and blackcurrant leaf flavours, granular tannins and some cigar box notes from 16% new wood.

Irene du Fleuriot uses the 548 Chardonnay clone to make this wine, relishing what she c alls the “mouthfeel” it gives her. Fermented in 50% new barrels, this has a touch of struck match reduction, stony zip and intensity and flavours of nutmeg, lemon zest and cardamom.

n: La Bri Limited Release Cabernet Sauvignon

d: Unusually for Franschhoek, red wines are the overwhelming focus at La Bri. Nodding in the direction of Côte Rôtie, this is a co-fermentation of Syrah and 3% Viognier from sand and clay soils. Matured in 10% new oak, it’s a spicy, cooler climate style with layers of gingerbread and summer berries and undertones of clove and fresh mint.

Do you have to be a Burgundy lover to make great Chardonnay in South Africa? Maybe not, but it surely helps. Nico Grobler buys the grapes for this excellent example from the Shannon farm, using the “feminine” 548 clone. Toasty, flinty, layered and precise, this has the weight of a Corton-Charlemagne and the racy acidity of a Puligny-Montrachet, with undertones of beeswax and butterscotch and scented 20% new oak.

Nico Grobler’s Pinot Noir comes from a 1.5-hectare plot on his farm in Elgin, predominantly planted with the 113 clone. A wine that will reward patience, it has layers of plum and black cherry fruit, stylish 20% new oak, plush tannins, finely judged acidity and a ferrous, earthy root vegetable undertone. Ambitious, concentrated stuff from what he calls a “special vintage”.

Making wine in Elgin is a bit like living in Europe, says Nico Grobler, who makes the most of the cooler conditions. This well-judged Chardonnay comes from nine different sites on ferricrete, shale and sandstone soils. Eschewing any malolactic, it has layers of lemon zest and grapefruit, a hint of toast and a sappy, refreshing finish.

n: La Brune The Valley Pinot Noir
d: The Valley is the second-tier Pinot Noir from La Brune, made with seven different Dijon clones from a dozen vineyards in Elgin. Eminently serious and well-structured at the price, it has plenty of colour for the variety, plum, bramble and black cherry flavours, a waft of 5% new oak and a slightly ferrous finish.

Sourced from Elim, rather than La Motte’s home base of Franschhoek, this is an exciting new premium Semillon that eschews oak entirely. Defiantly green and herbal, it has green bean and padrón pepper aromas, some mid-palate weight and texture from lees ageing and a saline, seashore undertone.

The 2024 release of Hanneli R represents a significant and welcome shift in style, blending Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah in a fresher, less extracted style. Curated in 90% new 600-litre barrels – another change – it has graphite, fynbos and coffee bean aromas, detailed, layered tannins, racy acidity and a core of red cherry, blackcurrant and aromatic green herbs. Hallelujah!

n: La Roche Estate Bacchus Brut Rosé CC
d: Named after the Roman god, rather than the grape variety that’s widely planted in England, this is a classic cuvée of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from consultant Tim Hoek. Lees aged for just ten months, it’s a modern, racy, textured bubbly with citrus, pain d’épices and wild strawberry flavours and a dab of crème fraîche.

n: La Roche Estate Pinot Noir Rosé
d: This is a very enjoyable rosé from this winery-cum-luxury venue in Franschhoek. Whole bunch pressed and stainless steel fermented on lees, it’s a bright, tangy, red-fruited style with pomegranate and hibiscus flavours, savoury tannins and a mineral core.

Just the kind of thing, wedding guests at La Roche would enjoy drinking, as long as they have the budget, this derives its texture and weight from good grapes and three months’ lees ageing as opposed to oak. Pear, citrus and honeysuckle notes are complemented by tangy acidity and an oyster shell finish.

As well as selling grapes to several top wineries, La Vierge makes a series of good wines under its eponymous label. Using barrel-aged and amphora components, Christo Kotze’s Chardonnay shows the quality of the site, with layers of beeswax, lemon zest and tangerine, subtle, scented oak and a petrichor undertone.

Using grapes from the Bokkeveld shale soils of the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, this is a youthful Pinot Noir that will develop further complexity in bottle. The 20% whole bunches are finely integrated here, bringing another layer to a palate of black cherry and wild strawberry, with sinewy tannins and a frame of second and third-use oak.

n: La Vierge Storyteller The Fairy & The Crocodile Pinot Noir
d: Sourced from La Vierge’s in-demand vineyard on the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, this uses a mix of Burgundy clones for extra complexity. Matured in second and third-fill barrels, with 10% whole clusters adding perfume and texture to the mix, this has goji berry and pomegranate flavours and a rose petal top note.

n: Landskroon Paul de Villiers Cabernet Sauvignon
d: Paarl might not be the first place you’d go looking for Cabernet Sauvignon in South Africa, but this is very attractive at the price from Fanie Geyser. Matured in 50% new wood, it has a touch of leafy bottle development, good underlying structure and a palate of cassis, mocha, dill and mint. Something of a bargain.

n: Landskroon Paul de Villiers The Heritage Cinsault
Le Bonheur Manor House Cabernet Sauvignon
Le Bonheur Manor House Sauvignon Blanc

d: The pick of the current Le Bonheur range, this is a comparatively rare example of a standalone Petit Verdot in the Cape. Keeping extraction and tannic heft to a minimum, this is far from a blockbuster, with deftly integrated 60% new wood, layers of mint, graphite and black cherry and an appealing violet top note.

Made with what Schalk-Willem Joubert calls “our most expensive grapes to grow” – yields were just two tons per hectare in 2024 – this is a varietal Chenin Blanc from a pair of old-vine parcels in the Polkadraai Hills planted in 1978 and 1988. Earthy, spicy and intense, it’s a tight, chiselled wine with aromas of white flowers and a granitic, lemon zest palate.

n: Le Grand Domaine Grand Vin de Stellenbosch Cabernet Sauvignon
Le Grand Domaine Grand Vin de Stellenbosch Cabernet Sauvignon/Merlot
Le Grand Domaine Grand Vin de Stellenbosch Sauvignon Blanc
d: Debbie Thompson makes this Stellenbosch Sauvignon Blanc with grapes from Le Grand Domaine’s Devon Valley property. Fermented cool in stainless steel tanks, this has tangy elderflower notes, a palate of lime and passion fruit and an appealingly herbal undertone.

n: Le Lude Limited Release Brut Rosé
d: Mature, complex and copper-hued, this cuvée of Pinot Noir, 40% Chardonnay and 6% Pinot Meunier uses raw material from Bonnievale, Elgin and Franschhoek. Boasting 13 years of autolysis, it’s a toasty, unwooded style with malt, wild strawberry and hazelnut flavours and a faint bitter twist on the finish.

n: Le Lude Madáme Brut Nature Millésimé CC
d: This is the third vintage of Madáme, made by the brilliant Paul Gerber during his time at Le Lude. An unwooded cuvée of Chardonnay from Franschhoek and Robertson, it’s a remarkable, bone-dry Cap Classique that rivals the best of Champagne, with tiny bubbles, layers of shitake mushroom and toast and a savoury, tapering finish. Not cheap, but worth every rand.

n: Le Lude Vintage Cuvée Extra Brut CC
d: Part of a brilliant current range from bubbly specialist, Le Lude, this partners Chardonnay and 20% Pinot Noir, using equal components from Franschhoek and Robertson. Disgorged after nine years on lees, it’s a poised, layered, effortlessly complex wine with chamomile and wildflower aromas, plenty of zip and acidity, flavours of toast and patisserie spices and a savoury, just off-dry finish.

Reflecting the power and tannic intensity of the 2024 vintage in South Africa, this uses grapes from 14 different parcels across the Stellenbosch region. Compact, chewy and made to age in bottle, it offers a lot of concentration and structure at the price, with damson, dark chocolate and blackcurrant flavours, stylish 29% new wood and the backbone to age for another decade or more.

“It all depended when you picked,” says Christo Le Riche of the 2023 vintage, who coped with the growing season as well as anyone in Stellenbosch. This excellent Cabernet Sauvignon used components from 13 different vineyards and the precision and breadth of the selection was important. Elegant, complex yet concentrated, it marries aromas of graphite, marjoram and violet with a polished palate of cassis, blueberry and cigar box and scented 74% new oak.

Made with the same eight rows on the Eendrag farm in Stellenbosch since 2019, this is a full-flavoured, 100% malolactic style of Chardonnay that benefits from the use of 25% new oak and 30% amphoras. Rich and nicely textured, it has some underlying ocean acidity and a core of pear, pineapple and butterscotch.

Right up there with the best Stellenbosch reds in 2023, this Mountain Cabernet Sauvignon comes from five vineyards on the Helderberg, all but one of which face north or north-west. Confident and self-assured, it’s a wonderful, layered, age-worthy expression of the variety with mint, coffee bean and tarragon aromas, sculpted tannins, subtle 60% new oak and a core of blackberry and blackcurrant fruit. Makes up 35% of the Reserve.

"I grew up drinking blends like this,” says Christo Le Riche, who makes this youthful assemblage with Cabernet Sauvignon, 27% Cinsault and 13% Cabernet Franc. Matured in 10% new oak, with some whole bunch fermentation on the Cinsault, it’s minty, savoury and sappy, with impressive underlying structure, flavours of plum, redcurrant and cassis and a dusting of wood spices.

The key to this wine, sourced from two sites on the Simonsberg, is that both were picked before the March rains. A component that makes up 21% of the Reserve Cabernet Sauvignon, this is also bottled on its own. Racy, focused and refreshing, it’s a wine with lots of zip and energy, deftly handled 60% new oak, tangy redcurrant and blackcurrant leaf flavours, savoury tannins and some underlying grip.

Le Sueur’s Cinsault comes from vineyards in the Swartland, showing the freshness and medium body that you normally associate with neighbouring Darling. Benefitting from 20% whole clusters, it has palate-caressing tannins, layers of red cherry and summer pudding, racy acidity and savoury balancing tannins.

Vineyards close to the Kammanassie mountains in the Klein Karoo, one of the more remote areas of the Western Cape supply the raw material from this pale, lightly pressed Grenache rosé. Aged in older oak, it’s a delicate, refined pink with cranberry, rosehip and watermelon flavours and a hint of supporting tannins.

Remote vineyards in the Klein Karoo are the source of this wild yeast fermented Chenin Blanc from Louis van der Riet. Showing some appealing struck match reduction, it has citrus, quince and subtle apricot flavours, nice palate weight and a subtle bitter twist.

Paradoks combines Pinotage’s two parents, Cinsault and Pinot Noir, in a single bottle here, blending components from the Klein Karoo and the Swartland. With a little bit of whole bunch spice, this is nicely textured and well balanced, with rose petal and subtle Negroni spice aromas and a juicy palate of strawberry and raspberry coulis.

n: Le Sueur Wild Card Sauvignon Blanc

d: Planted in the right place, modern, virus-free clones of Cabernet Sauvignon have a purity and a transparency that are remarkable. This one comes from three blocks at 250 metres on the Cordoba Road and is restrained, perfumed and beautifully balanced, with graphite, fresh herb and wet stone aromas, scented 33% new oak, plum and blackcurrant leaf flavours and filigree tannins.

It’s easy to overlook the fact that Andrea Mullineux makes one of the best Chardonnays in South Africa, given that she produces so many other excellent whites. The 2024 release is a stunner, sourced from a cool site at 400 metres on the Helderberg. With a pH of 3.1, even after full malolactic, is has granitic energy and focus, subtle nuanced of lemon butter, beeswax and coconut, flavours of citrus and clementine and a sappy, acid-driven finish.

Basson is the oldest Cinsault vineyard in South Africa, planted just after phylloxera on 20 different rootstocks. It’s not the prettiest site, but the wines it produces are remarkably elegant, serious and hauntingly poised, with rose petal, tea leaf, red cherry and goji berry flavours and more underlying structure than you think. Cinsault doesn’t get much better than this.

Inspired by the wines of López de Heredia in Rioja, even if it’s made with Chardonnay rather than Viura and Malvas’a Blanca, this was kept in barrels without added sulphites for five years. It tastes as if it was aged under flor, but has none, revelling in a palate of almonds, smoked lemons and marzipan, supported by lots of acidity and dry extract and a layered, lingering finish.

"Semillon in Franschhoek is magical," says Chis Mulllineux and it’s hard to disagree with him when you taste something like this. Sourced from a 62-year-old vineyard at 150 metres, it was fermented and lees aged in an amphora, with lovely focus, freshness, a palate of lanolin, saffron, oatmeal and citrus zest, with some subtle reduction, impressive texture and a petrichor top note.

The Leeu Passant is the top red from the winery, at least in terms of price. A seamless blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, 30% Cabernet Franc and 10% Cinsault, using components from Stellenbosch and Wellington, it’s a beautifully conceived assemblage with aromas of mint, coriander and graphite, subtle, granular tannins and flavours of red cherry, blackcurrant and vanilla spice.

Sourced from vines that are 55 years’ old, this is a wine that’s focused on place and terroir rather than oak. Wild fermented in concrete and neutral 500-litre barrels, it’s sappy, focused and intense with appealing quince and green apple flavours, a mid-palate of beeswax and wet stones, stony minerality and an underlying bitter twist.

Fans of Heritage Syrah had to do without their chosen drop in 2020 and 2021, so it’s good to see it back on the market. Boldly fermented with 50% whole clusters, it has subtle oak, brooding intensity, lavender, incense and rosemary aromas, dense blackberry, fig and damson flavours and the tannic backbone to age in bottle. Developing gratifyingly slowly in bottle.

Leeuwnekuil’s good value Chenin Blanc is one of my “go to” wine bar whites in South Africa, expressing everything that is enjoyable about the variety. Textured, layered and refreshing, it has nicely understated oak from a combination of foudres, stainless steel and older barrels, flavours of pear, lemon and orange zest and an undertone of stony reduction.

Natasha Williams makes her Chardonnay with grapes from Bosman’s extensive plantings in the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley. Dryland farmed, this is a well-balanced white with wooded and (for the first time) concrete components, lots of pithy acidity and appealing citrus, lemongrass and tangerine flavours.

n: Lelie van Saron Jade Red Blend
d: One of several wines under the attractive Jade brand from rising star Natasha Williams, this is a modern, Rhône style red that combines Syrah, 38% Grenache and 12% Petite Sirah from the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, the Swartland and Wellington. Floral, subtle and charming, it’s a youthful, joyful red with top notes of pine and fynbos and sappy bramble and red berry fruit.

It takes a bit of courage to plant a minority Hungarian grape like Hárslevelű in Tulbagh, but Lemberg has made a success of its 1.4-hectare plantings. Intensely aromatic and enticing, it has top notes of chamomile, honeysuckle and cardamom and an intriguing palate of pear, citrus zest and rose water underpinned by tangy acidity.

Something left field from Lemberg, a producer that likes to experiment, this delicious Syrah was fermented and aged in amphoras, with a 30% whole bunch component. Polished, perfumed and understated, it has classic white pepper and allspice aromas, sculpted tannins, a hint of petrichor and bramble, red cherry and blackberry flavours. Deliciously drinkable.

Unique in the Cape and almost certainly the world, this is a Tulbagh assemblage of Viognier, 29% Hárslevelü, 19% Sauvignon Blanc and 9% Chenin Blanc. Aged for seven months in barrel and Flexcubes, it has some subtle, stony top notes, layers of beeswax, quince, citrus and aromatic baking spices and lovely weight and texture.

Louis is an SMG blend of Syrah, 10% Mourvèdre and 8% Grenache. One for fans of Languedoc wines, it has alluring fynbos and garrigue aromas, refined plum, bramble and red berry flavours, some subtle Asian spices and the layered tannins that are a feature of Anri Botha’s winemaking style.

Part of an impressive line-up from Anri Botha, this is a stand-alone Pinotage that now comes entirely from the estate in Tulbagh. Subtly wooded in 10% new wood, it’s a wine for Pinot Noir rather than Cabernet Sauvignon lovers, with 10% whole bunch spices, redcurrant and wild strawberry fruit and fine-grained tannins.

Using grapes from Paarl and Stellenbosch, this is a subtly wooded Chenin Blanc from James Osche, offering plenty of wine at a reasonable price. Aromas of fennel and vanilla spice segue into a palate of pear, citrus and green apple and a touch of stone fruit sweetness.

This is a second release of a Cinsault under the Lievland label, sourced from two middle-aged blocks in Agter-Paarl. White pepper and Campari spice top notes lead you into a palate of pomegranate and blood orange, with a spicy top finish from 10% whole bunches.

Lievland’s Pinotage is a 70/30 blend from Agter-Paarl and the winery’s home farm in Stellenbosch. Benefitting from the addition of 6% Alicante Bouschet and 5% Grenache, it has subtle 10% new oak, some underlying ferrous grip and glossy bramble and summer berry fruit. Nicely judged at the price.

An ambitious Syrah that needs more time in bottle to lose its tannic carapace, this comes from decomposed granite soils on the farm in Stellenbosch and was blended with 6% Mourvèdre. Fermented with 20% whole clusters before ageing in 10% new wood, it has plenty of colour and intensity and a core of blackberry and damson fruit.

Combining components from Paarl and neighbouring Agter-Paarl, planted in the mid-1980s, this is a very lightly wooded Chenin Blanc from Riaan Möller, with appealing melon and passion fruit flavours and enough lime-like acidity to lift and freshen the finish.

Just the thing to drink by the glass if you are visiting Lievland’s stylish cellar door in Stellenbosch, this is a finely judged rosé made from an assemblage of Syrah, 22% Mourvèdre and 11% Cinsault. Pale, ethereal and delicate, it combines watermelon and pomegranate flavours with bright, tangy acidity and mineral-etched freshness.

Using equal proportions of grapes from Elgin, Greyton and Walker Bay, this is always one of the most complex Sauvignon Blancs in the Cape, showing the subtlety that’s the hallmark of Samantha O’Keefe’s winemaking. Combining foudre, concrete egg and new and old wood components, it’s savoury, briny and intense, with greengage, lime and pink grapefruit flavours and a kiss of kitchen spices.

After some tricky recent vintages out in Greyton, 2025 was plain sailing for Samantha O’Keefe. You have to say that she deserves a break. Made with dry-farmed “bonzi vines”, it’s a Chardonnay with corresponding structure and concentration that develops well in bottle. This has density and some phenolic grip, toasty 25% new wood and a racy, fynbos and citrusinfused finish.

Now on its fourth vintage, Cuvée Blanc remains as it was on first release. Roussanne supplies the core of the wine here, complemented by 5% each of Chardonnay and Viognier. Sappy, intense and very lightly wooded, it partners aromas of cardamom and honeysuckle with a palate of grapefruit, peach and aromatic spices and a spine of skin tannins. Unique in the Cape.

We’ve become so used to the quality of this wine that it’s easy to overlook how hard it is to make a Viognier of this quality. Enticingly intense and aromatic, it’s a wine that handles its 35% new oak with ease, marrying layers of tangerine, lychee and white peach with palatecoating texture and unmistakable cool climate acidity.

Often a slight weak link in the Lismore line up, the 2024 Pinot Noir has stepped up a gear. Made with equal components from Elgin and Kaaimansgat, with nothing from Stanford this time, it has subtle spices from 30% whole bunches, a waft of rose petal, and a juicy, lip-smacking palate of redcurrant and wild strawberry framed by 25% new wood.

Quite firm and shuttered when I tasted it, this is a serious, comparatively chewy cool climate Syrah that needs time in bottle to soften. Ferrous and firm, it has a palate of damson, tapenade, liquorice and steak tartare, fresh acidity and some much-needed sweetness from 25% new oak.

A huge step up on the basic Lismore Syrah in 2024, this is entirely sourced from Samantha O’Keefe’s own vines in the cool climate region of Greyton. Ethereal, perfumed and refined, it has violet and lily aromas, some texture from 50% whole clusters, layered tannins and a core of blackberry, white pepper and red berry fruit. The 35% new oak is right on point.

n: Lismore The Age of Grace Viognier
d: One of three different Viogniers from Samantha O’Keefe, the undisputed queen of the variety in South Africa, this uses grapes from Bot River, Elgin and Vyeboom and is typical of her restrained style. Very lightly wooed, it has a palate of clementine, ginger and apricot and a scoop of cream to hold everything together.

n: Longridge Blanc de Blancs Brut CC

d: One of the more unusual Cap Classique bubblies, this is made entirely from Verdelho, which is seldom used as a sparkling wine grape. Left on lees for 84 months to develop some nutty autolysis, this is still pretty tangy and focused, with Granny Smith apple and lemongrass flavours and a peppery, bone-dry finish.

Jasper Raats uses grapes from four different blocks, situated between 280 and 300 metres, to make his Reserve Chardonnay. Assertively fermented and aged in 55% new oak, it has aromas of toast, gunflint and wildflowers, racy, mouth-watering acidity and some mid-palate weight and texture from 90% malolactic.

Clos du Ciel is a celebrated, 1.2-hectare Chardonnay block, planted with a mix of clones at 280 metres on the side of the Helderberg. This is definitely on the chiselled side, with lots of youthful vim and energy, layers of lemongrass, wet stones and citrus zest, a waft of fynbos and smartly handled 40% new oak.

Longridge’s Chenin Blanc comes from a biodynamically farmed block that was planted on the lower Helderberg in 2007. Whole bunch pressed before fermentation in neutral wood, it’s a youthful, focused, lightly peppery style with quince, citrus and green apple flavours and an appealingly bitter twist.

The 20% new oak is nicely handled here, adding some ginger and vanilla spice to a red-fruited palate of raspberry and red cherry. Floral and approachable, this is the kind of Pinotage you could drink lightly chilled with fine, supple tannins and a refreshing core.

Made by Richard Kershaw MW, the King of South African Chardonnay, this comes from three blocks at Lothian planted with the 25% 76, 95 and 348 Burgundy clones. The 25% new wood is stylishly integrated here, complementing a palate that’s textured, refreshing and lightly toasty with citrus, gunflint and toffee fudge flavours and the acidity that comes with a cool climate.

n: Lothian Vineyards Lothian of Elgin Biosphere Chardonnay Sur Lie
d: Biosphere is an unwooded Elgin Chardonnay that derives some of its texture from eight months on lees. The sort of thing that Chablis used to make on an annual basis before climate change, it has good balance and texture, pithy acidity and core of citrus, lemon butter and orange zest.

n: Lothian Vineyards Lothian of Elgin Pinot Noir
d: Richard Kershaw MW is the consultant to this stylish, medium-weight Pinot Noir from Elgin. Very much a cool climate style, it’s precise, sappy and lightly reductive, with red cherry and pomegranate fruit, a spine of savoury tannins and subtle, well-integrated 25% new French oak.

n: Lothian Vineyards Lothian of Elgin Riesling

d: Now under the baton of winemaker Simon Smith, Louisvale has a deserved reputation for the quality of its varietal Cabernet Sauvignon. There’s plenty of good backbone and freshness here, typical of the best made 2024s, with subtle mocha oak, cassis and black cherry fruit and a minty undertone.

n: Louisvale CC Blanc de Blanc Brut

d: A fine follow up to the 2024 release, Louisvale is back where it belongs among the top Chardonnay producers in Stellenbosch. It’s a comparatively rich, toasty style, but it’s trim rather than overweight, attractive beeswax, patisserie, butterscotch and citrus zest flavours and a balanced, medium-bodied finish.

The Boris – nothing to do with a disgraced former British Prime Minister, thank goodness – is a well-judged assemblage of Cabernet Sauvignon, 12% Merlot, 7% each of Cabernet Franc and Malbec and 4% Petit Verdot. Savoury, leafy and balsamic, it’s a wine to drink sooner rather than later, but has subtle layers of tobacco leaf and coconut spice and cassis and summer berry flavours.

Named after Franco Lourens’ dad, who features on the label, this is a consistently impressive Rhône style cuvée made from Grenache, 39% Cinsault and 19% Syrah, combining three different sub-regions of the Swartland. Fermented with around 25% whole bunches, it’s an intense, still youthful blend that has appealing flavours of oregano, blood orange, blackberry and Campari spices and a tug of underlying tannins.

A white blend that lives up to its beautiful label, this combines Chenin Blanc, 20% Verdelho and 16% each of Colombard and Grenache Blanc, sourced from Paarl, Piekenierskloof, Stellenbosch and the Swartland. Featuring, wooded, concrete aged and skin contact portions, it has layers of agave, lime and gin botanicals and a sappy, tangy, mineral-etched finish.

n: Lourens Family Wines Lua Single Vineyard Grenache
d: Fermented and aged entirely in concrete for the first time, with slightly lower alcohol than in the past, this is the kind of Piekenierskloof Grenache that will appeal to fans of the Gredos region in Spain. Racy, ethereal and poised, it has a waft of tobacco leaf from 25% whole clusters, flavours of pomegranate, cranberry and wild strawberry and a top note of Angostura bitters.

n: Lourens Family Wines OVP Mathias Chenin Blanc
d: This is the last release of this wine from the Sonkop vineyard on the Paardeberg, alas, as Callie Louw will use the fruit to make his own Chenin Blanc. So, enjoy three 500-litre barrels while you can. White flower and fresh hay aromas lead you into a pithy, mouth-watering palate that has some subtle reduction, remarkable energy and focus and the racy minerality that often comes from grapes grown on granite soils.

n: Lourens Family Wines Piekenierskloof OVP Cinsault
d: "New block, new label, new everything," says Franco Lourens of this stand-alone Cinsault from sandstone soils in Piekenierskloof. Showing the concentration and low yields of its 1962 vines, this is muscular, sinewy and refreshing at the same time, with alluring rooibos tea, orange zest and Campari spice flavours, subtle oak and a lingering, energetic finish.

Hannes Nel makes very good bubbly, selling the result at an affordable price. This is a structured, layered, complex cuvée of Chardonnay and 15% Pinot Noir that has some subtle oak on the base wine and spent 63 months on lees. Toasty, dry and intense, this has layers of white flowers, aniseed and brioche and a chiselled, palate-cleansing finish.

A wine for Chardonnay lovers on a budget, this delivers a lot of flavour for less than R200. Fermented and aged in a combination of stainless steel, new and second use barrels and terracotta amphoras, this is tangy, focused and well balanced, with gunflint and petrichor top notes and a racy, slightly salty palate of citrus and grapefruit complemented by a subtle bitter twist.

Consistently among the better Viogniers from South Africa, this is particularly impressive in 2025, making the most of a stellar vintage. Fermented in 27% new oak, with ageing on primary lees for 11 months, it’s an engagingly scented white, with vanilla, pepper and sandalwood aromas and a palate that combines lovely, creamy intensity with flavours of apricot and clementine.

Prieska in the northern Cape is the source of this subtle, understated Viognier that draws on the talents of consultant, Lukas van Loggerenberg. Wild yeast fermented in older barrels, it’s not the fattest or creamiest expression of the variety, but it has gentle layers of lanolin, citrus and white flowers and a racy, acid-driven finish.

n: Loïc Du Toit Wines White Bait Chardonnay
d: An exciting maiden release from young winemaker Loïc Du Toit, who has a day job at De Wetshof, this is a stylish, racy, unwooded Chardonnay from Roberston’s classic limestonerich soils. Chalky, pithy and refreshing, it has flavours of cardamom, lime and lemongrass and a palate-cleansing wet stone finish.

Now featuring a 25% stainless steel component, alongside 50% new oak, this is a wellbalanced Franschhoek Viognier with a little bit of bottle age. Peach, apricot and subtle pineapple flavours are complemented by a creamy mid palate and some patisserie spices.

The Pinotage has been ditched in 2025, but the rest of this interesting blend remains, combining Syrah, 33% Mourvèdre and 17% Cabernet Franc. Fermented with 15% whole clusters and skin-macerated for 30 days, it’s a savoury, layered, refreshing cool climate red with redcurrant, plum and tobacco leaf flavours and a herbal undertone.

A brand that deserves to be better known, Maanschijn is a collaboration between Doulgas Mylrea and Paul Hoorwerf. Basket pressed and separately fermented this is a slightly savoury, oxidatively handled cuvée of Sauvignon Blanc, 27% Chenin Blanc, 20% Semillon and 18% Chardonnay. Aromas of nettle and stony reduction segue into a palate of elderflower, citrus zest and cardamom supported by some tannins.

The Contour is produced by one of two winemakers called Thys Louw in Durbanville. This is a full-bodied, barrel fermented style that uses 15% new oak, showing greengage, toast and passion fruit flavours, a hint of residual sugar and a subtle volatile lift.

New to Alex McFarlane’s range, Friday’s Child is an unusual blend of Pinotage, 30% Cinsault and 10% Grenache with around 30% whole bunches and negligible oak. Enticing aromas of rosehip and rooibos tea lead you into a palate of wild strawberry and Turkish Delight, savoury tannins and a tapering finish.

Rising star Alex McFarlane sources her nuanced, well-balanced Grenache from vineyards on Citrusdal Mountain, close to the West Coast. Denser and more backward than the more ethereal 2024 release, it has some subtle, stony reduction, redcurrant, tobacco leaf and aromatic spice flavours and a tangy, acid-fresh finish.

n: McGregor Winery Terroir Selection Chenin Blanc

d: The Heritage Block Pinotage comes from a Durbanville vineyard that was planted in 1955, making it one of the oldest in the region. Concentrated and intense enough to carry its 45% new oak lightly, it has plum and black cherry fruit, some toasty overtones and a backbone of sinewy tannin.

Ambitiously priced at over R1,000 a bottle perhaps, but this is an intriguing expression of Pinotage made with vine-dried grapes from a single block. With its 14.5% alcohol, it’s something of an Amarone style with 12.7 grams of residual sugar, flavours of liquorice, fig and blackberry and stylish, scented 20% new oak.

Wade Roger-Lund has done a very good job at Meerendal, so I’m sorry to hear that he’s leaving. This comes from three blocks on a farm that is rightly associated with Pinotage and is nicely textured and rose petal scented, with wild strawberry and pomegranate flavours and deftly intertwined 44% new oak.

The Chapel is a single-site Sauvignon Blanc from Wade Roger-Lund, fermented in 50% new French oak in a Blanc Fumé style. Slightly lighter this year because of growing-season rain, it has gooseberry and passion fruit flavours and a patina of wood spices.

Appealingly low in alcohol at just 12%, this is a Pinotage-dominated blend with support from seamlessly combined 28% Merlot and 22% Syrah. The 28% new oak adds a sheen of vanilla spice here, complementing a palate of bramble and wild strawberry and a herbal twist.

Picked before the rains that did so much damage in other parts of Stellenbosch, this stylish Cabernet Sauvignon comes from three main blocks in the lower part of the farm. Deftly aged in 50% new oak, it has the fine-grained, supple tannins that are part of the new Meerlust style, racy cassis and red plum flavours and a graphite top note.

The wine that has undergone the greatest stylistic shift under Wim Truter at Meerlust, this is much fresher and better balanced than it used to be, with only 5% malolactic and just 33% new oak. Sourced from two sites on granite and shale soils, it has a mineral core, a subtle mix of peach and lemon zest flavours, a hint of vanilla and a racy finish.

The Estate Red is Meerlust’s attempt to compete with brands like The Chocolate Block and Rupert & Rothschild's Classique. First made in 2020, it has quickly established itself in the market, with a stylish assemblage of Cabernet Sauvignon, 38% Cabernet Franc and 5% Merlot. Leafy, fresh and herbal, with appealing purity and subtle 20% new oak, it’s a deliciously drinkable glass of wine.

Meerlust handled the challenges of the 2023 harvest as well as anyone in Stellenbosch, as demonstrated by the quality of this varietal Merlot. Sourced from six different blocks on the estate, representing eight soil types, it has subtle coffee bean aromas, fine-grained tannins, layers of cassis, tarragon and summer berries and scented 35% new oak. A wine that carries its 14.7% alcohol lightly.

Fermented cool to retain perfume and freshness, Meerlust’s Pinot Noir comes from two parcels planted with the 115 clone. The 40% new oak is skilfully integrated here, with some help from ageing in concrete, revealing a palate of vibrant pomegranate and goji berry flavours supported by tangy acidity and filigree tannins. Improving with every vintage.

While some Stellenbosch producers struggled in 2023, Meerlust produced another very impressive Rubicon, even more impressive when you consider the 180,000 bottles produced. Partnering Cabernet Sauvignon, 36% Merlot, 11% Cabernet Franc and 7% Petit Verdot, this has plenty of colour, granite-derived freshness and minerality, youthful cassis, basil, damson and dark chocolate flavours and beautifully sculpted tannins. Bravo!

n: Mellish Family Vineyards Bakenkop Blanc Fumé
d: Not your boiler plate Durbanville Sauvignon Blanc by any means, this has partial fermentation on skins as well as 25% new barrels. Refreshing, tangy and refined, it wouldn’t look out of place in Pessac-Léognan, with layers of gunflint, nettle and pink grapefruit, chiselled acidity and gently integrated oak.

n: Mellish Family Vineyards Bakenkop Chenin Blanc
d: A name to keep an eye on in Durbanville, Andrew Mellish is making increasingly good wines at his family’s organic farm. Subtly wooded in older barrels, this is a racy, cooler climate style of Chenin Blanc with top notes of white pepper and sea breezes, a palate of citrus and yellow apple and a satisfyingly stony finish.

Andrew Mellish sells 95% of his grapes to other wineries, but there’s surely a strong case for producing more wine under his own label. Fermented with 13.5% whole bunches, this is a floral, medium-bodied style with fennel, pepper and fynbos aromas and a palate of redcurrant and summer berries. Subtle and refined.

Made with organically grown grapes from the Mellish family’s wheat and beef farm in Durbanville, this is a juicy, floral, enticing expression of Pinotage that sees a little oak. Supple and well balanced, it has plum and summer berry fruit and a bright, refreshing finish.

n: Metzer Family 3 Miles to Milk Bay OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Previously sold as Maritime, this comes from a single OVP block that was planted in 1980 on the coastal side of the Helderberg. Fermented with full malolactic, although you’d struggle to spot it, Wade Metzer’s superb Chenin Blanc has jasmine and chamomile aromas, layers of earth, citrus and oatmeal, a briny undertone and vivid, granite-influenced zip and minerality.

Sourced from two blocks on Chris Steyn’s Eendrag farm and Rustenhof, both close to False Bay, this is a varietal Cabernet Sauvignon of considerable focus and precision. Menthol, graphite and dried herb aromas are a scented introduction to a palate of plum, blackcurrant and subtle 30% new oak.

Mantra combines Syrah with 30% Cabernet Sauvignon and 20% Cinsault. “I love the way they hang together,” says Wade Metzer. Appealingly South African in all the best ways, it a nice medley of red cherry, plum and blackcurrant pastille fruit, sinewy, age-worthy tannins, top notes of mint and basil and some underlying tension and grip.

n: Metzer Family Montane OVP Chenin Blanc
d: The Montane label has been around for a while, but is effectively a new wine in 2025, as it uses grapes from a 1982 OVP block in the Blaauwklippen Valley for the first time. Intensely floral and herbal, it has wafts of fynbos and thyme, intense flavours of lemon verbena, quince and orange zest and a sappy, mineral-etched finish.

Made with grapes from what Wade Metzer calls “bonzai vines” on the Rustenhof farm overlooking False Bay, this is a finely balanced, nuanced Cinsault from sandy soils. Aged in older wood, it has some spices from 30% whole bunches, bramble and redcurrant flavours and a focused, tangy, granite-scented finish. Very classy.

I think of Wade Metzer as more of a Syrah than Shiraz guy, but what do I know? This comes from two Stellenbosch vineyards with an Atlantic influence, given further perfume and structure by 40% whole bunches. Pure, scented and appealingly granitic, it has tea leaf, white pepper and red cherry flavours and a frame of savoury tannins.

The decomposed granite soils of the Polkadraai Hills are the home of Miles Mossop’s mid-tier Cabernet Sauvignon. A serious wine that needs – and will get – more time in bottle, it has bold tannins, lots of grip and intensity, damson and blackcurrant flavours, sinewy tannins and deftly integrated 15% new oak.

Red clay soils next to Eben Sadie’s Treinspoor vineyard in Malmesbury are the source of this subtle, 50% whole bunch-fermented Cinsault. Fermented and aged in concrete eggs, it has rose petal and Negroni spice top notes, a juicy palate of cranberry and wild strawberry an a sappy, slightly earthy finish.

n: Miles Mossop Chapters OVP Chenin Blanc
d: The du Bois family’s vineyard in Stellenbosch supplies the grapes for this old-vine Chenin Blanc from clay shale soils. Rich yet focused, it’s a structured, intense Chenin Blanc with a subtle frame of older wood, pear and stone fruit flavours, some underlying stony intensity and the concentration to develop further in bottle.

n: Miles Mossop Chapters OVP Sauvignon Blanc
d: Weathered shale soils on the Sonop farm are the source of this Old Vine Sauvignon Blanc from a parcel planted in 1986. An engaging top note of petrichor and wet stones segues into a palate of greengage, pink grapefruit and yellow apple, with a dab of cream and some understated vanilla spice from 15% new wood.

Miles Mossop sources this brilliant sweet Chenin Blanc from two blocks on the Sonop farm, both of which were affected by full botrytis in 2025. Barrel fermented in older oak, it has rich flavours of crème brûlée, guava and citrus fruit, intense 223 grams of residual sugar, some aromatic baking spices and a lift of volatile acidity.

n: Miles Mossop The Introduction Chenin Blanc
d: Featuring grapes from Stellenbosch and a small percentage from the Swartland, this is a very quaffable blend of Chenin Blanc and 1% Clairette Blanche. Very lightly oaked in older barrels and stainless steel, it has a nice medley of quince, yellow apple and pear and a tangy, palatecleansing finish.

The Introduction is Miles Mossop’s by-the-glass red, made with a “heritage” blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, 21% Cinsault, 6% Merlot and 2% Petit Verdot. Spicy, floral and earthy, it has more grip and presence than you’d expect, with lively cranberry, cassis and forest floor notes and a fresh, leafy finish.

One of the staples of the expanding Momento line up, this is Marelise Niemann’s best seller. Combining Chenin Blanc and 35% Verdelho from six different vineyards, it’s a dryland delight, with yellow apple, quince and clementine flavours and some underlying tannic structure. A lot of wine at the price.

Marelise Niemann is the queen of Cape Grenache, whether white, gris or red. This comes from five different vineyards in Bot River, Stellenbosch, the Swartland and the Voor Paardeberg. Macerated on skins for 24 hours, it has good grip and freshness, quince, yellow apple and lemon zest flavours and a whisper of oak.

No prisoners taken here on this Voor Paardeberg Grenache Gris which spent 47 days on skins at 8¼C. Showing an attractive pink hue, it has appealing rose petal and ginger aromas, subtle quinine-like bitterness and flavours of citrus zest and green fig. Nicely understated.

Choosing between Marelise Niemann’s Grenaches isn’t easy – my advice is to buy all four – but this is (just) my favourite in 2024. Soured from Erasmus van Zyl’s farm in Piekenierskloof, it’s an ethereal, beguiling delight, with rooibos tea and saffron aromas and a racy, refreshing palate of redcurrant, raspberry and hibiscus. The 20% whole bunches add another layer of complexity.

The Anysbos farm in Bot River, where Marelise Niemann is the consultant, supplies the grapes for this consistently impressive Grenache from Bokkeveld shale soils. Suitably ferrous and intense, it has dried rose petal and fynbos aromas, plenty of structure and energy, flavours of goji berry and wild strawberry and well-integrated 20% whole bunches.

Kloovenburg’s vineyards in Riebeekberg supply the raw material for this Grenache – without the Garnacha Perluda that’s planted nearby. Showing the elegance and finesse that often seem to come from schist soils, it has scented wild strawberry and Turkish Delight flavours, some stony grip and a floral top note.

One of a quartet of region-specific Grenaches from Marelise Niemann, this comes from Scholtz Rossouw’s vines on the Paardeberg. Showing some subtle reduction and a waft of Campari spices, it has redcurrant and red cherry flavours, some texture from 30% whole bunches and a herbal undertone.

n: Mooiplaas Bush Vine OVP Chenin Blanc

d: Mercia hails from a young-vine block at 375 metres – high for the Bottelary Hills – on sandstone and decomposed granite soils. Carrying its 50% new oak lightly, it has good midpalate texture from 70% malolactic, appealing freshness and acidity, pear and citrus fruit flavours and a lightly stony finish.

Bertus Basson uses only 10% new wood on his Pinotage, reasoning that the wines have more than enough flavour and structure of their own. Sourced from 29-year-old bush vines, this is perfumed and engaging, with juicy bramble and summer pudding flavours, fine tannins and a sheen of aromatic spices.

It doesn’t claim Old Vine Project status, but this Bottelary Hills Sauvignon Blanc comes from a cool, dryland block that was planted in 1972. Given extended lees contact in stainless steel, it’s a wine with texture and intensity, with lots of acidity, flavours of lime, gooseberry and padrón peppers and a racy finish.

n: Mountain Ridge Romansrivier Grand Reserve Fire Lily
Mountain Ridge The Twins Cabernet Sauvignon

d: Elgin vines at 330 metres on Bokkeveld shale soils are the source of this stylish blend of the CY96 and 548 clones from very young vines. Savoury and complex, it’s about texture and acidity rather than simple fruit flavours, with layers of wet stones, sourdough bread and waxed lemons and top notes of aniseed and subtle oak spices.

A 60/40 combination of the 777 and 667 clones is responsible for this tangy, nicely judged Elgin Pinot Noir. Made without whole clusters because the stems are “too spicy”, according to Jean Smit, this is a bold, structured red with pink grapefruit, black cherry and blood orange flavours and top notes of rosewater and vanilla spice.

West-facing vines on Bokkeveld shale soils supply the raw material for this concretefermented, just off-dry Riesling from Jean Smit. The 5.5 grams of residual sugar are balanced by pithy acidity, with appealingly crunchy elderflower, lime and blackcurrant leaf flavours and a mineral-etched core.

"Epic" was my one-word summary of this brilliant Chenin Blanc from the Paardeberg. Sourced from comparatively young, 12-year-old vines on decomposed granite soils, it has amazing energy, vibrancy and focus, with salty, mouth-watering acidity, some struck match reduction, lemongrass, grapefruit and wet stone flavours and finish that lingers on the tongue for a minute. Bravo, Chris and Andrea Mullineux.

Adi Badenhorst’s Jakkalsfontein farm on the Paardeberg is the source of this Syrah, which is often served first of the three single-site bottlings at the winery. Fermented with 100% whole clusters, it has lots of structure, density and minerality, age-worthy tannins, plenty of energy and underlying structure and flavours of damson, blackberry and cooked meat.

The Iron Chenin Blanc comes from red clay soils in Malmesbury that can be challenging in hotter vintage but were ideally suited to the balanced 2025 growing season. Richer, broader and more textured than the Mullineux’s Granite release, with plenty of underlying concentration and grip, flavours of quince and pear, subtle oak and an intriguing, slightly ferrous finish.

Iron comes from red ferricrete soils in Malmesbury and has been part of the Mullineux’s supply base since their days as Tulbagh Mountain Vineyards. Dense, dark and appealingly brooding, it has top notes of clove and white pepper, intense blackberry, blueberry and steak tartare flavours and the concentration to reward cellaring.

n: Mullineux Kloof Street Old Vine Chenin Blanc
d: Chris and Andrea Mullineux buy in the grapes to make their crowd-pleasing Chenin Blanc, sourcing most of it from vineyards on the Paardeberg. Aged in a combination of mostly stainless steel and 15% older oak, it has some granitic energy, appealing flavours of fennel, greengage and yellow apple and some texture from full malolactic.

Kloof Street is made in good volumes and is a very accessible, reasonably priced introduction to the Mullineux’s range. Featuring Syrah, 15% Grenache and 10% Cinsault, it has appealing texture and clove spice from 40% whole bunches, some subtle meaty reduction, touches of thyme and fynbos and a core of vibrant redcurrant and blackberry fruit.

A white that no one should be in a hurry to drink, given how well it develops in bottle, this demonstrates Andrea Mullineux’s considerable skills as a blender. Combining Chenin Blanc, 11% Clairette Blanche, 8% Viognier, 6% Grenache Blanc and 5% Semillon Gris, it’s a wine that “defines who we are”, according to Chris Mullineux with lots of zip and acidity, layers of fennel, grapefruit and peach a dusting of wild mountain herbs.

The sixth release of this incredible solera Chenin Blanc has components dating back to 2008. Made in bijou quantities of less than 2,000 bottles, it’s both young and timeless at the same time, showing another side of Chenin Blanc. With layers of dried fig, honey, marzipan and orange zest, a subtle rancio undertone and a gorgeous interplay between acidity and 360 grams of residual sugar. One of the world’s greatest sweet wines.

One of an established trio of soil-specific Chenin Blancs from Chris and Andrea Mullineux, the power couple of the Swartland, this is the least extreme of the trio, combining elements of the other two. Sourced from a very windy site on the Roundstone estate, it has appealing texture and weight, flavours of pear, apricot and sourdough bread and plenty of supporting acidity and minerality.

Often my pick of the three top Syrahs from the Mullineux, this is a wine that has what Chris Mullineux refers to as a “calm confidence”. Ethereal top notes of fynbos, potpourri and aromatic spices segue into a palate of wild strawberry, plum and tobacco leaf complemented by appealing freshness, sappy acidity and wonderful texture. World class.

Like the Mullineux’s Granite Syrah, this stunning straw wine comes from Adi Badenhorst’s Jakkalsfontein farm on the Paardeberg. Combining natural acidity and a mind-boggling 358 grams of residual sugar, it’s a dehydrated, concentrated quintessence of Chenin Blanc, with lovely guava, honey and pawpaw flavours, a surprisingly refreshing palate and a lovely volatile lift.

At less than a third of the price of the three soil-specific Syrahs from the Mullineux, this is a relative bargain in the range. Combining grapes from granite, iron, quartz and schist, it’s a textbook Swartland expression of the variety, with fennel and violet aromas, a textured palate of blackberry, black olive and liquorice and very subtle oak.

People tend to forget that Muratie makes a Port-style fortified, but this is very enjoyable in its own way. Made from four Portuguese varieties – Tinta Barocca, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Francesa and Souzão – grown on a 1977 block, it’s youthful and sturdy, with fig and Black Forest gâteau flavours, age-worthy tannins and 90 grams of residual sugar.

One of a pair of impressive Chardonnays from Haittingh de Villiers and Rijk Melck, this comes from vines on the farm at 200 metres. The 28% new wood is well judged, adding a touch of cinnamon spice to a palate of clementine, lemongrass and cardamom complemented by some lees-stirring and subtle, crème fraîche malolactic notes.

Picked in two stages for balance and complexity, this is a fresh, appealingly light-bodied Chardonnay from a Simonsberg producer that deserves to be better known. Sandalwood and patisserie spice aromas segue into a palate of pear, quince and lemon zest framed by scented, first-rate French oak.

Laurens Campher says Chenin Blanc on the label, but it also contains 8% Sauvignon Blanc, 4% Verdelho and 3% Viognier. Fermented and aged in 5% new wood, it’s a seamless assemblage, with layers of musk, pear and citrus, bright, tangy acidity, subtle wood and some mid-palate texture from 40% malolactic.

It’s hard to go wrong with 2021 Stellenbosch Cabernets, the last great vintage until 2025. Skilfully curated in 10% new oak, it’s a proud, stand-alone expression of the variety, with sculpted tannins, lots of zip and energy, classic flavours of mulberry, cassis and red berries and the underlying concentration and freshness to develop further in bottle.

Well priced and easy to drink, this is the kind of thing you'd be happy to quaff at a braai. Combining Merlot, 37% Cabernet Sauvignon and 15% Shiraz, it’s a graceful, approachable cuvée, with a hint of stony reduction, bramble, plum and summer berry fruit and a dab of oak.

"It’s surprised us," says Rijk Melck of this dry-farmed Grenache, sourced from eight-yearold vines on the slopes of the Simonsberg. Showing that Stellenbosch can compete with Piekenierskloof, it has some clove spice from 20% whole bunches, subtle older wood, layers of redcurrant, pomegranate and Campari spices and fine-boned tannins.

Anything picked after the rains in 2023 was discarded, so there was quite a bit of selection involved to produce the latest release of MR. Based on Cabernet Franc, with 30% Cabernet Sauvignon, 15% Malbec, 11% Petit Verdot and 8% Merlot, this is grassy, herbal and refreshing, with fine-boned tannins, deftly handled cigar box oak, capsicum, cassis and red cherry flavours and a lingering finish. A lighter style of MR, but none the worse for that. Up a point after an extra year in bottle.

n: Myburgh Brothers Old Vine Chenin Blanc
d: A youthful Chenin Blanc that is mostly fermented and aged in stainless steel, with just 11% seeing older oak, this is sappy, bright and energetic, with subtle patisserie aromas, a palate of green apple and stone fruit and a slightly salty finish. Typically good value from Tyrrel Myburgh.

A new white from Alex Milner, ‘n Kaapse Ode is a “tribute to the Cape” made from Clairette Blanche from the Voor Paardeberg and 34% Chenin Blanc from Darling, both located on decomposed granite soils. Racy, tangy and mouth-wateringly fresh, this has aromas of white pepper and gin botanicals, palate of citrus and greengage and a lingering finish. An impressive début.

n: Natte Valleij Axle OVP Chenin Blanc
d: A block of old-vine Chenin Blanc planted in 1985 on decomposed granite supplies the raw material for this OVP white. The oak is kept to a minimum here, allowing the terroir to speak. Peach, yellow apple and nectarine flavours are supported and freshened by stony intensity and refreshing acidity.

A good value introduction to the magic Natte Valleij works with Cinsault, this is a bush-vine blend that combines components from Darling, Stellenbosch, the Swartland and mostly Wellington. Younger parcels are the focus, producing a wine with rose petal and rooibos tea aromas and a palate of pink grapefruit and summer berries.

NAT used to be a Pinotage, but is now what Alex Milner calls a “smashable” Cabernet Sauvignon from decomposed granite soils in Simonsberg-Paarl. Refreshingly medium bodied, it’s a racy, tangy refreshing style with cassis and summer pudding flavours and negligible oak. Only sold in South Africa.

One Night Stand – great name – is a new rosé from Alex Milner, sourced from vines on shale soils in Malmesbury. Made entirely with Cinsault, the house speciality, this is a pale, delicate, easy-drinking style with raspberry and redcurrant flavours and a nip of tannin.

It can be cool out there in Darling, a coastal region that sees considerable diurnal variation. Sourced from bush vines planted on decomposed granite in 1978, this is a wine that has freshness and zip as well as underlying backbone, with 15% whole bunches adding some texture and perfume to a palate of goji berry and wild strawberry. A Cinsault for Pinot Noir lovers.

“Not a lot of people understand tension in wine," says Alex Milner, so this Cinsault from a parcel on the Polkadraai Hills is intended to show them what they’ve been missing. Fermented with 10% whole bunches, it has redcurrant and goji berry flavours, lots of racy acidity, savoury tannins and a waft of potpourri.

Named in honour of three Italian prisoners of war who spent part of the Second World War at Natte Valleij, this is an unusual Coastal cuvée of Cabernet Sauvignon, 32% Cinsault and 9% Syrah. Floral and engaging, it’s a lighter style in 2023, with red cherry and blackcurrant leaf flavours and nicely understated oak.

Sampled just before bottling, this is a new wine from Jamie Willams, made with Pinot Gris from Darling and Stellenbosch. Very lightly wooded it’s musky and gently spicy, with top notes of ginger and cardamom and a textured palate of pear, citrus and white peach. Textured and refreshing at the same time.

Part of a good new range from Nederburg, where the winemakers get to experiment a little, this Darling Sauvignon Blanc was given an hour of skin contact before partial barrel ageing. Showing noticeable Atlantic Ocea freshness, it’s nettley and slightly briny, with some subtle nutmeg spice and flavours of grapefruit, gooseberry and green asparagus.

Ambitious stuff from Nederburg, this bubbly from Durbanville, Paarl and Stellenbosch spent 84 months on lees before disgorgement. Pairing Chardonnay and 21% Pinot Noir, it’s a lowdosage style with good concentration, bracing acidity, flavours of umami, brioche and citrus zest and a creamy, palate-coating mousse.

Double Barrel sounds like a wine with way too much wood for its own good, but that’s not the case here. Made from a blend of Merlot, 14% Cabernet Sauvignon, 12% Petit Verdot, 8% Malbec and 5% Cabernet Franc, this is a textured, modern red with top notes of mint, bay leaf and dark chocolate and a palate that marries plum and blackberry flavours with well-judged tannins.

n: Nederburg Heritage Heroes The Anchorman OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Tasted as a tank sample, this Chenin Blanc comes from a single Swartland parcel on granite soils. Partnering barrel, stainless steel and clay pot components, it has some added structure from partial skin contact, a touch of stony reduction, quince, cardamom and waxed lemon flavours and a textured, well-balanced finish.

n: Nederburg Heritage Heroes The Brew Master
d: Part of the Heritage Heroes range that honours individuals who have contributed to Nederburg’s story, this is a five-way Bordeaux-style red blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, 26% Merlot, 8% Cabernet Franc, 6% Petit Verdot and 4% Malbec. Subtly wooded in mostly new French and a little American oak, it marries blackcurrant, plum, coffee bean and vanilla flavours with fine tannins and a fresh finish.

n: Nederburg Heritage Heroes The Motorcycle Marvel

d: Based on Muscat de Frontignan from Simonsberg-Paarl with 19.5% Chenin Blanc and 11% Riesling from Darling, this is a very smart 100% botrytis-affected sticky with appealing freshness and commendably low volatile acidity. Very lightly wooded, it has layers of guava, passionfruit and honey, lime-like acidity and well-integrated 141 grams of residual sugar.

n: Nederburg The Manor House Cabernet Sauvignon
d: The Manor House is a well-priced, pan-Cape Cabernet Sauvignon that uses grapes from Paarl, Philadelphia and Stellenbosch. Assertively aged in 30% new French oak, good texture and intensity, toast, vanilla spice and blackcurrant pastille flavours and a firm, age-worthy finish.

n: Neetlingshof Short Story Collection The Caracal
d: A Stellenbosch red that weathered the tricky conditions in 2023, this is a modern, polished Bordeaux-style assemblage that partners Cabernet Sauvignon, 23% Merlot, 13% Cabernet Franc and 1% Malbec. Ageing in one-third new oak adds some toast and coffee bean notes to a palate of capsicum and blackcurrant pastille.

Neil Ellis was one of the pioneers of Darling Sauvignon Blanc, releasing his first wine back in 1991. Now made by his son, Warren, this has a briny top note that reflects the region’s proximity to the Atlantic Ocean, a salty introduction to a palate of citrus, grapefruit, parsley and green beans, understated older oak and a mineral core.

Two aspects and two picks contribute to this cool climate Syrah from the Groenekloof sub-region of Darling. Herbal, spicy and intense, it’s a lightly oaked delight, with savoury complexity, aromas of thyme and white pepper, red berry and tobacco leaf flavours and very subtle oak.

Warren Ellis sources this focused, well-structured Jonkershoek Cabernet Sauvignon from the lower part of the valley, close to Lanzerac. Aged in 70% new wood, it has lots of toast and coffee bean, layers of bramble and blackcurrant leaf, some herbal undertones and plenty of grip and ageing potential.

Sourced from the Marais family’s farm in Piekenierskloof, this is an intriguing, highaltitude blend of Palomino and 46% Chenin Blanc. Fennel and saffron aromas are a scented introduction to a palate of oatmeal, salted almond, beeswax and lemon zest underpinned by appealing extract and tannic structure.

Rodanos is a fine, well-balanced cuvée of Syrah from Darling and 40% Grenache from Piekenierskloof. Skilfully curated in 30% new wood, it has meaty grip and intensity, top notes of thyme and incense, fig and blackberry fruit and a refreshing, lifted finish.

Made in a very dry vintage in Elgin, which increased fructose levels in the wine, according to Warren Ellis, this is a refreshingly low-alcohol Chardonnay with lovely poise and balance. Barrel fermented in 40% new wood with 10% malolactic, it has clementine, citrus and cherimoya flavours, racy acidity and a mineral core.

n: Newstead Blanc de Blancs Brut CC
d: Rightly popular with the holidaymakers who flock to Plettenberg Bay, as well as bubbly aficionados in other parts of the country, this is a very tasty, all-Chardonnay bubbly from Anton Small. Based on the 2018 vintage, with a 12% component from 2017, it’s an off dry style with flavours of pear, aniseed and citrus zest, a hint of oak spices and a racy, palate-cleansing finish.

Using grapes from Plettenberg Bay – better known as a tourist destination than a winemaking region, at least until recently – this is a well-balanced, eminently drinkable cuvée of Pinot Noir and 19% Chardonnay. Showing some sweetness from 9.6 grams of dosage, it has succulent pomegranate and wild strawberry flavours, tiny bubbles, good texture and a slight bitter twist.

Now into its twelfth vintage, this comes from the oldest plantings of Albariño in the Cape. Fermented and aged in stainless steel, concrete eggs and foudres, it has good structure and phenolics, lime, pear and citrus fruit flavours and the concentration to develop further in bottle. Sappy, aromatic and appealingly refreshing.

Yields were very low in 2025 – think three tons per hectare – but this doesn’t seem like an overly concentrated Chardonnay. Sourced from three sites on the farm, two of which face south, it has wet stone and lime blossom aromas, a palate of tangerine and lemongrass, and appealing underlying texture from full malolactic.

n: Newton Johnson Family Vineyards Pinot Noir
d: Blended across the farm, this is a barrel selection from four different vineyards – Seadragon, Windansea, Sanford and a little bit of Mrs M. Fermented with 20% whole clusters and aged in 33% new oak, it has enticing rose petal and tobacco leaf aromas, layers of earth, raspberry and goji berry and a tang of granitic minerality. Expresses the energy of the superb 2025 vintage.

Right up there with the best cool climate Chardonnays in South Africa, this comes from a cool, south-facing parcel of just 0.6 hectares in the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley. Reflecting the zip and stony intensity of its granite soils, it’s a wine with remarkable focus and zip, unfurling flavours of citrus, pear and beeswax supported by scented 24% new oak and effortless density and gravitas. A Cape Corton-Charlemagne.

A great site in an historic vintage: what more could you ask of a Pinot Noir? Located on a single, north-facing site planted with the 113 clone, Seadragon is a Cape Grand Cru, with saffron and rose water aromas, flavours of wild strawberry, pomegranate and rooibos tea, plenty of racy acidity and fine, granular tannins. Delicious now, but will also evolve in bottle.

Three different clones – 3, 5 and 95 – planted in Tokara’s old Siberia vineyard supply the raw material for this full malolactic Chardonnay. Rich, textured, yet beautifully balanced and harmonious, it has top notes of sandalwood and vanilla spice and a palate of lime and lemon butter and a touch of passion fruit sweetness.

n: Newton Johnson Walker Bay Pinot Noir
d: The idea here is “over delivery”, according to Nadia Newton Johnson. Made entirely with the 113 clone, sourced from Bot River, the Upper-Hemel-en-Aarde Valley and the Hemel-enAarde Ridge, this has significant grip and intensity, redcurrant and pomegranate flavours and adroitly integrated 12% new oak.

Located next to Seadragon, but very different in style, the Windansea vineyard is planted with a trio of clones – 113, 115 and 777 – on clay and shale soils. Compact, focused and restrained, it’s a Pinot Noir to tuck away for a while, with bramble and black cherry flavours, a twist of orange peel, sinewy, serious tannins and beautifully interwoven 24% new oak. A winery at the top of its game.

"I wanted to make a Port-style wine," says Erni Leicht, who did exactly that as a one-off. Made with Syrah that had been in barrel for 18 years and had never been topped, this has 90 grams of residual sugar, rancio-rich flavours of dates, molasses and dried fruit and the underlying structure you’d expect from an LBV.

Made as a “proper white blend” in the words of Helgard van Schalkwyk, this partners Sauvignon Blanc and 48% Semillon, with the latter variety seeing oak. Creamy, sappy and herbal, it has tangy lime and pink grapefruit flavours and a whisper of patisserie spices.

On the cusp of qualifying for Old Vine Project status, this Durbanville Sauvignon was given two hours of skin contact before fermentation. Lees aged for 12 months, it’s a rich, full-bodied style with pear, lime and passion fruit flavours and an undertone of flinty reduction.

Durbanville Semillon sometimes gets overlooked because of the overwhelming focus on Sauvignon Blanc in the region. Unfairly so in my view. This is off-dry at 4.5 grams of residual sugar, with appealing beeswax and fennel aromas, scented 20% new oak and a textured palate of greengage and waxed lemons.

The Grande Matriarch is a Pinot Noir bubbly with a touch of colour. Matured for two years on lees before disgorgement, it has appealing toast, wild strawberry and summer pudding flavours, tangy acidity, fine bubbles and just 3.3 grams of dosage.

Fermented with yeasts that occur naturally in the vineyard, this is an off-dry Sauvignon Blanc with 8% Semillon for “backbone”, according to Helgard van Schalkwyk. Green-tinged flavours of asparagus and tarragon are complemented by vanilla-scented 10% new oak and some sweetness on the finish.

n: Noble Hill Brut Nature Blanc de Blancs

d: Field Atlas is a brilliant value Rhône style blend of Syrah, 7% Mourvèdre, 2% Grenache and 2% Viognier. Lightly wooded and refreshing, it has some clove spice from 10% whole bunches, top notes of rose petal and hibiscus, racy red cherry and bramble fruit and fine-boned tannins. Wonderfully drinkable and understated.

n: Noble Hill Simonskop OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Simonskop comes from the oldest block on the farm at Noble Hill, planted in 1987 and facing east on decomposed granite. Almost Sauvignon Blanc like in terms of raciness and flavour, it has some subtle stony reduction, a waft of jasmine, lots of zip and minerality, a touch of oak sweetness and a core of green apple and citrus.

Kristopher Tillery makes one of the Cape’s more restrained Viogniers from his organically farmed vineyards in Simonsberg-Paarl. Subtly wooded in 5% new barrels, it has engaging aromas of honeysuckle and white flowers, layers of tangerine, citrus and white peach, a touch of cream and a spicy finish.

Named after her family’s farm in Namibia, the Nuiba white is a deftly wooded blend of Sauvignon Blanc and 25% Semillon from Suzanne Coetzee, the latter being barrel fermented. Subtle kelp, sage and beeswax aromas guide you into a palate of gooseberry, citrus and green bean and a hint of subtle oak spices.

n: Oak Valley Beneath the Clouds Chardonnay
d: Beneath the Clouds is an impressive Chardonnay at the price from Jacques Du Plessis. Fermented in second and third-fill barrels and 15% foudres, it’s a perfumed, easy-drinking style, with lemongrass, cinnamon and wet stone flavours and a waft of white flowers.

n: Oak Valley Fountain of Youth Sauvignon Blanc
d: Featuring a highest-ever Semillon component at 9.5%, this blend with Sauvignon Blanc is a crowd-pleasing, easy-quaffing white blend. Greengage and passion fruit flavours are framed by scented 25% new oak with a herbal undertone and a tangy, cool-climate finish.

Made with selected parcels on the Oak Valley estate in Elgin, this Chardonnay is based on the 548 clone, with smaller amounts of 95 and 96. Fermented and aged in 31% new wood, it has sheen of cinnamon and nutmeg, a palate of pear and passion fruit and enough acidity to lift and freshen the finish.

Jacques Du Plessis uses four different Dijon clones – 114, 115, 667 and 777 – to make this mid-tier Elgin Pinot Noir.
