Showing a subtle undertone of whole bunch spices, it has aromas of rose petal and lily, scented 26% new oak, pomegranate and goji berry flavours and some patisserie sweetness on the finish.

n: Oak Valley Sounds of Silence Pinot Noir
d: A wine for Simon and Garfunkel fans perhaps, this is a very good-value Pinot Noir from Jacques Du Plessis, who makes some of the best examples of the variety in Elgin, but can play the volume game too. Floral, refreshing and enticing, this is a crowd-pleasing style with scented 16% new oak, layers of plum and wild strawberry and gentle, caressing tannins.

n: Oak Valley Tabula Rasa Chardonnay CY548
d: One of a series of clone-specific wines under the Tabula Rasa label, this was fermented in 50% new French oak to “manage the tannins”, according to Jacques Du Plessis. Flavours of peach, pear tart and mandarin orange are complemented by plenty of structure and acidity and a waft of vanilla spice.

n: Oak Valley Tabula Rasa Chardonnay CY95
d: Showcasing the widely planted CY95 clone, this Chardonnay was picked before the rains at the end of February, so suffered no dilution. The 43% new oak is expertly integrated here, adding a scented frame to a fresh, tangy, medium-bodied palate of aniseed and lemon zest. Racy and refreshing.

n: Oak Valley Tabula Rasa Pinot Noir PN667
d: There are only two barrels of this very tasty Pinot Noir, alas, made with the concentrated, tight-bunched 667 clone. Matured in 43% new oak (the second barrel is of 300 litres), this has top notes of mint, saffron and fynbos, plum and black cherry fruit, sinewy tannins and an appealingly savoury finish.

n: Oak Valley Tabula Rasa Pinot Noir PN777
d: Avoiding whole bunch fermentation in a cooler, wetter year, Jacques Du Plessis still ended up with what he calls “quite a wild wine”. Picked early for acidity, it has ginger spice and dried rose petal aromas, bramble, earth and summer berry flavours and the underlying freshness of site at 420 metres.

New to Duncan Savage’s portfolio, this is a small-volume Chardonnay from apple farmer Ian Cunningham’s five-year-old block in Elgin. The 25% new oak is well done here, with full malolactic adding some texture and weight to a palate of citrus, oatmeal and macadamia nut and a racy, mineral-etched core.

Part of a new, experimental range of small-parcel wines under the Observatory label, this high-altitude Grenache comes from a parcel at 770 metres on the Tierhoek farm in Piekenierskloof. It’s an ethereal expression of the variety, with plenty of chiselled acidity, flavours of cranberry, pomegranate and redcurrant and top notes of paprika and rose petal. Very promising.

Duncan Savage sources his Follow The Line Cinsault from this Darling vineyard, so he knows the site well. Grown in the teeth of the wind, it’s a racy, pithy red that is “helping us to understand Grenache better in South Africa”. Floral, herbal and nicely restrained, it has some texture and perfume from 20% whole clusters, red cherry, hibiscus and summer pudding fruit and a crunchy finish.

Bobby Wallace is one of the new faces of the Elgin region, although he also sources grapes from the Ceres Plateau. Sourced from Vrede en Lust’s Casey’s Ridge farm, this Chenin Blanc underwent 50% skin contact for added grip and complexity. Gunflint and struck match top notes segue into a palate of citrus, green apple and vanilla spice and a stony, palate-cleansing finish.

De Grendel’s farm at 1,050 metres on the Ceres Plateau is the source of this expressive cool climate Syrah from Bobby Wallace, all made with the SH9 clone. Fermented with 80% whole bunches, it has impressive concentration for a young-vine red, layers of fynbos, thyme and black pepper and a core of blackberry and wild strawberry fruit. “Back to where I like the wine,” as he puts it.

n: Old Road Wine Company 12 Mile Syrah
d: Picked early to retain acidity, this is a bright, medium-bodied Syrah from the granite soils of the Paardeberg that are so well suited to the variety. Fermented with 40% whole bunches, it’s a very lightly wooded style, with bramble, white pepper and red berry flavours, fine tannins and an energetic, acid-driven finish.

n: Old Road Wine Company Anemos Chenin Blanc
d: The vines are comparatively young by Swartland standards at 17 years’ old, but this has plenty of focus and intensity. Expressing the stony minerality that often comes with granite soils, it has citrus, grapefruit and petrichor notes, a floral top note, some lees-derived texture and a tapering finish.

n: Old Road Wine Company Grand-Mère OVP Single Vineyard Semillon
d: Using grapes from the celebrated La Colline vineyard in Franschhoek, planted in 1936, gives you a head start as a winemaker, and Ryan Puttick has handled them beautifully here. Fermented and aged in foudres, amphoras and some scented new oak, it’s a majestic Semillon with fennel and cinnamon aromas and a palate of lemongrass and cardamom complemented by a hint of struck match.

n: Old Road Wine Company Pepper Wind Single Vineyard Limited Edition Syrah
d: Pepper Wind comes from a vineyard at 450 metres in Franschhoek called, appropriately enough, La Montagne. Fermented with 50% whole clusters in amphoras and ceramic pots, with some old barrel ageing to follow, it has good zip and energy, aromas of clove and North Africa spices and a palate of redcurrant and bramble fruit.

n: Old Road Wine Company Stone Trail OVP Single Vineyard Chenin Blanc
d: Ryan Puttick makes the most of this parcel of old-vine Chenin Blanc in Franschhoek, planted close to the Boekenhoutskloof cellar on shale and decomposed granite soils. Naturally fermented in foudres and 15% amphoras, it has racy citrus zest and greengage flavours, a hint of gunflint and the underlying concentration of a parcel that’s been there since 1982.

Elizma Visser admits that she’s obsessed with Grenache Blanc and I’m more than happy that that’s the case. This uses grapes from a high-density planting at 450 metres and is wonderfully pithy, stony and intense, with layers of fynbos, lemon zest and Granny Smith apple, understated oak and a racy, mouth-watering finish. Delicious.

Lark makes an interesting contrast with Olifantsberg’s OVP Chenin Blanc, as it’s a tauter, more tucked in Breedekloof white from a younger vineyard planted in 2006. Floral, racy and appealingly sappy, it has fynbos and jasmine aromas, lots of zip, tension and minerality, a waft of vanilla spice from 9% new oak and a mouth-watering finish of lemon zest and green apple.

n: Olifantsberg Old Vine OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Showing a little of what Elizma Visser calls the “fruit plumpness” of the 2025 vintage, this comes a parcel of high-density bush vines planted in 1982. There’s nice texture and some glycerol here, with subtle oak, flavours of pear, citrus and a touch of banana and some tarte tatin sweetness.

Named after the pumpkins that were once grown, unsuccessfully, on the farm, Pampoeneland is a very smart new Grenache from this impressive Breedekloof estate. Made with the 70 clone and fermented with 15% whole bunches, it has lots of stony intensity, top notes of wild mountain herbs, redcurrant and Negroni spice flavours and an appealingly ferrous finish.

Among the best stand-alone Roussannes in the Cape, this comes from four different sites on the farm, planted between 2011 and 2014. Using oak as a “supporting act” in Elizma Visser’s words, it moves from floral, lightly spiced aromas to a palate of greengage and subtle stone fruit sweetness supported by steely acidity.

n: Olifantsberg Soul of the Mountain The Bull
d: South Africa’s answer to a very good southern French red – think Faugères or Pic St. Loup perhaps – this is a stunning cuvée of Syrah, 27% Grenache, 18% Carignan and 2% Mourvèdre from a property that’s taking the Breedekloof to a new level. Layered, complex and meaty, it has notes of pine needle, oregano, tapenade and garrigue and a core of plum and blackberry fruit.

n: Olifantsberg Soul of the Mountain The Matriarch
d: Drawing on raw material from different parts of this dramatic Breedekloof estate, this is a finely judged blend of Roussanne, 24% Grenache Bland and 10% Chenin Blanc. Performing well in a comparatively tricky year, it marries aromas of nutmeg, honeysuckle and saffron with a palate of pear, juniper and a hint of oak spice.

Following on from the brilliant, breakthrough 2021 release, Olifantsberg’s Syrah makes the most of five different sites on the farm, planted on rocky, shale and clay-rich soils. Thirty per cent whole bunches add some clove and rosemary notes to a palate of blackberry, blood orange, incense and lavender. Balanced and self-assured.

Sourced from vines planted at 375 metres on clay, shale and sandstone soils, this remarkable Chenin Blanc showcases the quality of the SN24 clone. Showing the zip and freshness of its mountain site, this has some subtle stony reduction, aromas of thatch, aniseed and chamomile, citrus, green apple and lemongrass flavours and a mouth-watering finish.

n: Opstal Estate Carl Everson Single Vineyard OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Carl Everson is a single-clone expression of Chenin Blanc, sourced from an old-vine block planted at 290 metres in 1982. Fermented and aged in concrete, foudres and older barrels, it’s racy, pure and appealingly focused, with yellow apple, greengage and lemon zest flavours, subtle wood and a subtle bitter twist.

n: Opstal Estate Eenvoud Single Vineyard OVP Chenin Blanc
d: This is the fifth release of Eenvoud from the brilliant Attie Louw, sourced from a 2.1-hectare parcel established at 290 metres in 1982. Planted with the SN1061 clone on sandstone soils, it’s a savoury, acid-driven expression of Chenin Blanc with a touch of oak, lots of energy and focus, fennel, cardamom and waxed lemon flavours and the concentration and structure to develop in bottle.

A rare sighting of an unblended Roussanne in the Breedekloof Valley, this hails from vines planted at 370 metres in 2014. One of the pithier, less exotic examples of the grape in the Cape, it’s taut, refreshing and well balanced with layers of citrus, pear and juniper, subtle oak, a nip of tannin from partial skin contact and a mineral core.

Guillermo is now a three-site blend from Breedekloof, the Swartland and Wellington. The French and 30% American oak are a little on the assertive side perhaps, but this is a textured, fleshy, full-bodied Pinotage with bramble, plum and strawberry flavours, a hint of dark chocolate and well-integrated tannins.

Now part of the Jordan stable, which should provide some investment and continuity for the Painted Wolf range, this uses grapes from a 1974 vineyard in Wellington. Curated in seasoned oak and 40% amphoras, it has a nice medley of pear and lemon zest flavours, a dab of cream from lees contact and full malolactic and a stony finish.

Jeremy Borg sources this impressive Viognier from Silkbush Mountain Vineyards at 550 metres in the Breedekloof Valley. Located at the more floral, refined end of the variety’s flavour profile, it has top notes of white flowers and tangerine and a creamy, textured palate of peach, juniper and lemon zest.

Martin Smith makes this Elgin Chardonnay with the widely planted CY95 clone. It’s a textured, cool-climate style that benefitted from full malolactic to put some extra flesh on its bones. Nutty, toasty and refreshing, it has stylish 33% new oak, flavours of citrus, patisserie spices and Greek yoghurt and a racy finish.

Union is sourced from Tulbagh, an area that has proved propitious for Syrah. This has some of the meaty reduction that is often a feature of the variety, plenty of muscular, tannic grip, flavours of tapenade, thyme and black fig and well-integrated 30% new oak.

n: Paul Clüver Clüver Prieur Colline du Matin
d: Colline du Matin Chardonnay is produced by Andries Burger alongside long-term consultant Martin Prieur from Meursault and is always one of the highlights of the Paul Clüver range. Sourced from a cooler, south-facing parcel on Bokkeveld shale, it has some texture from 30% malolactic, flavours of lemongrass, fennel and patisserie spices, a hint of sourdough bread and deftly integrated 36% new wood.

Still on the young and toasty side when I tasted it, this is a Chardonnay which should settle into its skin over the next year or two. Fermented in 33% new wood, with a similar amount of malolactic, it has orange peel, citrus and lemon butter flavours, pithy acidity and a stony finish.

n: Paul Clüver Seven Flags OVP Chardonnay
d: Seven Flags come from one of the oldest Chardonnay blocks in the Cape, planted back in 1987 on a cool site at 350 metres. Structured, intense and built to age, it has flavours of citrus, tangerine, peach and Digestive biscuit, a touch of beeswax, toasty oak and an intriguing bitter twist. One to tuck away for a few years.

n: Paul Clüver Seven Flags Pinot Noir
d: One of a pair of top Pinots from the same site – the other one is sold at the Cape Winemakers’ Guild Auction, this was still a little tight and shuttered when I tasted it at the winery. Fermented with 15% whole bunches before ageing in 38% new wood, it has redcurrant, raspberry and rhubarb flavours and a meaty, stony finish. Needs time.

Using a mixture of the 115, 667 and 777 clones, this is a great-value Pinot Noir that I’m always happy to find on a restaurant wine list. Lightly wooded in older barrels and foudres, it has a hint of favourable reduction, fleshy tannins, bright acidity and a core of raspberry, red cherry and pomegranate fruit. Supremely drinkable.

n: Paul René Brut Blanc de Blancs Extra Brut CC
d: As far as bubbly is concerned, Robertson grows some of the best Chardonnay in the country, which is why the grapes are so highly prized. This is a refreshing, comparatively low-alcohol style from Henk van Nieker and Izak de Vries, with fennel and citrus zest flavours, small bubbles and a pithy dry finish.

A name that deserves to be better known for the quality of its bubblies, Paul René is entirely focused on the Robertson Valley. This is a well-judged cuvée of Chardonnay and 15% Pinot Noir that spent 44 months on lees before disgorgement, showing flavours of malt, lemongrass and hazelnut and a toasty finish.

Not all Malbecs come from Argentina’s mostly warm, dry conditions. Think Cahors in the south-west of France. This has green herb and subtle violet aromas, deftly handled 20% new French oak, black cherry, bramble and redcurrant fruit flavours and a dusting of sweet spices. Refined stuff from Bobby Wallace.

Talented young winemaker Bobby Wallace is now back at his family’s estate in Elgin, working alongside his father Paul. This a sappy, elegant, cool climate Chardonnay that wears its 18% new oak lightly, with 30% malolactic adding some texture to a palate cardamom, lemongrass and subtle cinnamon spice.

n: Perdeberg Wines Endura Single Vineyard Chenin Blanc
d: Vines at 280 metres on the Paardeberg are the source of this granite-influenced Chenin Blanc from Albertus Louw. Lightly wooded in amphoras, cement, stainless steel and older barrels, it’s a racy, pithy white with notes of green apple, citrus and gin botanicals and a slightly salty finish.

n: Perdeberg Wines Endura Winemaker's Selection Cape Blend
d: Pinotage based with support from 20% Malbec, 19% Cabernet Sauvignon and 1% Merlot, this marries components from Paarl and the Swartland. Assertively wooded in 60% new oak, this is a bold, deeply coloured wine that's long on flavours of blackberry blackcurrant and coffee bean but short on subtlety.

n: Perdeberg Wines The Dry Land Collection Longevity Natural Sweet Chenin Blanc
d: One of a pair of contrasting Chenin Blancs from Albertus Louw, this was made with vinedried bunches that ended up looking like raisins. Barrel-fermented in second-fill oak, it has an intense 264 grams of residual sugar, flavours of honey, nectarine and patisserie spices and a volatile top note that adds complexity to the finish.

n: Pieter Ferreira Birdsong Extra Brut CC
d: Birdsong is a cuvée of Chardonnay and 29% Pinot Noir, using grapes from six different regions across the Western Cape from Darling to Napier. Showing some subtle, toasty autolysis from 26 months on lees, it’s just off dry at 3.7 grams of dosage, with good texture and weight and flavours of malt, stone fruit and citrus zest.

n: Pieter Ferreira Birdsong Rosé Extra Brut CC
d: The pink Birdsong is a varietal Pinot Noir that combines elements from Durbanville, Napier and Stellenbosch. Aged for 55 months, it has the finesse and focus that are typical of Pieter Ferreira’s wines, with rose petal and saffron aromas and a just off-dry palate of wild strawberry and goji berries complemented by creamy bubbles.

n: Pieter Ferreira Blanc de Blancs Extra Brut CC
d: Pieter “Bubbles” Ferreira may have retired from Graham Beck, but he continues to make exceptional sparkling wines under his own eponymous label. Blending components from Darling, Napier and Robertson, it has some subtle oak influence on the base wine, a very fine mousse, flavours of citrus zest and oyster shell and remarkable freshness for a Blanc de Blancs that spent 55 months on lees.

Pieter Ferreira made this first-ever Pinot Blanc bubbly with grapes from the oldest parcel of the variety, planted in the mid-1980s at Twee Jonge Gezellen in Tulbagh. It’s a racy, intense, jasmine-scented number with flavours of pear and citrus zest, a barely noticeable 3.9 grams of dosage and some weight and texture from 36 months on lees.

Pink Valley is something of a lifestyle brand, with the successful cellar door operation to prove it. This well-packaged rosé is a blend of Sangiovese and 30% Shiraz, with some mid-palate texture from seven months on lees succulent raspberry and watermelon fruit and a refreshing, tangy, medium-bodied finish.

A step up from the basic Pink Valley rosé, in terms of both concentration and price, this comes from a single parcel on decomposed granite and combines Sangiovese and Shiraz. Barrel fermented in older wood, it has appealing flavours of candy floss, summer berries and orange zest and a waft of Campari spices. An impressive début.

Understandably popular with bubbly drinkers looking for a relative bargain, this uses Chardonnay from across the Western Cape to produce sizeable quantities of wine. Using a wooded component and some reserve wine material, it’s tangy, nutty and refreshing, with flavours of hazelnut and citrus zest and nicely textured bubbles.

Porseleinberg is one of those wines where the analytical numbers don't make sense, as it has a pH of 4.06 but retains remarkable freshness and acidity, partly from the 100% whole bunch fermentation. Aged in large Stockinger foudres and 10% concrete eggs, it’s a denser wine than the 2023 release, with stony intensity, aromas of clove, fennel and tomato leaf, blackberry and North African spice flavours and seductive tannins. One of the New World’s greatest Syrahs.

n: Raats Eden High Density Single Vineyard Cabernet Franc
d: This small, high-density, 0.2-hectare parcel in Bruwer Raats’ garden has been so successful that’s he’s going to plant a further 0.3 of a hectare. The toasty new oak is quite assertive at the moment, but this is a wine that needs time to settle into itself, with damson, blackcurrant and cedarwood notes, a hint of gingerbread and serious, age-worthy tannins.

n: Raats Eden High Density Single Vineyard Chenin Blanc
d: Bruwer Raats doesn’t have to walk far to this 0.6-hectare block, as it’s located next to his house and was planted in 2009 with the low-yielding Montpellier clone. Combining concrete egg and 30% new oak components, it has lovely texture and weight, layers of pear tart, tangerine and vanilla spice and a refreshing, tangy, granite-rich core. Refreshing low in alcohol, with a lingering finish.

n: Raats Family Old Vine Chenin Blanc
d: Sourced from Bruwer Raats’ beloved Polkadraai Hills, this textbook Stellenbosch Chenin Blanc uses grapes from three different vineyards. Fermented and aged in a combination of stainless steel, concrete and older barrels, it segues from a nose of honeysuckle and baking spices into a palate of peach, nectarine and yellow apple.

Three sites in the Polkadraai Hills – Karibib, Bluegum Grove and Skoonheid – supply the grapes for this serious, well-structured Cabernet Franc. The whole bunch component has increased from 10% to 30%, adding more structure to the wine. Dense, grippy and firm, it has layers of graphite, damson and black cherry and a sheen of 25% new French oak.

The 2024 release of Vlag is a triumph, made with grapes from Karibib and Skoonheid, both of which are in the Polkadraai Hills. Exhibiting the freshness and energy that often seem to come with decomposed granite soils, this is a refined, polished, beautifully weighted Cabernet Franc with 33% whole bunches, subtle ageing in concrete, foudre and barrel, sculpted tannins and flavours of black cherry, tarragon and coffee bean.

n: Radford Dale Freedom Organic Pinot Noir
d: Burgundy lover Alex Dale uses three different Dijon clones – 115, 667 and 777 – to make this organic Pinot Noir from Elgin. Matured in just 5% new oak, with a similar whole bunch component, it has good structure and focus, cool climate acidity and flavours of wild strawberry, plum and orange zest.

n: Radford Dale Higher Purpose Organic Cabernet Franc
d: Cabernet Franc is what Alex Dale describes as the “revelation” on Radford Dale’s Elgin farm, sourced from parcels with a greater clay content. Concrete egg fermented and aged, with 10% whole bunches adding perfume and texture, this has juicy bramble, plum and black cherry flavours, a waft of basil and a firm, sinewy finish.

Making the most of the excellent 2025 vintage, this superb Chenin Blanc comes from a single block with five different soil types. Youthful, pithy and acid driven, it has beautifully understated oak, a nip of tannin from a night on skins, racy citrus, cardamom and green apple flavours and a taut, stony finish.

Something of a swansong release, alas, this impressive Semillon came from an Elgin vineyard that has been grubbed up in favour of Cabernet Franc. Macerated on skins over night before fermentation, it’s a very lightly wooded style with aromas of chamomile and lanolin, a palate of pear and lemon zest and a herbal twist.

Sourced from Radford Dale’s organically farmed estate in the Elgin Valley, this a winningly elegant, restrained Chardonnay from Petrone Thomas. Aromas of chamomile and jasmine segue into a palate of aniseed, green olive and lemon juice complemented by a waft of vanilla spice and an appealing bitter twist.

Alex Dale knows a thing or two about Chardonnay, having spent a good deal of his life living and working in Burgundy. Gently wooded in older barrels and foudres, this one comes from several different Stellenbosch sites, marrying aromas of chamomile, vanilla and wet stones with a palate of waxed lemon and fennel and a poised finish.

Radford Dale are the Gamay kings of South Africa, with 3.5 hectares of the variety to their name, planted across three different sites. This one comes from a single site in the Polkadraai Hills and reflects the granite soils of its terroir. Serious and concentrated, it has some subtle reduction, plum and black cherry flavours and a hint of oak.

Great value from the Radford Dale team, this is a 70/30 blend of bush vine fruit from Stellenbosch and the Swartland. Made in a Pinot Noir style, with ageing in second to fourth use Burgundian barrels, it has layers of pomegranate, red cherry and raspberry fruit, textured tannins and appealing freshness and palate length.

Cabernet Franc is something of a signature grape at Rainbow’s End. Made with a 60/40 combination of the 214 and 1 clones, it has some subtle, stony reduction, scented 25% new oak, flavours of damson, plum skin and wild mountain herbs and a carapace of tannins. Needs more time in bottle to soften.

n: Rainbow's End Limited Release Cabernet Franc
d: Anton Malan’s top Cabernet Franc is a single-site bottling from a 0.7-hectare parcel planted with the 312 Bordeaux clone at 520 metres. Matured in 35% new French oak, it has appealing mint, wet stone and capsicum aromas and a dense, layered palate of damson and black cherry framed by intense mountain tannins.

Anton Malan’s Merlot comes from one of the most beautiful farms in the Banghoek Valley. Made in a firm style with at least one eye on the future, this has plenty of tannin and backbone, layers of damson and black cherry, well-handled 20% new oak and a compact finish.

A nice contrast with the Noa Chenin Blanc, as it comes from schist soils on the other side of the Swartland, this is a plusher, more textured wine, although it still weighs in at just 12.5% alcohol. Fermented and aged in old foudres, it has yellow apple, pear and subtle stone fruit flavours and a savoury finish.

A wine to drink before the more shuttered 2024 Ava Syrah, this is also structured but is more approachable in its youth. Sourced from the schist soils of the Kasteelberg, it has the effortless concentration of vines that yielded just 1.5 tons per hectare, violet, thyme and lavender aromas, fig and blackberry fruit, a touch of steak tartare and a refreshing, mediumbodied finish. A wine of impressive self-assurance.

Labelled as a coastal wine because it has equal components from Darling and the Paardeberg, this is a low-alcohol style that was fermented with 100% whole bunches for perfume and structure. Matured in a large foudre, it has redcurrant, watermelon and wild strawberry flavours and an appealing nip of tannin.

Donovan Rall’s Grenache is a wine that will repay a degree of patience. Now in its second vintage, it’s a taut, pithy style from a one-hectare parcel on the Paardeberg, with clove and tobacco leaf notes from 100% whole bunches, mouth-watering acidity and flavours of cranberry, redcurrant and allspice.

"F****** brilliant" is Donovan Rall’s succinct description of the 2025 vintage. This Grenache Blanc comes from a 30-year-old vineyard at 750 metres on sandstone soils and has the focus and freshness that are typical of Piekenierskloof. Salty, pithy and mouth-wateringly fresh, it has greengage and beeswax flavours and a hint of stony reduction from fermentation and ageing in concrete eggs.

The fifth vintage of Noa is arguably the best yet, fully justifying Donovan Rall’s high praise for the vintage. Sourced from a 21-hectare block planted on the Paardeberg in 1969, it has a petrichor and wet clay note from concrete eggs, impressive focus, purity and palate length, chiselled flavours of green apple and lemon juice and a salty, pithy tang from granite soils.

"It used to be hard to sell red blends," says Donovan Rall, “but that’s changing.” This wine is part of the reason why. Combining Syrah from schist soils with 20% Cinsault from granite, it has the depth, concentration and intensity of the 2024 vintage, a spine of chewy tannins, some subtle reduction and a palate of blackberry, damson, fennel and dried herbs.

Made with grapes from the same vineyard as BLANKbottle’s Little William, this is just the second crop from this parcel. Showing the freshness of its 800m altitude, it’s an engagingly perfumed, refreshing style with white pepper, fynbos and paprika aromas and a palate of redcurrant and chorizo complemented by savoury tannins.

The regular Rall Syrah comes from the same site as the Ava bottling, located between the Kasteelberg and Porseleinberg. Entirely concrete fermented, it marries aromas of violet and incense with a serious, layered palate of blackberry and liquorice, complemented by sappy acidity, lots of colour and well-structured tannins.

Donovan Rall has been making this wine since 2008, although the style has become more focused and refreshing over the last couple of decades. Chenin Blanc dominated, with 30% Verdelho and a splash of Viognier, it’s a wine that shows the influence of granite soils, with subtly integrated oak, flavours of citrus, chamomile and cardamom and a hint of apricot sweetness. Beautifully balanced, it’s a white that ages well too.

Appealingly off the wall, this méthode ancestrale bubbly is what Keyleigh Hattingh describes as her “cash cow”. With 11 grams of residual sugar, it’s deliberately made in a gluggable, crowd-pleasing style, with pear, yellow apple and stone fruit flavours and more than enough acidity to lift and freshen the finish.

n: Rebel Rebel Old Vine OVP Colombar
d: Kayleigh Hattingh sources this old-vine Colombar(d) from a 1986 bush vine parcel on the Kaapzicht farm, where she works as assistant winemaker. Treated like a top Chenin Blanc, with classy French and Austrian oak, it has a touch of botrytis, the chiselled, mouth-watering acidity that’s part of the variety’s DNA and flavours of citrus, quince and orange peel and a long finish.

Ava Marie comes from the oldest Chardonnay vineyard in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, planted in 1998 with three sparkling wine clones, and is a world-class expression of the variety. Focused, pithy, layered and refined, it has granitic energy, a sappy, savoury palate of gunflint, aniseed and lemon butter and very subtle 10% new oak. The 40% malolactic puts just the right amount of flesh on the bones.

The latest addition to the mouth-watering line of Chardonnays from Restless River, sourced from four-year-old plantings of the CY95 and CY96 clones at 300 metres. More Meursault than Puligny-Montrachet, it has appealing texture and weight, aromas of toast, Digestive biscuit and hazelnut and a palate of lemon butter, vanilla spice and racy acidity.

Cuvée Cru is a five-barrel selection of Ava Marie and reflects what Craig Wessels considers a more textured, less chiselled style of Chardonnay. It’s an impressive wine in its own right, but doesn’t have the tension and focus of the 2024 Ava Marie. Struck match, toast and cheese rind aromas guide you into a palate of beeswax, citrus and juniper framed by 20% new oak.

“We want to be known for Pinot Noir as well as Chardonnay,” says Craig Wessels, and I’d say he’s nearly there. This is only the second crop from these vines and it’s very promising indeed, with some subtle reduction, a frame of 30% new oak, some savoury intensity and tangy redcurrant, Negroni spice and wild strawberry flavours.

n: Restless River Klein Hemel Pinot Noir
d: The entry-point wines from Craig and Ann Wessels are made with the same attention to detail as the top wines, so are well worth tracking down. Younger vines planted with the 113, 115 and 777 clones supply the raw material here, producing a smooth, crowd-pleasing Pinot Noir that’s deceptively easy to drink with 10% whole clusters and juicy goji berry and summer pudding flavours.

n: Restless River Le Luc Pinot Noir
d: Craig Wessels sources his top Pinot Noir, named after his son, Luke, from older vineyards at Restless River, planted with the 113, 115 and 777 clones in 2013. The 25% new oak is adroitly handled here, adding structure and perfume to a savoury, nicely layered palate with 20% whole clusters, an undertow of granite, racy acidity and a core of raspberry, clove and red cherry.

n: Restless River Main Road & Dignity Cabernet Sauvignon
d: Main Road & Dignity uses grapes from the oldest virus-free Cabernet Sauvignon vines in South Africa, established in 1998. Picked into early May in a tricky vintage, this is a tribute to excellent viticulture and selection in the winery. Green yet ripe at the same time, it has a frame of refined 38% new oak, mint, dill and blackcurrant flavours, a waft of cigar box and an herbal, well-balanced finish.

Mooirivier is a new single vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon from Restless River, confirming Craig Wesssels’ conviction that the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley can produce exceptional examples of the variety. This comes from a unique patch of Cederberg shale soils at 400 metres on the farm and is a very impressive début, with Loire-like aromas of graphite, violet and cut grass and a palate of red berries, fynbos and blackcurrant leaf supported by fine-grained tannins.

Reyneke’s Cabernet Franc used to be a component of the Cornerstone Red, but was bottled on its own in 2023 and 2024. Concrete fermented before ageing in second and third-fill barrels, it’s a refined, confidently balanced red from Barbara Melck with lots of youthful energy, aromas of tarragon and pencil shavings, some underlying clove and pepper spice and paprika and black cherry flavours.

Barbara Melck sources this unblended Cabernet Sauvignon from two biodynamically farmed parcels on the estate. Big, bold and intense, it has considerable backbone and concentration, assertive new French oak, top notes of graphite and green herbs and a core of damson and blackcurrant fruit. Good, but needs a friend.

Reyneke’s Chenin Blanc sometimes gets overlooked in a tasting with the estate’s Sauvignon Blanc, but that’s an injustice. Mostly sourced from a single, old-vine parcel, it marries aromas of chamomile and summer meadows with flavours of pear, greengage and lemon verbena with pithy acidity, subtle wood and plenty of extract.

The Cornerstone Red is an equal cuvée of Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah from the Polkadraai Hills that will reward further time in bottle. A little shuttered when I tasted it at the winery, it has a sheen of toasty, cigar box oak, firmish tannins and layers of blackberry, plum and red berries.

A feel-good wine that donates part of the profit from the entire value chain back to nine families who work on the Reyneke farm, this is a new blend of Sauvignon Blanc, 24% Semillon and 6% Chenin Blanc. Featuring amphora and old barrel components, it has plenty of life and energy, citrus, elderflower and yellow apple flavours and a petrichor top note.

Sauvignon Blanc has become such a commodity in South Africa and elsewhere that you really notice the outstanding examples. Source from two blocks on decomposed granite, it’s almost ludicrously good, with a flinty top note, flavours of elderflower, lime and cucumber, a subtle bitter undertone and a touch of vanilla from 33% new oak.

Formerly sold as the Reserve Red, Reyneke’s Syrah may have changed name but is as thrilling as ever. A textbook expression of the Polkadraai Hills, it has rose petal, potpourri and ginger spice aromas, fine-grained tannins from submerged cap fermentation, subtle 30% whole bunches and a palate of blackberry and cooked meat. Delicious now but will evolve beautifully in the bottle.

n: Rickety Bridge Regna Loca OVP Cinsault
d: One of a pair of very impressive wines under the Regna Loca label, this Cinsault is a single parcel expression of a 1954 vineyard in Agter-Paarl. Ethereal and engaging, it’s a subtle, floral red that tastes lighter than its 14.2% alcohol, with rose petal and allspice aromas, raspberry and red cherry fruit and sinewy tannins.

n: Rickety Bridge Regna Loca OVP Semillon
d: Young winemaker Kelsey Shungking is making an impact at Rickety Bridge, if the maiden release of this Semillon is a guide. Sourced from the La Bri block, planted on sandy soils in 1905, it has saffron, honeysuckle and wild herb aromas, very well handled 40% new oak, an earthy touch from an amphora component and a core of lime, lemongrass and wet stones.

n: Riebeek Valley Wine Company Kasteelberg OVP Chenin Blanc
d: This Old Vine Project Chenin Blanc uses raw material from a vineyard that was planted between 1984 and 1989. Made in a modern style, it’s floral, racy and subtly wooded, with some stony reduction, layers of pear, green apple and patisserie spices and a focused, pithy finish. Impressive value from the Riebeek Valley Wine Company.

n: Riebeek Valley Wine Company Kasteelberg Premium Chenin Blanc
d: Sheree Nothnagel sources this top-of-the-range Chenin Blanc from a single block that was planted in 1969. Fermented and aged in older 300 and 500-litre barrels, it’s a refreshing, pithy, acid-driven style with pear, citrus and cardamom flavours, underlying concentration and a touch of oak spices.

n: Riebeek Valley Wine Company Kasteelberg Premium Syrah
d: Part of a consistently impressive range from this well-run Swartland co-operative, this is an elegant, well-balanced Syrah from Sheree Nothnagel. Benefitting from the inclusion of 30% whole bunches, it marries aromas of thyme, white pepper and allspice with a palate of redcurrant and black cherry underpinned by some ferrous grip.

n: Riebeek Valley Wine Company RAAR Carbonic Maceration Shiraz
d: Fermented, Beaujolais-style, with full carbonic maceration, this is a lovely Syrah sourced from iron-rich soils in the Swartland. South Africa’s answer to a good-value CrozesHermitage, this has layers of bramble, blackberry and summer pudding flavours, top notes of violet and liquorice and a textured, well-balanced finish.

n: Riebeek Valley Wine Company RAAR Grenache Blanc
d: it’s good to see a former co-operative, now known as a producers’ cellar, hanging its winemaking hat on Grenache Blanc, a variety that has huge potential in the Cape. Using grapes from bush vines on sandy soils, this has the variety’s characteristic zip and energy, layers of white pepper, wet stone, greengage and lemon zest and the faintest touch of oak.

The Burger family still employs techniques that were used back in 1864 (and since) to produce this intense Robertson fortified. Made with Muscat de Frontignan and some skin contact, it has lovely texture and weight, subtle fortification, 170 grams of residual sugar and layers of rose petal, musk, molasses and raspberry coulis.

Fermented in 20% new oak, with an important concrete component adding some zip and freshness, this is a complex, wild yeast-fermented Chenin Blanc from Coenie Snyman that has a coastal feel to it. Fresh hay and white flower aromas segue into a palate of vanilla spice, citrus and yellow apple and a stony, granitic finish.

Making the most of very good grapes from the Rustenhof farm, close to False Bay, this is a Cinsault for Pinot Noir lovers, with graceful rose petal and petrichor aromas, plenty of zip and acidity, flavours of redcurrant, raspberry and hibiscus and some clove spice and tobacco leaf notes from 30% whole clusters.

At 1,520 metres, the vineyard that supplies the raw material for this Chardonnay is the highest commercial planting of the variety in South Africa. Showcasing the 95 clone, this is a racy, naturally fermented delight with aromas of oyster shell and brine, despite its continental terroir, and a palate of citrus and subtle passion fruit.

Rogge Cloof is a new wine from Johan Kruger, made with a young vineyard of the 113 clone. The altitude of the site – at 1,500 metres – comes through in the wine on this racy, cool climate Pinot Noir, combining flavours of tomato leaf, redcurrant and pomegranate with a spine of tannin and a mineral core.

A wine for people who like the sound of remote places, this comes from high-altitude plantings in the Karoo which are also the source of the Kruger Family Syrah. Showing plenty of guts and concentration, it has flavours of blackberry and steak tartare, sinewy tannins and a top note of wild mountain herbs.

n: Roodekrantz Brand Se Berg OVP 1975 Chenin Blanc
d: A wine that has fattened up over the last year, Brand Se Berg uses raw material from a Paarl vineyard that was planted in 1975. Sweeter than the other OVP Chenin Blancs in the range, it has some honey from a little botrytis, layers of patisserie spices, pear and peach and 4.5 grams of residual sugar balanced by acidity.

n: Roodekrantz Die Kliphuis OVP 1977 Chenin Blanc
d: Few wineries in South Africa have as many Old Vine Project Chenin Blancs as Roodekrantz Wines, who treat the variety with Gallic reverence. Die Kliphuis hails from a windy site planted in 1977 and is typically subtle and well balanced, wit flavours of pear and apple pie, lees-derived texture and a stony finish.

My pick of the old-vine Chenin Blanc line up from Marius Burger and Danie Morke, this comes from a Stellenbosch bush vine parcel that was planted in 1974. Floral, racy and intense, it’s more refreshing than the 2023 was at the same stage, with subtle vanilla and honeysuckle aromas, layers of aniseed and tarte tatin and a salty finish.

n: Roodekrantz Old Bush Vine OVP 1974 Chenin Blanc
d: Showing the concentration you’d expect from a parcel of 1974 bush vines in warmer climate Paarl, this has lots of texture and weight, the understated oak that’s a feature of the Roodekrantz style, pear, peach and orange zest flavours, good weight from extended lees contact and 3.9 grams of residual sugar.

Marius Berger and Danie Morkel source this Swartland Chenin Blanc from two vineyards, planted on the Paardeberg in 1983, although it’s not sold as an OVP wine. Lightly wooded in older barrels, it has the energy, zip and concentration of the vintage, flavours of aniseed and pear tart, good texture from extended lees ageing and a hint of juniper on the finish.

Roundstone Red only uses grapes from Chris and Andrea Mullineux’s farm of the same name near Riebeek-Kasteel and is a stylish Mediterranean combination of Grenache, 30% Syrah and 20% Cinsault. Matured in older oak and foudres, it’s enticingly floral, stony and refined, showing the perfume that often seems to come with schist soils, plum, bramble and red cherry flavours, chiselled acidity and finely wrought tannins.

Showing the ripeness and texture of the 2022 vintage, this is a serious, concentrated Baron Edmond made from a seamless assemblage of Merlot, 28% Cabernet Sauvignon, 24% Cabernet Franc, 6% Petit Verdot and 1% Malbec. Curated in 47% new oak, it’s a delicious wine from Kayla Oertle-Morse with aromas of toast, cedarwood and North African spices, polished, glossy tannins, layers of mint, tarragon and blackcurrant and the underlying concentration to develop further in bottle.

One of a pair of Baron Edmonds that I tasted at Rupert & Rothschild, the 2023 features components from Faure, Flottenberg, the Helderberg and the Simonsberg. Marrying Cabernet Sauvignon, 27% Cabernet Franc, 25% Merlot and 4% Petit Verdot, it has assertive 47% new oak, commendable intensity and concentration for the vintage, youthful cassis, bramble and dark chocolate flavours and refined tannins.

Baroness Nadine is made with an equal split of grapes from Elgin and the Polkadraai Hills. Matured in a combination of 28% new barrels and 20% larger foudres, it’s a wine that needs more time for the oak to integrate. The underlying fruit is pithy, stony and racy, with layers of citrus, cardamom and fennel and a white flower top note.

A wine that helps to promote Brand South Africa at home and overseas, Classique is a commendably reliable blend of 1.2m bottles. Combining Cabernet Sauvignon, 38% Merlot, 12% Cabernet Franc, 10% Petit Verdot and 1% Malbec, it has toasty, coffee bean aromas from 20% new wood, a red cherry and blackcurrant pastille palate and a leafy finish.

Made with barrels that don’t quite make it into John X Merriman, as well as other bits and pieces, this is a great value Stellenbosch Cabernet Sauvignon from Murray Barlow that shows the quality of the 2024 vintage. Textured, perfumed and well balanced, it combines subtle aromatic spices from 10% new wood with a palate of capsicum and blackcurrant pastille.

This Chardonnay is a pan-Stellenbosch blend that combines grapes from the estate with lots from Bottelary, Deveon Valley, the Helderberg and the Polkadraai Hills. Wild yeast fermented with 50% malolactic, it has toasty oak, flavours of patisserie, orange zest and almond and a tangy, refreshing finish.

Five Soldiers hails from a single, 1.5-hectare block at 450 metres on the Simonsberg, planted entirely with the 548 clone. Fermented with full malolactic in 70% new oak, it’s a rich, palatecoating style, with flavours of butterscotch and stone fruit, a hint of beeswax and enough acidity and minerality to lift and freshen the finish.

Back on form after the very difficult 2023 vintage on the Simonsberg, John X Merriman is a seamless cuvée of Cabernet Sauvignon, 34% Merlot, 6% Malbec and 4% Petit Verdot. Curated in 35% new oak, it has aromas of sandalwood and coffee bean, racy plum and blackcurrant fruit flavours, a hint of basil and detailed, well-integrated tannins.

Murray Barlow has done a good deal to put Malbec on the map in South Africa. Made with the 46 and 71 clones, it uses grapes from Devon Valley, the Helderberg and Stellenbosch and is a smooth, crowd-pleasing expression of the variety, with appealing texture and weight and a palate of liquorice, blackberry and vanilla spice.

Back after skipping the 2023 vintage - a brave decision that others should have emulated - this is a textbook Peter Barlow Cabernet Sauvignon. Made with the 163 and 169 clones, it has scented, beautifully integrated 50% new French oak, plenty of structure and energy, flavours of coffee bean, cassis and black cherry and top notes of graphite and fynbos.

A vineyard that was established in 1887 – the oldest in the Cape – ‘T Voetpad has grown slightly in size to 1.4 hectares thanks to some additional plantings. Partnering equal parts Chenin Blanc, Palomino and Semillon with a little Muscat d’Alexandrie, this is a subtle, layered, effortlessly complex wine with orange zest and beeswax aromas, flavours of lime, greengage and pear and considerable depth and underlying structure.

The best Columella since 2019 in my opinion – a wine that also achieved a “perfect” 100-point score – this is now a nine-variety Mediterranean blend from a dozen different Swartland sites, dominated by the Paardeberg. Syrah takes the lead, accounting for 40% of the cuvée, but this is a collective effort that includes Grenache, Cinsault and even a little Pinotage among other grapes. Violet, thyme and fynbos aromas lead you into a palate of wonderful density and energy, with sculpted tannins, subtle minerality and flavours of tangerine, blackberry and red cherry framed by 5% new oak. One of the greatest-ever South African wines.

Henk Laing may have passed, but his remarkable vineyard on Citrusdal Mountain continues to deliver the goods. Pairing Semillon with around 30% of its mutation, Semillon Gris, this is more focused and less exotic than it can be in the excellent 2025 vintage, with aromas of struck match, angelica root and curry leaf, layers of lanolin, pear and lime and a tangy, refreshing finish.

In a year when the Sadie Family’s whites are uniformly good, Mev Kirsten is the boldest and broadest of his Chenin Blancs. Sourced from the oldest vineyard of the variety in the Cape – the core dates back to 1905 – this is often the last picked of the line up. Textured, leesy and intense, it has some subtle reduction, flavours of oatmeal, citrus and lemon butter and a subtle bitter twist.

Palladius gets better and more complex with every passing vintage, thanks to the addition of new components and an ongoing refinement of the style. Now at 11 varieties from 17 vineyards, built around a core of Chenin Blanc, it’s pithier and more focused than most of its predecessors with engaging flavours of lemongrass, greengage and pink grapefruit and a hint of orange zest. The oak is just a whisper here, allowing the grapes to sing.

People sometimes think that Pofadder hails from Darling, but it uses grapes from the schist-based soils of the Riebeeksrivier farm in the Swartland. Like Soldaat, this had some meaty reduction when I tasted it in June 2026 – hence the lower than usual score – that may disappear in bottle. The wine is a little tight, but has potential, with lots of pithy acidity, redcurrant and rhubarb flavours and fine-grained tannins. Another wait and see wine.

Despite being based there, it’s only recently that Eben Sadie has produced a Chenin Blanc from the Paardeberg, thanks to the acquisition of a nearby parcel planted in 1974. The result is Rotsbank. Showing aromas of flint, iodine and struck match, it’s a wine that builds slowly to a crescendo on the palate, with the tang of decomposed granite, lime and pink grapefruit flavours and an umami top note.

Anyone who has visited the vineyard - a combination of beach sand and limestone sitting next to the Atlantic - will know why this remarkable blend of equal parts Chenin Blanc and Palomino tastes the way it does. It’s like you’re tasting the essence of the place. Aged in three foudres, this has engaging sea breeze, kelp and honeysuckle aromas, layers of gunflint, salted almond and lemongrass and a chiselled, bone-dry finish.

The Van Lill family’s farm on Citrusdal Mountain is one of the Cape’s unofficial Grands Crus. The Sadie’s use Chenin Blanc from a 1.8-hectare parcel on red sand, producing a 2025 of remarkable power, concentration and coiled intensity. Structured, stony and refreshing, it’s a stunning old-vine white with layers of aniseed, wet stone, fynbos, green apple and sea breeze and a savoury finish.

Soldaat comes from Erasmus van Zyl’s vineyard in Piekenierskloof and is normally one of the most scented and refined wines in the Sadie Family range. When I tasted the 2025, it seemed a little shuttered to me, with an overtone of minty reduction. The underlying wine has fine tannins and some subtle spices from 30% whole clusters, with negligible oak and layers of cranberry and pomegranate. One to come back to in another five years or more.

My discovery of the year in its maiden vintage, Sonvang is every bit as good in 2025. Sourced from a 2.4-hectare parcel of six-year-old vines below the cellar, it combines a dozen different Mediterranean varieties in equal proportions. Fermented with 30% whole clusters and aged in concrete and a Stockinger foudre, it has racy, granite-enhanced freshness, floral bramble, pomegranate and red cherry flavours and fine, sculpted tannins.

Made with the smallest ever crop from this sandstone, granite and quartz vineyard outside Malmesbury, Treinspoor has shifted in style towards greater elegance and less extraction in 2025. Fermented in concrete and conical oak containers with 30% whole bunches, it has layers of plum, redcurrant and mint, a waft of graphite and layered, granular tannins.

Planted as recently as 2018 with equal amounts of a dozen different varieties Mediterranean varieties and now some Assyrtiko, this is a wine of place, somehow expressing the soul of the Paardeberg. Fermented and aged in concrete tanks and old foudres, it has top notes of musk, white flowers and oyster shell, pithy focused flavours of lime, lemongrass and cardamom and a salty finish.

First made in 2014, this Chenin Blanc, or Steen, put the Montagu region on the map. Sourced from two 43-year-old blocks on slate soils, it’s a wild, intense, fynbos-scented white with arrowhead acidity, layers of wet stone, lime and juniper, a hint of almond paste and a pithy, focused, mouth-watering finish.

Wit Versnit is a blend of more or less equal parts Colombard and Chenin Blanc from the slate soils of Montagu, made with multiple picks in the vineyard. Pithy and intense, it shows the benefit of having vines at 800 metres in a hot region, all lime, citrus and gin botanicals with a touch of oak, effortless structure and a subtle bitter twist.

Unfiltered Syrah is how Reenen Borman describes Sons of Sugarland, which comes from the Karibib farm in the Polkadraai Hills. Fermented in concrete with 100% whole bunches, it’s youthful, tangy and hauntingly perfumed, revealing aromas of sage, black pepper and lavender and a palate of blackberry, clove and black olive. Utterly delicious young, but will develop further complexity in bottle.

n: Sakkie Mouton Full on Misfit Blanc
d: Finding freshness on the West Coast is easier, says Sakkie Mouton, who proves it with this amusingly labelled assemblage of Chenin Blanc, 18% Colombard and 7% Hárslevelü. Combining stainless steel and old wood components, it has piercing acidity, top notes of white flowers and lime blossom and a racy palate of lemon zest, grapefruit and cherimoya and a lees-rich mid-palate.

n: Sakkie Mouton Revenge of the Crayfish
d: Rejoicing in one of the most memorable labels in South Africa, this is a brilliant West Coast Chenin Blanc from Sakkie Mouton. Sourced from a low-yielding parcel of just one hectare in Koekenaap, it has good texture from full malolactic, aromas of kelp, white flowers and aniseed, a hint of oak spices and a tangy, chiselled palate of lemongrass and green apple. More generous than the 2024 release.

Sakkie Mouton is rightly regarded as one of the most exciting young winemakers in the Cape right now, producing a series of characterful whites. This Colombard comes from vines planted in sandy soils in 1987 and has more than a touch of Austrian Grüner Veltliner about it, marrying aromas of bay leaf and white pepper with a palate of pear and white peach supported by classic West Coast acidity.

The 2023 and 2024 wines were lost to the floods on the West Coast, so it’s good to see this young-vine Assyrtiko back on the market in 2025. Fermented with full malolactic, although the tangy acidity remains at the core of the wine, this has lots of intensity and savoury depth, a nip of tannin and flavours of pear, citrus and rock salt.

At the recent Vinoble conference in Jerez, the biggest queue was to taste Adi Badenhorst’s South African “Sherries”, and no wonder. This Amontillado is the real deal, spending four years under flor followed by exposure to oxidative ageing. Walnut and incense aromas lead you into a palate of dried fruits and savoury intensity.

The sort of thing that will appeal to Sherry lovers with a sweet tooth, but don’t want to drink a raisin-like Pedro Ximénex, this is what Adi Badenhorst calls a “special blend that we made up on the spur of the moment”, combining different barrels from a solera. Nutty, intense and date-like, it has wonderful maturity, masses of concentration and extract and a savoury finish.

The best of the three Creams in the Saldanha range – there are Pale and Medium versions too – this is a blend of Chenin Blanc and Palomino that was sweetened to 156 grams of sweetness with 3% Hanepoot grapes. Made in a Sherry-style solera system of fractional blending, it has flavours of molasses, hazelnut and dried fruits and a subtle volatile top note.

Fortified Hanepoots are rare in the Cape these days, so congratulations to Adi Badenhorst for keeping this historic wine alive. A wine that carries its 231 grams of sugar lightly, it’s a mature, nutty delight, with a rancio top note, effortless concentration and flavours of date, blood orange and salted caramel.

The younger of the two current Jerpigo releases from Saldanha, this is a lightly fortified, time-burnished Hanepoot at a comparatively restrained 16% alcohol. Quince, patisserie and orange peel flavours coat the palate, with ample sweetness from 239 grams of residual sugar and a slightly spirity finish.

Made with a South-Africa-meets-Jerez combination of Chenin Blanc and Palomino, this Oloroso was fortified to 18% alcohol, so did not develop a veil of flor yeast. Comparatively dry at just 13 grams of sugar – many Cape examples are considerably sweeter – it’s nutty, savoury and intense, with subtle oxidation and a salty tang.

Part of a range that’s taking South African fortified wines to a new audience, this is a subtle, nuanced cuvée of Palomino and Chenin Blanc. Modelled on a Spanish Fino, with ageing under flor yeast, it has flavours of oatmeal and salted almonds, tangy, sea breeze acidity and a balanced, just off-dry finish of 4 grams of residual sugar.

My pick of the extensive Saldanha range, this is a wine that could fool the most ardent Sherry aficionado, despite being made from Chenin Blanc, rather than Palomino. Enticing aromas of incense and old library books are a prelude to a layered, beautifully nuanced palate of citrus, toast and salted almonds and impressive dry extract.

Carla Pau’s bubbly is a pan-Cape cuvée of Pinot Noir and 47% Chardonnay that is sold as a non-vintage wine because it has 20% older barrel-aged reserve wines from previous years. Aged on its lees for 30 months, it’s a bone-dry style with subtle wild mushroom, toast and macadamia nut flavours and a racy, well-balanced finish.

Full Circle has a legion of fans, and you can see why, as it’s among the best reds in Tulbagh. Partnering Syrah, 18% Grenache, 7% Mourvèdre and 4% Viognier, it’s intense, smooth and full-bodied, with aromas of gingernut, vanilla and Asian spices, glossy blackberry, liquorice and peach skin flavours and skilfully integrated 80% new oak.

Grounded Chenin Blanc is part of a new, small volume range from Saronsberg, where winemaker Daniela Briedenhann picked one barrel out of ten from a parcel on clay soils. Ripe, textured and intense, it has a creamy, stone fruit palate that’s almost a little Viognier like, with subtle oak and balancing minerality.

Saronsberg’s Grounded Grenache comes from a bush-vine parcel that was planted on the farm in 2006. Fermented with 20% whole bunches and aged in third and fourth-fill oak, it has juicy, sappy bramble, plum and summer berry fruit, supporting freshness and acidity and a waft of Asian spices.

The best of the new Grounded range, this is a rare example of an unblended Mourvèdre in South Africa. Violet aromas that are reminiscent of Malbec segue into a palate of subtle, vanilla-scented French oak, smooth, polished tannins, bramble and black cherry fruit and a savoury, well-structured finish.

Provenance Shiraz is the wine that keeps the lights on at Saronsberg, accounting for half of its production. Using grapes from the Ceres Plateau, Darling and the Swartland, it’s a fruit driven style with juicy layers of blackberry and bramble, savoury tannins, understated older oak and a refreshing, well-balanced finish.

Saronsberg is strongly associated with Rhône varieties, but don’t overlook this Bordeaux style blend. Featuring the classic five varieties, it’s an assemblage of Cabernet Sauvignon, 12% Cabernet Franc, 11% Merlot, 9% Petit Verdot and 8% Malbec. Sensitively wooded in older barrels, it has dark chocolate, dill and cedarwood top notes, flavours of fig and blackcurrant pastille and supporting acidity.

Hand harvested at night to get cooler grapes into the winery, this is a bold, intense, fullthrottle Tulbagh Shiraz that handles its 80% new French oak with aplomb. Toasty, plush and consumer friendly, it has layers of fig, blackberry and damson, notes of chocolate and Asian spices and the concentration to develop further in bottle.

Daniela Briedenhann sources this attractively priced Viognier from three vineyards on the estate in Tulbagh. Barrel fermented in 30% new oak, it has honeysuckle and vanilla spice aromas, appealing texture and weight and flavours of pear and apricot skins.

Boom is a new wine from Jessica Saurwein, made “like a Pinot Noir”, from ten-year-old Nebbiolo vines at Domaine des Dieux on the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge. Light, perfumed and ethereal, it has less tannin than many examples of the variety, with savoury intensity, classic rose petal and fennel aromas and a palate of cranberry, tobacco leaf and red cherry.

One of the best Rieslings in South Africa – the variety seems to be in German-born Jessica Saurwein’s blood – this is blended with 10% Crouchen Blanc and uses components from Elgin, the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley and Paarl. Pithy lime and green apple flavours are complemented and embellished by 12 grams of residual sugar and a hint of stem ginger.

There is no OM Pinot Noir in 2025, so Saurwein fans will have to buy more Nom as a result. This is a fresh, lively, beautifully delineated style that reflects its origin at 680 metres in Elandskloof. Racy and acid driven, it has tangy redcurrant, goji berry and wild strawberry fruit, fine-boned tannins, a touch of reduction and a subtle volatile undertone.

Are We There Yet? is a reference to the remoteness of the Sijnn estate in Malgas, where Duncan Savage buys the grapes for this cuvée of Touriga Nacional and 44% Syrah. Showing the intensity of tiny berries, it has an engaging violet, thyme and fynbos aromas, a palate of blackberry and blood orange, plenty of underlying grip and structure and a fresh, stony finish.

Duncan Savage shares this 4.4-hectare vineyard in Darling with Donovan Rall, both of whom get the best out of these 44-year-old bush vines close to the Atlantic Ocean. Firmer and more savoury than the sweeter 2024 release, this has layers of pomegranate and Campari spices, sinewy, grippy tannins and a white pepper top note.

Girl Next Door used to come from a single 0.38-hectare site on the Cape Peninsula but has been joined in recent years by a second 0.2-hectare vineyard in Noordhoek. The most maritime of Duncan Savage’s Syrahs, it has top notes of sage and white pepper, a waft of sea breeze, redcurrant, plum and black cherry flavours and some tobacco leaf texture from 100% whole bunches.

n: Savage Never Been Asked To Dance
d: Never Been Asked To Dance comes from the fourth oldest Chenin Blanc vineyard in South Africa, planted on decomposed granite in Paarl in 1956. Fermented and aged in older 600-litre Stockinger barrels, it has understated power and concentration, racy green apple, citrus and wet stone flavours and a mouth-watering finish.

Now a varietal Syrah – it included other things in the past – this superb red uses grapes from Kuils River and the nearby Polkadraai Hills in Stellenbosch. Fermented with 70% whole clusters before ageing in older barrels and foudres, it’s very much a northern Rhône style, with top notes of white pepper and lavender, savoury tannins, flavours of blackcurrant and fennel and a hint of cola.

This is the best-ever release of Thief in the Night, beautifully expressing the quality of Grenache grown on sandstone soils at a lofty 704 metres in remote Piekenierskloof. Fermented with 20% whole bunches, it’s a wonderful, graceful expression of what Duncan Savage calls a “ripper year”, with engaging flavours of pomegranate, goji berry and Turkish Delight and fine-boned, filigree tannins.

Savage White is one of the finest Bordeaux style white blends in the Cape, delivering its magic on a consistent basis. Pairing Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon from three different sites, located between 213 and 677 metres, it’s a subtle, saline, typically graceful cuvée with sea spray and blackcurrant leaf aromas and a palate of lime, elderflower and beeswax complemented by vanilla-scented 20% new oak.

Saxenburg’s Chardonnay comes from vines on sandstone soils at 170 metres in the Polkadraai Hills. Fermented in 14% new oak, with some mid-palate texture from 35% malolactic, this has appealing layers of pear, lemongrass and vanilla spice, racy acidity and top notes of aniseed, cardamom and toast.

One of the first wineries to plant Syrah in the Polkadraai Hills, Saxenberg deserves to be better known. Violet and cracked pepper aromas are an enticing introduction to a palate of tapenade, blackberry and rosemary complemented by grippy tannins and some subtle whole bunch spices.

Rudi Schultz has a day job at Thelema, but also makes a little wine under his own name. This is a restrained, medium-bodied Stellenbosch Chardonnay that has a nice interplay between 15% new oak, pear and lemongrass flavours, gentle baking spices and a subtle bitter twist.

Three vineyards on the lower Helderberg supply the grapes for this blended Pinotage from Bernhard Bredell. Very lightly wooded in stainless steel and 5% barrels, it has a touch of whole bunch spices, raspberry and wild strawberry flavours, detailed, fine-boned tannins and a stony finish. An excitingly modern expression of the variety.

Part of Pinotage’s new wave, with not a single new oak barrel in site, this is one of several Scions of Sinai wines that hails from the Rustenhof farm overlooking False Bay. Fermented with 30% whole clusters, it has plenty of colour, the concentration of its 1976 vines, layers of oregano, garrigue and black cherry and a spine of tannin.

n: Scions of Sinai Gramadoelas Grenache Blanc
d: Bernhard Bredell buys his Grenache Blanc grapes from a vineyard at 460 metres in the remote Klein Karoo, where the diurnal variation is a significant factor. The vines are nowhere near the coast, but there’s a saltiness to this wine, with chiselled, obsidian acidity, lemongrass and green apple flavours and some mid-palate texture from lees ageing.

n: Scions of Sinai Granietsteen Chenin Blanc
d: A great wine from a great site in a great vintage: what’s not to enjoy? This stunning Chenin Blanc uses grapes from a 1.2-hectare block on the Rustenhof that was planted in 1978. Fermented and aged in concrete and (since 2024) 20% foudres, it’s a stunning, self-assured wine with a noticeable sea breeze top note, flavours of citrus, pear and juniper, a waft of jasmine and a racy, granitic finish. Fast becoming a must-buy wine for me.

This is the second vintage of Granitas, featuring Chenin Blanc, 26% Grenache Blanc, 8% Chardonnay and 6% Roussanne from Stellenbosch and the Voor Paardeberg. A little skin contact in the press adds some structure here, complementing the palate of citrus, pear and a hint of nectarine, supported by granite-derived freshness.

Sourced from a one-hectare parcel on his cousin Peter’s Rustenhof farm, Bernhard Bredell’s old-vine Cinsault was planted in 1988. Very much a cooler climate style – False Bay is close by – it has more tannin and grip than the 2024 release, complementing a palate of redcurrant, hibiscus and pomegranate, some aromatic spices from 30% whole bunches and a savoury finish.

n: Scions of Sinai Krummelklip Cabernet Sauvignon
d: Krummelklip is a varietal Cabernet Sauvignon from a 0.5-hectare block on granite soils, planted with the earlier ripening 163 clone on the Rustenhof farm. Pure, perfumed and refined, it has graceful tannins, layers of blackcurrant leaf, bramble and red berries and a whisper of older oak. Typically elegant from Bernhard Bredell.

Bernhard Bredell has sourced this Syrah from the same 0.8-hectare block since 2018, making the most of the decomposed granite soils. Fermented with 70% whole bunches using the gentle submerged cap technique, it’s a pure, focused, nuanced expression of the grape, with top notes of clove and cumin, fine-boned, savoury tannins and a core of red cherry and bramble fruit.

In the past, Black was made with either the Italian or French clones that are planted in the vineyard, depending on the vintage, but now includes both. Inky and concentrated, as its name implies, it’s a serious, dense, 50% new-oak aged Merlot that also retains the acidity of Elgin’s cool climate. Floral and herbal, it has layers of graphite, damson and black cherry flavours and a spine of robust tannins. One to cellar for a while.

“We didn’t get the same rainfall as many surrounding areas,” says James Downes of the 2023 vintage. Mount Bullet is arguably a little more leafy than normal, but there’s nothing dilute about it whatsoever. Matured in 25% new oak, it’s dense yet refreshing, combining five Merlot clones to good effect. The tannins are still on the firm side here, framing a palate of cassis, bramble and dark chocolate and a subtle herbal twist.

Three clones, two picks is how James Downes describes this classic Elgin Chardonnay, referring to the 76, 95 and 548 selections. Sandalwood and ginger spice aromas are a scented introduction to a sappy, tangy, acid-driven palate of lemongrass and aniseed, complemented by 25% new oak and 20% malolactic.

n: Shannon Rock n Rolla Pinot Noir
d: Rock n Rolla comes from a 0.5-hectare parcel at Shannon that’s entirely planted with the 113 clone. Now made by Johann Fourie at Benguela Cove, rather than Gordon Newton-Johnson, it’s a more concentrated Pinot Noir in 2024, with well-handled 50% new oak, black cherry and summer berry flavours, some whole bunch spices and a firm finish.

Rockview Ridge has been part of the Shannon range since 2007 and continues to deliver good value for money. Featuring the 113, 115 and 667 clones, it has impressive structure and concentration, firmish, savoury tannins and alluring red cherry, pomegranate and wild strawberry fruit. The 20% new oak is right on point.

This wild yeast fermented Semillon hails from a 0.5-hectare parcel that was planted 22 years ago. Barrel fermented in 30% new oak, it’s a graceful, refined, cool-climate expression of the grape with layers of lemongrass, oatmeal and marjoram, a sheen of scented vanilla spice and a stony, slightly flinty finish.

Sijnn specialises in blends, as a rule, so it’s fun to come across this varietal Chenin Blanc from Charla Bosman and successor Kruger Theunissen. Matured in Austrian foudres, it has some tannic structure from whole bunch pressing, layers of coconut, pineapple and brioche, appealing underlying zip and minerality and a sappy, slightly salty finish. Intriguing.

Appropriately named, Low Profile is the second-tier red from this pioneering Malgas property, featuring an unusual blend of Syrah, 14% Viognier, 15% Tempranillo and 10% Chenin Blanc. Green, sappy and slightly earthy, it has flavours of sage, rooibos tea and redcurrant, understated oak, racy acidity and a subtle volatile lift.

Always a wine that takes a while to come together in bottle – it’s well worth buying some to tuck away – this is a seamless, gloriously unique assemblage of mostly Syrah with 16% Grenache, 14% Mourvèdre, 12% Cabernet Sauvignon, 9% Tempranillo, 5% Tinta Amarella, 3% Carignan and 2% Malbec. Bloody, intense and appealingly ferrous, it has layers of garrigue, blackberry and chopped liver and a slightly green, herbal finish. Needs time.

Confirming the promise of the maiden 2024 release, this is a small-volume bottling of just 500 bottles, suggesting that Vermentino has a promising future in South Africa. Subtle juniper and aniseed aromas lead you into a palate of lemon zest and white pepper and an appealingly briny, oyster shell finish.

Remote Malgas supplies the raw material for this Cape white blend of Chenin Blanc, 14% Viognier, 8% Verdelho and 3% Roussanne. Showing some tannic presence from whole bunch pressing, this has aromas of saffron, petrichor and wildflowers and an intriguing palate of citrus, lemongrass and gin botanicals.

Back after a break in 2020 – a good vintage to skip, according to John Loubser – the 2021 Jewel Box is every bit as good as its distinguished predecessors. Combining Chardonnay and 15% Pinot Noir, it’s appealingly dry at just 4.5 grams of dosage, with subtle brioche and oatmeal autolysis from 42 months on lees, a mineral spine and a core of citrus, lemongrass and cream.

Who says that Cap Classique bubblies must be made from Chardonnay or Pinot Noir? John Loubser uses four old-vine parcels of Roberston Colombard to produce River Dragon and it’s very tasty, with flavours of lime, green apple and freshly squeezed lemon juice, a hint of wood spice and mid palate texture from full malolactic.

John Loubser bottled some of his River Dragon in magnums in 2024 to see how it would evolve. As you’d expect, it’s a little more reticent on the nose and palate, but has a similar fruit profile, with layers of aniseed, pear and green apple, mouth-coating bubbles and an appealing undertone of spice from 40% acacia fermentation on the base wine.

Sparkling wines made with Shiraz are an Australian specialism, but are still very rare in the Cape. This has a bronze-pink hue from red wine dosage of 3.1 grams of sugar, classic limestone-derived freshness, layers of redcurrant and strawberry and a dusting of Campari spices.

Experienced bubbly hand John Loubser uses a little wood on the base wine of this allChardonnay Blanc de Blancs from Robertson. Benefitting from the addition of a little reserve wine, it shows the chalky intensity of Robertson fruit, with subtle 6.5 grams of dosage, creamy bubbles, layers of citrus and macadamia nut and a satisfyingly dry, refreshing finish.

n: Simonsig Cuvée Royale Blanc de Blancs CC
Simonsig Kaapse Vonkel Brut Rosé CC
Simonsig Kaapse Vonkel Satin Nectar CC
Simonsig Pick of the Bunch Pinotage

d: Carl Schultz bought this varietal Cabernet Sauvignon from Danie Steytler at Kaapzicht so that he would have a red to sell under his new Solo Wine label. Aged in 40% new wood, it has impressive concentration for a 2023 Stellenbosch red, with layers of mint, dried herbs, plum and blackcurrant and a sheen of toasty oak.

Part of a new range from experienced winemaker Carl Schultz, formerly the long-term supremo at Hartenberg, this Chardonnay comes from Baleia’s plantings in the cool-climate Lower Duivenhoks River area. Fermented in older oak without malolactic, it’s an expression of his “go to” CY95 clone, with subtle lemongrass, oyster shell and cardamom flavours and a dab of crème fraîche.

Something a little left field under the Solo Wines banner, this Merlot was purchased as a finished wine from Joubert-Tradouw in the Klein Karoo. Paired with 8% Cabernet Sauvignon, it’s a fine, floral red from slate and schist soils, with fine-boned, graceful tannins, plum, red berry and paprika flavours and a leafy top note.

The Engela is a tribute to Carl Schultz’s mother, made with grapes from the Alexander Block at Ataraxia on the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge. It’s an ambitious expression of Chardonnay from Bokkeveld shale soils, with understated 20% new oak, plenty of zip and stony minerality, a hint of brine and a chiselled, lemon zest palate. Like an old school Chablis.

n: Sophie Germanier Old Vine Chenin Blanc
Sophie Germanier Old Vine Chenin Blanc
d: Swiss-born Sophie Germanier makes this old-vine Chenin Blanc with grapes from Durbanville and Wellington, with 20% of the final blend seeing oak. Showing a hint of good, stony reduction, it has white flower and jasmine aromas, a nettley undertone and a palate of aniseed, oatmeal and citrus zest.

Southern Right uses grapes from four different regions across the Western Cape, three of which could be classified as cool climates. Ambitiously priced it may be, but that’s partly the point. Entirely matured in older wood, it has impressive concentration and texture, plum and black cherry flavours, smooth tannins and a kiss of aromatic spices.

Twenty-nine parcels, five clones and three soil types is Emul Ross’s summary of the components that go into this Cape Coast Sauvignon Blanc. A burst of stony, gunflint reduction announces the arrival of a palate of elderflower, white pepper and bay leaf, complemented by a racy, mouth-watering finish.

A wine that has an army of fans, due to the name as well as the style, this is a concretefermented blend of Carignan, 23% Syrah, 17% each of Grenache and Tannat, 10% Mourvèdre and 9% Durif. Showing a touch of meaty reduction, it has plum, blackberry and cranberry flavours, savoury tannins and a dusting of Asian spices.

Saffron is a pale, elegant, whole bunch-pressed rosé from Darling showing the zip and freshness that reflect the region’s Atlantic Ocean-influenced climate. Sappy, perfumed and easy to drink, it’s a juicy pink with cranberry and wild strawberry flavours and a zesty finish.

n: Spice Route Tarragon OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Tarragon is a naturally fermented Chenin Blanc from a 1978 block next to the Rooidraai farm outside Malmesbury. Subtly wooded in 5% new barrels with a hint of malolactic, it’s all about texture rather than simple fruit flavours, with layers of lanolin, fennel and beeswax, bright acidity and a subtle bitter twist.

A textbook expression of Stellenbosch Cabernet Sauvignon in the warm 2022 vintage, this is a red with time on its side. Stylishly wooded in 70% new barrels, with more than enough structure and concentration to cope, this has smooth, nicely polished tannins, blackcurrant, plum and blueberry fruit and supporting acidity.

Ripe and concentrated for a Durbanville Chenin Blanc, this comes from a 38-year-old vineyard on the Tygerberg. The 40% new oak is well handled here, adding some toast and cinnamon spice to a palate that’s creamy, intense and well balanced, with some subtle gunflint reduction and a medley of yellow apple, peach and quince.

Big, bold and ripe, this is a wine for Pinotage drinkers who want the grape to be handled like a Cabernet Sauvignon. Nearly touching 15% alcohol, it has plenty of structure and texture, flavours of plum, blackberry and dark chocolate and a backbone of grippy tannins supported by 60% new French, American and Hungarian oak.

Turning its attention to the Rhône Valley, as it were, this is a ripe, full-throttle assemblage of Syrah, 5% Mourvèdre and 3% Viognier, with assertive 40% new French and American oak, flavours of fig, blackberry and Asian spices and a structured finish. Good enough, but a little too international in style.

The quantities may vary from vintage to vintage, but Creative Block 5 is always a blend of the five red Bordeaux grapes. Based on Cabernet Sauvignon, with a supporting cast of 36% Merlot, 7% Cabernet Franc, 6% Petit Verdot and 1% Malbec, it’s modern, compact, dense and lavishly oaked in 50% new barrels, all mint, blackcurrant pastille and damson and a waft of green herbs.

n: Spier Frans K Smit White Blend
d: Named after Spier’s winemaking supremo, Frans K. Smit, this is an ambitious Cape Town white from the Durbanville region, combining Sauvignon Blanc and 33% Semillon. Racy, perfumed and lightly wooded, it has brine, toast and lime blossom aromas, lots of green herbs and a core of elderflower and asparagus.

Anyone who loves Riesling will be familiar with this wine, which is rightly regarded as the best interpretation of the variety in the Cape. Made by eccentric Belgian ex-sommelier Koen Roose, it’s just off dry at 5.5 grams of residual sugar, with plenty of extract and grip, stony intensity and flavours of lime, green apple, wet stones and toast. More Alsace than Germany, but with a distinctive South African personality. Delicious.

A significant step up on previous releases, this shows the influence of the time that Emma Bruwer spent at top bubbly producer, Le Lude. Deftly pairing Chardonnay and 40% Pinot Noir from the 2021 and 2022 vintages, it has a subtle wooded component, layers of patisserie, Digestive biscuit and toast and a racy, well-balanced finish.

n: Springfield Life from Stone Sauvignon Blanc
d: A wine that is deservedly popular with Sauvignon Blanc fans, this textbook expression of the grape spent 100 days on primary lees in stainless steel tanks. Flavours of gooseberry, passion fruit and kiwi are complemented by an appropriately stony finish.

Just the sort of thing you could imagine drinking on winemaker Abrie Bruwer’s boat, this is a summer wine with a difference. Combining Sauvignon Blanc, 25% Pinot Gris, 24% Semillon and 14% Sauvignon Gris, it has alluring aromas of musk and rose petal, flavours of pear and passion fruit and a tangy, well-balanced finish.

Bottled unfined and unfiltered, this is an intense, textured style of Chardonnay from Abrie and Emma Bruwer. Fermented and aged in 30% new 600-litre Stockinger barrels, it has a subtle note of struck match reduction, layers of toast, lemongrass and crème fraîche and an appealingly savoury finish.

The Special Cuvée vineyards were badly hit by the floods in the winter of 2026, after these grapes were picked, so enjoy this wine while you can. Sourced from vineyards on sandier soils, it has a touch of classic sweat on the nose, layers of passion fruit and lime, some texture from lees ageing and a racy, palate-cleansing finish.

Entirely fermented with ambient yeasts, this is an unwooded Chardonnay from limestone soils. Showing nice texture and weight from full malolactic, it combines flavours of sourdough bread and lemon butter with a racy, nicely focused finish.

How do Jeanne Vito and Johst Weber come up with these names? They certainly make me smile. This is the only Pinotage from the Springfontein Rim sub-region of Walker Bay, showing the freshness and brightness that show the variety at its best.
