Floral, scented and acid driven, it has top notes of gingerbread and patisserie spices and a sappy, tangy palate of raspberry, pomegranate and plum.

n: Springfontein Limestone Rocks Dark Side of the Moon
d: Made with grapes from the Springfontein Rim, a ward in Walker Bay, this is an intriguing cuvée from Jeanne Vito and Johst Weber, produced from a unique blend of Chenin Blanc, 33% Chardonnay and 22% Pinotage of all things. Fermented and aged in a combination of concrete eggs and 30% older French and American oak, this is floral, subtle and ethereal with a flinty, struck match top note, layers of dried honey and aromatic spices and a racy, wellbalanced finish.

Angus Paul gets half the fruit from this Syrah block on the Karibib farm in the Polkadraai Hills, while Chris Alheit gets the rest for his Fogwell brand. Fermented with whole bunches to make the most of the site, it’s a recognisably granitic style, with aromatic 25% new oak, impressive tannic structure and grip and flavours of sage, tapenade, black cherry and toast.

Blended with 4% Petit Verdot and 2% Cabernet Franc for added layers of complexity, this uses grapes from five sites on the property. Structured and intense, it’s a wine that needs more time, with blackcurrant and mocha flavours, detailed tannins and pink grapefruit acidity. One to tuck away for a while.

Vines close to the entrance of Stark-Condé’s ludicrously picturesque estate are the source of this brilliant white field blend, which has hit new heights of complexity in 2025. Roussanneled with support from 27% Chenin Blanc, 11% Verdelho and 10% Viognier, it’s salty, savoury yet somehow refreshing with pear, lime and citrus flavours and aromas of musk and wet stones.

The only wine at Stark-Condé that’s made with a trio of Rhône grapes, this is an assemblage of equal parts Syrah and Mourvèdre and 10% Grenache, sourced from a neighbouring farm. Peppery, spicy and almost chiselled on the palate, it has aromas of rosemary and essential oils, a palate of plum, redcurrant and dried herbs and a meaty undertone.

Even more impressive when you learn that this comes from a six-year-old vineyard in the cool Jonkershoek Valley, this is a subtle, racy, refined expression of Chenin Blanc that has the raciness of a Sauvignon Blanc. Petrichor, jasmine and aniseed aromas segue into a palate of citrus, greengage and pink grapefruit embellished by 15% new oak.

Always among the highlights of any tasting at Stark-Condé, Oude Nektar comes from an isolated vineyard at 550 metres and is one of the Cape’s unofficial Grand Cru sites. Curated in 40% new wood, it wouldn’t look out of place in a line-up of Bordeaux Crus Classés, with lots of energy and refinement, layers of graphite, cigar box and blackcurrant and a waft of mint and mountain herbs.

Stand-alone Petite Sirahs are rare in South Africa – maybe it’s José Condé’s American roots that make him a fan of the variety – but this is a textbook expression of the variety. Easily handling its 75% new French oak, it has the tannin and acidity you’d expect, with intense damson and blackberry fruit flavours and a backdrop of toasty wood.

Stark-Condé is generally regarded as a red wine producer, but it makes some very smart whites, too. This Sauvignon Blanc comes from a block at 400 metres and has the freshness and zip of its terroir. Stylishly fermented in 5% new oak, it has appealing layers of wet stones, white pepper and pink grapefruit, subtle baking spices and a tangy, chiselled finish.

Part of a superb crop of current releases, this serious, stony red hails from three parcels on the property, located between 250 and 360 metres. Marrying Syrah, 7% Mourvèdre and 1% each of Roussanne and Viognier, it’s a Cape-meets-the-northern-Rhône style with clove and rose petal aromas, plum and red berry fruit and a savoury granitic undertow.

Some of the older vines on the property contribute to the blend here, partnering Cabernet Sauvignon, 10% Petit Verdot and 5% Cabernet Franc. Showing the influence of decomposed granite soils, this has a scented frame of toasty 35% new oak and a palate of plum, redcurrant and cassis complemented by fine-grained, sculpted tannins.

Black Swan showcases the top three Sauvignon Blanc vineyards on Steenberg’s extensive Constantia estate. It’s a very pithy cool climate expression of the variety, where you can almost taste the sea breeze. Salty, tangy and granitic, it has notes of nettle, lime and oyster shell and a mouth-watering finish.

Previously sold as Steenberg’s Barrel-Fermented Sauvignon, this is now a blend with 10% Semillon. Made in a Blanc Fumé style, this uses grapes from selected blocks on the estate and is all about what Elunda Basson calls “texture and mouthfeel”. Subtle, toasty, mostly older oak frames a palate of grapefruit, dill and gooseberry supported by palate-cleansing acidity.

Lady R is a very smart cuvée of Chardonnay from Darling and Philadelphia with 40% Pinot Noir from Robertson. Lees-aged for five years, it’s an appealingly dry, very complex bubbly with full malolactic adding some cream and texture to a palate of aniseed, citrus, hazelnut and dried mushroom. Complex, focused and very long on the finish.

Magna Carta is Steenberg’s most ambitious white, expressing all that is best about the Constantia Valley. Back in 2023 after skipping a vintage in 2022, it’s a seamless cuvée of Sauvignon Blanc and 40% Semillon with very subtle baking spice and kelp top notes, flavours of grapefruit, rock salt and cardamom and a savoury finish.

Merlot is the most planted red grape at Steenberg, so it’s something of a specialism. Picked early in a demanding vintage, this uses grapes from five different blocks on the farm and is enjoyably refreshing and elegant, combining aromas of mint and dill with a palate of plum and blackcurrant leaf framed by subtle oak sweetness.

Elunda Basson uses grapes from 23 different blocks of Sauvignon Blanc to make this good value wine, blending them with 13% Semillon. Entirely unwooded, it’s tangy, refreshing and appealingly dry, with kiwi fruit, lime ad cucumber flavours and a herbal tang.

There’s a little more love for Semillon out there, says Elunda Basson and it’s surely about time. This comes from a single parcel of just over a hectare and is a stylish cool climate expression of the variety, with scented 20% new oak, layers of iodine, tarragon, beeswax and lemon zest and a waft of vanilla spice.

n: Stellenrust 61 Barrel Fermented OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Sixty-one is the age of the vineyard here, planted on a mix of iron and granite soils. Blended with 0.4% botrytis-infected bunches – it’s surprising what an impact they have – this is a comparatively large volume top Chenin Blanc, with scented 30% new oak, layers of honey citrus and passion fruit and a bright, acid-driven finish.

n: Stellenrust ArtiSons Series Rare Blueberry Hill Shiraz
d: Historically, the reds played second fiddle to the whites at Stellenrust, but not anymore. This 100% whole cluster Syrah comes from richer soils with a higher clay content and will delight northern Rhône Valley fans with its aromas of incense, oregano and white pepper, its freshness and focus, its subtle, understated oak and its confident, well-structured finish.

n: Stellenrust ArtiSons Series Rare The Albatross White Cinsault
d: The Albatross is a very rare sighting of White Cinsault, made from a mutation of the more common red form of the grape. Using raw material from two blocks planted in 1971 and 1972, respectively, it’s a chiselled, super racy curiosity, with subtle barrel fermentation, mouthwatering acidity and flavours of lime, fennel and lemon zest.

n: Stellenrust ArtiSons Series Rare The Basket Child OVP Cinsault
d: “Our red Chenin Blanc” is how Tertius Boshoff describes Cinsault, as it’s “hard to fuck it up”. This one comes from a 1971 bush vine parcel and is a delight. Fermented with 32% whole bunches, it has appealing aromas of ginger and Campari spices, ambitious, savoury tannins and a core of redcurrant, hibiscus and rooibos tea.

n: Stellenrust ArtiSons Series Rare The Mothership Chenin Blanc
d: Chenin Blanc lovers are almost spoilt for choice at Stellenrust, such is the range and quality of the wines on offer. This is my pick of the bunch in 2025, a wine of perfume, poise and intensity sourced from a three-hectare vineyard planted in 1964. White flower and honeysuckle aromas are a scented introduction to a sappy, racy, beautifully defined palate of citrus, quince and passion fruit, steely acidity and a (just) off-dry finish.

Reflecting the quality of the “cool, early” 2025 vintage, this is consistently one of the bestvalue Chenin Blancs in South Africa, all of it sourced from the Bottelary Hills. Very lightly wooded in older barrels and stainless steel, it marries flavours of pear, green apple and stone fruit with balancing acidity and a touch of sweetness.

n: Stellenrust Chenin d'Muscat OVP Noble Late Harvest
d: This old-vine noble late harvest sticky combines botrytis-affected Chenin Blanc with 33% vine-dried Muscat d’Alexandrie. Reasonably priced by the standards of some Cape sweet wines, it has lovely pear, peach and pineapple flavours, plenty of racy acidity, a subtle volatile lift and a refreshing, acid-driven finish.

Corner Stone comes from a parcel of old-vine Bottelary Pinotage that was planted back in 1962. Showing the concentration of its raw material, it has the density and concentration to age, but without excessive oak. Plum and black cherry flavours are grounded by plenty of grip and backbone and top notes of liquorice and wood smoke.

n: Stellenrust Indecent Obsession OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Generally the most intense and concentrated of the three Chenins sourced from Stellenrust’s three-hectare 1983 block, this is sweet, yet refreshing, with 8.8 grams of residual sugar from some blended back botrytis-affected bunches and a chiselled pH of 3.18. Floral and intense, it has flavours of patisserie spices, yellow apple and nectarine, subtle wood integration and a racy, tapering finish.

n: Stellenrust Naked Truth OVP Chenin Blanc
d: One of a trio of wines sourced from a dryland Chenin Blanc vineyard planted in 1983, this unwooded, “naked” iteration of the variety is dry, focused and intense, with flavours of passion fruit, green apple and cherimoya, a nip of tannin from partial skin contact and some mid-palate texture from seven months on lees.

Despite its name, this Shiraz is less peppery than the Blueberry Hill release, but is no mean wine in its own right. Sourced from a 1978 parcel of dry-farmed vines, it has lovely granitic intensity, top notes of clove and liquorice, redcurrant and blackberry fruit, sinewy tannins and the effortless concentration that comes with very low yields.

n: Stellenrust Secrets and Lies OVP Chenin Blanc
d: "A bit of wood and a bit of sugar," is how Tertius Boshoff describes this old-vine Chenin Blanc, fermented with 1.4% botrytis-affected grapes and aged in 20% new oak. Vanilla and patisserie spice aromas segue into a palate of pear, citrus and yellow apple, with a hint of sweetness and a racy, tapering finish.

Stellenzicht was one of the first farms in South Africa to make a name for Syrah, so there’s an historic connection with the variety. This is a refreshing, medium-bodied style, with some subtle stony reduction, plum and blackberry fruit flavours, scented 30% new oak and an undertow of tannin.

It’s good to see Stellenzicht undergoing a renaissance under German owner Hans von StaffReitzenstein. This is a very smart red at the price, combining Cinsault and 30% each of Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon. Racy, floral and refreshing, it has some subtle whole bunch spice, a sappy palate of redcurrant, plum and subtle oak spices and lots of zip and energy.

As its name suggests, Ignis hails from a 2.4-hectare parcel on the classic, granite-based soils of the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley. More immediate and charming than Vrede, it has rose petal and kitchen spice aromas, refined sculpted tannins, plenty of underlying zip and energy, stylish 23% new oak and flavours of redcurrant and wild strawberry. Long, detailed and very complex.

Hannes Storm’s brilliant Ridge Chardonnay uses grapes from an 18-year-old parcel that was planted with a highly unusual 8,000 plants per hectare on Bokkeveld shale soils. Subtly wooded in 29% new oak and some clay amphoras, this has the elegance and restraint of a cool site, with some texture from full malolactic, a pithy, mineral-etched core and flavours of citrus, aniseed and vanilla spice.

Ridge uses raw material from the coolest of Hannes Storm’s three single vineyards, located at 330 metres on the Bokkeveld shale soils of the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge. Showing more acidity as a result, it’s a crunchy, tangy Pinot Noir that can be a little tight in its youth but ages beautifully in bottle. Pomegranate, watermelon and pink grapefruit flavours are embellished by finely wrought tannins, mouth-watering minerality and fine 27% new oak.

A best-ever bottling of Vrede Chardonnay, at least in my book, this is a superb, textured white from a man who has grasped the potential of the exceptional 2025 vintage with both hands. Fermented in 29% new oak with full malolactic, it’s a textured, layered, self-assured wine with notes of lanolin, lemon butter and patisserie spices, a hint of earth from 10% clay amphoras and balanced, mealy finish.

Hannes Storm often says that his Vrede Pinot Noir has a lot of bass notes, and I know what he means. Sourced from a warmer, north-facing slope on Bokkeveld shale soils, it has effortless concentration, depth and poise, with 20% new oak, finely integrated 15% whole bunches, notes of forest floor, black cherry and plum and a steady heartbeat of tannin.

Adamastor is an almost equal blend of Sauvignon Blanc and 48% Semillon from two separate vineyards in Elim, with the latter undergoing barrel fermentation. Wet stone, parsley and curry leaf aromas segue into a palate of cream soda, grapefruit and cardamom and a herbal, lightly wooded finish.

Made with a highest-ever Semillon component (10%), this is a stylish Sauvignon Blanc from Conrad Vlok. There’s no missing its cool climate origins, down in wind-buffeted Elim, which have produced a wine with layers of green bean, fynbos and blackcurrant leaf complemented by an unmistakeably salty tang.

You need to tread warily if you’re using whole bunches in a cool climate like Elim’s, but Conrad Vlok has got it just right with 20%. Matured in 30% new wood, this is savoury, intense and ocean-influenced, with fynbos and subtle seaweed aromas, flavours of anchovy, tobacco leaf and black olive and a grippy, sinewy finish.

Commendably consistent given what can be challenging conditions at the foot of Africa, this is a southern Rhône style blend of Syrah, 37% Grenache, 11% Mourvèdre and 10% Viognier. Made with 25% added stems, it’s a savoury, intense, peppery red, with fine tannins, lots of tangy acidity, flavours of red cherry, tea leaf and oregano and a meaty undertone on the finish.

Named after the great white sharks that Conrad Vlok is happy to share the ocean with – rather him than I and all that – this is the second bottling of this impressive Sauvignon Blanc from Elim. Made with a 15% botrytis component, it’s rich yet refreshing at the same time, with impressive structure and density, layers of petrichor, pink grapefruit and toast and an oyster shell finish.

n: Survivor Cellar Master Series Cabernet Franc
d: This Cabernet Franc used to be blended with 25% Merlot, but is now a varietal wine from 17-year-old vines in Tradouw. The 40% new oak is deftly folded into the wine – a feature of the Survivor reds – adding an espresso coffee note to a capsicum and black cherry palate that’s supple and well balanced, carrying its 14.7% alcohol lightly.

Pierre Wahl sources this Chardonnay from the continental climate of Tradouw, using grapes from a 27-year-old block on shale soils. Subtly wooded in one-third new barrels, it’s a comparatively exotic style with peach and pineapple flavours and enough supporting acidity to lift and freshen the finish.

Keeping it in the family, this wine comes from a dryland Chenin Blanc vineyard that belongs to Pierre Wahl’s second cousin. Benefitting from comparative proximity to the Atlantic on the Darling side of the Swartland, it has citrus, yellow apple and tarte tatin flavours, some granitic freshness and stylish 40% new oak.

“Power with elegance” is Pierre Wahl’s motto when it comes to Pinotage, a variety with which he’s often associated. Sourced from 28-year-old vines on the Weldie farm in the Swartland, this is succulent, intense and self-confident, with toast, vanilla-scented 40% new oak, blackberry and summer pudding flavours and good balance for a wine with 14.7% alcohol.

Vines on iron-rich clay soils supply the fruit for Pierre Wahl’s Swartland Syrah, giving the wine a ferrous, almost red meat-like undertone. Fermented with 25% whole bunches and aged in 15% new oak, it has blackberry and dark chocolate flavours, savoury tannins and a herbal undertone.

The Vinekeeper is a pan-Cape blend of Stellenbosch Cabernet Sauvignon with 32% each of Syrah and Pinotage from the Swartland and 4% Cabernet Franc and 1% Merlot from Tradouw. Produced in small quantities, it’s a smooth, seamless red blend with herbal top notes, perfumed oak and layers of cassis, red cherry and paprika framed by fine-grained tannins.

Sutherland’s Anna Chardonnay comes from a 0.5-hectare parcel in Elgin, from which the best barrels are selected. Richer, creamier and more concentrated than the regular bottling, it has impressive weight and texture, pear and smoked lemon flavours and a saline, oyster shell, acid-driven finish.

Fresher and sappier than the Thelema Chardonnay – that’s Elgin’s cooler climate for you – this is a very complete, self-assured expression of the variety with subtle baking spice aromas from 25% new oak, layers of cardamon, crème fraîche, pear and lemon tart and a long, tapering finish.

One of only a handful of stand-alone Petit Verdots from the Cape, this is a wine that expresses the variety’s personality with aplomb. Intensely coloured, compact and built for the longer haul, it has sturdy tannins, layers of chocolate, damson and liquorice and enough structure to handle the 100% new oak.

Up a point with an extra year in bottle, this is a fresh, tangy, acid-driven Pinot Noir from Elgin that showcases the 777 clone, with a little 114 and 115 for good measure. Rose petal and Turkish Delight aromas lead you into a palate of redcurrant, raspberry and hibiscus complemented by 10% each of new oak and whole bunches.

Part of an impressive range from the Webb family’s Sutherland property in Elgin, this is a textbook Cape Riesling that’s scented, racy and light on its feet. Just off dry at 6 grams of residual sugar, with the chiselled acidity to match, this has classic lime and wet stone notes, a waft of white flowers and a mineral-etched finish.

Elgin is not usually considered the ideal spot for red Bordeaux grapes, but Sutherland is a warm site that can ripen them consistently. This is a partnership of Cabernet Sauvignon and 19% Merlot that will reward further time in bottle, with good grip and palate weight, toasty 55% new oak, a palate of mint, bramble, blackcurrant and plum and a firm finish.

Described by Thomas Webb as a “wine from a warm site in a cool region”, this is a stylish, attractively priced Sauvignon Blanc that sees no wood. Tangy lime and gooseberry flavours are complemented by a touch of passion fruit sweetness and a racy, stony finish.

A very rare example of a blend of Viognier and 15% Roussanne from Elgin’s cool climate, this was entirely fermented in larger used barrels. Engagingly spicy, with hints of white pepper, musk and cardamom, pear, peach and greengage flavours. Beautifully judged by the talented Rudi Schultz.

"I’m very excited about the future of Assyrtiko in South Africa," says Dirk Swanepoel, and you can see why. Ideally suited to Tulbagh’s warmer conditions, it’s serious, dense and complex, with aromas of wet stone and fynbos, mouth-watering acidity, citrus and fennel flavours and impressive underlying extract and concentration.

Great value from the youthful Dirk Swanepoel, this is an elegant, direct-pressed rosé made from Grenache, 38% Pinot Noir and 11% Syrah. Rose petal and rooibos tea aromas segue into a graceful palate of raspberry and watermelon, supported by palate-cleansing acidity.

n: Swanepoel Old Vine OVP Chenin Blanc
d: A wine that is showing much better now than it was a year ago – hence the higher score – this comes from a 45-year-old Chenin Blanc block at 500 metres on Citrusdal Mountain. Racy, pithy and refreshing it’s very much a West Coast style, with a note of sea breeze, some subtle stony reduction and a citrus, cardamom and green apple core.

Garnacha, or Grenache if you prefer, is the star red grape from the Piekenierskloof plateau to the north of Cape Town. This is a very refined expression of the variety that tastes like a Mencía from Bierzo in Spain, with ethereal aromas of rose petal, tobacco leaf and aromatic spices and a palate of raspberry, red cherry and grapefruit framed by filigree tannins.

Sourced from a 1964 Piekenierskloof parcel that is “planted on rocks”, according to Rudiger Gretschel, this is a rare example of a dry white Palomino in South Africa. Wild fermented in foudres and clay amphoras, it’s a mealy, complex, low-intervention white with notes of citrus and salted almonds and a briny finish.

Unusual for a Piekenierskloof red as it’s based on Syrah with 20% Grenache, rather than the other way around, this needs a little more time to shed a touch of meaty reduction, but has plenty of structure, concentration and minerality. Lightly wooded in concrete, amphoras and older wood, it has redcurrant, plum and blackberry flavours and a firm, upright spine of tannin.

Miracle Bush comes from the coastal side of Piekenierskloof, where you can sometimes sense the proximity of the Atlantic Ocean in the wines. Led by Grenache Blanc, with support from 35% Chenin Blanc and 5% Palomino, this is a racy, West Coast-style white with appealing aniseed and lemongrass flavours and a racy, palate-cleansing finish.

What a wine! Pinotage doesn't get much better than this example from the brilliant Rudiger Gretschel, who also features on the label in a fetching hat. Sourced from vines at 700 metres, it’s racy, floral and engagingly elegant with sculpted, fine-grained, palate-caressing tannins, flavours of sweet spices, strawberry and goji berry and a waft of fynbos herbs and flowers.

n: Swartland Winery Bush Vine Chenin Blanc

d: A brand that has rapidly established itself as one of the best red blends in Stellenbosch, Taaibosch has crept up in price but still represents good value for money. Based on Cabernet Franc, with support from 38% Cabernet Sauvignon and 19% Merlot, the 2022 is more approachable than the 2021 was at the same stage, with floral, graphite top notes, fine-boned tannins and a fine, layered palate of red berries, paprika and rocket. Classy stuff.

Melanie van der Merwe’s Blanc de Blancs uses the greatly prized Chardonnay grapes from the Mont Blois farm in Robertson. Racy, youthful and rifle-sight focused, it marries aromas of white pepper and Shiitake mushrooms with a structured, stony, limestone-rich palate and tangy, acid-driven energy.

Grapes from Gawie du Bois’ Sonop farm in Stellenbosch make up the blend here, with 20% from a 1993 block in Darling. Wild yeast fermented in older oak, it has the subtlety and balance that are the hallmarks of the Tembela style, with jasmine and wet stone aromas and a structured palate of citrus and greengage and a pithy finish.

Building on the success of the 2024 release, this is a brilliant new Syrah from rising star Banele Vakele. Blending grapes from Karibib in the Polkadraai Hills and Langverwacht in nearby Kuils River, it has perfume and structure from 80% whole bunches, subtle old wood integration, aromas of pepper and incense, lovely granitic precision and a core of blackberry and tapenade. Utterly delicious.

n: Terblanche Family Vineyards Elmie Pinotage Rosé
d: Top viticulturist Etienne Terblanche, also one of the partners in Thistle & Weed, makes this excellent rosé under his own label. Sourced from vines planted in 1976, it’s a Pinotage pink that out-Provences Provence, with rosehip, raspberry and wild cherry flavours, a hint of wood and a savoury, dry finish.

n: Terra Loci Déjà Vu Grenache Blanc
d: Sourced from a north-facing slope where it’s “baking hot”, according to Johann Fourie, this wine shows you why Grenache is so well suited to an increasingly hot climate. On the palate, it’s like licking a wet stone, with lemon zest and apple cider flavours, a sheen of gin botanicals and nicely understated third and fourth-use oak.

Terra Loci is the personal project of Benguela Cove winemaker Johann Fourie, made with gapes sourced across the Western Cape. This Chardonnay comes from the Pascall family’s Oneiric farm in Elgin and reflects its cool climate origin. Mealy, stony and refreshing, it has some stony reduction, layers of citrus, vanilla and beeswax and some mid-palate texture from 30% malolactic.

n: Terra Loci Planted by Chance Chenin Blanc
d: Planted By Chance comes from 58 Chenin Blanc vines that were planted, quite possibly by error, in a 48-year-old Pinotage vineyard. Fermented and lees-aged in older barrels, this has the granite-derived freshness of the Paardeberg, aromas of lanolin and aniseed and a palate of juniper, yellow apple and nutmeg spice.

Berene Sauls uses the winemaking skills of Emul Ross of Hamilton Russell Vineyards to make her in-demand Chardonnay from the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge. Featuring the CY95 clone, it’s a very lightly wooded style that combines amphora and a 30% wooded component. Pithy and stony, with layers of petrichor, lemon zest and cardamom and a waft of struck match.

A slightly warmer, north-east facing site on the shale soils of the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge supplies the raw material for this appealing, if ambitiously priced Pinot Noir. Showcasing the refined 115 Dijon clone, it has scented, toasty 30% new François Frères oak, racy acidity, a spine of tannin and plum and black cherry fruit. Needs more time in bottle.

Thamnus’ Chardonnay has experienced a meteoric rise, quickly establishing itself as a wine of impressive quality and personality since its first release in 2021. Made with ten and 15-year-old vines from the Overberg, it’s a seamless mix of three clones (95, 96 and 76) that looks towards Burgundy. Subtle toast and gunflint top notes are complemented by a pithy, stony, beautifully balanced palate of oatmeal and waxed lemon and a hint of nougat sweetness.

Now vinified without a whole-bunch component, this is a riper, more textured style of Pinot Noir from PJ Geyer. Featuring the 115 and 777 Dijon clones, with ageing in 30% new oak, it’s the best Thamnus release yet, with juicy black cherry and raspberry fruit, textured tannins and a floral lift.

Part of a very smart selection under The Bothey label, this Elgin Chardonnay sits proudly at the racier end of the varietal spectrum. Aromas of chamomile and jasmine guide you into a lightly wooded palate of citrus and green apple complemented by a savoury note from wild yeast fermentation and a lightly buttery mid palate.

Combining Chenin Blanc grapes from the Swartland and Stellenbosch - hence the Coastal label - this is deftly selected by Katja Leinbgerger and Marcel Hartman. Showing old-vine concentration, it has subtle aromatic spice notes from second and third-fill oak, a touch of beeswax and a palate of citrus, cardamom and wet stones.

Named after The Bothey House in Somerset West, this is part of a range of wines produced for the property at other unnamed premium estates. This scented Grenache from Piekenierskloof is very smart indeed, with hibiscus, fynbos and rooibos tea aromas, lots of zip and energy and a core of pomegranate and red cherry.

n: The Dog Star Chardonnay Barrel Fermented
d: Fermented and aged in older 500-litre barrels, this is one of the best Chardonnays from Roberston, using grapes from shale and limestone soils. Subtle sandalwood and vanilla spice aromas segue into a palate that’s vibrant and energetic, revealing layers of lemongrass and wet stones and a tangy, palate-cleansing finish.

n: The Dog Star Chardonnay Sur Lie
d: He may be better known for his Cap Classiques, but John Loubser can also turn his hand to still Chardonnays. Sourced from shale and limestone soils, this is an unwooded, lees-aged style with appealing purity and focus, racy acidity and flavours of lemon zest and cardamom spice.

n: The Fledge & Co Cape White Fortified
d: The Fledge doesn’t normally make fortified wines, but Margaux Nel’s day job is at Boplaas, so it was only a matter of time. This intriguing new cuvée is Chenin Blanc-based, with a “bit of everything else, except Muscat”. Produced in an off-dry, lightly rancio style with 41 grams of residual, it’s nutty, waxy and intense, with notes of citrus, pear and honey and well-integrated spirit.

Reflecting The Fledge’s attachment to what Leon Coetzee calls “terroir by truck”, this blend of Sauvignon Blanc and 10% Semillon was sourced from Darling, Elgin and Stellenbosch. The flinty, struck match note is quite assertive on the nose, but integrates on the palate, adding complexity to a palate of tarragon, lime, green beans and cream soda and a taut, pithy finish.

n: The Fledge & Co Hoeksteen Chenin Blanc Reserve
d: Labelled with both of its origins, Montagu and three vineyards in the Swartland, this is no longer a Stellenbosch Chenin Blanc. Fresh bread, oatmeal and citrus fruit flavours are complemented by lees-derived texture, a hint of salt and a spine of racy acidity.

n: The Fledge & Co Lone Leopard Grenache
The Fledge & Co Praeteritus Bosstok OVP Tinta Barroca
d: One for lovers of stand-alone Portuguese varieties, this comes from the granite-based soils of the Jakkalsfontein vineyard on the Paardeberg. Sage, earth and tobacco leaf aromas lead you into a palate of damson, fynbos and black cherry supported by grippy, faintly rustic tannins.

n: The Fledge & Co Redemption of a Rogue Viognier
d: Redemption of a Rogue – great name, Leon Coetzee – is a new release from The Fledge, made entirely from Elgin Viognier. Fermented and matured in Hungarian and 20% French oak, it’s an appealingly restrained style, marrying aromas of white pepper and stem ginger with a palate of citrus, beeswax and cream and a hint of peachy sweetness.

This the Fledge’s tenth vintage of this “humble and faithful donkey” variety, this comes from a single site on the Doornbosch farm in Calitzdorp. Showing the colour and acidity that are part of Souzão’s DNA, this has some subtle, stony reduction, flavours of bramble, redcurrant and cranberry and an unabashedly chewy finish.

Elgin got too expensive, says Leon Coetzee, explaining the The Fledge’s move to the Klein Karoo for this Chardonnay from Keisie and Tradauw. Stony, pithy, focused and intense, it’s a smart, tucked in, continental white with appealing mid-palate texture, lemongrass and wet stone flavours and a bright, chalky finish.

Vagabond is The Fledge’s version of the Sadie Family’s Palladius, made with ten varieties from 17 different vineyards, with Chenin Blanc and Roussanne accounting for nearly half the blend. Showing a salty note from a hint of flor, it has some structure from partial skin contact, layers of peach, quince and lemon zest and a subtle juniper twist.

It was sad to be reviewing these wines just after owner Les Sweidan had passed away. Representing excellent value for money, this is a Stellenbosch blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, 8% Merlot and 4% Petit Verdot that’s very serious at the price, with mint, bramble and blackcurrant flavours, scented oak and some tannic ballast.

Classique is a four-way Bordeaux style blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, 40% Merlot, 13% Cabernet Franc and 5% Petit Verdot. It’s a lighter style, reflecting the wetter vintage, but is elegant in its way, with racy acidity, sinewy tannins and red cherry and blackcurrant leaf flavours and a patina of older oak.

Not quite up to the high standard of recent vintages, but that’s got more to do with the harvest conditions than anything else. Cabernet Sauvignon takes the lead here, supported by 27% Merlot, 11% Petit Verdot and 5% Cabernet Franc. Top notes of rose petal and mint segue into a palate of bramble, graphite and blackcurrant pastille and well-handled 50% new oak.

n: The Vinoneers Orpheus & the Raven Chenin Blanc
The Vinoneers Orpheus & the Raven Eye of the Tiger Cinsault
The Vinoneers Orpheus & the Raven No# 7 Pinotage

d: One of those wines that never seems to disappoint, this unblended Cabernet Sauvignon uses grapes from two blocks in the middle part of the farm, located between 400 and 440 metres. A wine that's forward but has the structure to develop further in bottle, this has a scented sheen of 40% new oak, classic mint, green herb and blackcurrant flavours, fine tannins and a racy, refreshing finish.

Rudi Schultz’s skills as a white winemaker are sometimes under-valued, such is the focus on his reds. This Simonsberg Chardonnay from three blocks on the farm is a finely judged white, with 30% new oak, a hint of malolactic, cream, clementine, pear and waxed lemon flavours and a touch of peachy sweetness.

Stand-alone Merlots of this quality are very rare in South Africa - and the world for that matter. Intense, focused, layered and well structured, it has basil, toast and mocha aromas, lots of energy and drive, well-defined, sinewy tannins and a core of blueberry and cassis. Delicious now but will improve further in bottle. A fine expression of what Rudi Schultz calls a “super elegant vintage”.

Rabelais doesn't always receive the plaudits it deserves, especially from critics, but I’m a huge fan of this accomplished blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and 10% Petit Verdot. The 75% new wood is right on point, the palate structured, detailed and built to last, with violet, fynbos and cedarwood aromas and flavours of cassis blueberry and mint complemented by fine tannins. Good now and will improve further.

Benefitting from the judicious inclusion of 10% whole clusters, this has potpourri, clove and subtle mint aromas, flavours of blackberry tapenade and cola, savoury, nicely integrated tannins, lots of underlying energy and stylish 15% new French oak. A classy Simonsberg Syrah.

In challenging years like 2023, it’s important to “read the vintage”, according to Rudi Schultz. Picked in four stages, this superb Cabernet Sauvignon is a case in point, with the eucalyptus top notes that give the wine its name, notes of pine, laurel and blackcurrant, stylish, coffee bean-scented 35% new oak and a lingering finish.

n: Thelema Vin de Hel Muscat Late Harvest
d: Picked late in early April, with around 3% botrytis, the 2025 Vin de Hel is slightly sweeter than usual at 211 grams of sugar. A varietal expression of Muscat de Frontignan, this is intensely exotic and concentrated with aromas of rose water and orange blossom and a palate of pineapple and guava balanced by racy acidity.

n: Thiart Wines The Pope's New Crib
Thistle & Weed Brandnetel OVP Chenin Blanc
d: A wine that tastes every bit as good as it looks, this wonderful Chenin Blanc is sourced from two parcels on sandstone soils in Stellenbosch, both planted in 1980. Bold, intense, yet racy at the same time, it has white pepper and nettle aromas, very subtle oak integration, a touch of residual sugar, layers of pear and wet stones and a engaging bitter twist. Very smart indeed.

n: Thistle & Weed Duwweltjie OVP Chenin Blanc
d: One of a trio of impressive single site Chenin Blancs from Stephanie Wiid and Etienne Terblanche, this intense white hails from 64-year-old vines on a gravel ridge at Joostenberg in Paarl. Fermented with full malolactic, it’s a relatively rich wine with layers of pear, cardamom and waxed lemons, subtle wood spices and ample concentration.

Khakibos is a wine that is blended across the Western Cape, with components from Paarl, Piekenierskloof, Stellenbosch, Wellington and Worcester and is a clever assemblage of Verdelho, 26% Palomino, 15% Chenin Blanc, 10% Albariño and 2% Fernão Pires. Racy, pithy and mouth-wateringly fresh, it has plenty of grip, layered flavours of lime, pear, citrus peel and coriander and engaging palate length.

Occupying a stylistic space between the Loire and Rhône Valleys, this is a Cabernet Franc that tastes as if it’s been blended with a little Syrah. Fermented with 15% whole clusters, it marries aromas of graphite, basil and white pepper with a palate of black cherry and bramble complemented by savoury, granular tannins.

Showing her considerable skills as a blender, Stephanie Wiid makes this effortlessly complex blend with Tempranillo, 17% Touriga Nacional, 16% Alicante Bouschet, 11% each of Souzão and Touriga Franc, a further 8% each of Merlot and Syrah and 4% Pontac. Think of it as Portugal meets South Africa, with violet, clove and fennel aromas and a palate of bramble, blackberry and cranberry supported by deftly integrated tannins.

n: Thistle & Weed Springdoring OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Springdoring comes from decomposed white granite soils on the Paardeberg, using grapes from a Chenin Blanc block that was established in 1982 on the Uitvlucht farm. Showing the weight and intensity of a comparatively warm site, it was picked in two stages for complexity, combining aromas of quince, stone fruit and fennel with a racy, stony finish.

We’ve always wanted to make a bubbly, says Stephanie Wiid, and here it is for the first time. Made with a block of Chenin Blanc planted on the Simonsberg in 2020, this is fresh, lively and well made with subtle bready autolysis from 12 months on lees, flavours of yellow apple and citrus zest and an appealingly earthy finish.

n: Thokokani Diemersfontein The Clockmaker OVP Chenin Blanc

d: Blended with 5% botrytis-affected fruit for texture and a little sweetness, this is a wild yeast fermented Chenin that’s focused on fruit rather than oak. Savoury, scented and nicely textured, it has a waft of kitchen spices, yellow apple, citrus and stone fruit flavours and a nice interplay between acidity and 4.8 grams of residual sugar.

Nieuwoudtville in the Northern Cape is the source of this Sauvignon Blanc from Emile Gentis, which was given a day’s skin contact before fermentation in stainless steel and six months of lees ageing. Racy, refreshing and appealingly briny, it has lots of zip and energy, lime and passion fruit flavours and a dry finish.

n: Thor Vintners Boshmeshier Chenin Blanc/Grenache Blanc
d: New to the report, Thor Vintners & Co is the personal project of Emile Gentis, who used to work at DeMorgenzon. This is a well-judged blend of Swartland Chenin Blanc and 40% Grenache Blanc, with some structure from three days on skins, flavours of citrus, pear and yellow apple and a subtle, underlying bitter twist.

n: Thor Vintners Megan Mari Cabernet Franc/Merlot
Thor Vintners The Phoenix Petite Sirah
Thorne & Daughters Cat's Cradle OVP Chenin Blanc
d: John Seccombe is not given to exaggeration, so when he tells you that 2025 is a “very, very good year”, you know you can believe him. This is a greater Swartland blend of different Chenin Blanc components from the Paardeberg and Malmesbury, using grapes from vines planted between 1971 and 1983. Showing some flinty reduction, it’s a low-intervention style with beeswax, fennel, citrus and juniper flavours and a mouth-watering finish.

n: Thorne & Daughters Paper Kite OVP Semillon
d: Paper Kite is a blend of Semillon and around 5% of the much rarer Semillon Gris. Sourced from a single 0.75-hectare parcel planted on the Paardeberg in 1983, it has very classy, understated 25% new Stockinger oak, layers of musk, black tea and quince and the density and structure that are often features of John Seccombe’s whites.

n: Thorne & Daughters Rocking Horse Cape White Blend
d: Rocking Horse is a wine that never lets you down, a skilfully blended cuvée of Roussanne, 23% each of Chardonnay and Chenin Blanc, 20% Semillon and 7% Clairette Blanche. Made in a low-intervention style, it has savoury intensity and unusual structure for a white, with layers of quince, gin botanicals and lemongrass and very subtle wood.

n: Thorne & Daughters Snakes & Ladders Sauvignon Blanc
d: "You can’t dilute yourself to please everyone," says John Seccombe, “otherwise, you are vanilla.” This wine is a case in point, as it’s proudly individual. Sourced from the Van Lill and Oudam farms on Citrusdal Mountain, it’s a low-intervention, old-vine Sauvignon Banc with a difference, with lots of grip and extract, layers of nettle, elderflower, cardamom and wet stones and a touch of neutral oak.

n: Thorne & Daughters Tin Soldier Semillon Gris
d: Something of a curiosity in the Cape, this is made entirely with Semillon Gris, which is a natural mutation of much more widely planted Semillon. Bronze pink in colour, it’s a smallvolume release that is much coveted by aficionados, with 50% skin contact adding some grip and tannin, flavours of pear tart and orange peel and an appealing bitter twist.

Mahalia Kotjane is something of a rosé specialist, having worked at Lievland for a while. This is a restrained, youthful cuvée of more or less equal parts Cinsault, Grenache, Mourvèdre and Syrah, with subtle watermelon and raspberry flavours and enough acidity to drive and lengthen the finish.

Buying Syrah grapes from the adjacent Karibib and Bluegum Grove farms gives anyone an advantage in the cellar. This pepper and sage-scented red has plenty of depth, concentration and tannic grip, some clove spice from 30% whole clusters and no oak whatsoever.

Good bubblies from Piekenierskloof are rare, but the high altitude of the Tierhoek farm is ideally suited to fizz. This is stony, pithy Blanc de Blancs that used ten months of lees contact on the base wine, adding texture to a palate of citrus and apple pie supported by racy acidity and a fine mousse.

Charl van Schalkwyk makes this Sauvignon as a Blanc Fumé style, using wild yeast fermentation in older oak. Pithy, chiselled and mouth-wateringly fresh, it has layers of elderflower, lime and pink grapefruit, a savoury undertone and a bone-dry finish.

Tierhoek’s grapes are in demand, not only to make dry Chenin Blancs, but sweet ones too. This is a solera style blend dating back to 2007, with fermentation of air-dried bunches in older barrels. Fig, molasses, marmalade and apricot flavours are complemented by 246 grams of residual sugar, countervailing acidity and a rancio finish.

The price is certainly on the ambitious side, but there’s no denying the quality of this all-Chardonnay bubbly. Lees-aged for seven years, it has some subtle barrel fermentation on the base wine, impressive freshness for a wine that’s nearly a decade old, notes of citrus, oatmeal and dried mushroom and a nutty finish. Very tasty.

When people talk of the best Bordeaux style white blends in South Africa, Tokara is always in the mix. Made as a separately fermented cuvée of Sauvignon Blanc and 27% Semillon, it has appealing 31% new oak, layers of pink grapefruit, toast and lemongrass, impressive underlying structure and a touch of beeswax.

All sourced from a single block of the CY95 clone on the farm, this is a youthful Chardonnay that is just beginning to get into its stride. Fermented in 28% new oak, with full malolactic, it’s a small volume release that’s only sold in Tokara’s tasting room. Spicy cinnamon and aromatic herb aromas lead you into a palate of toast, pear and lemon butter and supporting acidity.

Stuart Botha uses three different Chardonnay clones (95, 242 and 377) to make this welljudged Simonsberg white. Less oaky than the 2024 release, it’s still on the toasty side, with good structure and intensity, some subtle struck match reduction, flavours of waxed lemon, brioche and baking spices and some cream from 90% malolactic fermentation.

n: Tokara Reserve Collection Chenin Blanc Straw Wine
d: Inspired by Tokaji Esencia, this is a very sweet, yet well balanced straw wine made from Chenin Blanc. Boasting 368 grams of residual sugar, it’s a wonderfully pure, unoaked expression of the style, with honey and crystallised fruit flavours, layers of nectarine and pineapple and an alluring interplay between racy acidity and intense, palate-coating sweetness.

Entirely lees-aged in stainless steel, this comes from sandstone over granite soils in Elgin. Nicely focused and restrained, it has wet stone and hedgerow aromas, flavours of lime and gooseberry, plenty of palate-cleansing acidity and a pithy dry finish.

Tokara may be best known for its Bordeaux style reds and white, but Stuart Botha has a long history of making excellent Cape Syrahs. Fermented with 30% whole bunches, it’s a scented, spicy, medium-bodied style with aromas of iodine and lavender and a palate of pepper, blackberry and red cherry framed by 55% new wood.

Production is limited to 1,000 bottles, so Telos is something of a collectors’ item, even at R5,600 a bottle. A wine that lives up to the hype, this is a pure Cabernet Sauvignon from a 17-year-old vineyard on the Simonsberg, with beautifully handled 100% new oak, aromas of mocha, mint and fynbos, glossy, palate-coating tannins and a youthful, intense core of blueberry and blackcurrant fruit.

Italian grapes are still something of a rarity, so it’s always a pleasure to taste this nicely framed Barbera from the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge. Showing the savoury tannins and pronounced acidity you expect from the variety, it has a medley of plum and black cherry and top notes of clove spice and cola.

One of a handful of top Cape Syrahs from outside Stellenbosch and the Swartland, this is a wonderful, ocean-kissed expression of the variety that has top notes of kelp, sage, tar and fynbos, a palate of black olive, white pepper and black cherry, understated oak, racy acidity and a slightly salty finish.

n: Trizanne Signature Wines Lower Duivenshokrivier Chardonnay
d: The cool climate Lower Duivenshokrivier region is the source of this finely crafted Chardonnay from Trizanne Barnard. Wild fermented in 20% new oak, it has kelp and oyster shell top notes, a waft of patisserie spices and a palate of lime, oatmeal and macadamia nut. A Chardonnay that reflects the proximity of the ocean.

n: Trizanne Signature Wines Napier Blanc Fumé
d: Sourced from a hilltop vineyard called Kroonport in Napier, this is an old-vine Sauvignon Blanc that illustrates Trizanne Barnard’s fine touch with the grape. Sappy, stony and lightly briny, it has gently interwoven oak, layers of pink grapefruit and mountain herbs and a touch of passion fruit sweetness.

Pairing components from the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge and the Overberg, this is a crowd pleaser of a Pinot Noir that’s all about immediate pleasure, with aromas of rooibos tea and Turkish Delight, scented 10% new French oak and a palate of red cherry, potpourri and pomegranate.

Sondagskloof is one of the Cape’s cooler corners, ideally suited to top-of-the-range Sauvignon Blancs such as this one from the talented Trizanne Barnard. Wild yeast fermented in 50% new wood, it’s a tangy, chiselled white with greengage, nettle and elderflower flavours, racy acidity and a hint of cherimoya.

To make great Cabernet Franc, you need to know what great Cabernet Franc tastes like, and that’s certainly the case with Lukas van Loggerenberg. This is a 70/30 blend from Pierre Winshaw’s farm and Bluegum Grove and is a Loire-meets-Bordeaux-meets-the-Cape style with floral graphite and fresh parsley aromas, racy black cherry, paprika and vanilla spice flavours, lots of energy and beautifully manicured tannins.

Geronimo comes from the celebrated Rustenhof farm next to False Bay, where the “fruit profile is darker than in Darling”, according to Lukas van Loggerenberg. Showing the purity and transparency of the 2025 vintage, it has rose petal and ginger spice aromas, some texture and structure from 60% whole bunches and flavours of plum redcurrant and rhubarb.

Lukas van Loggerenberg shares this Syrah block with Jean Smit of Damascene and Reenen Borman of Boschkloof, all of whom make exceptional wines from it. The 2025 is more approachable than the 2024 release at the same stage, with real sense of purpose and selfconfidence, effortlessly integrated 100% whole clusters, layers of fennel, sage, white pepper and blackberry, structured, sinewy tannins and wonderful focus. A red for grown-ups.

Formerly made as a red blend, High Hopes is a varietal Syrah for the first time in 2025, using grapes from schist-dominated soils in Riebeek-Kasteel. Demonstrating Lukas van Loggerenberg’s magic touch with the variety, it has lots of perfume and structure from 100% whole bunches, flavours of cooked meat, blackberry and thyme and a spicy finish.

Kameraderie mostly comes from the Lammershoek farm, with a 15% component from nearby La Rhine, which also the source of Donovan Rall’s Noa Chenin Blanc. More exotic than Trust Your Gut, it has a medley of pear, passion fruit and fennel, a waft of white flowers and impressive underlying weight and concentration.

Yields were more than four times what they were in 2024 at the Lötter vineyard, which is fantastic news for this wine’s many fans. Sourced from iron-rich, granite-based soils in Franschhoek, it’s as “serious as Cinsault gets”, according to Lukas van Loggerenberg, with sinewy, even muscular tannins, flavours of plum, bramble, redcurrant and Negroni spices, 100% whole bunches and a structured, almost intellectual finish.

n: Van Loggerenberg Trust Your Gut Chenin Blanc
d: "I hope my kids get to see a vintage like this," says Lukas van Loggerenberg, who has made some of his greatest-ever wines in 2025. This superb Chenin contains equal components from the Paardeberg and Piekenierskloof, with a 20% addition from the Polkadraai Hills, showing saffron and wet stone aromas, good texture from 80% malolactic and flavours of lime and yellow apple.

n: Van Loveren Christina Noble Late Harvest Moscato
d: Something a little left field from this large Robertson winery, this is a low-alcohol Muscat de Frontignan that was given extended skin contact in stainless steel before ageing in old Chardonnay barrels. A mini Vin de Constance, it has flavours of pear, nectarine and honey, a hint of raisin and well-integrated 201 grams of sugar.

n: Van Loveren VRL Special Late Harvest Gewürztraminer
d: An unashamed crowd pleaser of a wine, this is simply a delicious drink, especially if you have a bit of a sweet tooth. Indulgently aromatic, it has rose petal and ginger spice aromas, a palate of lychee and cherimoya and a nice interplay between 47 grams of sugar and supporting acidity. A fruit cocktail in a glass.

Rachel Rose is a skin fermented white from Justin van Wyk, one of the best winemakers in the Constantia Valley. Combining Chenin Blanc, 29% Roussanne and 28% Viognier, it has a herbal, musky, saffron-infused nose, flavours of quince, peach and sourdough bread and nicely understated older oak.

Rebecca May is a pan-Cape blend of mostly Cinsault with 13% Syrah and 6% Grenache that’s deliberately made in a lighter, fresher style. The oak is very subtle here, leaving plenty of space for aromas of rose petal and aromatic spices and a palate of redcurrant, pomegranate and rooibos tea and finely judged tannins.

A Syrah for people who like a tangy, savoury, cool climate expression of the variety, this has plenty of zip and intensity, classic clove, fennel and white pepper aromas, racy plum, cooked meat and tobacco leaf flavours and a subtle undertone of oak spices. Elgin at its best in a wetter year.

Cabernet Sauvignon is the stellar variety at Vergelegen. This one hails from ten different parcels on the sizeable estate, making the most of varying aspects and altitudes. Curated in 30% new French oak, it reflects the shift in style under Luke O’Cuinneagain, with mint and basil aromas, racy plum, blackcurrant leaf and red cherry flavours and granular tannins.

Often overlooked in the range at Vergelegen because of the property’s reputation for red and white Bordeaux style wines, this Chardonnay deserves to be better known. Wild yeast fermented in 20% new oak, it’s a waxy, leesy, nicely balanced style with pear, citrus and white peach fruit, a savoury undertone and a scoop of crème fraîche.

A textbook example of what Luke O’Cuinneagain calls a “sleeper vintage”, the Estate Red is Cabernet Sauvignon based with support from 36% Merlot, 17% Cabernet Franc and 1% Petit Verdot. The 30% new oak is adroitly handled here, framing a palate of cassis, blueberry and dried herbs. The tannins are on point and guarantee further bottle development.

Previously sold as GVB, the revamped Estate White combines Semillon and 49% Sauvignon Blanc, all sourced from the farm. Fermented and aged in larger foudres and 20% new oak, this reflects what Luke O’Cuinneagain learnt as a young intern at Château de Fieuzal in Bordeaux, with aromas of honeysuckle and gunflint, stylish oak spices and a palate of beeswax, subtle herbs, toast and pink grapefruit.

Based on Syrah from the estate, with 17% Grenache and 15% Mourvèdre purchased from DeMorgenzon, this is a rosé that looks towards the south of France in terms of style. Racy and bone dry, it has mouth-watering acidity, flavours of pink grapefruit and watermelon and a twist of pepper.

There was a time, when Michel Rolland was the consultant, when Vergelegen was making way too many Merlots, so the slimmed down range is welcome. This comes from three distinct parcels and is fresher and less oaky than it used to be, combining blackcurrant and bramble fruit with some coffee bean oak, filigree tannins and a balanced finish.

Pretty smart for an entry-point red, The Mill puts Cabernet Sauvignon in the spotlight, with a supporting cast of 29% Merlot, 11% Syrah, 10% Cabernet Franc, 4% Petit Verdot and 3% Malbec. Youthful and well-structured it outperforms its price point, with scented 17% new oak, flavours of cassis, plum and dark chocolate and a refreshing finish.

Part of a very good run of V releases, the 2024 V marks Luke O’Cuinneagain’s second vintage in charge at Vergelegen. Combining Cabernet Sauvignon and 2% Petit Verdot from some of the highest red wine blocks on the farm, it’ a serious, tightly wound red that will reward cellaring. Layers of damson, cassis and black cherry are framed by 35% new French oak and supported by a spine of tannin and acidity.

Appropriately named, given how blustery it can get at the top of the estate, Wild Winds is a varietal Sauvignon Blanc that combines stainless steel and 5% barrel-fermented components. Fresh, tangy and well balanced, this has wet stone and elderflower aromas and a palate of greengage, passion fruit and pink grapefruit.

Now working with experienced consultant Abrie Beeslaar, Vergenoegd is a revitalised property to keep an eye on. This varietal Cabernet Sauvignon has plenty of grip and structure, layers of mocha, blackcurrant leaf and cassis, deftly judged tannins and the structure to develop further in bottle.

Fermented and aged in a combination of concrete eggs, 30% older barrels and 20% new wood, this is a step up on the previous release, with subtle cinnamon spice, a waft of white flowers and chamomile, lemongrass and clementine flavours and a bright, refreshing finish.

n: Vergenoegd Löw Family Collection Lara Cabernet Sauvignon
d: Made as a barrel selection by the talented Vusi Dalicuba, this is a very impressive Cabernet Sauvignon from four-year-old vines in Faure. Matured in second-fill barrels, it’s fresh, detailed, minty and light on its feet for a wine with 14.5% alcohol, with bramble, black cherry and green herb flavours and a dash of cedarwood on the finish.

Maximilian is a Bordeaux style blend that features Cabernet Sauvignon, 30% Merlot and 5% Petit Verdot, all sourced from vines planted in 2020. Impressive in a challenging vintage, this has a scented frame of 40% new oak, lively cassis and bramble fruit, a hint of pencil shavings and a fresh finish.

n: Vergenoegd Löw Family Collection Valentina Chardonnay
Vergenoegd Löw Family Collection White Bordeaux Blend
d: New to the range at Vergenoegd, this is a finely judged cuvée of Sauvignon Blanc and 30% Semillon from young vines. Fermented and aged in older barrels, this is herbal and appealingly waxy, with notes of tarragon, citrus and cream, some sourdough bread and a racy pink grapefruit finish. Promising stuff from Vusi Dalicuba.

Benefitting from a rare outcrop of limestone in Stellenbosch, this is a young-vine Merlot with lots of potential. Deftly matured in 30% new oak, it combines aromas of graphite and marjoram with a palate of plum and black cherry underpinned by sinewy tannins.

Generally the more structured of the two top Vilafonté wines – soon to be united under one label – this is Cabernet Sauvignon based with support from 24% Merlot, 12% Malbec and 7% Cabernet Franc. Gracefully wooded in 73% new French oak, it’s international in style, yet somehow quintessentially South African at the same time, with cassis, liquorice and damson fruit, beautifully judged tannins and appealing freshness and palate length. Picked before the rains, and it shows.

One of a pair of excellent Vilafonté Series wines from Chris de Vries in 2023, this is a plush, finely judged assemblage of Merlot, 38% Malbec, 16% Cabernet Sauvignon and 5% Cabernet Franc. Coffee bean and all spice top notes from 30% new oak are a scented introduction to a rich, supple, well-balanced palate of blackberry, black cherry, plum and dark chocolate supported by granular tannins and fresh acidity.

Now up to 450,000 bottles, Seriously Old Dirt is a seriously commendable brand from Arlene Mains. Combining purchased grapes from Robertson with 30% from Vilafonté’s own vineyards in Paarl, it’s a cuvée of Cabernet Sauvignon, 3% each of Malbec and Merlot and 1% Cabernet Franc. Appealing aromas of violet and gingerbread segue into a palate of plum, blueberry and cassis framed by supple tannins.

Kobie Viljoen buys his Chardonnay from cool climate Elgin, which is one of the three best sources of the variety in the Cape. Gently fermented in 30% new barrels, it’s a floral, detailed, well-balanced style with a touch of malolactic for texture, layers of waxed lemon and patisserie spices and a lingering, medium-bodied finish.

Sourced from Barton’s vineyards in Bot River, planted in 1983, this is always among the best Chenin Blancs in the region, not far behind what Beaumont produces. Fermented in 35% new oak, it has a nicely judged interplay between aromas of gunflint, aniseed and lemon verbena and a palate of pear, green apple and subtle stone fruit sweetness.

This is the second release of Silence from characterful English ex-pat, Samantha Suddons, made a solera-aged blend of the 2020, 2021 and 2022 vintages. Matured under a veil of flor, like a Fino Sherry, it’s a complex, medium-bodied style with flavours of saffron, rock salt, citrus and almond paste and a spine of tannin from whole bunch pressing.

It’s made from Chenin Blanc, as opposed to Palomino, but this reminds me of a good, unfortified vino de pasto from Jerez. Macerated on skins for 27 days and aged without topping in old French barrels, it’s earthy, savoury and challenging with aromas of thatch and tamarind and a palate of quince and black tea.

Old bush vines in the Swartland – planted in the 1980s, presumably – supply the grapes for this solo project from Rudi von Waltsleben. A Chenin Blanc that completed malolactic and was lees-aged for six months, it has pithy acidity, layers of fennel, citrus, lime and wet stones and a waxy mid-palate.

n: Von Family Wines The Thief Durif

d: Babiana uses grapes from the original Vondeling farm on the Voor Paardeberg and is a blend of Chenin Blanc, 24% Viognier, 9% Grenache and 7% Roussanne. Fermented and aged in 15% new French oak, it has appealing texture and concentration, pear, peach and grapefruit flavours and a tangy, mineral-etched finish.

Monsonia comes from Vondeling’s estate on the Voor Paardeberg and is a Languedoc-style assemblage of Syrah, 35% Mourvèdre and 20% Carignan. Matured in 20% new oak, it’s a structured, compact, serious red blend with clove, cumin and garrigue aromas, meaty fig and blackberry flavours and a spine of sinewy tannins.

The idea behind this charming red is to make something that’s "light and chillable” in the words of Max Ward, and it’s certainly that and maybe a little more. Made with a young vine cuvée of Grenache, 32% Syrah, 16% Cinsault, 14% Tempranillo and 4% Agiorgitiko, it’s a delicious Mediterranean blend with lots of zip, savoury tannins, redcurrant, pomegranate and white pepper flavours and a fresh finish.

A new wine in the Vondeling range, made with an unusual combination of Chenin Blanc, 13% Marsanne and 6% each of Assyrtiko, Roussanne and Verdelho from very young vines, this was fermented and aged in older wood and concrete eggs. Showing some granitic freshness, it has layers of citrus fruit, banana and apricot and a dusting of aniseed and white pepper. A wine to watch under consultant Callie Louw.

Vonn is the second release from Chardonnay specialist, Yvonne Lester, who learnt her craft at Rupert & Rothschild and Eikendal. Fermented and aged in older barrels and a ceramic pot, it makes of limestone-based grapes from Robertson, with subtle skin phenolics, notes of beeswax, oatmeal and fresh lemons, a hint of brine and a stony finish.

n: Vrede en Lust Barrique Semillon/Sauvignon Blanc
d: Barrique is often among my favourite whites from Vrede en Lust, showcasing the quality of the winery’s Casey’s Ridge farm in Elgin. Pairing Semillon and 10% Sauvignon Blanc, it has deftly handled 20% new wood, some flinty reduction, layers of citrus, green herbs and cream soda and plenty of crisp, palate-cleansing acidity.

Reflecting the predominance of whites in the Vrede en Lust range, this Blanc Fumé comes from what is judged the best block in a given vintage from Vrede en Lust’s Casey’s Ridge vineyard. Subtly wooded in 20% new oak, it has appealing flavours of blackcurrant leaf, pink grapefruit and toast and a racy, slightly stony finish.

n: Vrede en Lust Early Mist Riesling
d: Mostly sold from the farm, which has a flourishing cellar door, this is a very well-judged Riesling from Karlin Nel. The residual sugar of eight grams per litre is well done, adding some texture to the wine’s steely acidity. Lime and passion fruit flavours combine appealingly on the palate, leading to a long, tapering finish.

n: Vrede en Lust Kogelberg Chenin Blanc
d: Kogelberg is a single, north-facing block in Elgin that was planted in 2004 on shale soils. Deftly oaked in 20% new French oak, it has a nice medley of greengage, nectarine and citrus fruit flavours, a hint of subtle, stony reduction, a waft of patisserie spices and racy, cool climate minerality.

Elgin is rightly recognised as one the best regions in the Cape to grow Chardonnay. Refreshing and medium bodied, this has more than enough acidity to carry its 100% malolactic, with crisp flavours of citrus, pear and lemongrass, nuanced 20% new oak and the zip and acidity that come with the terroir.

White Mischief is a seven-variety blend, based in Chenin Blanc, with the remainder made up of Pinot Gris, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon, Riesling, Chardonnay and Viognier. Showing the zip and precision of Elgin, it has a touch of wood spices, flavours of lime, grapefruit and cherimoya and a stony finish. Complex at the price.

n: Vulpes Wines Vulpes Cana Cabernet Sauvignon
d: Biodynamic guru Johan Reyneke grows the grapes that Nuschka de Vos buys for her Polkadraai Hills Cabernet Sauvignon. Firm, dense and still youthful, this is a wine that will reward a degree of patience, showing flavours of damson, blackberry and cassis, negligible oak, a waft of clove and mint and a core of granitic intensity.

n: Vulpes Wines Vulpes Chama Chenin Blanc
d: Nuschka de Vos uses grapes from two Paardeberg sites – Jakkalsfontein and Sky – to make her impressive Chenin Blanc. Expressing the freshness and tension that are a feature of many wines grown on decomposed granite soils, this has jasmine and sourdough bread aromas, flavours of cumin, lemongrass and oatmeal and nicely understated, fifth-use oak.

n: Vulpes Wines Vulpes Velox Chenin Blanc
d: Yields were much higher in 2025 than in 2024 – a relief to this wine’s growing band of fans – but production is still small from Johann Ferreira’s one-hectare parcel on Citrusdal Mountain. Showing a ferrous note from iron-rich clay soils, it has aromas of fynbos, hay and honeysuckle, flavours of lemon zest and yellow apple and a subtle bitter twist.

Brilliant stuff from JD Pretorius, who has a special touch with the variety, this is one of the best Cabernet Francs of the vintage. Sourced from a single site planted in 2008, it’s engagingly floral and leafy, with tangy plum and black cherry flavours, top notes of tarragon and pencil shavings and a mineral core. Picked, wisely, before the rains.

n: Warwick Old Vines OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Made with old-vine Chenin Blanc from the Du Bois family’s Sonop farm in Stellenbosch, where the soils are a mix of rock, gravel and shale. Showing plenty of concentration for a wine with 13% alcohol, this has nuanced 6% new oak, layers of quince and green and yellow apple and some subtle gin botanicals underpinned by stony acidity.

Pitch Black is a Cape assemblage of Cabernet Sauvignon, 24% Cabernet Franc, 14% Cinsault, 10% Merlot, 7% Malbec and 6% Petit Verdot. Needly sidestepping the worst of the later rains in 2023, it’s a light, refined, elegant cuvée with cassis and sweet red berry flavours, graceful tannins and perfumed 24% new oak.

JD Pretorius makes this unwooded Sauvignon Blanc with purchased grapes, mostly from the Polkadraai Hills. Located at the greener end of the variety’s spectrum, it has aromas of dill and elderflower and a palate of pithy kiwi fruit and gooseberry.

Considerably richer and denser than the 2023 release, this Pinotage comes from a very warm, north-west facing site on the farm. Picked before the end of January in a warm, early vintage, it’s a juicy, glossy textured expression of the variety, with raspberry and wild strawberry flavours, supple, savoury tannins and subtle 31% new French oak.

n: Warwick The Blue Lady Cabernet Sauvignon
d: The Blue Lady is a stand-alone Cabernet Sauvignon from a pair of sites on the Warwick farm and is another example of how well JD Pretorius handled the 2023 vintage. Racy, pure and well structured, it’s a textbook Simonsberg expression of the variety, with scented 44% new wood, flavours of mint, blackcurrant and liquorice and a fresh finish.

White Lady uses grapes from four different sites in Stellenbosch and is a stylish, well-judged expression of the hot, dry, early 2024 vintage. Deftly fermented in 21% new oak, it’s a comparatively forward style, with clementine, quince and apricot flavours, decent underlying acidity and enough structure to balance the fruit sweetness.

Always dominated by Pinotage, this is a three-way blend with 26% Cabernet Sauvignon and 15% Cabernet Franc in 2022. Now sold in a Burgundy bottle, this is a well-structured, engaging red that’s more than the sum of its parts, with plum, raspberry and black cherry flavours and a patina of aromatic spices.

As its name suggests, Trilogy is a three-way blend of mostly Cabernet Franc, 19% Cabernet Sauvignon and 7% Merlot. Billed as the “best wine we can make” by JD Pretorius, it’s a beautifully judged assemblage, with vanilla and mocha-scented 39% new oak, flavours of blackcurrant, capsicum and fennel and textured, finely judged tannins.

Antigo uses grapes from a comparatively extensive 5.5-hectare block on red clay soils in the lower part of the farm, alongside the Blaauwklippen Road. Pairing Cabernet Sauvignon and 11% Merlot, it’s floral, forward and appealingly racy, with red cherry and bramble fruit, a touch of tobacco leaf and nicely understated oak.

Now into its third iteration, this is a nicely mature, all-Chardonnay bubbly from the estate that had a little wood on the base wine and six years of autolysis. Layers of white pepper, citrus and oyster shell are complemented by some toast and Digestive biscuit and an appealingly bone-dry finish. A below the radar bubbly.

Blended with 4% Merlot and 3% each of Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot, this Cabernet Sauvignon comes from a combination of gravel and loam soils on the eastern end of the Helderberg. Structured and still youthful, it needs time to grow into itself, with fynbos, dried herb and cedarwood aromas, firmish tannins and a core of cassis and summer berry flavours.

Kevin Arnold may have left, but the wine to which he gave his name lives on at Waterford. Lighter and less oaky than it once was, this is an elegant Shiraz from a comparatively warm vintage, with layers of white pepper, bramble and black cherry, fine-boned tannins, a waft of rose petal, ample concentration and a refreshing, balanced finish.

n: Waterford Estate Single Vineyard Grenache Noir
d: You don’t find many stand-alone Grenaches from the Helderberg, but Mark le Roux’s wine shows that the variety works well in this part of Stellenbosch. Fermented with just 4% whole clusters, it’s a supple, succulent expression of the variety, with a nice medley of pomegranate and wild strawberry fruit and a scented, floral finish.

n: Waterford Estate Single Vineyard OVP Chardonnay
d: One of very few Old Vine Project Chardonnays in the Cape, this comes from a vineyard planted in 1988 on the lower slopes of the Waterford Estate. Using the rare Davis CY3 clone, it’s exotic, soft and peachy, with good weight for a wine with 12% alcohol, scented 12% new oak and layers of guava and passion fruit.

As you’d expect from the 2021 vintage, the latest release of The Jem is an absolute corker. Based on Cabernet Sauvignon, with seven other French and Italian grapes and 2% Tempranillo for the first time, it’s youthful yet already self-assured with some subtle, stony reduction and violet aromas, understated oak, granular, layered tannins and a medley of cassis, bramble and red cherry fruit complemented by top notes of fynbos and Mediterranean herbs. A delight.

n: Waterford Library Collection Spring Cabernet Franc
d: You will almost certainly have to visit the cellar door to sample or buy this Cabernet Franc, made with two clones (1 and 312) from a single parcel, but it will be worth it. A success in a tricky vintage, this is a blind taster’s dream wine, with tarragon, dill and graphite aromas, finely judged tannins, understated oak and capsicum and black cherry flavours.

n: Waterford Old Vine OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Gawie du Bois’s Sonop farm supplies the raw material for this Chenin Blanc, featuring grapes from a parcel planted in 1966. Lightly wooded in older oak, it has appealing pear, quince and greengage fruit flavours, a twist of aniseed spice and a sappy, palate-cleansing finish.

It’s worth trading up from the Circumstance Chenin Blanc to enjoy this more complex iteration of the variety. Soured from a 1.2-hectare block planted with a Loire Valley clone, it’s racy, refreshing and mineral-etched, with aromas of thatch and honeysuckle, zesty pink grapefruit and green apple flavours and some underlying grip from 21 days on skins.

Nadia Langenegger makes her Circle of Life White with Sauvignon Blanc, 22% Chenin Blanc and 3% Semillon. Fermented in older 600-litre barrels with a little malolactic, it has plenty of zip and acidity, grapefruit, gooseberry and cherimoya flavours and good underlying weight and structure. No longer organic, but as appealing as ever.

Nadia Langenegger thinks that people are unnecessarily down on the 2023 vintage, which was fine if producers picked before the rains in late February. Lightly wooded in 10% new oak, this is an elegant Cabernet Sauvignon with aromas of sage and fresh mint and a palate of bramble, red plum and blackcurrant leaf.

n: Waterkloof Circumstance Cape Coral Mourvèdre Rosé
d: A rare example of a South African rosé made entirely from Mourvèdre, this is a savoury, smartly packaged delight from the windy slopes of the Waterkloof farm, with a touch of residual sweetness, layers of hibiscus, fynbos and watermelon and a tangy, tapering finish.

A series of bush vine parcels overlooking False Bay are the source of this well-priced Chenin Blanc from Nadia Langenegger. Barrel fermented in older barrels, without malolactic, it has appealing pear drop, quince and yellow apple flavours, a touch of beeswax and an appealing bitter twist.

The cooler slopes of the Waterkloof estate are well suited to Merlot, a variety that can struggle in the heat of the Cape. This is a bright, engagingly floral expression of the variety, with stylish 10% new oak, wafts of graphite, cut grass and rose petal and a palate of liquorice, summer berry fruit and fine tannins.

Mourvèdre is the most planted red variety at Waterkloof and something of a speciality as a result. Showing the influence of whole bunch fermentation, it has pressed rose, fynbos and rosemary aromas, flavours of forest floor, plum and damson, a spine of tannin and nicely understated oak.

Part of a well-priced, ultra-reliable range under the Circumstance label, this a wild yeast fermented Sauvignon Blanc from low-yielding blocks on the farm. Salty and tangy it has appealing elderflower, greengage and fresh herb flavours and a lightly savoury finish from older oak ageing.

The Circumstance Syrah comes from a cooler, south-east facing block that’s buffeted by the winds from False Bay. The 100% whole clusters give the wine perfume, personality and structure, adding to a palate of blackberry, redcurrant and tapenade, with muscular tannins and the concentration to age further in bottle.

Seriously Cool uses grapes from Bottelary and Lower Helderberg, fermented with 100% whole bunches. Lightly wooded in older, larger-format barrels, it has notes of candyfloss and wild strawberry, plenty of tangy acidity and a backdrop of Campari spices.

n: Waterkloof The Last of The First Pinotage
d: A new wine from Waterkloof, this comes from a 1994 block on the Schapenberg, not far from where Pinotage was first planted by Professor Perold. Fermented with 100% whole clusters, it has top notes of fynbos and Asian spices, some Cola and subtle wood and a palate of bramble, summer berries and clove.

Made by consultant Albert van Niekerk from grapes grown on Jo and Tessa Neser’s farm in Bot River, this is a savoury, slightly earthy cuvée of Syrah and 43% Grenache that has a touch of fun, aromas of potpourri and Asian spices, plum, leather and red cherry flavours and nicely understated oak.

n: Wellington Wines La Cave Cape Blend
Wellington Wines La Cave OVP Chenin Blanc
d: OVP-certified vines planted between 1979 and 1984 are the source of this impressive Chenin Blanc from producers’ cellar, Wellington Wines. Fermented in 50% new oak, as well as amphoras and concrete eggs, this has a nice medley of peach, pineapple and yellow apple fruit complemented by fresh acidity and scented vanilla spice.

n: Weltevrede Philip Jonker Entheos Brut CC
Weltevrede Philip Jonker Rosetta Brut Rosé CC
Weltevrede Philip Jonker The Ring Blanc de Blancs Brut CC
d: One for Tolkien, or Wagner, fans perhaps, The Ring is the top-of-the-range bubbly from Weltevrede. Sourced from Robertson’s classic limestone-rich soils, it spent 24 months on lees and includes a reserve wine component from 2014 in the 5.6 grams of dosage. Pear, citrus and brioche flavours combine winningly on the palate here.

Place of Rocks comes from shale and limestone soils in Robertson and shows why Chardonnay is so well suited to the region. The 50% new French oak is well handled here, with ten months on lees adding some mid-palate weight. Toasty, tangy and lightly salty, it has good underlying structure and a stony finish.

Made in small quantities, which partly explains the ambitious price, this comes from a site that is rich in active limestone. The new oak is a little assertive perhaps, but this has enough acidity to complement the flavours of butterscotch, toast and popcorn. One to tuck away for a year or two to see how it evolves.

A couple of bush-vine parcels, planted in 1992 and 1993, are the source of this modern, medium-bodied Pinotage from DeWet Viljoen. Lightly oaked in 20% new barrels, it has bramble, plum and strawberry flavours, a sprinkling of dried herbs, fine tannins and supporting acidity. A wine that still has time on its side.

Using the talents of experienced winemaker, De Wet Viljoen, this is a subtly wooded cuvée of Grenache Blanc and 40% Chenin Blanc that also has an amphora component. Aromas of fennel and gin botanicals lead you into a palate of pear, quince and lemongrass complemented by a pithy, lightly savoury finish.

To sell an Old Vine Project Chenin Blanc of this quality from a Voor Paardeberg vineyard planted in 1974 for R110 is almost a crime, but that’s the current state of the wine market for you. Barrel fermented in 20% new oak, it has pear, cream, citrus and white peach flavours and a waft of aromatic spices. Ludicrously good at the price.

n: Wine of Brocha One Man Band Red
d: Blessed with a great label, One Man Band is an unusual, separately fermented cuvée of Syrah, 24% Petit Verdot, 8% Mourvèdre and 5% Viognier from the Brocha farm in Elgin. Showing a touch of good reduction, this is savoury, meaty and intense, with aromas of clove, mint and pepper, damson, blackberry and redcurrant fruit and sinewy tannins.

Back after a break in 2023, this comes from Rozy Gunn’s farm next to Iona, where Rhône grapes do especially well. Fermented with10% whole clusters and aged in 10% new wood, it’s very much a cooler climate style of Syrah mixing aromas of clove, pepper and oregano with a palate of red berries, black cherry and tobacco leaf and a balanced, refreshing finish.

n: Wolf and Woman Wines Always Present, Often Invisible OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Vredendal on the West Coast is the source of this OVP Chenin Blanc, sourced from a vineyard that was planted in 1988. Later picked and put through full malolactic, it’s a salty, slightly earthy white with attractive quince and green apple flavours, a waft of gin botanicals and a pithy, nicely focused finish.

n: Wolf and Woman Wines Glen Frank Syrah
d: Now into its third vintage, Glen Frank is a superb, late-picked Syrah from a cooler, southfacing slope in Darling. You can smell the proximity of the Atlantic here, with a briny top note adding to a nose of thyme and incense. Fresh, peppery and well structured, it has clove spice from 100% whole bunches and a palate of blackberry and redcurrant framed by sinewy tannins.

n: Wolf and Woman Wines Grenache Blanc
d: An equal pairing of grapes from Piekenierskloof and the Voor Paardeberg, this is a Grenache Blanc that has the focus and structure you expect from the variety. Lightly wooded in older barrels, it has plenty of steely intensity, flavours of yellow apple, citrus and peach, stony intensity and some underlying tannic grip.

n: Wolf and Woman Wines OVP Chenin Blanc
d: Jolandie Fouché uses grapes from four different vineyards, planted between 1976 and 1984, to make her superb Swartland Chenin Blanc. Mixing granite and iron-rich soils, it has enticing white flower and jasmine aromas, impressive structure and concentration, understated oak and layers of waxed lemon, juniper and aniseed.
